en: Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume One, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huijiao of Jiaxiang Temple in Kuaiji during the Liang Dynasty. Part One:
Translators of Scriptures, Upper Section. Translators of Scriptures, Upper Section.

1. Kāśyapa Mātanga: Kāśyapa Mātanga was originally a native of Central India. He possessed refined manners and was well-versed in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras; he made it his constant mission to travel and propagate the teachings. 2. Zhu Falan 3. An Shigao 4. Zhi Loujiachen 5. Dharmakāla 6. Kang Senghui 7. Vighna 8. Zhu Tanmoluoche 9. Bo Yuan 10. Bo Shilimi 11. Saṃghabhūti 12. Dharmaratna 13. Saṃghadeva 14. Zhu Fonian 15. Dharmayaśas 1. **Kāśyapa Mātanga**: Kāśyapa Mātanga was originally a native of Central India. He possessed refined manners and was well-versed in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras; he made it his constant mission to travel and propagate the teachings.
Formerly, while traveling to a small vassal state in India to lecture on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, a hostile nation invaded the borders. Daoteng reflected and said:
"The sutra states:
'One who can preach this Dharma of the sutra...'"
"Protected by the earth deities,
he shall cause those who dwell there to be at peace and happy.
Now that the clash of spears and arrows has only just begun, could this possibly be of benefit?
He then vowed to sacrifice his own life and went in person to mediate and persuade them; consequently, the two nations entered into friendly relations, and through this, he rose to prominence.

During the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the Emperor dreamed one night of a golden man flying through the air and arriving; he immediately assembled his ministers to interpret the dream.
The learned official Fu Yi respectfully replied:
"Your servant has heard that there is a deity in the Western Regions whose name is 'Buddha.
That which Your Majesty dreamed of must surely be this one."
The Emperor agreed with this and immediately dispatched Langzhong Cai Yin, Bo Shi disciple Qin Jing,
and others as envoys to India to seek out the Buddha-dharma.
When Cai Yin and his companions encountered Kāśyapa Mātanga there, they invited him to return to the land of Han.

Mātanga vowed to propagate the Dharma and, undaunted by exhaustion or hardship, braved the shifting sands to reach Luoyang. Emperor Ming received him with great honor and provided a vihāra outside the West Gate of the city for him to reside in; this marked the beginning of the existence of śramaṇas in the land of Han.

However, as the Great Dharma was first being transmitted, there were yet no converts who placed their faith in it; thus, he retained his profound understanding within himself and had nothing to proclaim or describe.
Later, after a short time, he passed away in Luoyang.
A record states:
An Shigao translated one fascicle of the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*.
It was initially sealed away in the fourteenth chamber of the Stone Chamber at the Lan Tai.
The place where [Kāśyapa] Mātanga resided is the Baima Monastery (White Horse Monastery) outside the Yong Gate to the west of present-day Luoyang.
Tradition relates that a foreign king once destroyed various monasteries, yet only the Zhaoti Monastery had not yet been demolished.
One night, a white horse circumambulated the stupa while neighing mournfully. He immediately informed the king, who thereupon halted the destruction of the various monasteries.
Consequently, he changed the name of the *jātī* (monastery) to "White Horse."
Therefore, many monasteries adopted these names as their models. 2.
Zhu Falan: Zhu Falan was also a native of Central India. He claimed to have recited several tens of thousands of chapters of sutras and śāstras, serving as a teacher to scholars in India.
When Cai Yin arrived in that country, Kālayaśas and Dharmaratna had already entered into an agreement to travel together for the purpose of conversion; thus, they proceeded in company.
However, as the disciples there created obstacles for them, Kālayaśas traveled by a separate route and arrived [at Luoyang] independently.
Having reached Luoyang, he stayed with Tan; in a short time, he became proficient in the Chinese language.

In the Western Regions, Zhi Cien had obtained scriptures, which he immediately translated into five works: the *Daśabhūmi-vinīvaraṇa*, the *Buddhajātakas*, the *Dharmasāgaragarbha*, the *Buddhacarita*, and the *Forty-two Sections*.

Due to the upheavals caused by the relocation of the capital and the rebellions, the original texts of the four sections were lost and did not reach the region south of the Yangtze River; only the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* remains extant today, consisting of approximately two thousand words.
Among all the scriptures currently extant in the land of Han, this alone is the very first.
Kang Sengyin also obtained in the Western Regions a painted image of Śākyamuni in a reclining posture; it was the fourth work produced by the master of sandalwood images, King Udayana.

Once they had arrived in Luoyang, Emperor Ming immediately ordered painters to produce copies, which were placed within the Qingliang Terrace and atop the Xianjie Mausoleum; the original images no longer exist today.
Furthermore, in the past, when Emperor Wu of Han dredged the bottom of Kunming Lake, he found black ash. He questioned Dongfang Shuo about it, and Shuo replied:
"I am not certain.
You may ask a person from the Western Regions."
Later, when Dharmaratna arrived, the crowd pursued him to question him.
Dharmaratna said, "This is the ash from the world's final end, when the kalpa-fire burns everything through."
Shuo’s words were subsequently verified, and those who believed him were very numerous.
Later, Lan passed away in Luoyang at the age of over sixty. 3. An Qing:
An Qing, whose courtesy name was Shigao, was the crown prince of the chief queen of the King of Parthia (Anxi).

From his youth, he was renowned for his filial conduct; moreover, his aspirations and talents were sharp and keen. He applied himself with diligence to learning, mastering foreign classics as well as the seven luminaries, the five elements, medical prescriptions, and diverse arts—even down to the cries of birds and beasts—leaving nothing that he did not thoroughly comprehend.
Once, while traveling, he saw a flock of swallows and suddenly said to his companions,
"The swallows say there will surely be someone bringing food.
Shortly thereafter, food was indeed delivered.
The multitude all marveled at him; thus, his reputation for brilliance and extraordinary talent spread early to the Western Regions.

Although Gao remained a layman, he observed the precepts with rigorous precision. Upon the death of the king, he succeeded to the great throne, yet he contemplated deeply the suffering and emptiness of existence, feeling weary of and detached from the physical body. Once his period of mourning was complete, he abdicated the kingdom to his uncle and left the household life to cultivate the Way.
He was extensively learned in the Piṭaka of the Sūtras and was particularly proficient in the study of Abhidharma; he recited and mastered the Dhyāna-sūtras, exhausting their subtle nuances.
Subsequently, he traveled abroad to propagate the teachings, traversing many kingdoms, and arrived in China at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty.
Possessing keen insight and quick wit, he was able to grasp everything upon hearing it once; not long after his arrival, he had mastered the Chinese language.

Thereupon, he translated various scriptures, rendering them from the foreign (Hu) tongue into Han Chinese, producing the *Ānāpāna-smṛti* (*Anban shouyi*), the *Śarīrārthagāthā* (*Yinchi ru*), the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* in both its larger and smaller versions, and the *Ṣaṣṭipañcāśat-prakaraṇa* (*Baishi liupin*).

Initially, the foreign Tripiṭaka master Saṃgharakṣa compiled the essentials of the sūtras into twenty-seven chapters. Baoyun then analyzed seven of those chapters compiled by Saṃgharakṣa and translated them into Chinese; this is precisely the *Dàodì jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages of the Path).
The scriptures and treatises he produced, both earlier and later, total thirty-nine works in all.

Their principles are clear and analytical, and their phrasing is accurate and correct. They are eloquent yet not flowery; substantial yet not rustic. All who read them find themselves tirelessly engaged, never growing weary.

Tao Gao had thoroughly investigated principle and fully realized his nature; he personally understood the conditions of his own karma and manifested many spiritual traces that the world could not fathom.

Initially, Gao claimed that in a previous life he had already left the household life. He once had a fellow student who was prone to anger; whenever they went on alms rounds and encountered donors whose offerings were unsatisfactory, the student would invariably give vent to his resentment.
Gao repeatedly issued reprimands and admonitions, yet [his companion] ultimately did not reform.
After more than twenty years had passed in this manner, he took leave of his fellow student, saying:

"I am going to Guangzhou to settle the karmic retribution from past lives. You have been diligent and thorough in your study of the scriptures, no less than I; however, your nature is prone to anger, and after your life ends, you will likely receive an evil form. If I attain the Way, I shall certainly deliver you."
Thereupon, he set out for Guangzhou.
Encountering a great upheaval caused by bandits, he met a youth on the road who spat in his hand, drew a blade, and said,
"I have truly caught you!"
He laughed loudly and said, "I owe you a debt from my past lives; therefore, I have come from afar to repay it.
Your anger is precisely the same intention as that of your previous existence."
He then extended his neck to receive the blade, his countenance showing no sign of fear, and the bandit consequently killed him.
Spectators lined the streets, all of whom were struck by the wonder of this extraordinary event.
Subsequently, his consciousness returned as the crown prince of the King of Anxi—this is none other than the present-day Kang Senghui.

After Kāśyapa Mātanga had completed his mission of traveling and preaching throughout China, he encountered the turmoil of Guanzhong and Luoyang at the end of Emperor Ling’s reign. He then took up his mendicant’s staff and traveled south to Jiangnan, saying:
"I shall pass through Mount Lu to visit my former fellow student."

When his journey reached the temple of Tingtihu, this shrine had long possessed divine power; merchants and travelers would offer prayers there, and it would divide the winds for them—blowing one way above and another below—so that none were ever detained.
Once, there was someone who begged for some "divine bamboo," but before permission was granted, he took it; immediately, the boat capsized and sank, and the bamboo returned to its original place.
From then on, the boatmen respected and feared him, and none failed to be struck with awe at his very shadow.

Thirty-odd ships of his traveling party offered sacrifices and prayed for blessings; the deity then descended through the medium of the invoker and said, "There is a śramaṇa on board; you may call him up immediately.
The guests were all struck with amazement and requested Baogao to enter the shrine.
The deity told Gao:

"In the past, in a foreign land, I went forth from home to study the Way together with you. I was fond of practicing giving, yet my nature was prone to anger; I am now the deity of the Yangting Temple, governing a territory extending for a thousand li in every direction."
Because of my practice of giving, my treasures and playthings were exceedingly abundant; yet because of my anger, I have fallen into this retribution as a spirit.
Now, seeing my former companions, my sorrow and joy are beyond words.
"My life will end within days; my hideous form has grown large, and if I were to die here, I would defile the rivers and lakes. I should instead pass away in the marshes west of the mountains.

Fearing that after this body perishes I might fall into hell, I have a thousand bolts of silk along with various precious objects. You may use these to establish the Dharma and construct a stupa for me, so that I may be reborn in a good realm."
Gao said, "I have come specifically to deliver you; why do you not manifest your form?
The spirit replied:
"The form is extremely ugly and strange; everyone will surely be terrified," Gao said.
"Just go out, and the people will not find it strange."

The deity emerged its head from behind the bed; it was a great python, and its tail could not be seen for its length. When it reached the edge of [the Buddha’s] knees, it addressed him several times in the Sanskrit language and chanted several verses of praise. The python wept with tears like rain, and after a short while, it withdrew and vanished.

Gao immediately took the silk goods, bid them farewell, and departed. As his fellow travelers hoisted the sails, the python again emerged from its body, climbed the mountain, and watched; only after the crowd raised their hands did it vanish.
In the blink of an eye, they reached Yuzhang. He immediately used the temple’s assets to build Dongsi Temple; after Hui'gao had departed, the deity passed away.
At dusk, a young man boarded the boat and knelt long before Hui'gao to receive his blessing and vows, then suddenly vanished.
Hui'gao said to the boatmen, "The youth just now was the spirit of the Boting Temple; he has finally been freed from his malevolent form."
Thereupon, the temple deity ceased its activity, and from then on there were no further miraculous responses.
Later, people saw a dead python in a marsh to the west of the mountain, its head and tail spanning several li; this is the present-day Snake Village (Shecun) in Xunyang Commandery.

After this, Guo returned to Guangzhou to seek out the youth who had harmed him in his previous life; the youth was still alive at the time. Guo went directly to his home and recounted the matters of retribution from their past encounter, as well as their karmic connection from former lives.
They faced one another with joy, and the youth said: "I still have remaining retribution; I shall now go to Kuaiji to complete the settlement."

A traveler from Guangzhou named Wu, realizing that [the Master] was extraordinary, attained sudden enlightenment; he repented his past transgressions and provided him with generous support, accompanying him on his journey eastward until they reached Kuaiji.
Upon arriving, he entered the marketplace, where it happened that a disturbance was occurring. One man, while fighting another, mistakenly struck his own head with a weapon and died instantly.

The Guangzhou traveler had personally witnessed these two retributions; he subsequently applied himself diligently to the Buddha-dharma and recounted the circumstances in detail. When those far and near heard of this, there were none who were not moved to grief and lamentation, realizing that the three periods of time are indeed evidenced by such signs.
Since Kāśyapa Mātanga was of royal lineage, the travelers from the Western Regions all addressed him as "An Hou" (Lord An), a title that remains in use to this day.

In the kingdom of India, they refer to their own writing as "Celestial Writing" (Tian-shu) and their speech as "Celestial Speech" (Tian-yu); its phonology and terminology are obscure and complex, differing greatly from those of Han China.

Throughout successive generations of transmission and translation, many errors and corruptions have occurred; only that which was produced by [Kumārajīva] stands as the foremost among all translations.

Master Dao’an considered that to receive instruction from him in person would not differ from seeing a sage, and thus the men of illustrious virtue across the ages have all praised and reflected upon his work.

I have searched through various records, noting that the accounts of Master Gao appear and disappear inconsistently; this may be because his traces were intentionally concealed or manifested according to the many circumstances of his ministry, or perhaps due to errors by the transmitters, resulting in these contradictions. I have therefore set forth these various discrepancies in full, hoping that they may serve as a basis for discussion.
According to Shi Dao’an’s *Catalogue of Scriptures* (*Jinglu*), it states:
"An Shigao translated more than thirty scriptures over a period of twenty-odd years, from the second year of the Jianhe era of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty until the Jianning era of Emperor Ling."
Furthermore, the *Biézhuan* (Separate Biography) states:
"At the end of the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty, the Daoist Anhou arrived at Sangyuan. After he finished reciting the scriptures, he sealed a casket in the temple and said:
'It may be opened after four years.'"
At the end of the Wu dynasty, he traveled to Yangzhou, where he had a man sell a chest of goods to purchase a slave named Fushan, saying, "He is my spiritual friend."
He then took the slave to Yuzhang; after he had completed the construction of a temple for the deity of the Duting Shrine, Fushan stabbed Anhou in the ribs with a knife, whereupon he died.
The people of Sangyuan then opened the sealed casket they had found; the contents were naturally inscribed with characters that read:
"He who honors my Way is the layman Chen Hui; he who transmits the Chan scriptures is the bhikṣu Senghui."
"This was precisely the fourth year [of the Jianwu era].
Furthermore, Yu Zhongyong’s *Record of Jingzhou* states:

"At the beginning of the Jin dynasty, there was the śramaṇa An Shigao, who converted the deity of the Baoting Temple; having obtained wealth and goods, he established the Baima Monastery at the southeastern corner of the city of Jing."
The *Xuanyanjiji* (Records of Verified Manifestations) by Prince Kang of Linchuan of the Song dynasty states:
"The python died at the end of the Wu dynasty.
The *Tasiji* (Records of Stupas and Temples) by Tanzong states:

"The Waguan Monastery in Danyang was established during the reign of Emperor Ai of the Jin dynasty by the śramaṇa Huili; later, the śramaṇa An Shigao renovated it using materials remaining from the Boting Temple."
"However, since Dharma Master Dao’an had already collated and verified the various scriptures and compiled records of their translation, there must certainly be no errors.

From the second year of the Jianhe era of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty until the end of the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty, a total of more than one hundred and forty years elapsed. If Master Gao were long-lived, he might indeed have been able to do so; yet the facts cannot be thus. Why is this?..."
According to the preface to the *Anban Shouyi Jing* (The Scripture on Guarding the Mind through Ānāpāna) annotated by Kang Senghui, it says:
"This scripture was translated by An Shigao, but for a long time it had been submerged and obscured.

There were three worthies—Han Lin of Nanyang, Wen Ye of Yingchuan, and Chen Hui of Kuaiji—who were deeply and sincerely devoted to the Way. They collectively requested instruction from me; thus, Chen Hui set forth the meanings while I assisted in refining and deliberating them."
Soon after, Senghui died in the first year of the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty, having already stated:
"After this sutra emerges, it will remain obscured for a long time.
Furthermore, the inscription on the casket of Lokakṣema says:
"He who honors my Way is the layman Chen Hui;
he who transmits the *dhyāna* sūtras is the bhikṣu Senghui.
Thus, what is elucidated in the *Ānāpāna-smṛti* extensively explains the practice of *dhyāna*; one can therefore know that the record on the sealed casket was indeed not written in vain.
Since it has already been stated that two individuals were to transmit my Way, how could they have coexisted in the same world?
Furthermore, the *Biézhuan* itself states:
"The one who transmitted the Chan scriptures was the bhikṣu Senghui."
"Since Huiyi died at the beginning of the Taikang era, how could there have been the Dharma Master Anhou at the end of that same era?

The statements regarding the beginning and the end are self-contradictory; it must be that some document erroneously dates [the event] to the early Jin period, and subsequently, various authors either cited the Taikang era or the end of the Wu dynasty, following suit in their competition for conformity without any means of verification."
Since the accounts from the early Jin period are already difficult to reconcile, the *Tanzong ji* states:
"During the reign of Emperor Ai of the Jin, An Shigao was just then restoring the temple."
Such a claim regarding his errors is, therefore, far-fetched.

Zhi Loujiachan—also simply called Zhi Chen—was originally a person from Yuezhi. His conduct was pure and profound, his character open and quick-witted; he maintained the Dharma-precepts and was renowned for his diligent application.
He recited various sutras with the intent of propagating the Dharma.

During the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, while traveling in Luoyang between the Guanghe and Zhongping eras, he translated Indic texts and produced three sutras: the *Pratyutpanna*, the *Śūraṅgama*, and the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, there were more than ten other scriptures, such as the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra* and the *Ratnakūṭa*, which had long been lost from the catalogs.
Master Dao’an compared ancient and modern versions and meticulously examined their literary styles, remarking:

"These appear to have been produced by [Dharmakṣema] Yìchèn. All these various scriptures faithfully capture the original intent without adding any embellishment; they may truly be called works of those who excel at proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma and propagating the Way."
Afterwards, his final whereabouts were unknown.

At that time, there was also an Indian śramaṇa named Zhu Foshuo, who, during the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, brought the *Daoxing jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) to Luoyang and translated it from the Indic language into Chinese.

The translator was occasionally delayed, and although there were instances where the original intent was lost, he abandoned ornate style to preserve the substance, thereby deeply capturing the meaning of the sutra.

In the second year of the Guanghe era, Zhu Shuo also produced the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* in Luoyang; An Shigao acted as the oral transmitter (*chuan yan*), while Meng Fu and Zhang Lian of Luoyang in Henan received the text in writing.
At that time, there was also the upāsaka An Xuan, a native of the country of Parthia (Anxi), whose character was upright and pure, and who was profound, steady, and possessed of logical acumen.
He had extensively recited the various scriptures and was well-versed in many fields of learning.
Furthermore, at the end of the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, he traveled to Luoyang as a traveling merchant and was granted the title of Qiduwei (Commandant of Cavalry) for his services.
By nature he was serene, tranquil, gentle, and respectful; he constantly took the affairs of the Dharma as his own responsibility.

Gradually mastering the Chinese language, he was determined to propagate the scriptures; he frequently engaged in discussions on the meaning of the Way with śramaṇas—those whom the world called the Commandant (Duyou).

Together with the śramaṇa Yan Fotiao, Zhu Fashuan translated the *Fajing jing* (Sūtra of the Dharma Mirror). Fashuan orally translated the Sanskrit text while Fotiao received it in writing; thus the principles were correctly captured and the phonology made precise, exhausting the subtle purport of the scripture. This excellence, like that of the master carver of Ying, was praised by later generations.

Fotiao was originally a native of Linhuai; from his youth, he was exceptionally intelligent and keen-witted, being both quick-minded and fond of learning. The world praised these three—An Hou, Duwei, and Fotiao—as being such that their skill in translating and transmitting the scriptures was difficult to equal.
Dharmamitra also compiled the *Daśajñāna*, which has likewise been transmitted to the world.
Master Dao’an praised Dharmamitra’s translations of the sutras, noting that they were concise yet not tedious, and entirely elegant in their composition.

Furthermore, there were the śramaṇas Zhi Yao, Kang Ju, Kang Mengxiang, and others, who, during the reigns of Emperors Ling and Xian of the Han dynasty, enjoyed a reputation for their study of wisdom and were renowned throughout the capital of Luoyang.
Zhu Faya translated the *Siddhārthasamādhi-sūtra* and the *Laghuvastu-vibhaṅga*, while Zhu Faju translated the *Pratyutpanna-naraka-prcchā-sūtra*;
both spoke with direct language and profound meaning, adding no literary embellishment.
Meng Xiang translated the *Madhyama-vastu-vibhaṅga* and the *Caryā-vastu-vibhaṅga*.
Previously, the śramaṇa Tanguo obtained a Sanskrit manuscript in the kingdom of Kapilavastu; Mengxiang, together with Zhu Dalì, translated it into Chinese. Master Dao’an remarked:
“The version produced by Mengxiang is magnificent and fluid, sufficient to convey the profound significance.”
5. Dharmakāla: Dharmakāla, translated here as "Dharma-Time," was originally a native of Central India.
His family had been wealthy for generations and constantly cultivated meritorious deeds through the practice of the Brahma-faring life.
Kāla was gifted and perceptive from a young age; his physical bearing surpassed that of ordinary men. Upon reading a book only once, he thoroughly mastered both its literary style and its meaning.

He was skilled in studying the *Catur-Veda* treatises, and there was nothing—from the movements of wind and clouds to the stars, or from diagrams and prophecies to the shifts of fortune—that he did not master. He declared of himself, "The principles and patterns of the world are all contained within my heart."

At the age of twenty-five, he entered a monastic dwelling where he happened to see the *Dharmatrāta-vibhāṣā* (Fasheng Pit'an). He took it up for a casual perusal but found it utterly incomprehensible; though he examined it with diligent persistence, his confusion only increased. He then sighed, saying:

"I have devoted many years to my studies, setting my ambitions upon the ancient classics and moving with ease through the scriptures. Yet their meaning required no second thought, and their texts needed no repeated reading."

Now, upon reading the Buddhist scriptures, I find they suddenly transcend the realm of my ordinary sentiments; they must surely penetrate the profound through their logical principles and possess a distinct, essential core.

Thereupon, he took the scrolls into his room and requested a bhikṣu to provide a brief explanation. He subsequently attained a deep realization of cause and effect and a subtle mastery of the three periods of time, finally understanding that the Buddhist teachings are vast and expansive, beyond the reach of secular texts.

He then renounced worldly glory and left the household life to practice asceticism with diligence, reciting the sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna as well as the various sections of the *Vinaya*.
Always valuing travel and conversion rather than remaining fixed in one place, he arrived in Luoyang during the Jiaping era of the Wei dynasty.

At that time, although the Buddha-dharma existed within the borders of the Wei dynasty, the spirit of the Way had become corrupted and degenerate; there were also members of the monastic community who had not yet received the precepts of refuge, being distinguished from the laity merely by their shaven heads.
Furthermore, although they established fasts and repentances and performed rituals according to the methods of ancestral sacrifices, once Kālaya arrived, he extensively propagated the Buddha-dharma.

At that time, various monks collectively requested that Kālaya translate the Vinaya; however, Kālaya considered that because the detailed regulations of the Vinaya-piṭaka were so voluminous in both text and language, and as the Buddhist teachings had not yet flourished, they would certainly not be accepted or put into practice.
He then translated the *Mahāsāṃghika-śīlacitta*, which was sufficient for his daily morning and evening observances.
He further invited a Brahman monk to establish the *karmavācanā* ritual for conferring the precepts; thus, the Vinaya tradition in China began from this point.
Kāla’s final whereabouts were unknown.
At that time, there was also a foreign śramaṇa named Kang Sengyai,
who likewise arrived in Luoyang at the end of the Jiaping era and translated four scriptures, including the *Ugra-paripṛcchā*.

Furthermore, there was the śramaṇa Danti from the kingdom of Anxi, who was also well-versed in the Vinaya studies. During the Zhengyuan era of the Wei dynasty, he came to Luoyang and produced the *Tánwúdé Jīemó* (The Karma of the Mahāsāṃghika).
There was also the śramaṇa Bo Yan, of whom it is unknown who he was.

He too was talented and intelligent, possessing profound understanding; during the Gānlù era of the Wei dynasty, he translated six scriptures in total, including the *Wúliàng qīngjìng píngděng jué jīng*.
His final whereabouts were unknown thereafter. 6.
Kang Senghui: Kang Senghui was originally from Kangju; his ancestors had lived for generations in India, but his father moved to Jiaozhi for commercial purposes.
When he was about ten years old, both his parents passed away; having completed the period of mourning with the utmost filial piety, he left the household life.
His practice of the precepts was exceedingly rigorous, and he was magnanimous, elegant, and possessed of great discernment; he was profoundly sincere and fond of learning.

He had a clear understanding of the Tripiṭaka and read widely in the Six Classics; he was extensively versed in astronomy, the *tu* and *wei* charts, and other fields, possessed a sharp intellect for critical discernment, and was quite adept at literary composition.
At that time, Sun Quan had already established his control over the region east of the Yangtze River, yet Buddhism had not yet spread there.

Previously, there was the lay devotee (upāsaka) Zhi Qian, courtesy name Gongming, also known as Yue, who was originally a person from the Yuezhi and came to travel within the borders of the Han realm.
Initially, during the reigns of Emperors Huan and Ling of the Han dynasty, there was Zhi Chen, who translated numerous scriptures.
There was Zhi Liang, whose courtesy name was Jiming; he studied under Chen, and Daoqian in turn received his instruction from Liang.
He read widely across the classics and scriptures, mastering them all without exception; he was thoroughly practiced in many worldly arts and crafts.
Having studied diverse texts extensively, he was proficient in the languages of the six kingdoms.
He was thin, tall, dark, and lean, with eyes that were mostly white and pupils that were yellow. At that time, people had a saying about him:
"Zhi Lang’s eyes are yellow; though his frame is slight, he is a treasury of wisdom."

At the end of the reign of Emperor Xian of the Han, during a period of turmoil, he sought refuge in Wu. Hearing of his talent and wisdom, Sun Quan summoned him for an audience and was pleased with him; he appointed him as a *boshi* (Erudite) and tasked him with instructing the Crown Prince, working together with Wei Yao and others to provide counsel and benefit. However, because he was originally from a foreign land, he is not recorded in the *Wu zhi*.

Although the Great Teaching had already spread, many scriptures remained in Sanskrit and had not yet been fully translated. Xuanzang, being already proficient in local dialects, collected various manuscripts and translated them into the Chinese language.

From the first year of the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty until the Jianxing period, he translated forty-nine sutras, including the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, the *Dharmapada*, and the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses and Original Arisings*. These works accurately capture the sacred meaning and are elegant in their diction and style.

Furthermore, based on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* and the *Madhyamāgama*, he composed three sections of *bodhi-lianju-fanbai* (Buddhist liturgical chants in linked verses), as well as annotated the *Liaoben shengsi jing* (Sūtra on Understanding the Origin of Birth and Death) and other works, all of which have circulated in the world.

At that time, the land of Wu had only recently been converted to the Great Dharma, and its customs and teachings were not yet fully established. Desiring to cause the Way to flourish throughout the region east of the Yangtze River and to establish monasteries there, Senghui took up his monk’s staff and traveled east. In the tenth year of the Chiku era of the Wu dynasty, he first arrived at Jianye, where he constructed a thatched hut, installed an image of the Buddha, and performed religious practices.

At that time, as it was the first time the state of Wu had seen śramaṇas, people observed their outward appearance but had not yet encountered their Way; thus, they suspected them of practicing eccentricity.
An official submitted a memorial, saying:
"There is a barbarian who has entered our borders, claiming to be a śramaṇa. His appearance and attire are unusual, and he should be investigated."
Zhang Quan said, "In the past, Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty dreamed of a deity whom he called the Buddha; is that which you practice not perhaps the lingering influence of his tradition?
He immediately summoned the assembly to interrogate them as to what spiritual efficacy they possessed.

Hui said: "Since the Tathāgata passed away, more than a thousand years have suddenly elapsed; his remaining relics, the śarīra, manifest divine radiance without limit. In the past, King Aśoka erected eighty-four thousand stūpas."
"Generally, the rise of stupas and monasteries is intended to manifest the legacy of the Buddha's teachings.
Sun Quan considered this to be boastful and empty, and said to Senghui:
"If you can obtain a śarīra relic, I shall have a stupa built for it; if your claim proves false, the state has established punishments."
He requested a period of seven days and then said to his followers:
"The rise or fall of the Dharma depends upon this single undertaking; if we do not now act with utmost sincerity, how can it be remedied hereafter?"
They then purified themselves together in a quiet chamber, placing a copper vessel upon an altar, burning incense, and making their invocation.
When the seven-day period concluded, there was no response; they requested to extend it for another seven days, but the result was the same.
Sun Quan said, "This is truly a deception; I am about to punish you. It happened that Zhihui requested another seven-day period, and Sun Quan again granted this special request.
Zhihui said to his disciples: "Confucius once said:
'Since King Wen has passed away, does not the cultural legacy now reside with us?'"
"The Dharma-spirit ought to descend in response, yet we have felt nothing. What need is there for royal punishment? We shall simply take death as our limit.
At the end of the twenty-first day, still nothing was seen; everyone was struck with trembling fear.
When the fifth watch had passed, he suddenly heard a metallic "clang" from within the jar. He went to look personally and indeed obtained the śarīra.
The following morning, he presented them to Quan; the entire court assembled to observe, as five-colored flames of light shone brilliantly upon the jar.
Sun Quan personally took hold of the jar and poured its contents onto a bronze basin; as the śarīra struck it, the basin shattered immediately.
Sun Quan was deeply moved with awe and, starting up in alarm, exclaimed:
"This is a rare and auspicious omen!"
Huìjìn then spoke, saying:
"The majestic spiritual power of Śāriputra is not limited to his radiant marks alone; even the fires at the end of an eon cannot burn him, nor can the vajra-pestle shatter him."
The magistrate ordered them to test him, whereupon he made a renewed vow, saying:
"The Dharma-cloud is now spreading, and the common people look up to its bounty; I pray that you will further manifest divine traces to broaden the display of your majestic power."
He then placed the śarīra upon an iron anvil and had a strong man strike it; consequently, both the anvil and the mallet were indented, yet the śarīra remained undamaged.

Sun Quan sighed in great admiration and immediately erected a stūpa for it. Because this was the first Buddhist temple ever built, it was named "Jianchu Temple" (Temple of the Foundation), and the site was accordingly called "Buddha Village."
Consequently, the Great Dharma flourished throughout the region east of the Yangtze River.
When Sun Hao ascended the throne, his laws and decrees became harsh and tyrannical; he abolished excessive sacrifices and extended this policy even to Buddhist temples, intending to destroy them all.
Sima Hao said, "From what did this arise? If its teachings are authentic and correspond with the sacred scriptures, then we shall preserve and honor that Way.
If they lack substance, then burn them all."
The ministers all said:
"The power of the Buddha is not equal to that of other deities.
Since the auspicious signs were manifested at Kanghui and the Great Emperor founded the temple, if you now treat it with such contemptuous destruction, I fear it will lead to future regret."

Sun Hao dispatched Zhang Yu to the monastery to interrogate Senghui. Zhang Yu was naturally gifted with eloquence and skillful debate; his questions were swift and far-reaching. However, Senghui responded to each point with rapid wit and his arguments emerged with sharp precision. From morning until evening, Zhang Yu was unable to defeat him.
After he had retired, they gathered to see him off at the gate. At that time, there was a practitioner of licentious sacrifices nearby, and Sengyu said:
"The profound transformation has already gained credence; why is it that these people remain close by and have not reformed?"
Hui said: "When a thunderclap shatters a mountain, the deaf do not hear it; this is not because the sound is faint.
If the principle is unobstructed, there is a response across ten thousand li; if it is blocked, then the liver and gallbladder are as far apart as Chu and Yue."
Upon his return, Sun Yu sighed, "Zhihui’s brilliance exceeds what I can fathom; I pray that Your Majesty will examine him.
Emperor Hao then convened a great assembly of court scholars and went out to welcome Zhihui in a carriage drawn by horses.
Once they were seated, Sun Hao asked,
"In what the Buddhist teachings clarify regarding the retribution for good and evil, what exactly constitutes this?
Hui answered him, saying:
"When a sagely ruler instructs the world with filial piety and compassion, vermilion phoenixes soar and the Old Man appears;
when he nurtures all things with benevolence and virtue, sweet springs gush forth and auspicious sprouts emerge."
As there are auspicious omens for good, so it is likewise for evil.
Therefore, when one commits evil in secret, the ghosts apprehend and punish them; when one commits evil in public, other people apprehend and punish them.

The *I Ching* proclaims, "The accumulation of goodness brings forth abundant blessings," and the *Book of Poetry* sings, "Seeking fortune without turning back. Though these are the maxims of the Confucian classics, they are precisely the clear instructions of Buddhism.
Sun Hao said, "If that is so,
then since the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius are already clear, what need is there for Buddhism?
Zhu Fawei replied:
"What Zhou and Kong spoke merely indicated superficial traces; as for the teachings of Śākyamuni, they exhaustively reveal the most profound and subtle truths.
Thus, committing evil leads to the long-lasting suffering of hell, while cultivating goodness results in the eternal bliss of celestial palaces."
"To cite this as an illustration for encouragement and deterrence—is it not grand?
At that time, Sun Hao had no means to refute his words.

Although Hao had heard the True Dharma, his nature of darkness and violence could not overcome his cruelty; later, he ordered the palace guards to enter the inner quarters to tend the gardens. There they found a golden image several feet high in the ground and presented it to Hao. Hao ordered it to be placed in an impure location and doused with filthy liquids, laughing with his ministers to take pleasure in the act.
In an instant, his entire body swelled up greatly, with the private parts being especially painful; his cries reached the heavens.
The Grand Astrologer divined that this was caused by offending a great deity; consequently, sacrifices were offered at various shrines, yet there was never any recovery.
Among the palace ladies was one who had previously served the Dharma;
she asked in greeting, "Does Your Majesty seek merit within the Buddhist temples?
Sun Hao raised his head and asked:
"Is the Buddha a great deity?
The court lady replied,
"The Buddha is indeed a great deity."

Sima Hao’s mind was thus awakened as he fully grasped the meaning of the words; consequently, the court ladies immediately escorted the image into the palace hall, where they bathed it with scented water dozens of times, burned incense, and performed repentance. Sima Hao prostrated himself upon his pillow, confessing his transgressions. After a short while, his pain subsided, and he dispatched a messenger to the monastery to inquire after the Master and invite him to preach the Dharma at the assembly. Huì then followed the messenger into the palace.
Sun Hao questioned him in detail about the origins of sin and merit; Daohui analyzed these matters for him with words that were exceedingly precise and essential.
Sun Hao, who already possessed some talent for understanding, was filled with joy and delight, and consequently requested to see the *śramaṇa* precepts.

Considering that the text of the precepts was strictly secret and could not be lightly proclaimed, he took the one hundred and thirty-five vows from the *Bunyaku* (Original Acts) Sūtra and divided them into two hundred and fifty items; whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he dedicated these vows for the sake of all sentient beings.

Upon seeing that his compassionate vows were so vast and universal, Emperor Hao’s benevolent intentions increased all the more; he immediately joined the assembly to receive the five precepts. Within ten days, his illness was cured. He then further renovated the residence at the site of the assembly and issued a proclamation to the imperial clan, ensuring that everyone without exception would observe them.

During the Wu dynasty, he frequently expounded the True Dharma; however, because Emperor Sun Hao was by nature fierce and coarse, he did not reach the subtle meanings, but instead recounted matters of retribution and immediate consequences to open his mind.

At Jianchu Monastery, he translated numerous sūtras, including the *Ānapanasmṛti*, the *Rājādarśa*, the *Rājavatsa*, and the *Brahmarāja-sūtra*. He also produced the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya* (Small Version), the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*, and the *Avadāna-śataka*. In all these works, he excelled at capturing the essence of the scriptures, ensuring that both the phrasing and the meaning were perfectly accurate.
Furthermore, he transmitted the chanting of the *Nirvāṇa*, which was refined, plaintive, and resonant, serving as a model for his generation.

He also annotated the three scriptures—the *Ānāpānasmṛti* (Anban shouyi), the *Dharmādarśa* (Fajing), and the *Bodhivṛkṣa* (Daoshu)—and composed prefaces for them; their phrasing was elegant and accessible, while their doctrinal meanings were subtle and profound, all of which have been preserved for the world.
In the fourth month of the fourth year of the Tianji era of the Wu dynasty, Sun Hao surrendered to the Jin. In the ninth month, he fell ill and passed away.
This was the first year of the Taikang era of Emperor Wu of the Jin.

During the Xianhe era of the Jin dynasty, when Su Jun incited a rebellion, he burned down the stupa built at the assembly hall. He Chong, the Minister of Works, subsequently renovated and constructed it once more.
Zhao You, General Who Pacifies the West, had for generations failed to uphold the Dharma and treated the Triple Gem with arrogance.

Upon entering this monastery, he said to the various monks, "I have long heard that this stupa frequently emits light; such empty exaggerations are contrary to the scriptures and are things I cannot believe. If I must see it for myself, then there will be no further discussion."

When he had finished speaking, the stupa immediately emitted light of five colors that illuminated the hall and its pinnacle. Kang Su was so moved by awe that his hair stood on end; from this, he came to believe with deep reverence.

To the east of the temple, he further erected a small stupa. This was due, in the long run, to the spiritual inspiration of the Great Sage, and in the short term, to the power of Kang Hui; thus, he depicted the Buddha’s image, which has been passed down to the present day.
Sun Chuo composed a eulogy for him, saying:
"Lord Hui’s zither and lutes are truly of noble substance;
his mind is free from worldly burdens, and his spirit possesses abundant leisure."
Amidst this profound darkness, he shook off those who were particularly base and excluded.
Transcending all, he reached afar; eminent and lofty indeed was his height.
A record states that Sun Hao struck and tested the śarīra, claiming it was not from the time of [Emperor] Quan.
According to my examination of the case where Emperor Hao intended to demolish the temple, all his ministers replied:
"Kang Senghui was moved by an auspicious omen, and Your Majesty established the temple.
From this we know that the initial manifestation of the śarīra must have been a provisional measure for the time being.

Therefore, the records of the numerologists all state that Sun Quan was moved by the śarīra in the palace of Wu; subsequently, its divine efficacy was further tested, and it may have been brought there by Sun Hao.
7. Weizhinan: Weizhinan was originally a person from India.
The people of the world followed heterodox paths, regarding fire worship as orthodox.

At that time, there was a Śramaṇa from India who studied the Hīnayāna and frequently practiced various arts and techniques. As he was traveling a great distance and evening was approaching, he wished to stay overnight at the house of Nán.
Since the Nans family followed a different path, they harbored suspicion toward the śramaṇas and placed them outside their gate to sleep on the open ground.

At night, the śramaṇa secretly applied incantations, causing the fire upon which the Nans family relied to suddenly vanish. Thereupon, the entire household came out together, prostrated themselves to entreat the śramaṇa to enter the house for offerings.
The śramaṇa then used his incantations to transform the fire so that it would ignite.

Having witnessed that the śramaṇa’s supernatural power surpassed his own, Nanda immediately conceived great faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma; he then abandoned what he had previously served, left the household life to pursue the Way, and took this śramaṇa as his upādhyāya.
He studied the Tripiṭaka and became exceptionally proficient in the four Āgamas. As he traveled and converted people in various kingdoms, there were none who did not revere him.
In the third year of the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty, he accompanied his fellow practitioner Zhu Lüyan.
He arrived at Wuchang, bringing with him the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Dhammapada*.
"Dhammapada" is the same as the *Faju jing* (Sūtra of the Dharma Verses).

At that time, the scholars of Wu collectively requested that he bring out the scriptures. Since his knowledge of the local language was not yet proficient, they worked together with his companion, Zhu Fayan, to translate them into Chinese.

Fayan was also not well-versed in the Chinese language; consequently, there were some points left incomplete, as their primary aim was to preserve the fundamental meaning, resulting in a style of expression that was somewhat plain and unadorned.
Toward the end of the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, there was the śramaṇa Fali, who retranslated it in five fascicles.
The śramaṇa Faju served as the scribe; its phrasing is somewhat refined.

Dharmarakṣa, whose name is translated as "Dharma Protection," was originally a person of Yuezhi descent; his ancestral surname was Zhi, and his family had resided for generations in Dunhuang Commandery.

During the turmoil at the end of the Yongjia era, he produced another approximately ninety minor sūtras, most of which no longer survive. [8] Zhu Tanmoluoche (竺曇摩羅剎): Zhu Tanmoluoche is translated as Dharmarakṣa. His ancestors were of Yuezhi origin; his original surname was Zhi, and his family had lived for generations in Dunhuang Commandery.
At the age of eight, he left the household life and took the foreign śramaṇa Zhugaozuo as his teacher. He could recite ten thousand words of scripture daily, mastering them upon a single reading.

By nature pure and noble, his conduct was refined and austere; he was devoted to learning and sought out teachers even at a distance of ten thousand li. Consequently, he read widely across the Six Classics and let his mind roam through the Seven Writings; yet, regarding worldly affairs such as praise or blame, he never allowed them to disturb his heart.

At that time, during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, although temples and images were highly revered in the capital, the profound *Vaipulya* sutras remained hidden beyond the Pamir Mountains.
Dharmarakṣa was filled with resolute indignation and resolved to propagate the Great Way; he subsequently followed his master to the Western Regions, traveling through various kingdoms.

There were thirty-six different foreign languages and an equal number of scripts; Dharmarakṣa studied them all exhaustively, mastering their glosses and commentaries, and there was no aspect of phonology, meaning, or calligraphy that he did not fully comprehend.
He then brought back a vast collection of Sanskrit scriptures to return to China. From Dunhuang to Chang’an, he translated them along the way, transcribing them into the language of Jin.
The works he obtained and examined included one hundred and sixty-five sections, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra) and the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (The Light of Praise).
Diligently devoted to his task, he made the propagation [of the Dharma] his sole vocation.
Throughout his life, he transcribed and translated [the scriptures], never complaining of weariness.
It is because of him that the sutras and dharmas have spread widely throughout China.
This was due to the power of his protection.

During the final years of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, Hu lived in seclusion deep in the mountains. There was a clear stream there from which he constantly took water for washing and rinsing; later, a woodcutter defiled the waterside, and in an instant, the water dried up.
Huguo then paced back and forth and sighed, saying,
"How lacking in virtue people are!
They have thus caused the clear spring to cease its flow."
"If the water were to dry up forever, I would truly have no means of sustenance; I must simply move elsewhere.
As soon as he finished speaking, the spring surged forth, filling the ravine; such was the response to his profound sincerity.
Therefore, Zhi Dun composed a eulogy for his portrait, saying:
"Master Hu is serene and tranquil; his virtue and character are profound and beautiful. He chants softly in the remote valleys, rinsing his mouth with water from dried-up springs."
"Lofty was Master Hu, born of Heaven with vast and noble virtue; he washed his feet in the shifting sands and grasped the profound ultimate.
Later, he established a monastery outside the Qing Gate in Chang’an, where he practiced the Way with diligent devotion.
Thereupon, his virtuous transformation spread far and wide, and his reputation covered the four quarters; several thousand monastics all revered and served him.
When Emperor Hui of the Jin fled westward and Guanzhong fell into turmoil, the common people were displaced, and Baohu, along with his disciples, moved eastward to escape the unrest.
Upon reaching Mianchi, he fell ill and passed away at the age of seventy-eight.

Later, Sun Chuo composed the *Treatise on the Worthies of the Way* (*Daoxian lun*), in which he compared seven monks from India to the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, matching Dharmarakṣa with Shan Juyuan.
The treatise states:

"Master Hu’s virtue abides in the source of all things, and Master Ju’s rank has ascended to the Way of Discourse; the character and virtue of these two masters are lofty and far-reaching, such that they are truly worthy of being held as models for their contemporaries."
His reputation for excellence was thus esteemed by later generations.

At that time, there was the lay devotee Nie Chengyuan, who was intelligent, talented, and devoted to the Dharma; he assisted Master Hu in translating the scriptures and frequently participated in refining the wording and phrasing.
The first translation of the *Sūtra of the Sun-Moon Radiance* was quite verbose and redundant; Chengyuan revised and edited it, resulting in the two-fascicle version currently in circulation.
His detailed determinations were generally of this nature.

Shengyuan had a son named Daozhen, who was also well-versed in the study of Sanskrit. This gentleman and his son were elegant and fluent in their phrasing, without detracting from the classical style.
Furthermore, there were Zhu Fashou, Chen Shilun, Sun Bohu, Yu Shiya, and others, all of whom assisted in upholding the master’s intent, taking up the pen to carefully edit and verify the text.
Master Dao’an said:
“Regarding what Master Hu has produced, if one can truly discern his own handiwork, the essential framework will surely be correct.

Although his translated scriptures may not always distinguish between the subtle and the manifest with refined elegance, they are grand, expansive, and exhilarating; he is particularly adept at conveying the doctrine of non-arising.”
"Rely on wisdom rather than literary elegance; simplicity is closer to the fundamental.
Such was the acclaim he received.
Daohu lived in Dunhuang, yet his transformative teachings reached everywhere; the people of the time all called him the "Dunhuang Bodhisattva."
9. Bo Yuan, whose courtesy name was Fazuo, was originally surnamed Wan and was a native of Henei.
His father, Wei Da, was renowned for his refined and elegant character; he declined all appointments offered by the provincial and regional governments.

From his youth, Huizang developed the aspiration for the Way and petitioned his father to leave the household life. His arguments were so earnest and compelling that his father could not resist him; he subsequently changed his attire to follow the Way.

Huizang’s talent and insight were brilliant and penetrating, and his quick-witted clarity was peerless. He would recite eight or nine thousand words of scripture daily, and through his profound study and savoring of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) sutras, he entered their subtle and mysterious depths with mastery.
He was extensively versed in both secular and canonical literature.

Consequently, he constructed a vihāra in Chang’an, making the study and exposition of the teachings his primary vocation; monks and laypeople alike took him as their spiritual guide, numbering nearly a thousand.

Toward the end of the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, Grand Chancellor Hejian Wang Yong was stationed in Guanzhong; he held [Dao’an] in high esteem with an open mind, treating him with the respect due to a teacher or a friend, and whenever there was leisure time or a quiet night, they would invariably discuss and lecture upon the Way and its Virtue.
At that time, the Western Capital was first established and subsequently flourished greatly; those eloquent scholars all acknowledged his profound insight.
Seeing the various factions contending for power and the onset of war, Zuo desired to withdraw secretly to the region beyond the Long Mountains (Lung-yu) to preserve his refined integrity.
Zhang Fu was appointed as the Imperial Protector of Qinzhou to govern the region of Longshang, and Zuo accompanied him on his journey.
Because Zuo’s reputation for virtue and wisdom was so prominent that he was the natural choice for all, Zhang Fu wished to have him return to secular dress and serve as his own subordinate official.
Sengzu’s resolve remained unshakable, and because of this, [Wang] harbored a deep resentment toward him.

Previously, there had been a local man named Guan Fan who had engaged in debate with Sengzu; having been repeatedly defeated by him, Fan bore a profound sense of humiliation and hatred, constantly engaging in slanderous intrigues against him.
When the Patriarch reached Qian County, he suddenly said to the practitioners and his disciples:
"I shall arrive at my destined destination in a few days.
He then took his leave and composed a plain letter, after which he completed the distribution of the scriptures, images, and all his worldly possessions.
The next morning, he went to visit Fu and spoke with him; suddenly, however, he offended Fu's sentiments, and Fu ordered him to be arrested and punished.
The assembly all felt strange and regretful, but Zu said:
"I have come here to settle this matter; it is a long-standing karmic bond from past lives, not something that concerns the present."
He then invoked the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Regarding the karmic conditions of his past offenses, he joyfully confessed them all and made this vow: "From this day forward, may you be my spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); do not let me suffer the retribution for the sin of killing."
He was subsequently whipped fifty times and died suddenly.
When Fu later heard the full account of these events, he was filled with great regret and resentment.

Initially, the reputation of Zu Dao’s transformation had spread throughout Guanzhong and Longyou; to the right of the Xiaohuan Pass, people revered him as if he were a deity, such that both the Rong and Jin peoples lamented his passing and those on the roads wept.

The Qiang and Hu tribes of the Long Mountains led five thousand elite cavalry, intending to escort Fu Zu back to the west. Hearing on the way that he had been murdered, they were overcome with grief and regret at not having reached him in time; the entire host was filled with indignation and desired to take revenge for Zu. When Fu’s army advanced toward the Long Mountains, the Qiang and Hu led their light cavalry to meet them in battle. At that time, Fu Zheng, the former Commandant of Xianxia in Tianshui, took advantage of the fury to slay Fu. Once the tribesmen had avenged their grievance and shame, they praised the deed and returned, dividing Zu’s remains and each erecting stupas and temples in his honor.
Fu, whose courtesy name was Shiwěi, was a native of Nányáng and a descendant of Zhāng Héng.

Although he possessed talent and understanding, he was cruel and lacked principle; he perversely murdered Fēng Shàng, the Governor of Tiānshuǐ. The common people were filled with suspicion and alarm, and amidst the ensuing chaos, Fu himself was executed.
Guan Fan also ultimately met with defeat due to his treacherous and perilous nature.
A short time later, there was a man named Li Tong who died and then returned to life, saying:
"I saw Master Zu at the abode of King Yama, where he was lecturing on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* for the King. He continued:
"Once the lecture is finished, you should go to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
He also saw Wang Fu, the Sacrificial Libationer—also known as Daoist Master Ji—who was bound in shackles and chains, seeking the Patriarch’s repentance.

"In the past, during his ordinary days, Zu frequently debated matters of heterodoxy and orthodoxy with Fu; Fu was repeatedly defeated. Unable to restrain his anger, Zu then composed the *Laozi huahu jing* to slander the Buddha-dharma. Since the retribution for such calamity has its destination, it was only upon his death that he finally felt remorse."
In his *Discourse on the Worthies of the Way* (*Daoxian lun*), Sun Chuo pairs Fazu with Ji Kang, stating in his commentary:

"Bai Zu’s misfortune arose from Guan Fan; Zhongshan’s disaster was brought about by Zhong Hui. These two worthies both possessed an air of extraordinary brilliance, yet they were oblivious to the considerations necessary for self-preservation. They withdrew their minds from worldly affairs and, by holding the world in low esteem, invited calamity; in this, they were hardly different."
His reputation was thus acclaimed.

The Master was extensively learned and versatile, proficient in both Sanskrit and Chinese. He once translated three scriptures—the *Vaidalya*, the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, and the *Pañcavargika*—and also annotated the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
There were also several other translations of minor sutras in multiple fascicles that were lost during the chaos; their titles are now unknown.
His younger brother, Fazuo, also enjoyed a distinguished reputation from his youth and was summoned as a court scholar, but he did not accept the appointment.
At the age of twenty-five, he left the household life; he profoundly penetrated the principles of the Buddha-dharma and became renowned throughout Guanzhong and Longyou.
At that time, Zhang Guang, the Regional Inspector of Liangzhou, had executed Sengfu because Sengzuo’s elder brother refused to wear mourning clothes for him.

Emperor Guang again pressured Sengzuo to renounce the Way; however, Sengzuo remained firm and steadfast in his resolve, swearing to die rather than comply, until he was ultimately murdered by Guang at the age of fifty-seven.
He annotated the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Fàngguāng Bōrě Jīng) and authored works such as the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Xiǎnzōng Lùn).
His courtesy name was Jǐngwǔ, and he was a native of Jiāngxia. Later, while Wǔdù was besieged by Yang Nándí, he died out of indignation.
During the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, there was also the Upāsaka Wei Shidu, who translated the two-fascicle *Daoxing Banruo Jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra).

Shidu was originally a native of Ji Commandery in Sizhou; though he remained submerged among the commoners of a humble lineage, he was content in poverty and delighted in the Way, constantly taking the Buddha-dharma as his core concern.

On the day of his passing, he purified himself by washing and rinsing his mouth, recited more than a thousand words of scripture, and then drew his robes over his corpse to lie down, whereupon he died suddenly.
10. Śrīmitra: Śrīmitra is translated here as Jiyǒu (吉友). He was a man from the Western Regions, whom the people of the time called Gāozuò (高座).
The tradition states:
He was the son of a king who, being entitled to succeed to the throne, yielded the kingdom to his younger brother, An-gui (Tàibó).
Subsequently, having attained awakening through a celestial inspiration, he became a śramaṇa.
Mili possessed a naturally lofty and radiant countenance and an exceptionally transcendent spirit; even upon first meeting him, one was struck by his outstanding superiority over all others.
During the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty, he first arrived in China; encountering turmoil, he subsequently crossed the Yangtze River and stayed at Jianchu Monastery.
When Prime Minister Wang Dao saw him once, he marveled at him, considering him one of his own kind; thus, his reputation became prominent.

The Grand Marshal Yu Yuan gui, the Court Herald Zhou Bo ren, the Director of the Imperial Clan Office Xie You yu, and the Minister of Justice Huan Mao lun—all renowned scholars of their generation—upon meeting him, sighed repeatedly throughout the entire day and opened their hearts to form a deep bond with him.
Zhi Dao once visited HuiMi; as Mi unfastened his belt and lay down prostrate, Dao was moved by the spiritual resonance of their conversation.

At that time, Bian Wangzhi, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was also on intimate terms with Mi. After a short while, Wangzhi arrived, whereupon Mi adjusted his collar, composed his countenance, and sat upright to face him.
When someone asked him the reason for this, Sengmi replied:
"The Prince [Wang Gong] aspires to others through the Way and its influence, while Magistrate Bian measures things according to their standards; that is precisely why it is so."
Thereupon, the gentlemen marveled at how his spirit was so vigorous and refined, and that he had found his true place.
Once, the Magistrate of the Court (Huan Tingwei) wished to compose a character sketch for Śrīmitra; after a long time, he could not find the right words, until someone remarked:
"Śrīmitra may truly be called 'exalted and brilliant' (zhuōlǎng)."
Thereupon, Huan sighed deeply and uttered words of supreme praise, regarding them as the ultimate in titles.

When General of the State Wang Chuzhong was in Nanxia, he heard that the various lords, including Wang Zhou, all held Mi in high esteem; suspecting this to be an exaggeration, he went to see Mi. Upon meeting him, he was so moved by joy that he rushed forward, showing the utmost reverence from their very first encounter.
Zhou Yi served as the Director of the Imperial Secretariat and presided over the selection of officials.

As he was about to enter the office, he stopped by to visit Wang Mi. He then sighed and said, "If, in an age of Great Peace, we could fully select such worthy men for office, it would truly leave one with no regrets."

Shortly thereafter, Huiyi was killed. Sengmi went to visit his orphaned child; as they sat facing each other, he chanted the *huabei* (foreign hymns) three times, the resonance of the Sanskrit sounds soaring above the clouds.
He then recited several thousand words of dharanis, his voice lofty and resonant yet his facial expression remaining unchanged.
Having finished, he wiped away his tears and composed himself, his spirit and countenance as calm as before.
Their expressions of sorrow and joy, and their rise and fall, were all of this nature.
A prince once said to Mi:
"In foreign lands, there is but one true sovereign."
Mili smiled and said,
"If I were like you gentlemen, how could I be here today? At that time,
these were considered excellent words.

Hui-mi’s nature was profound and simple; he did not study the Jin language. When the various gentlemen conversed with him, although Hui-mi relied on interpreters, he grasped the spirit and captured the meaning intuitively, exhausting the essence of what was said before a single word was uttered. All marveled at his natural genius and extraordinary insight, realizing that his realization surpassed the ordinary.
Saṃghavarman was skilled at maintaining esoteric incantations, and his efforts were invariably efficacious.
Initially, the methods of incantation did not yet exist in Jiangdong; Saṃghavarman translated the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra*, elucidating various divine spells.
He also taught his disciples the *mili* (seeking the path) chant in a loud voice, the resonance of which continues to this day.
He passed away during the Xiankang era of the Jin dynasty at over eighty years of age.
When the various officials heard of it, they mourned him with tears flowing.
Huan Xuanwu often remarked that he had rarely seen anyone so eminent in his youth, praising his spiritual presence as being preeminent among his contemporaries.
Wang Min of Langya took him as his teacher and composed a preface for him, saying:

"In the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, the states of Wu and Chu are referred to as 'Zi' (Son of Heaven). Commentators consider this to mean placing the Central Kingdom first and the four barbarian tribes second. Is it not because, though they were descendants of the Three Dynasties, they practiced the rites of foreign customs, and because the Rong and Di were greedy and lacked the nature of benevolence and yielding?"

Nevertheless, the world’s most outstanding talents have occasionally arisen among them, and those of extraordinary genius may at times equal those found here; thus we know that when Heaven bestows brilliance and greatness, it does not wait for the distinction between Chinese and barbarians. Since that time, only the Han dynasty produced Jin Midi; yet while Midi’s worth was consummate in his benevolence, filial piety, loyalty, and sincerity—his virtue and integrity being pure and ultimate—he cannot be considered a match for those of profound insight and discernment.
"Gaoseng’s mind reaches the highest peaks, and he exchanges brilliance with the divine; his character is lofty and transcendent—how far he surpasses others!
After Huiji was constantly practicing *dhūta* austerities on the eastern side of Shizigang, he passed away and was consequently buried there.
Emperor Cheng admired his character and established a stupa at the site of his grave.
Later, a śramaṇa from Guanyou came to travel in the capital and subsequently built a monastery on the grounds of the grave.
Xie Kun of Chenjun supported his undertaking and commemorated these past events by retaining the name "Gaozuo Temple. 11.
Saṃghabhūti (Sengqiebacheng): Saṃghabhūti means "Manifestation of the Multitude" in Chinese; he was a native of Jibin.

Possessing a resolute and profound magnanimity, he traveled extensively to seek out renowned masters, thoroughly studying the Tripiṭaka and broadly surveying various scriptures. He was particularly adept at the Abhidharma texts; he could recite the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra* from memory and had mastered its subtle principles.
He had always harbored the ambition to travel abroad to observe the customs and propagate the teachings.
In the seventeenth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, he arrived in Guanzhong.

Prior to this, the Mahayana scriptures had not yet spread widely, while the study of meditation and numerical analysis (Abhidharma) was very prevalent; once he reached Chang’an, everyone hailed him as a master of the Dharma.

Zhao Zheng, a Secretariat Drafter under Fu Jian, held the Great Dharma in high esteem. Having heard that foreigners were devoted to the study of the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā* and that Saṃghabhūti could recite it from memory, he provided him with the fourfold offerings and requested the translation of the Sanskrit text. Consequently, together with renowned and virtuous Dharma Masters such as Shi Dao’an, they assembled the monastic community to proclaim and translate the work.

Bazheng orally recited the original text of the sūtra; the foreign śramaṇa Dharmalati transcribed it into Sanskrit characters, and Fotuoluoche provided the oral translation. The Qin śramaṇa Minzhi transcribed it into the Jin version. It was translated out during the nineteenth year of the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin, beginning in the first month of summer and concluding in the middle month of autumn.

Initially, Saṃghabhūti had also brought a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Vasumitra-śāstra* with him. The following year, Zhao Zheng again requested that it be translated. Saṃghabhūti, together with Dharmaratna and Saṃghadeva—these three men—held the Sanskrit manuscript, while the Qin śramaṇa Fo-nian orally translated it, Hui-song took it down in writing, and Master Dao’an and Fa-he compared and finalized the text together. Consequently, these two scriptures were disseminated and have been transmitted for study to this day.
Bhadrapāla was of strict and lofty moral integrity; he was serene and detached from the mundane world. The monastic community in Guanzhong took him as their model.
His ultimate end is unknown. Buddharakṣa was a man of unknown nationality; his virtuous conduct was pure and refined, and he had thoroughly mastered the scriptures.
Having traveled extensively through the Central Kingdom for a long time, he was well-versed in the Chinese language; his translations of Sanskrit texts were highly esteemed by Emperor Fu Jian.
12. Dharmaruci (曇摩難提): Dharmaruci means "Dharma-Joy" (法喜) in Chinese; he was a person from Tukhāra.
Having left secular life at the age of seven, his intelligence was precociously developed; he studied and recited the scriptures with single-minded dedication.

Having perused the entire Tripiṭaka and memorized the *Ekottarika Āgama* by heart, his vast knowledge and extensive learning encompassed everything, such that those far and near throughout the realm all held him in high esteem and submission.

Having traveled abroad in his youth and journeyed through many countries, he often maintained that the essence of propagating the Dharma lay in proclaiming what had not yet been heard. Thus, braving the shifting sands from afar and carrying his treasures, he entered the East and arrived at Chang’an during the Jianyuan era of the Fu clan.
Since Dharmanandi’s learning was already excellent and his reputation for the Way was very great, Fu Jian received him with profound respect and courtesy.

Previously, among the various scriptures in the Central Lands, the four *Āgamas* had not yet appeared. Fu Jian’s minister, Zhao Zheng, the Governor of Wuwei, wished to request that these scriptures be translated.

At that time, Tuoba Chong had already rebelled and raised troops to attack Yao Jian, causing turmoil throughout Guanzhong. Although Yao Zheng was deeply devoted to the Dharma, he forgot his own person for the sake of the Way.

He then invited Master Dao’an and others to assemble monks specializing in the study of meaning within the city of Chang’an. He requested that Saṃghadeva translate the *Madhyama-āgama* and the *Ekottarika-āgama*, as well as previously untranslated works such as the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* and the *Tridharmaka-śāstra*, totaling one hundred and six fascicles.
The Buddha’s teachings were translated by Founian, with Huisong receiving them in writing. From summer until spring, spanning two full years, the texts were finally completed.
When Yao Chang’s forces threatened the Guannei region and public morale was in peril, Kumārajīva took his leave to return to the Western Regions, and his ultimate fate remains unknown.

At that time, Fu Jian had recently been defeated, rival factions were rising in conflict, barbarian rebels were acting with lawless violence, and the people were fleeing in all directions; yet, it was still possible to transmit and translate the great Mahāyāna scriptures, which was largely due to the efforts of Zhao Zheng.
Zhengzi Wenyè was a native of Qingshui in Luoyang, though some say he was from Jiyin.
At the age of eighteen, he served as the Court Historian (Zuozhíjué láng) for the pseudo-Qin dynasty; later, he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Huángmén láng) and Governor of Wuwei.
He was hairless and thin, and though he had wives and concubines, he had no children; thus, his contemporaries called him a eunuch.

Nevertheless, his temperament and discernment were acute and penetrating, and his learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular traditions. By nature, he delighted in offering satirical admonitions, never shrinking from anything.
During the final years of Fu Jian’s reign, he was infatuated with the Xianbei and brought his administration into ruin. Consequently, [Wang] Zheng composed a song of admonition, saying:
"I have heard of the Mengjin River, Which forms a single bend for a thousand li. This water was originally clear; Who has stirred it to become turbid?"
Jian moved his expression and said,
"This is I. He then sang this song:
"In the northern garden there is a jujube tree; its leaves are spread wide, casting a heavy shade. Though thorns abound on the outside, within it truly possesses a red heart.
Sengjian laughed and said, "Could this not be Zhao Wenye?"
His playful wit and quickness of mind were all of this nature.

Later, because the Buddha-dharma was flourishing in Guanzhong, he wished to leave the household life; however, his father Sengjian cherished him deeply and did not grant permission. Only after Sengjian’s death was his aspiration fulfilled, and he changed his name to Daozheng.
He then composed a verse, saying:
"Why was the Buddha born so late, and why did his nirvana come so soon? I take refuge in Śākyamuni; now I come to entrust myself to the Great Way."
Later, he withdrew into seclusion on Mount Shangluo, where he devoted himself exclusively to the study of the Sūtras and the Vinaya.
Xi Hui, the Governor of Yongzhou during the Jin dynasty, admired his character and lifestyle and urged him to travel with him; he eventually passed away in Xiangyang at the age of over sixty.
13. Saṃghadeva: "Saṃghadeva" means "Heavenly Host" (Zhòngtiān) in Chinese; it is also sometimes written as "Tihe," which is due to a phonetic corruption.

His original surname was Gautama, and he was a native of Jibin. Having entered the path to study, he traveled afar in search of enlightened masters. His learning permeated the Tripiṭaka, and he was particularly adept at the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, penetrating its subtlest principles.
He constantly recited the *Tri-dharmaka-śāstra*, admiring and savoring it day and night, regarding it as the treasury for entering the Way.
He was brilliant and possessed profound discernment, yet his deportment was mild and respectful; he was dedicated to instructing others, remaining earnest and untiring.
During the Jianyuan era of the Fu clan, he came to Chang’an to propagate the Dharma and transform others.

Initially, Saṃghabhūti had translated the *Vasumitra-śāstra*, and Dharmaratna had produced two versions of the *Āgamas*, the *Abhidharma*, the *Vistara*, the *Tri-dharmaka*, and other texts totaling over one million words.

During the turmoil caused by the troubles of the Murong clan, the non-Chinese enemies were in a state of chaotic disturbance; furthermore, as the translators worked in haste, their work was not yet thorough or detailed, and thus the essential meanings and the nuances of the phrasing were often left incomplete.
Shortly thereafter, Master Dao’an passed away before he could correct [the calendar].
Later, when the region east of the mountains became peaceful, Guṇabhadra then traveled to Luoyang together with the śramaṇa Fǎhé of Jī Prefecture.

For four or five years, he studied and lectured on the aforementioned sutras; having resided in China for some time and become proficient in the Chinese language, he finally realized that there were many errors and discrepancies in the scriptures previously translated.
While Fǎhé was still lamenting that [the teachings] were not yet settled, he further commissioned Saṃghadeva to produce the *Abhidharma* and various extensive sūtras.
Shortly thereafter, Yao Xing ruled over the Qin state and Buddhist affairs flourished greatly; consequently, Fǎhé entered Guānzhōng, while Saṃghadeva crossed the Yangtze River.

Previously, Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu had been devotedly diligent in the wondrous scriptures and had extensively collected the Tripitaka. With an open mind and humble posture, he waited expectantly for eminent guests; upon hearing that [the Master] had arrived, he immediately invited him to enter Mount Lu.
