During the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, he requested the translation of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Tridharmaka-śāstra*.

Deva then, at the Prajñā Terrace, held the Sanskrit texts in his hands while orally proclaiming them in the Jin language; he stripped away ornamentation to preserve the substance, striving to exhaust the fundamental meaning of the doctrines. What is transmitted today is likely his literary version.

In the first year of the Long’an era, he came to travel in the capital. Among the princes and dukes of the Jin court, as well as the eminent men of refined culture, there were none who did not visit his quarters to pay their respects.

At that time, Wang Xun of Langya—the General of the Guards and Marquis of Dongting—was a man of profound virtue and deep faith who upheld the True Dharma. He had established a vihāra and widely invited a multitude of students. Once Deva arrived, Xun immediately extended an invitation; Deva subsequently lectured on the *Abhidharma* in Xun’s residence, where renowned monks gathered in full assembly.
Deva’s doctrinal system was already refined and his phrasing and intent were clear and analytical; as he expounded the principles, the assembly all attained joyful realization.
At that time, Wang Mi was also present in the audience listening. Later, when Wang Mi gave a lecture on his own in a separate room, Sengxun asked the Dharma Master Gang, "What has Wang Ami attained?"
He replied, "In its broad outlines it is entirely correct; it is only in minor details that it has not yet been thoroughly scrutinized.
Such was the clarity of his analytical exposition, capable of awakening the minds of others with such ease.

That winter, Sengxun gathered more than forty śramaṇas from the capital’s monastic academies, including Shi Huichi, and again requested Guṇabhadra to retranslate the *Madhyama Āgama* and other texts. The Kasmīrian śramaṇa Saṃgharakṣa held the Sanskrit manuscripts while Guṇabhadra translated them into the language of Jin; it was not until the following summer that the work was completed.
The various scriptures he produced in the regions along the Yangtze and Huai rivers total more than one million words.

Having traveled extensively among both Chinese and foreign lands, he was thoroughly acquainted with their customs; composed yet quick-witted, he excelled in conversation and humor. His reputation for spiritual transformation and his renown were heard everywhere.
His final whereabouts were unknown. 14. Zhu Fonian:

A native of Liangzhou, Zhu Fonian entered the monastic order in his youth; his aspirations and practice were pure and firm. He was harmonious outwardly and lucid inwardly, possessing a discerning mind of great penetration and agility.

He recited and studied various sutras and had a superficial acquaintance with the external classics; he was particularly proficient and well-versed in the glosses and explanations of the *Cangjie* and *Shuowen Jiezi*.

From his youth, he delighted in traveling to distant regions, observing customs thoroughly. His family lineage was from Xihe, so he was intimately familiar with foreign dialects; there were no sounds or meanings of either Chinese or non-Chinese languages that he did not understand simultaneously. Thus, although his reputation for scholastic expertise was lacking, his fame for extensive learning was very prominent.

During the Jianyuan era of the Fu clan’s reign, the monks Saṃghabhūti, Dharmanandi, and others entered Chang’an. Zhao Zheng requested that they translate various scriptures; however, at that time, none of the renowned virtuous masters were able to transmit the translations. As everyone unanimously recommended Dharmarakṣa, Saṃghabhūti then held the Sanskrit texts while Dharmarakṣa translated them into Jin Chinese.
He resolved doubts and clarified meanings, so that the sounds and characters finally became clear.
In the first month of the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era, he again requested Dharmānanda to bring forth the *Ekottarika Āgama* and the *Madhyama Āgama*.

Within the city of Chang’an, he assembled śramaṇas specializing in the study of doctrine and invited Dharmarakṣa to serve as the translator. Through detailed exposition, analysis, and rigorous verification, the work was completed in two years.
The manifestation of the two *Saṃyuktāgama* collections is due to the merit of Dharmarakṣa’s proclamation and translation.

Since the time of An Shigao and Zhi Qian, none has surpassed Zhu Fonian; during the two reigns of Fu Jian and Yao Xing, he was the preeminent master among translators, and thus the monastic community in Guanzhong all held him in high esteem.

Subsequently, he produced the *Bodhisattvālaṃkāra*, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga*, as well as the *Udānavarga*, the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*, the *Antarābhava-sūtra*, and others; he had just begun to edit and finalize them when his intentions remained largely unfulfilled. He then fell ill and passed away in Chang’an, at which all those far and near, both monastics and laypeople, sighed with lamentation.
15. Dharmayaśas: Dharmayaśas, translated here as Faming (Dharma-illumination), was a native of Jibin.
From his youth he was fond of learning; at the age of fourteen, he was recognized by Puṇyatāra.
As he grew up, his physical frame was tall and vigorous, and he possessed a refined spiritual intelligence. He had mastered the sutras and vinayas, and his clear insight surpassed that of his peers.
Cultivating his thoughts within the eight dhyānas and letting his mind roam through the seven factors of enlightenment, his contemporaries compared him to Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.
He traveled alone through mountains and marshes, not avoiding even jackals and tigers; dwelling in solitude in contemplation, days and nights passed as he moved about.
He would often reproach himself beneath trees, saying:
"My years are approaching thirty, yet I have still not attained the fruit; how negligent I am!"
Thereupon, for several days he neither slept nor ate, applying himself with singular intensity and reaching the limit of austerity in order to repent for his past transgressions.
He then dreamed that the Heavenly King Vaśavartin spoke to him, saying:

"A śramaṇa should contemplate the various directions and propagate the transformation [of others], making vast salvation his concern; why do you cling to minor rules and seek only your own solitary perfection?"
"The Way relies upon manifold conditions and must further await the ripening of the time; to seek it by force beyond one's lot leads to death without realization.
Thus he reflected within himself, desiring to travel afar to transmit the Way. Thereupon, he traversed famous lands and journeyed through various provinces and kingdoms.
During the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, he first arrived at Guangzhou and resided at Baisa Temple.
Yaśas was skilled at reciting the *Vibhāṣā-vinaya*, so people all called him "Mahāvibhāṣā. At that time, he was already eighty-five years old, and his assembly consisted of eighty-five disciples.

At that time, there was a laywoman of pure faith named Zhang Puming, who sought instruction in the Buddha’s teachings; Dharmayaśas expounded for her the *Buddhajanma-utpatti* (The Origin of the Buddha’s Birth) and translated the *Kṣemaka-sūtra* in one fascicle.
During the Yixi era, he arrived in Chang’an.
At that time, Yao Xing had usurped the title of emperor and held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem; once Guṇabhadra arrived, Yao Xing treated him with profound courtesy and exceptional honor.

There would come a day when the Indian śramaṇa Dharmagupta entered Guanzhong; seeking out those of like mind, they felt as though they had known each other for a long time. Consequently, they collaborated with [Dharmayaśas] to translate the *Śāriputrābhidharma*. Beginning in the first year of Hongshi of the Later Qin, they transcribed the Sanskrit text, and by the sixteenth year, the translation was finally completed, totaling twenty-two fascicles.
The false Crown Prince Yao Hong personally managed the *wei* (flavor) [meditation], and the śramaṇa Daobiao composed a preface for it.

Later, Guṇabhadra traveled south to Jiangling and stayed at Xin Temple, where he extensively propagated the methods of dhyāna. Among those who sought the stillness of flavor, there were over three hundred people who came through the brushwood to join him.
Whenever officials or commoners visited him, even those who previously lacked faith would all feel reverence and joy upon seeing him.
He himself said that there was once a master and a disciple who practiced their studies together and both attained arhatship; however, the transmitter of this account has lost their names.
Furthermore, on one occasion, while he was sitting in meditation with the doors closed at the outer gate, suddenly five or six śramaṇas entered his room.
On other occasions, he frequently saw śramaṇas flying to the tops of trees; such instances were not limited to a single occurrence.

He constantly maintained communion with the divine while condescending to mingle with the ignorant masses; although his traces of the Way were not yet fully manifest, people of the time all claimed he had already attained the fruit of sainthood.
During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he took his leave to return to the Western Regions, and his ultimate end remains unknown.
Yaśas had a disciple named Fadu, who was proficient in both Sanskrit and Chinese and frequently served as an interpreter.

Fadu was originally the son of Zhu Poluo; Poluo had resided in Guangzhou for a long time, traveling back and forth to seek profit. Along the way, in Nankang, he fathered a son whom he named Nankang. When the boy grew up, his name was changed to Jinka; upon entering the monastic order, he was named Fadu.
At first, Fadu was a disciple of Yaśas and received the transmission of the sutras and the Dharma.

Once Yaśas had returned to his foreign land, Fadu began to maintain eccentric views on his own, intending to win over followers. He claimed that one should study exclusively the Hīnayāna and prohibit the reading of the *Vaipulya* (Mahāyāna) scriptures; he asserted that one should worship only Śākyamuni and that there were no Buddhas of the ten directions; furthermore, he maintained that one should use copper bowls for eating and that there were no other separate alms vessels.
Furthermore, he commanded that the nuns walk holding one another’s hands, and on the day they repented their transgressions, they were to merely prostrate themselves facing each other on the ground.

Only the nun Fahong, daughter of Yan Yuan, former Governor of Danyang during the Song dynasty, and the nun Puming, daughter of Zhang Mu, the Regional Inspector of Jiaozhou, initially received his teachings.
Nowadays, the nuns of Xuanye and Hongguang Monasteries in the capital study her legacy, and among the nunneries of the eastern lands, her teachings are likewise occasionally transmitted.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huijiao of Jiaxiang Monastery in Kuaiji during the Liang Dynasty.
Among the translators of the Chinese Tripitaka:

1. Kumārajīva; 2. Dharmaruci; 3. Vimalākṣa; 4. Buddhayaśas; 5. Buddhabhadra; 6. Dharmakṣema. 1. Kumārajīva: Kumārajīva, here translated as "Child-Life" (Tongshou), was a native of India whose family had served as ministers of state for generations.
Kumārajīva’s grandfather, Datta, was unconventional and stood out from the crowd; his reputation was esteemed throughout the kingdom.

His father, Kujūla-Kaśyapa, was intelligent and possessed noble character; when he was about to succeed to the position of prime minister, he declined the appointment, left the household life, and traveled east across the Pamir Mountains.

When the King of Kucha heard that he had renounced his glory, he felt profound admiration for him; he went out to the outskirts of the city to welcome him in person and invited him to serve as the National Preceptor.

The king had a younger sister who was twenty years of age; she possessed a keen and lucid intelligence, such that she could master anything after a single glance and recite it immediately upon hearing it once.
Furthermore, her body bore a red mole, a sign that she would give birth to a son of wisdom; consequently, when various kingdoms sought her hand in marriage, she refused to go with any of them.
Upon seeing Māyā, her heart desired him as her husband, so he was compelled to take her as his wife, and she subsequently conceived Śāriputra.
While Kumārajīva was in the womb, his mother felt her spiritual awakening and superior understanding increase twofold compared to her usual state.

Hearing that the Great Kukkutārāma Monastery possessed many men of renowned virtue and monks who had attained the Way, she immediately provided daily offerings together with noble ladies of the royal clan and nuns of virtuous conduct, inviting them for a vegetarian feast and to listen to the Dharma.

Śīma’s mother suddenly became able to communicate in the language of India; when faced with difficult questions and inquiries, she invariably exhausted the depths of their meaning, and the assembly all marveled at her.
The arhat Dharmaghoṣa said, "This child must surely be one who harbors wisdom."
He recounted for him the evidence regarding Śāriputra’s time in the womb;
however, after Kumārajīva was born, he forgot what he had previously said.
Shortly thereafter, Kumārajīva’s mother wished to leave the household life, but her husband would not permit it. Consequently, she gave birth to another son, named Puṣyadeva.

Later, while traveling outside the city for sightseeing, he saw withered bones scattered in various places amidst the burial mounds; thereupon, he deeply contemplated the root of suffering and made a firm vow to renounce the household life, swearing that he would not swallow food or drink until his hair was shorn.
By the night of the sixth day, his strength was exhausted and he feared he would not survive until dawn; his husband, filled with dread, finally consented.
Because he had not yet shaved his head, he still did not partake of food.
He immediately ordered someone to shave his hair and then provided him with food and drink.
On the following morning, he received the precepts; continuing to delight in the methods of dhyāna, he applied himself with focused diligence and attained the first fruit of the path.

At the age of seven, Kumārajīva also left the household life together with him; he received the sūtras from his teacher and recited a thousand gāthās daily, each gāthā consisting of thirty-two syllables, totaling thirty-two thousand words.

Once he had finished reciting the *Abhidharma*, his teacher transmitted its meaning to him; Kumārajīva immediately attained thorough mastery, such that there was no profound point he could not elucidate.

At that time, because the people of Kucha regarded him as the maternal uncle of their queen, the offerings and honors bestowed upon him were exceedingly great; consequently, he took Kumārajīva with him to avoid this situation.

When Kumārajīva was nine years old, he accompanied his mother across the Indus River to Kapiśī, where he met the renowned and virtuous Dharma Master Bandhudatta, who was the younger cousin of the King of Kapiśī.

Profound and pure, he possessed a vast capacity; talented, brilliant, and widely learned, he was peerless in his time. There were no works among the Tripiṭaka or the nine divisions of scripture that he had not mastered.
From morning until noon, he would transcribe a thousand verses by hand; from noon until evening, he would likewise recite a thousand verses.
His fame spread throughout various countries, and those both near and far took him as their teacher.

Upon Kumārajīva’s arrival, [the King] honored him with the rites due to a teacher and followed him to receive the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka* and the two *Āgamas*—the *Madhyama-āgama* and the *Dīrgha-āgama*—comprising a total of four million words.

Dharmadatta constantly praised Kumārajīva’s divine brilliance, and his reputation eventually reached the King. The King immediately invited him into the palace and assembled non-Buddhist masters of logic to engage him in debate and challenge him.
When their breaths first mingled, the non-Buddhist disparaged Kumārajīva for his youth, speaking with considerable insolence.
Kumārajīva seized the opportunity to humble him; the non-Buddhist was defeated and, filled with shame and regret, remained speechless.
The king’s respect and admiration for him increased further; he provided daily a pair of goose carcasses, three pecks each of non-glutinous rice and flour, and six liters of ghee.
These were the finest offerings from foreign lands.

The monks of the monastery where he resided appointed five senior bhikṣus and ten śrāmaṇeras to attend to him, sweeping and cleaning as if he were their own disciple; such was the reverence shown to him.
When he reached the age of twelve, his mother took him back to Kucha; although various kingdoms offered him invitations with high-ranking titles, Kumārajīva paid them no heed.
At that time, Kumārajīva’s mother took him to Bactria (Yuezhi).
On North Mountain, an arhat saw him and marveled at his extraordinary nature.

He said to the boy’s mother, “You must always protect this śrāmaṇera. If by the age of thirty-five he has not broken any precepts, he shall greatly propagate the Buddha-dharma and deliver countless people, no different from Upagupta.”
"If one's precepts are incomplete, they are incapable of achieving anything; they can only rely on their talent and intelligence to accompany a Dharma Master.
When Kumārajīva arrived at the kingdom of Kashgar, he took up the Buddha’s alms bowl and thought to himself:
"The shape of this bowl is very large; why is it so light?"
It was so heavy that he could not bear it; losing his composure, he set it down.
His mother asked for the reason, and he replied, "My mind harbors discrimination; therefore, the bowl feels heavy or light."
He remained in Śākala for one year.
That winter, he recited the *Abhidharma*.

Regarding the chapters on the "Ten Gates" (*Daśamukha*) and "Cultivating Wisdom" (*Jñānabhāvanā*), though he had no teacher from whom to receive instruction, he thoroughly mastered their subtleties; furthermore, regarding the various questions in the "Six Feet" (*Ṣaṭpāda*), he encountered no obstruction.
In the kingdom of Śākala, there was a *tripiṭaka* śramaṇa named Priyadarśana who said to his king:
"This śrāmaṇera must not be underestimated; Your Majesty should invite him to first open the gateway of the Dharma. There will be two benefits:
first, the śramaṇas within the realm will feel ashamed of their own shortcomings and will surely exert themselves."
"The King of Kucha will surely think that since Kumārajīva has come from our country and is honored there, he must honor us as well; he will certainly come to establish friendly relations.

The King agreed and immediately organized a great assembly, inviting Kumārajīva to ascend the seat and preach the *Dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra*. Consequently, the King of Kucha dispatched an important envoy to reciprocate his personal goodwill.
In his leisure time from preaching the Dharma, Kumārajīva sought out non-Buddhist scriptures and became proficient in the study of the *Vedānta-śāstra*.

He was particularly well-versed in the composition of prose and verse, as well as the art of debate and dialogue; furthermore, he extensively read the four Vedas and various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).

In the calculations of the Yin-Yang and the stars, there was nothing he did not master; he attained a profound understanding of auspiciousness and misfortune such that his words were like a tally and its seal.

By nature, he was straightforward and open, not insisting on minor points of propriety; consequently, practitioners often harbored doubts about him, yet Kumārajīva remained self-possessed in his heart and never gave it a second thought.
At that time, there were two brothers, a prince of Śākya and a prince of the Cāṇūra clan, who abandoned their kingdoms to seek following [the Buddha] and became śramaṇas.
The elder brother was named Śūryabhadra, and the younger brother was named Śūryasoma.

Sūma’s talent and skill were peerless; he specialized in converting others through the Mahāyāna, and both his elder brother and various scholars took him as their teacher. Kumārajīva also revered and followed him, their personal intimacy reaching its highest degree.

Later, Sūma preached the *Anavatapta-sūtra* for Kumārajīva. Upon hearing that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are all empty and signless, Kumārajīva was astonished and asked:
"What further meaning does this sūtra contain, such that it utterly dismantles all dharmas?"
He replied, "The eye and other such dharmas do not exist as ultimate realities.

Since Kumārajīva maintained that the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya) exists, while the other relied on the fact that things lack reality because they are established through causes, they investigated the Great and Small Vehicles, engaging in a back-and-forth debate that occupied much time.
Only then did Kumārajīva realize that the truth had its proper destination, whereupon he devoted himself exclusively to the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) sūtras.
He then sighed and said:
"In the past, when I studied the Hīnayāna, it was like a person who does not recognize gold and mistakes brass for something exquisite."
Thereupon, he extensively sought out the essential meanings of the teachings and received and recited the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, and other treatises.
Shortly thereafter, he traveled with his mother to the kingdom of Wensu, which lies on the northern border of Kucha.
At that time, there was a Daoist master in Wensu who possessed divine eloquence and brilliant talent, renowned throughout many lands. He struck the king’s drum with his own hand and made this vow:
"Should anyone defeat me in debate, I shall behead myself as an apology."
Once Kumārajīva arrived, he examined [the opponent] with two principles; the latter immediately became bewildered and lost his composure, bowing his head in submission and taking refuge.
Thereupon, his fame filled the region east of the Pamirs, and his reputation spread beyond the Yellow River.
The King of Kucha went in person to Wensu to welcome Kumārajīva back to his kingdom. There he extensively expounded various sūtras; those from all directions revered him, and none could oppose him.

At that time, there was a princess who had become a nun, named Ajita (阿竭耶末帝). She had read widely across the various sūtras and possessed a particularly profound mastery of the essentials of dhyāna, claiming she had already realized the second fruit of the path.
Filled with joy upon hearing the Dharma, he then organized a grand assembly and requested Kumārajīva to expound the profound depths of the *Vaipulya* sūtras.

Kumārajīva analyzed and elucidated how "all dharmas are empty and devoid of self," and distinguished that the "aggregates and elements are merely provisional designations and lack substantial reality."
At that time, none among those present in the assembly failed to feel profound grief and lamentation, regretting that their awakening had come so late.
When he reached the age of twenty, he received the full precepts in the royal palace and studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under Vimalākṣa.
After a short while, Kumārajīva’s mother took her leave to travel to India, saying to the King of Kucha, Baima (Bai Chun):
"Your kingdom will soon decline; I shall depart.
Upon arriving in India, she advanced in her practice and attained the third fruit of the path.

As she was about to depart, Kumārajīva’s mother said to him, “The profound teachings of the Vaipulya sutras should be extensively propagated in the Land of the Great Tang; it is solely through your power that they shall be transmitted to the Eastern Lands.”
"It will bring no benefit to yourself; what can be done about that?
Kumārajīva replied, "The way of a Great Being is to benefit others while forgetting one's own body."
"If I can ensure that the Great Transformation spreads and awakens the ignorant masses, I shall have no regrets even if my body must endure the suffering of the cauldrons and furnaces.
Thereupon, he remained in Kucha and stayed at the New Temple.
Later, within the ruins of an old palace beside the monastery, he first obtained the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Fàngguāng jīng*).

As he began to open and read it, a māra came and obscured the text so that he saw only blank pages. Kumārajīva recognized this as the work of a māra and his resolve became even firmer; when the māra departed, the characters reappeared, and he continued to study and recite them.
Again, he heard a voice from the air saying, "You are a wise man; why do you need to read this?
Kumārajīva replied:
"You are but a minor Māra; you should depart at once. My mind is like the earth, and it cannot be turned.
He remained there for two years, extensively reciting Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras until he thoroughly penetrated their secret mysteries.
The King of Kucha had a golden lion throne constructed for him and spread it with brocade cushions from Da Qin, commanding Kumārajīva to ascend it and preach the Dharma.
Kumārajīva said, "My teacher has not yet realized the Mahāyāna; I wish to go there in person to convert him by example, so I cannot remain here."
Before long, the Great Master Pāṇḍubhadra arrived from no great distance away.
The King said, "Great Master, how is it that you have deigned to come so far to visit me? Pāṇḍubhadra replied:

"First, I heard that the disciples have attained a realization beyond the ordinary; second, I heard that Your Majesty extensively praises the Buddha-way. For these reasons, I have braved hardships and dangers to journey from afar to this divine land."

When Kumārajīva obtained his master’s arrival, he rejoiced that his original aspiration had been fulfilled. He then preached the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Virtuous Woman* (*Guṇavatī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*) for him; as it extensively clarifies the emptiness and conventionality of causes and conditions—topics they both previously did not believe—he preached it first.
The Master said to Kumārajīva,
"What extraordinary features do you perceive in the Mahāyāna that you wish to hold it in such high esteem?
Kumārajīva replied:
“The Mahāyāna is profound and pure, clarifying that ‘all phenomena are empty,’ whereas the Hīnayāna is narrow and biased, rife with omissions and errors.
The Master said:
“Your claim that everything is empty is truly terrifying; how can you abandon existing phenomena while craving emptiness?”

Once, there was a madman who had a weaver weave thread, commanding it to be made extremely fine and excellent. The weaver applied himself with great care until the thread was as fine as a mote of dust; yet the madman still complained that it was too coarse. The weaver, filled with great indignation, pointed to the empty air and said, "This is the fine thread."
The madman asked, "Why do you not see it?
The Master said:
"This thread is extremely fine; even I, a master craftsman, cannot see it, let alone others.
The madman was greatly delighted and handed it over to the weaver.
The Master also imitated this, and both received rewards from the Emperor, yet in reality they possessed nothing.
"Your 'empty dharma' is also like this," [the Emperor said].
Kumārajīva then proceeded to present a series of analogies, engaging in a rigorous and exhaustive debate for over a month before the Emperor finally came to believe and accept his words.
The Master sighed and said,
"That I was unable to reach [the truth] myself, yet instead inspired his resolve— this is now proven.
Thereupon, he paid homage to Kumārajīva as his teacher and said:
"The Upādhyāya is my teacher of the Mahāyāna, while I am the Upādhyāya’s teacher of the Hīnayāna.

Throughout the various kingdoms of the Western Regions, all were humbled by Kumārajīva’s divine brilliance; whenever he gave a lecture, the kings would all kneel long at the side of his seat and have Kumārajīva step upon them to ascend, showing him such high esteem.

Since Kumārajīva’s Way had spread throughout the Western Regions and his fame had reached the eastern lands, at that time Fu Jian—who had usurped the title of ruler in Guanzhong—received envoys from the King of the Frontier State of Foreign Nations and the younger brother of the King of Kucha.
They both came to pay court to Fu Jian; Jian received them in audience, and the two kings said to him:
"The Western Regions produce many rare and precious things; we request that you dispatch troops to bring them under control so that they may submit to our rule."
In the first month of the year Dingchou, the thirteenth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, the Grand Astrologer submitted a memorial, saying:
"A star has appeared in the celestial division corresponding to foreign lands; there shall be a man of great virtue and wisdom who enters to assist the Middle Kingdom."
Fu Jian said, "I have heard that there is Kumārajīva in the Western Regions and the śramaṇa Shi Dao’an in Xiangyang; could it not be one of these two?
He immediately dispatched envoys to seek them out.
In the second month of the seventeenth year, King Shanshan and King Qianbu again petitioned Yao Xian with earnest entreaties to dispatch troops for a western expedition.

In the ninth month of the eighteenth year, Yao Xian sent General of the Light Cavalry Lü Guang and General Who Crosses Rivers Jiang Fei, leading King Qianbu, the King of Che-shi, and others, with an army of seventy thousand to campaign westward against the kingdoms of Kucha, Uḍḍiyāna, and other states.
As they were about to depart, Fu Jian saw Kālaya off at the Jianzhang Palace and said to him:
"The sovereign and his ministers respond to Heaven in their governance; they take loving the common people as their fundamental principle. How could they covet its territory and wage war against it?"
"This is precisely because of those who cherish the Way.

I have heard that in the Western Regions there is Kumārajīva, who profoundly understands the characteristics of dharmas and is well-versed in the principles of yin and yang; he is a master for later scholars, and I long for him greatly."
"The wise and sagacious are the great treasure of a nation; if you conquer Kucha, you must immediately dispatch a messenger on horseback to send for Kumārajīva.
Before King Guṅga’s army had even arrived, Kumārajīva said to the King of Kucha, Bai Chun:
"The destiny of your kingdom is declining; there shall surely be a powerful enemy."
"A man from beneath the sun comes from the east; you should receive him with reverence and not oppose his advance.
But Xuan did not follow this advice and went to battle. Gao Guang subsequently defeated Kucha, killed Xuan, and installed Xuan’s younger brother, Zhen, as the ruler.

After Yao Xing had captured Kumārajīva, he could not yet fathom the depth of his wisdom and capacity; seeing that the master was still young in years, he treated him as an ordinary man and playfully forced him to marry the daughter of the King of Kucha. Kumārajīva refused and would not accept her, his refusal being most earnest and poignant.
Faguang said, "The integrity of a Daoist does not exceed that of my late father; how can you so firmly decline?
He then gave him strong wine and confined them both in a sealed room.
When Kumārajīva was driven to such extremes, he ultimately maintained his integrity.
Some ordered him to ride an ox or mount a vicious horse, intending to cause him to fall;
however, Kumārajīva always maintained patience and showed no sign of distress, leaving Guṇabhadra ashamed and bringing the matter to an end.
As they were returning on the road, Fo Guang halted the army at the foot of a mountain; once the officers and soldiers had rested, Shi said, "We must not remain here;
we will surely face disaster. We should move the army to the ridge above."
Faguang did not accept [the invitation].
That night, it indeed rained heavily; a sudden flood surged forth, with the water reaching several zhang in depth and thousands of people perishing. Only then did Faguang secretly marvel at this.
Kumārajīva said to Guṇabhadra, "This is a place of misfortune and ruin; it is not fitting to linger here.
Inferring from the movements of fate and calculating the numbers, you should speak of returning home quickly; along the way, there will surely be a blessed land where you may dwell."

Foguang followed this advice and reached Liangzhou, where he heard that Fu Jian had already been killed by Yao Chang. Foguang’s three armies donned white mourning garments and wailed loudly south of the city; thereupon, they assumed a title outside the pass and styled their era Taian.
In the first month of the first year of the Tai’an era, a great wind arose in Guzang. Kumārajīva said:
"This is an inauspicious wind; there will surely be treachery and rebellion, yet it shall settle of its own accord without the need for effort."
Shortly thereafter, Liang Qian and Peng Huang rebelled in succession, but both were soon exterminated.

In the second year of the Guanglong era, Juqu Nancheng, a Hu leader of the Lu-shui tribe from Lin-song in Zhangye, along with his younger cousin Juqu Mengxun, rose in rebellion. They deposed Duan Ye, the Governor of Jiankang, as their sovereign. Emperor Guang dispatched his younger son, Crown Prince Chuan, the Governor of Qingzhou and Duke of Taiyuan, leading fifty thousand troops to suppress them.

At that time, the public discourse claimed that Kumārajīva’s followers were merely a motley crowd, whereas Zhu Fashou possessed a formidable reputation and his power would surely ensure a total victory.
Daoguang consulted Kumārajīva about this,
and Kumārajīva said, "Observing this course of action, I see no benefit in it."
Shortly thereafter, Fu Jian suffered a defeat at Heli.
Soon after, Guo Xing incited a rebellion; Jian abandoned his main army and fled on light chariots, only to be defeated again by Xing, escaping with his life alone.
Zhang Zi, the Director of the Imperial Library under Emperor Guang, was refined and elegant in his literary style; Guang held him in high esteem.
When Zhang fell ill, Guang extensively sought means for his medical treatment. A foreign monk named Luocha declared, "I can cure Zhang's illness."
Guangxi bestowed upon him very generous gifts.
Kumārajīva, knowing that Xun Cha was deceitful, told Sengzhi:
"Xun Cha cannot accomplish this; it would only serve to increase our needless expenses. Although the workings of the unseen realm are hidden, they can be tested through practical matters."

He then had a rope made by tying together threads of five colors; this was burned to ash and cast into water. If the ashes emerged from the water and reformed into a rope, the illness could not be cured.
In a short while, the heap of ashes floated up and returned to the original form of the rope.
Although he treated him again, it was without effect, and after a few days, Sengzhi passed away.
Shortly thereafter, Senglue also died, and his son Sengshao succeeded him on the throne.
A few days later, Sun Chuan, the younger son of Sun Guang, murdered Sun Shao and established himself as ruler, styling his era Yuan Xianning.

In the second year of Xianning, a pig gave birth to offspring with three heads on one body; a dragon emerged from the well in the eastern corridor and coiled itself before the palace hall, only to vanish by dawn. Sun Chuan took this to be an auspicious omen and renamed the main hall the Longxiang Hall (Dragon Soaring Hall).
Suddenly, a black dragon ascended at the gate of the Jiugong Palace in Dangyang; consequently, the name of the Jiugong Gate was changed to Longxing Gate (Dragon Ascension Gate).
Kumārajīva memorialized, saying:
"Recently, a hidden dragon has gone out on a tour, and a boar-demon has manifested its anomaly."

Dragons belong to the Yin category; they appear and disappear according to fixed seasons. That they are now seen repeatedly constitutes an omen of calamity; there must surely be a rebellion of subordinates plotting against their superiors. You ought to restrain yourself and cultivate virtue to respond to this celestial warning.
Zuan did not accept this.
While playing a board game with Kumārajīva, he killed one of the pieces and said,
"I am chopping off the head of that barbarian slave."
Kumārajīva said,
"If you cannot chop off the head of the barbarian slave, the barbarian slave will chop off your head.
These words were full of meaning, yet Sengzuǎn ultimately did not realize it.

Guang’s younger brother Bao had a son named Chao, whose childhood name was Hunu; later, Chao indeed killed Zuan, beheaded him, and established his elder brother Long as the ruler, whereupon people of the time finally verified the words of Kumārajīva.

Kumārajīva resided in Liangzhou for many years; since Lü Guang and his son did not propagate the Way, he retained his profound understanding without being able to spread its transformative teachings. By the time Fu Jian had already passed away, they never met.

When Yao Chang usurped power over Guanzhong, he too admired Shi’s lofty reputation and extended a sincere invitation for him to come. However, because the Lü brothers were aware that Shi possessed many strategic insights and feared he might devise schemes for Yao, they refused to allow him to enter the east.
Upon the death of Yao Chang, his son Yao Xing succeeded him to the throne and again sent envoys to invite [Kumārajīva].

In the third month of the third year of Hongshi, a tree with interlaced branches grew in the expansive courtyard, and the leeks in the Xiaoyao Garden transformed into fragrant herbs; these were regarded as auspicious omens, leading to the belief that a man of wisdom was destined to enter [the capital].
In the fifth month, Yao Xing dispatched Shiduo, Duke of Longxi, to campaign westward against Lü Long; Long’s army was decisively defeated.

In the ninth month, Long submitted a memorial of surrender, finally permitting the welcome of Kumārajīva into Guanzhong. On the twentieth day of the twelfth month of that year, he arrived in Chang’an.
Xing treated him with the etiquette due to a National Preceptor and showed him great favor and honor.
When they conversed face to face, they would remain together until the end of the day; when investigating subtle mysteries to their ultimate limit, they would do so for years without weariness.

Since the Great Dharma was first transmitted to the East during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, and passing through the Wei and Jin dynasties, the number of sūtras and śāstras gradually increased; yet, among those translated by Lokakṣema, Dharmarakṣa, and others, many were hindered by archaic phrasing and interpretive schemata.
Xing had attained a profound understanding of the Three Jewels since his youth and was resolute in his commitment to lecturing and assembling commentaries.
Once Kumārajīva arrived, Xing invited him to the Ximing Pavilion and the Xiaoyao Garden to translate various scriptures.

Since Kumārajīva had memorized and recited most [of the scriptures], there was nothing he did not master; moreover, he was proficient in the Chinese language, and his phonetic translations were fluent and elegant.

Upon examining the older translations, he found that their meanings were frequently erroneous and deviant, all because the earlier translators had missed the essential intent and failed to correspond with the Sanskrit originals.

Thereupon Yao Xing dispatched over eight hundred people, including the śramaṇas Sengqie, Sengqian, Faqin, Daoliu, Daoheng, Daobiao, Sengrui, and Sengzhao, to consult with and receive the instructions of Kumārajīva, and to have him retranslate the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Kumārajīva held the Sanskrit manuscript while Xuánzàng held the old translation; as they compared them against one another, those new passages that differed from the old were found to be perfect in meaning and thorough in principle. The assembly was deeply impressed and submissive, all of whom rejoiced in and praised them.

Xing [observed] that the Buddha-way is profound and subtle, its practice being solely goodness; he believed it to be the excellent ford for escaping suffering and the grand principle for governing the world.

Therefore, he applied his intent to the Nine Classics and let his mind roam through the Twelve Divisions of the Canon, subsequently composing the *Tongsanshi lun* (Treatise on the Three Times) to exhort and demonstrate the law of cause and effect. From the princes and dukes downward, all revered and praised his style.
The General of the Household, Duke of Changshan, Xian, and the General of the Left Army, Marquis of Ancheng, Song,
both possessed profound faith in the principle of causes and conditions. They repeatedly invited Kumārajīva to the Great Monastery in Chang’an to lecture on newly translated sutras,
subsequently producing the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra in Eight Thousand Lines*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The Vimalakīrti, the Saṃghāṭa, the Śūraṅgama, the Lokasthiti, the Buddhapiṭaka,
the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, the Śāsanāntima, the Acaryācintya, the Kāmanindā, the Īśvararāja, and the Pratītyasamutpādadarśana.
*The Shorter Sukhāvatīvyūha*, *The New Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*, *The Dhyāna Sūtra*, *The Essentials of Dhyāna*,
*The Commentary on the Essentials of Dhyāna*, *Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood*,
*Maitreya’s Descent to Rebirth*, *The Ten Recitations Vinaya*, *The Ten Recitations Prātimokṣa*, *The Bodhi...*
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, its commentary (*Śāstra*), the *Tattvasiddhi*, the *Daśabhūmika*, the *Madhyamaka*,
the *Śata-śāstra*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*— altogether totaling more than three hundred fascicles.
He fully elucidated the divine source and brought forth its profound subtleties.
At that time, scholars from all quarters gathered from ten thousand li away; his magnificent achievements became enduring and vast, and even today they are universally revered.

Shi Daosheng of Longguang Temple possessed an insight so subtle it reached the profound; his metaphysical constructions transcended the literal text. Fearing constantly that his words might deviate from the truth, he traveled to Guanzhong to seek resolution.

Shi Huiyuan of Mount Lu had mastered the various scriptures and served as a pillar for the surviving teachings. Yet, as the time since the Sage had long passed, points of doubt remained unresolved; he therefore sealed his inquiries and consulted Kumārajīva, as recorded in the *Biography of Huiyuan*.
Initially, the śramaṇa Sengrui was of exceptionally high talent and insight.
He frequently accompanied Kumārajīva as he transcribed texts.
Kumārajīva often discussed the literary styles of the Western Regions with Sengrui, deliberating upon their similarities and differences, saying:
"The customs of the kingdom of India place great importance on literary composition. Regarding the tonal patterns and rhythmic cadences, it is considered excellent when they can be set to strings.

Whenever one has an audience with a king, there must be praise for his virtues; as for the ritual of seeing the Buddha, the chanting of hymns is held in high esteem. The verses and stanzas within the sutras all follow this model."
To merely transcribe the Sanskrit into the Qin (Chinese) language is to lose its elegance and refinement.
Although the general meaning may be captured, the literary style is profoundly alienated.
It is like chewing food and giving it to others; not only is the flavor lost, but it causes one to vomit.
Kumārajīva once composed a verse to present to the śramaṇa Fǎhuó, saying:
"The mountain of mind nurtures brilliant virtue, its fragrance wafting for ten thousand yojanas.
Like a grieving crane atop a solitary paulownia tree, its pure sound penetrates the nine heavens."
In total, there were ten verses; the phrasing and metaphors were all of this nature.
Kumārajīva had always been fond of the Mahāyāna and was intent on its propagation, often sighing:
"If I were to take up my pen and compose a Mahāyāna *Abhidharma*, it would not be comparable to that of Kātyāyanīputra."
"Now that I am in the land of Qin, those with deep understanding are few; having had my wings broken here, what more could I possibly discuss?
Thereupon, he desisted in sorrow.
He composed only two fascicles of the *Shixiang lun* (Treatise on True Reality) for Yao Xing, as well as a commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
When he spoke, his words formed elegant compositions without the need for deletion or revision; his phrasing and metaphors were graceful and subtle, all of them profound and mysterious.
Kumārajīva was a man of brilliant and penetrating spirit, standing aloof and towering above his peers; in his ability to respond to circumstances and grasp their essence, few could equal him.
He was sincere by nature, benevolent and generous, and took universal love as his guiding principle; he humbled himself to provide excellent guidance, never tiring throughout the day.

Lord Yao often said to Kumārajīva, "The Great Master’s intelligence and transcendent realization are peerless in the world. If you were to pass away one day, how could we allow the lineage of the Dharma to remain without an heir?"
He then compelled her to accept ten female entertainers.
From that time forward, she no longer resided in the monastic quarters but established a separate residence for herself, which was provided with abundant supplies.
Whenever he gave a discourse, he would always first speak of an analogy, such as: "A lotus flower grows from foul mud; one should take only the lotus flower and not the foul mud."

"Initially, when Kumārajīva was in Kucha, he received the Vinaya from the Dharma Master Vimalākṣa. Later, when Vimalākṣa entered Guanzhong, Kumārajīva heard of his arrival and was filled with joy; he paid him the utmost respect and observed all the rites of a disciple."
Vimalākṣa was unaware that he had been coerced, and so he asked Kumārajīva:
"You have great karmic ties with the land of Han; how many disciples have you who have received the Dharma from you?"
Kumārajīva replied:

"In the land of Han, the sūtras and vinayas are not yet complete; most of the new sūtras and various śāstras have been transmitted by me. My three thousand disciples all receive the Dharma from me, yet because my accumulated karmic obstructions are deep, I do not accept formal instruction from a teacher."
Furthermore, while the bhikṣu Beidu was in Pengcheng, he heard that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an and sighed, saying:

“I have been separated from this youth for over three hundred years; our paths are now so distant that we have no expectation of meeting again in this life, and I can only hope to encounter him in a future existence.”

Before Kumārajīva had completed the day, he felt his four elements were somewhat failing him; he then recited the Threefold Divine Incantation from his own mouth and instructed his foreign disciples to chant it to save himself. Before he could exert much effort, he felt his condition grow increasingly critical.
Thereupon, despite his failing strength, he took leave of the assembly of monks, saying:
"We have met because of the Dharma, yet I have not yet fully expressed my heart's intent. As we are about to part for future lives, what words can suffice to express my sorrow?"

Considering myself ignorant and dull-witted, I have mistakenly been charged with the task of transmitting and translating; in total, I have produced over three hundred fascicles of sutras and śāstras. Only for the single work, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, have I not yet managed to prune away redundancies, as I have preserved its original intent without any deviation or error.
"I vow that whatever I have proclaimed and translated shall be transmitted to future generations and universally propagated by all.
Now, before this assembly, I make this sincere and truthful oath: if what I have transmitted is free from error, may my tongue not be scorched or consumed after my self-immolation."
He passed away in Chang’an on the twentieth day of the eighth month in the eleventh year of the Hongshi era of the pseudo-Qin dynasty; this was the fifth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty.
He was cremated according to foreign rites in the Xiaoyao Garden; when the firewood was consumed and his body reduced to ashes, only his tongue remained unburnt.
Later, foreign śramaṇas arrived and said,
"Not even one-tenth of what Kumārajīva was familiar with has been brought out.
Initially, Kumārajīva’s name was simply Kumārajīva.
Names given by foreigners are generally based on those of their parents.
Kumārajīva’s father was named Kujūla-Kaśyapa and his mother’s name was Jīvā; therefore, his name was formed by combining elements from both.

However, regarding the year of Kumārajīva’s death, various records differ: some say the seventh year of Hongshi, some the eighth, and others the eleventh. Examining these dates, it appears that the characters for "seven" and "eleven" may have been subject to scribal error.
Yet, within the records of translated scriptures and biographies, there is still mention of a single year [of activity].
Fearing that this might be confused with the accounts of the three other masters, I have provided no means to correct it.
2. Puṇyatāra (弗若多羅): There were two Puṇyatāras; here [in Chinese] it is translated as "Flower of Merit" (功德華). He was a native of Kaśmīra.

He left home to become a monk at a young age and was renowned for his observance of the precepts. He was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and specialized in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, becoming a preeminent master among foreign teachers; people of the time all claimed that he had attained the fruits of sainthood.
During the Hongshi era of the spurious Qin dynasty, he took up his staff and entered the Guanzhong region.
Yao Xing, the ruler of Qin, treated him with the etiquette due to a guest of highest honor.
Kumārajīva also held him in high esteem for his monastic discipline, honoring and respecting him deeply.
Previously, although the Sūtras had been transmitted, the Vinaya-piṭaka had not yet been expounded. Hearing that Guṇavarman was well-versed in this collection, everyone felt a deep longing for him.

On the seventeenth day of the tenth month in the sixth year of the Hongshi era of the pseudo-Qin dynasty, several hundred monks specializing in the study of the Dharma gathered at Zhong Temple in Chang’an. They invited Guṇavarman to recite the Sanskrit original of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which Kumārajīva then translated into the literary language of the Jin.
Having achieved two-thirds of his task, Tāra fell ill and suddenly passed away.
As his great undertaking remained unfinished and the master craftsman had perished, the depth of the assembly’s grief and regret surpassed ordinary sorrow.
3. Dharmaruci. Dharmaruci, meaning "Dharma-joy" in this language, was a native of the Western Regions.
Having left his home to enter the path, he became particularly renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya Piṭaka. In the autumn of the seventh year of Hongshi, he arrived in Guanzhong.
Initially, when Puṇyatāra had recited the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, he passed away before it was completed.

When Shi Huiyuan of Mount Lu heard that Saṃghadeva was well-versed in the Vinaya and hoped to obtain the complete corpus of the disciplinary texts, he sent a letter to establish friendly relations, saying:
"The rise of the Buddha's teachings first occurred in the Central Kingdom; since their dissemination here, more than four hundred years have passed."
As for the virtuous standards of the śramaṇas, there are particularly many deficiencies.
Recently, the Western monk Puṇyatāra, a native of Kaśmīra,
was highly proficient in reciting the Sanskrit version of the *Daśabhāṇavāra*.
There was the Dharma Master Kumārajīva, a man of versatile talent and vast erudition, who served as the translator for this work.

Within the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when the text had barely surpassed the halfway mark, Tārā died prematurely; thus the project was suspended mid-course, and the great undertaking could not be brought to completion. My regret and lamentation over this are truly profound. Hearing that you, O Virtuous One, have carried this scripture with you, I am greatly delighted by such a meeting. Is it not the case that the arrival of such a providential destiny is something that transcends mere human effort?
I conceive that propagating the Way for the sake of all beings involves acting in response to the times; when one is called upon, there must be no stinginess in one's heart.

If you can act as a follower of the Vinaya studies to complete this scriptural text, thereby revealing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and cleansing the ears and eyes of others, ensuring that those who have only recently entered the path do not lose the unsurpassed ferry, and causing those who harbor superior aspirations to become ever more radiant like the sun and moon—then your wisdom will be profound and your virtue substantial, and both humans and spirits will be moved by it in common.
"I hope you will deign to consider this and not fail to fulfill our previous intentions;
all that the various practitioners possess is hereby submitted.
Once Kumārajīva had received the letter from Huiyuan and Yao Xing’s earnest invitation, he completed the joint translation of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* with him.
After conducting detailed research and thorough examination, the regulations were carefully reviewed and finalized; yet Kumārajīva still regretted that the text was too verbose and not yet perfected.
Shortly thereafter, Kumārajīva passed away, and the work could not be further edited.
While Dharmaruci resided at the Great Monastery in Chang’an, Huìguān wished to invite him to the capital, to which Dharmaruci replied:
"That land has both people and the Dharma sufficient to benefit the world; I shall proceed further to places where there is no teaching of the Vinaya.
Thereupon, he traveled and transformed others in other regions, and it was not known where he passed away.
Some say he ended his life in the land of Liang, but this is not certain.
4. Vimalākṣa: Vimalākṣa (卑摩羅叉) means "Stainless Eye" (無垢眼) in Chinese; he was a native of Kaśmīra.
Shen Jing was a man of great resolve and vigor; he left the household life to tread the Way, achieving his purpose through rigorous discipline.

Previously residing in Kucha, he propagated and expounded the Vinaya-piṭaka, drawing scholars from all quarters who vied with one another to become his disciples; Kumārajīva was among those present at that time.
When Kucha fell to the enemy, he fled to those regions.

Shortly thereafter, hearing that Kumārajīva was extensively propagating the *Sūtra-piṭaka* in Chang’an and wishing further to ensure that the supreme categories of the *Vinaya* would also reach the eastern lands, he took up his staff and traveled across the shifting sands. Braving the perils, he entered the east and arrived in Guanzhong in the eighth year of the Hongshi era of the Later Qin. Kumārajīva received him with the reverence due to a teacher, and Saṃghabhūti likewise rejoiced at this long-awaited encounter.
When Kumārajīva passed away, Faxu traveled to the region east of the Guanzhong area, staying at Shijian Temple in Shouchun.
There, a multitude of monks specializing in the Vinaya gathered, and he extensively expounded upon the monastic discipline.

The version of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* translated by Kumārajīva consists of fifty-eight fascicles; its final section, which elucidates the methods for receiving the precepts as well as various matters concerning the accomplishment of wholesome dharmas, is named the *Śubhabhāṇavāra* (Good Recitation) according to its essential meaning.

Later, Saṃghabhadra took it to Shijian (Stone Gully) and divided it into sixty-one fascicles; he changed the title of the final recitation to the *Vinaya-saṃgīti*, and thus both names still exist today.
Shortly thereafter, he traveled south to Jiangling and sat in summer retreat at Xin Temple, where he lectured on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Having mastered the Chinese language and being exceptionally adept at conveying the meaning, he extensively expounded upon the wondrous essence of "non-action" (*anabhisamskāra*) during that time. Those who analyzed the text to seek its principles gathered like a forest, and those who understood the clear rules and prohibitions were likewise numerous; that the Vinaya-piṭaka was so widely propagated was due to the efforts of Daocha.

Hui guan of Daochang deeply encompassed the essential tenets [of the Vinaya]; he recorded the regulations for internal prohibitions according to their gravity and compiled them into two fascicles, which he sent back to the capital. Monks and nuns studied them with diligence, vying with one another to copy them;

at that time, those who heard of it had a proverb: "The vulgar speech of Vimalākṣa was skillfully recorded by Hui guan; the people of the capital transcribed it so fervently that paper became as precious as jade."
His teachings still circulate in the world today as a source of Dharma for future generations.

Faying also cherished virtue and loved seclusion; he abandoned clamor and distanced himself from the mundane. In the winter of that year, he returned once more to Shijian in Shouchun and passed away at the temple at the age of seventy-seven.
Facha’s eyes were blue, so his contemporaries also called him the "Blue-Eyed Vinaya Master.
(5) Buddhayaśas: Buddhayaśas, translated as "Awakened Brilliance," was a native of Kaśmīra of Brahmin descent; in his youth, he had served the non-Buddhist heretics.

There was a śramaṇa who begged from his house; his father became enraged and sent someone to beat him. Consequently, the father’s hands and feet became cramped and withered, so that he could no longer walk or move.
He then consulted a sorcerer, who replied, "This is because you have offended a worthy man; it is the work of ghosts and spirits.

He immediately invited this śramaṇa to perform a sincere repentance on his behalf, and after several days, he was cured. Consequently, he caused Yaśas to leave the household life as the śramaṇa’s disciple; at that time, Yaśas was thirteen years old.

He was once traveling a long distance with his teacher when they encountered a tiger in the wilderness. As the teacher wished to flee and avoid it, Yaśas said, "This tiger has already eaten its fill; it will certainly not harm anyone."
Shortly thereafter, the tiger departed; as he proceeded forward, he indeed saw the remains left behind, which the Master perceived with a sense of secret wonder.
By the time he was fifteen years old, he could recite two to three ten-thousand-word passages of scripture each day.

At the monastery where he resided, he constantly went out for alms, neglecting his recitation and study; a certain arhat, valuing his intelligence and acuity, would regularly beg for food to provide for him.
By the age of nineteen, he had recited several million words from the Mahayana and Hinayana sutras.

However, his character was simple and haughty; he was somewhat self-important regarding his knowledge and views, claiming that few were capable of being his teachers. Consequently, he was not held in high esteem by the monastics; yet, as his deportment was graceful and he was skilled in conversation and laughter, those who saw him forgot their deep resentment.
When he reached the age for receiving full ordination, there was no one to preside over the ceremony; consequently, even at the age when he should have stood as a monk, he remained a śrāmaṇera.
He then studied the various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) under his maternal uncle and practiced extensively in worldly arts and techniques.
At the age of twenty-seven, he finally received full ordination.
He made the constant practice of recitation his primary task, never letting the scriptures leave his hands.
Whenever he sat upright to contemplate the meaning of the teachings, he would say that he was unaware of time passing by in vain; such was his single-minded devotion.
Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Kāśmira (Shale). The king was unwell and convened an assembly of three thousand monks, of whom Guṇavṛddha (Ye-she) was one.

At that time, the crown prince Dharmaputra—which means "Son of the Dharma"—observed that Guṇavṛddha’s appearance and attire were dignified and elegant, and asked where he had come from. Guṇavṛddha replied with such clarity and eloquence that the prince was delighted; he subsequently invited him to remain within the palace to receive offerings, treating him with great honor and generosity.
Kumārajīva arrived later and again studied under Guṇavarman, who held him in the highest esteem.
When Kumārajīva returned to Kucha with his mother, Guṇavarman remained behind.

Shortly thereafter, the king passed away and the crown prince ascended the throne. At that time, Fu Jian dispatched Lü Guang to campaign westward against Kucha; as the King of Kucha was in urgent distress, he sought military aid from the King of Śākala. The King of Śākala personally led his troops to his rescue, leaving Guṇavarman behind to assist the prince and entrust him with the affairs of state.
Before the relief army had arrived, Kucha was already defeated. When the king returned, he related in detail how Kumārajīva had been captured by Gao; thereupon Sengque sighed and said:
"Although I have known Kumārajīva for a long time, we have not yet fully shared our inner thoughts. Now that he has suddenly been taken captive, when shall we meet again?"
After staying for more than ten years, he traveled east to Kucha, where his propagation of the Dharma flourished greatly.

At that time, Kumārajīva was in Guzang and sent a messenger to invite him; as he prepared to set out with provisions, the people of the country detained him, and he remained there for another year or so.
Later, he said to his disciples:
"I wish to seek out Kumārajīva; you may prepare secretly and set out at night, ensuring that no one knows.
His disciples replied:
"Fearing that they will catch up tomorrow, I shall not avoid returning once more.

Yaśas then took a bowl of clear water, cast medicine into it, and recited several dozen words of incantation; he then had his disciples wash their feet and immediately set out under the cover of night.
At dawn, he had traveled several hundred li.
He asked his disciples,
"What have you perceived?"
He replied, "I have heard only the sound of a gale, and tears have flowed from my eyes.
Yaśas then gave him consecrated water to wash his feet, and he rested.
At dawn the next day, the people of the country pursued him, but having already gained several hundred li, they could not catch up.

When they reached Guzang, Kumārajīva had already entered Chang’an; hearing that Yao Xing was pressuring him with concubines and female attendants and urging him toward unrighteous acts, he sighed and said, “Kumārajīva is like fine cotton;
how can one allow it to enter a thicket of thorns?”
When Kumārajīva heard that [Buddhayaśas] had arrived in Guzang, he urged Yao Xing to welcome him, but Xing did not yet accept the request.
Shortly thereafter, Xing ordered Kumārajīva to translate the *piṭaka* (scriptural treasury). Kumārajīva said:

"In propagating the Dharma teachings, one should ensure that both the phrasing and the meaning are perfectly integrated. Although I, a poor monk, can recite the texts, I have not yet mastered their underlying principles. Only Buddhayaśas has a profound understanding of their subtle depths; he is currently in Guzang. I pray that you issue an edict to summon him. Let there be three detailed examinations for every single word before setting pen to paper, so that these subtle words do not fall into ruin and may be trusted for a thousand years."
Xing followed his advice and immediately dispatched a messenger to invite him, offering him generous gifts; yet [the monk] would not accept any of them and said with a smile:

"Since Your Excellency’s gracious decree has been issued, I ought indeed to set out at once. However, as the donor treats scholars so generously, were my treatment to be like that accorded to Kumārajīva, then I would not dare to accept your command."

The messenger returned and recounted everything in detail. Daoxing sighed in admiration of his extreme prudence and sent messengers again with earnest exhortations; only then did he proceed to Chang’an.

Daoxing went out in person to welcome and inquire after him, establishing a new academy for him within the Xiaoyao Garden and providing the four types of offerings; yet [Dao’an] would not accept them, going instead on alms rounds at the appropriate time and taking only a single meal.
At that time, Kumārajīva was translating the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
For over a month, he remained hesitant and in doubt, having not yet set pen to paper.

Once Guṇabhadra arrived, they consulted together to resolve his difficulties; only then were the words and principles finalized. More than three thousand monastics and laypeople all marveled at how perfectly essential the exposition was.
Śīlabhadra had red whiskers and was well-versed in the *Vibhāṣā*; his contemporaries called him "Red-Whiskered Vibhāṣā.
Since he served as the teacher of Kumārajīva, he was also referred to as the "Great Vibhāṣā."

He provided the four requisites for his support—robes, alms bowls, and bedding—filling three rooms; yet he did not set his heart upon them. Yao Xing sold these goods and used the proceeds to construct a monastery south of the city.

Previously, Yaśas had recited the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Yao Shuang, the Acting Commandant for the Supervision of Slaves, requested that he produce it; however, Yao Xing suspected there might be omissions or errors. He therefore invited Yaśas to recite five ten-thousand-word medicinal prescriptions from the Qiang records. After two days, they compared the text against the original manuscript and found not a single character was mistaken. The assembly marveled at his prodigious memory.
In the twelfth year of the Hongshi era, he translated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* in forty-four fascicles, along with the *Dīrgha-āgama* and other texts.
The Kuchean śramaṇa Zhu Fonian translated them into the Qin language, while Daohan acted as the scribe.

In the fifteenth year, when the assembly was dissolved, Daoxing offered ten thousand bolts of silk and cloth as a religious gift (*dakṣiṇā*) to Guṇabhadra, but he accepted none of it. Daohan and Buddhabhadra each offered one thousand bolts of silk and cloth, and five hundred śramaṇas of renowned virtue all presented him with generous offerings.

Afterwards, Yaśas took his leave and returned to foreign lands; upon reaching Jibin, he obtained one fascicle of the *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* and entrusted it to merchants to transmit to the monks of Liangzhou. His ultimate end was thereafter unknown.

6. Buddhabhadra. Buddhabhadra (six times). Buddhabhadra is translated here as Jue-xian (Awakened Virtue). His original surname was Śākya; he was a native of Kapilavastu and a descendant of King Amṛtodana.
His grandfather was Dharmadeva, which in this language means "Dharma-Heaven. He once engaged in trade in Northern India and subsequently settled there.
His father was Dharmasūrya, which in this language means "Dharma-Sun," who passed away in his youth.
At the age of three, Xian was orphaned and lived with his mother; at five, he lost his mother as well and was raised by his maternal relatives.
His paternal great-uncle, Jūvalī, hearing of his intelligence and feeling pity for his state of being left alone and exposed, welcomed him back and ordained him as a śrāmaṇera.

When he reached the age of seventeen, he was among several fellow students who all took the recitation of scriptures as their vocation; while the rest required a month, Xian would finish his recitation in a single day.
His teacher sighed in admiration and said, "Xian accomplishes in one day what thirty men could do."
Upon receiving full ordination, he applied himself with diligent effort to his practice, extensively studying the various scriptures and attaining mastery in many areas.

From his youth, he was renowned for his expertise in meditation and the Vinaya. He frequently traveled together with his fellow student Saṃghadatta through Kaśmīra, staying in each other’s company for many years; although Saṃghadatta was humbled by his brilliance and learning, he could not yet fathom the man himself.
Later, while sitting in meditation in a private room with the door closed, he suddenly saw Xian coming and asked in surprise,
"Where have you come from? He replied:
"I shall go briefly to Tuṣita Heaven to pay my respects to Maitreya.
Having spoken these words, he vanished. Upatiṣya knew him to be a holy man, yet he could not fathom his depth.

Later, having repeatedly witnessed the sage's supernatural transformations, he prayed to him with a reverent mind for instruction; only then did he learn that [the sage] had attained the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).

He had always desired to travel abroad to propagate the teachings and observe the customs of various lands. It happened that the Qin monk Zhìyán traveled west to Jibin and, seeing that the assembly of practitioners there was pure and eminent, he looked toward the east with a sigh of regret and said:
"My fellow practitioners here possess the will for the Way, yet they have not encountered a true master; thus, they have no means by which to achieve awakening."
He immediately consulted the assembly of the kingdom as to who was capable of propagating the teachings in the eastern lands.

They all said: "There is one named Buddhabhadra, born in the city of Nagarahāra in India; his family lineage has been hereditary, and for generations they have followed the study of the Way. He left home at the age of childhood and had already mastered the sūtras and śāstras; in his youth, he received instruction from the Great Meditation Master Buddhayaśas."
Previously, while also in Kaśmīra, he said to Yan:
"The one who can uphold and guide the monastic community and propagate the teachings of dhyāna is Buddhabhadra."

As Yan insisted on inviting him to the hardship, Xian was moved by compassion and granted his request; he then left the assembly and took leave of his teacher, packing his provisions and heading east.

He traveled for three years, enduring both winter and summer, and having crossed the Pamir Mountains, his route passed through six kingdoms; the rulers of these lands, admiring his mission of distant propagation, all devoted their hearts to providing him with support and offerings.
Upon reaching Jiaozhi, he boarded a ship and traveled along the coast; as they passed beneath an island, Xian pointed to a mountain and said, "We may stop here."
The ship’s captain said, “Travelers must cherish their time; favorable winds are difficult to encounter, so we cannot stop.

After traveling some two hundred li, the wind suddenly shifted and blew the ship back toward the island. Only then did the people realize his divine power; they all took him as their teacher and followed his every command regarding their progress or halt.
Later, they encountered a favorable wind, and his companions all set sail;
Xian said, "You must not move.
The shipowner then halted, and subsequently those who had set out first were all capsized and destroyed at once.

Later, in the middle of a dark night, he suddenly ordered all the ships to set sail; none were willing to comply, but Bhadra rose up himself to gather in the mooring ropes, and one ship alone departed. Before long, the pirates arrived, and all those who remained were plundered and harmed.

Shortly thereafter, he arrived at Donglai Commandery in Qingzhou and heard that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an; he immediately went there to follow him. Kumārajīva was greatly delighted, and together they discussed the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), elucidating the profound and subtle mysteries, from which [Dao’an] gained much insight and benefit.
Daohui said to Kumārajīva, "The interpretations you provide do not go beyond what others have conceived; how is it that you have attained such a high reputation?
Kumārajīva replied:
"I am merely old, so how could I possibly be capable of delivering an eloquent discourse?
Whenever Kumārajīva encountered points of doubt, he would invariably consult with him to reach a resolution.
At that time, Prince Hong of Qin wished to hear Kumārajīva preach the Dharma; he therefore summoned the assembly of monks and gathered them for a discussion at the Eastern Palace.
Kumārajīva and Buddhabhadra exchanged several rounds of questions and answers;
Kumārajīva asked, "In what way is the Dharma empty?
Buddhabhadra replied:
"Since form is composed of atoms, and form lacks intrinsic nature, form is eternally empty despite its appearance.
He asked again:
"If you have already refuted the emptiness of form by means of the ultimate atom, how then do you refute the atom itself?"
He replied: "Some masters may break down and analyze a single atom, but in my view, that is not so.
He asked again:
"Is this atom permanent? He replied:
"Because of the single atom, the multitude of atoms is empty; because of the multitude of atoms, the single atom is empty."
At that time, Baoyun translated these words but did not understand their meaning; both monastics and laypeople alike claimed that Xuan’s calculation was that atoms are eternal.
On another day, when monks from Chang’an requested a further explanation, Xuan said:
"Now, phenomena do not arise of themselves; they arise because conditions converge."
Because one atom serves as a condition, there are many atoms; yet since the atom lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty.
How then can you say that one atom is not destroyed, being permanent and non-empty?
This is the general purport of the dialogue.

Emperor Yao Xing of the Qin dynasty was single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha-dharma and supported more than three thousand monks; they all frequented the palace and engaged extensively in worldly affairs, yet only Kumārajīva maintained his tranquility and did not conform to the crowd.
Later, he told his disciples:
"Yesterday I saw five ships setting sail together from my native village.
Subsequently, when his disciples spread this report to outsiders, the veteran monks of Guanzhong all considered it a display of eccentricity intended to delude the masses.
Furthermore, while Xian was in Chang’an, he extensively propagated the practice of dhyāna; those from all quarters who delighted in tranquility came to him upon hearing his reputation.

However, as their immersion in the study varied in depth and their realization of the Dharma differed in intensity, there were among them those of corrupt and false character who consequently became deceitful and slippery.

There was a disciple who, due to some slight practice of contemplation, claimed for himself that he had attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin. Before the Venerable One could immediately investigate and question him, rumors spread, leading to widespread slander and accusations that threatened him with unforeseen calamity.

Thereupon, some of the disciples hid their names and departed in secret, while others scaled the walls and fled by night; within half a day, the assembly had dispersed almost entirely, yet Xian remained composed and took no heed of it.
At that time, the senior monks Sengshou, Daoheng, and others said to Xian:
"Even the Buddha did not permit [his disciples] to preach the Dharma they had attained themselves.

Your previous claim that five ships were about to arrive proved false and unsubstantiated; furthermore, your disciples have misled and confused others, giving rise to mutual disagreements. Since this violates the Vinaya and is logically inconsistent with our cohabitation, you should depart at once and must not remain."
Xian said, "My body is like a drifting duckweed; it is very easy for me to go or stay. I only regret that my inner aspirations have not yet been fully realized, which is why I feel such deep sorrow.

Thereupon, he set out together with over forty disciples, including Hui-guan, his spirit and composure remaining serene without the slightest change in expression. Those who recognized his true nature all sighed in lamentation; more than a thousand people, both monastics and laypeople, escorted him.
Upon hearing of his departure, Yao Xing was filled with regret and said to Daoheng:

"The śramaṇa Fotudeng came here in harmony with the Way, intending to proclaim the Bequeathed Teachings. That his words remain unspoken is truly a matter of deep lamentation; how can a single transgression of speech cause ten thousand men to be without a guide?"
Thereupon, he ordered that [Bhadra] be pursued.
Bhadra replied to the messenger, saying:
"I truly acknowledge your gracious command, yet I have not been consulted regarding this order."
Thereupon, leading his companions, he set out under the cover of night, heading south toward Mount Lu.

The śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan had long admired his reputation; hearing of his arrival, he rejoiced as if meeting an old friend. Huiyuan considered that because Daoyuan had been expelled, the fault lay with his disciples. Furthermore, regarding the prophecy of the five ships, it was merely spoken in reference to those of like mind, and thus did not constitute a violation of the Vinaya.

He then dispatched his disciple Tanyong to deliver a letter to the ruler Yao and the monastic community of Guanzhong to resolve the matter of his exclusion; subsequently, Huiyuan requested that various sutras on meditation and Abhidharma be translated.
Xian’s aspiration was to travel for the sake of conversion; he had no desire for personal comfort in his dwelling. After staying there for about a year, he again traveled west to Jiangling.
There he encountered foreign ships arriving; upon inquiry, it turned out they were indeed the five ships from India that he had previously seen.

The commoners and gentry of the surrounding region vied with one another to come and pay their respects; whatever offerings they presented, he accepted none of them. Carrying his alms bowl, he went on his rounds for food, making no distinction between the noble and the lowly.

At that time, Yuan Bao of Chenjun served as the Chief Secretary to the Grand Marshal of Emperor Wu of Song. When Emperor Wu marched south to campaign against Liu Yi, Bao followed the headquarters to Jiangling.
Daoyuan’s disciple Huiguan went to Bao to beg for food; however, Bao had long been one who lacked faith and respect, treating him with great scantiness, so Huiguan took his leave before he was full.
Bao said, "It seems not yet sufficient; please stay for a short while longer. Xian replied:
"The donor’s intention for giving was limited, which is why what has been prepared has already been exhausted," he said.
Baofu immediately called his attendants to bring more rice; when the rice was indeed finished, Baofu felt great shame.
Shortly thereafter, he asked Huiguan,
"What kind of person is this śramaṇa?
Huiguan replied:
"His virtue and capacity are so lofty and remote that they cannot be fathomed by ordinary people.
Bao deeply marveled at this excellence and informed the Grand Marshal (Taishou).
