The Grand Marshal invited him for an audience and revered him with great respect, providing him with the most abundant material support.
Shortly thereafter, the Grand Marshal returned to the capital and invited [Seng]xian to return with him, whereupon he was settled at Daochang Temple.
Sengxian’s deportment was simple and unadorned, differing from the refined customs of the Chinese; yet his aspirations were pure and far-reaching, possessing a profound elegance.
The Dharma Master Sengbi of the capital wrote a letter to the śramaṇa Baolin, saying:
"The Meditation Master of Douchang possesses a truly great mind; he is truly a man of refined elegance in the tradition of the Indian kings and the [Chinese] Wanghe."
Such was the acclaim he received.
Previously, the śramaṇa Zhi Falin had obtained the first portion of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* consisting of thirty-six thousand gāthās in Khotan, but it had not yet been translated or propagated.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, Meng Yi,
the Interior Administrator of Wu Commandery, and Chu Shudu, General of the Right Guard, invited Master Xian to serve as the master translator.
Thereupon, holding the Sanskrit manuscript in his own hand, he translated it at the Daochang Monastery together with more than one hundred people, including the śramaṇas Faye and Huiyan.

He elucidated the meaning of the texts and harmonized the traditions of China and the Western Regions; having masterfully grasped the intent of the sutras, the Huayan Hall still exists at Daochang Monastery today.

Furthermore, regarding the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* obtained by the śramaṇa Faxian in the Western Regions, he again requested Kumārajīva to translate it into the language of Jin; this account is recorded in the *Biography of Faxian*.

The works he produced earlier and later—including the six-fascicle *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Pratipattisādhana-śāstra*—total fifteen sections comprising one hundred and seventeen fascicles; in all of them, he thoroughly investigated their profound purports and exquisitely exhausted the meaning of the texts.
Xian passed away in the sixth year of the Yuanjia era at the age of seventy-one.
7. Dharmakṣema: The seventh [section] concerns Dharmakṣema. He is also called Tanmochan or Tanmochan; these variations likely stem from differences in the transcription of the Sanskrit sound.
He was originally a native of Central India. At the age of six, he lost his father and followed his mother, who made her living by hiring out her labor to weave woolen cloth (*karpāsa*).

He encountered the śramaṇa Dharmayaśas—translated into Chinese as Faming—who was revered by both monastics and laypeople and received abundant offerings. His mother admired him greatly, and thus she took Śīlādharma as her disciple.
At the age of ten, he studied incantations alongside several of his peers; his intelligence surpassed the crowd, and he could recite over ten thousand words of scripture every day.
Initially, he studied the Hīnayāna while also surveying the various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*); his expositions were so precise and eloquent that none could challenge him.
Later, he encountered the White-Headed Meditation Master (Baidou Chanshi) and engaged him in debate. As their respective practices were different, they contended for ten months.

Although Daorong’s challenges arose like a sharp point, the Meditation Master ultimately refused to yield; Daorong was so impressed by his profound reasoning that he said to the master, "Are there any scriptures you might allow me to see?"
The Zen Master then gave him a copy of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* written on tree bark.

Upon reading it, Baoyun was struck with sudden awakening; he felt deep remorse for his former self, realizing that his knowledge had been as limited as that of a frog in a well and that he had long been lost within the Great Way. Thereupon, he assembled the community to repent his transgressions and subsequently devoted himself exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
By the time he was twenty years old, he had recited more than two million words from the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras.

Guṇavarman’s elder brother was skilled at training elephants; while riding one, he killed the white-eared great elephant that the king was mounting. The king was enraged and executed him, issuing a decree:
"Whoever dares to look upon [the corpse] shall have their three clans exterminated."
None of his relatives dared to go there.
Śāṇakavāsin wept as he buried him. The King was enraged and wished to execute Śāṇakavāsin, but Śāṇakavāsin said:
"The King kills me for the sake of the law, while I bury him out of kinship; neither of us violates the great principle of righteousness. Why, then, do you show such anger?"
Those standing nearby were struck with cold dread, yet his countenance remained composed; the King, marveling at his spirit and resolve, subsequently retained him to provide for his needs.

Dharmakṣema was profoundly adept at incantations and sorcery, and whatever he directed invariably proved effective; thus, throughout the Western Regions, he was hailed as the "Great Master of Incantations."

Later, he followed the King into the mountains. When the King became thirsty and required water but could not find any, Śīlamati then secretly recited mantras, and water gushed forth from a rock. He then offered this praise:
"Moved by the Great King’s benevolent grace, this withered rock has been made to produce a spring."
Those in neighboring countries who heard of this all marveled at the King’s virtue.
At that time, the rains were perfectly regulated, and the common people sang praises; the King, delighted by his spiritual arts, bestowed upon him profound favor and honor.

After some time, the King’s interest gradually waned and his treatment of him became increasingly perfunctory. Realizing that his long stay had led to weariness on the part of the court, Daochan took his leave and departed for Kaśmīra.
He carried with him ten fascicles of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* (the earlier portion), as well as the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-mūla*, and other texts.
In that country, many studied the Hīnayāna and did not believe in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; consequently, he traveled east to Kucha.
After some time, he proceeded further to Guzang and stayed at an inn.
Fearing he might lose the original text of the sutra, he placed it under his pillow and fell asleep.
Someone pulled it down to the ground; when Moksala woke up in alarm, he thought it was a thief.
This happened for three nights until he heard a voice from the air saying:
"This is the treasury of the Tathāgata’s liberation; why do you use it as a pillow?
At these words, Baoyun Chen was filled with shame and realization, and he set the scripture aside on a high place.

That night, there were thieves who came several times to lift it, yet they could not move it. When Chen took the scripture away the next morning, he did not consider it heavy. Seeing this, the thieves thought he was a sage and all came forward to bow and offer their thanks.

Juqu Mengxun, the King of Hexi, who had usurped the territory of Liang and styled himself king, heard of the man’s name from the prophecies and summoned him for an audience, treating him with great hospitality.

Jianmenson had long venerated the Great Dharma and was intent upon its propagation; he wished to request the original texts of the scriptures. However, because Kumārajīva had not yet mastered the local language and there were no translators available, he feared that the words might deviate from the principles of the doctrine and thus refused to translate them immediately. Consequently, he studied the language for three years before finally translating and transcribing the *Dīrgha Āgama* (the "First Division") in ten fascicles.

At that time, the śramaṇas Huìsōng and Dàolǎng, who were peerless in Hexi, encountered his translation of the scriptural treasury; they held him in profound esteem and assisted in transposing the Sanskrit texts, with Master Sōng receiving the oral dictation by pen.

Several hundred monastics and laypeople raised difficult questions from all sides; as Baoyin confronted these challenges, he resolved their confusions with clarity and eloquence that flowed like a stream.

Furthermore, he was richly endowed with literary talent, and his compositions were both elegant and profound. Sengsong, Falang, and others further requested that he extensively produce various scriptures; subsequently, he translated over six million words, including the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the *Mahāmegha*, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Upāsakaśīla*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā*, and the *Bodhisattva-śīlasūtra*.

Daōchèn found that the manuscript of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was incomplete in its chapter count; he returned to a foreign land to search for the missing portions, but upon arriving, his mother passed away, so he remained there for over a year.
Later, in Khotan, he further obtained the middle portion of the sūtra text and returned to Guzang to translate it.
Subsequently, he again dispatched an envoy to Khotan and sought out the final portion; he then continued the translation, completing it in thirty-three fascicles.

The translation began in the third year of the Xuan-shi era of the Former Qin; it was completed in three fascicles on the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the tenth year of the Xuan-shi era, which corresponds to the second year of the Yongchu era of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty.
The prophecy states:

"This sūtra originally consisted of thirty-five thousand gāthās in its Sanskrit version; here in this land, it has been reduced by one million words, so that what is now produced consists of only slightly more than ten thousand gāthās."
Dharmakṣema once told Juqu Mengxun: "A ghost has entered the village; there will surely be much pestilence.

Mengxun did not believe him and wished to see it for himself as proof. Dharmakṣema then employed his esoteric arts upon Mengxun; when Mengxun saw [the apparition], he was struck with terror. Dharmakṣema said:
"You should purify yourself with sincerity and observe the fasts; I shall drive them away with divine incantations.
He then recited the incantations for three days and said to Xun:
"The ghosts have already departed.
At that time, those at the border who had seen ghosts said:
"We saw several hundred pestilence spirits fleeing in rapid haste."
The peace within the borders was achieved through the power of Lü Chèn; thus, Juṅ treated him with even greater reverence.

When Juṅ, under his assumed reign title Xuán-èr, crossed the river to attack Qífú Mùmò at Bǎohàn, he dispatched his eldest son, Xíngguó, as the vanguard; however, they were defeated by Mùmò’s army, and Xíngguó was captured.
Later, when Qifu lost his stronghold, Murong Mo and Xingguo were both captured by Helian Ding; subsequently, when Ding was defeated by the Tuyuhun, Xingguo was killed by the rebel troops.

Fu Jianxun was greatly incensed, claiming that his worship of the Buddha had yielded no response; he immediately dispatched messengers to expel the śramaṇas and ordered all those aged fifty and under to abandon the monastic life.

Previously, Fu Jianxun had commissioned a sixteen-foot stone statue for his mother, which subsequently began to weep and shed tears. When Yao Chèn further offered earnest admonitions, Jianxun finally changed his mind and repented.
At that time, Tuoba Tao of the Wei barbarians, having heard that Moksala possessed supernatural arts, dispatched an envoy to invite him and warned Xun, saying:
"If you do not send Moksala, we shall immediately deploy our troops."
Since Juqu Mengxun had served Foṣhuān for a long time, he could not bear to let him go.

Later, he dispatched Li Shun, the Marquis of Gaoping and Acting Minister of Ceremonies, to confer upon Mengxun the appointment of *shizhong* (Attendant-in-Ordinary) with the rank of *shichijie* (General with Seal of Authority), Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Liangzhou and the Western Regions, Grand Tutor (*taifu*), General of the Flying Cavalry (*piaoyi dajiangjun*), Governor of Liangzhou, and King of Liang, while bestowing upon him the nine emoluments (*jiuxi*). He further commanded Mengxun, saying:

"I have heard that you possess the Dharma Master Dharmakṣema, who is widely learned and erudite, a peer of Kumārajīva; his secret mantras are divinely efficacious, making him a match for Master Tanyao."
"I am considering that if you wish to discourse on the Way, I shall dispatch an imperial post to escort you. Xun feasted with Li Shun at the Xinle Gate;

Xun said to Shun, "I, the old minister of the West, Juqu Mengxun, serve the Imperial Court and dare not fail my duty. Yet the Son of Heaven has placed his trust in the words of sycophants; having seen me pressed by such constraints, I previously sent an envoy requesting that Dharmakṣema be retained, but now he is being summoned back."
"This is my master; I must die together with him, for I truly do not begrudge the remainder of my years.
Once born, one must die—how could one perceive when that moment will come? Shun said:

"Your Majesty’s sincerity was first established when you sent your beloved son to serve as an attendant; the Imperial Court held your loyal services in high esteem and thus bestowed upon you exceptional honors.

Yet, because of this one foreign monk, Your Majesty allows the merit of your great achievements to be diminished by an impulse of momentary anger, thereby damaging your long-standing reputation. How could such an act reflect the profound courtesy with which the Court treats you? I venture to say, Great King, that this is not a course worthy of you."
"The Sovereign’s utmost sincerity in opening his breast is something known to Hongwen.
Hongwen was the envoy sent by Sun to the Wei court. Sun said:
"Taichang’s mouth is as eloquent as Su Qin’s; I fear his inner sentiments do not match his words.

Since Sengxun was stingy and refused to send Daochen, and furthermore felt pressured by the power of the Wei state, in the third month of the third year of Yihé, Daochen earnestly requested to travel westward to further seek the *Latter Part of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Enraged by Daochen’s desire to depart, Sengxun secretly plotted to harm him, feigning permission for his journey while providing him with provisions and generously bestowing precious goods upon him.
On the day of his departure, Baoli Chen wept and addressed the assembly, saying:
"The retribution for my karma is about to arrive; even the multitude of sages cannot save me.
Because of his original vow, it was right that he should not remain.
Shortly before his departure, Xun indeed dispatched an assassin to waylay and kill him; he was forty-nine years of age. This was the tenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
Monastics and laypeople alike, both far and near, all lamented his loss.
Shortly thereafter, Xuun’s attendants frequently saw ghosts and spirits by day striking Xuun with swords; in the fourth month, Xuun fell ill and passed away.
Previously, while Daochen was in Guzang, there was a śramaṇa from Zhangye named Daojin who wished to receive the bodhisattva precepts from him, to which Daochen replied:
"First, you must repent."

He then exerted himself with utmost sincerity for seven days and seven nights; on the arrival of the eighth day, he went to Baoshan Chanshan to request ordination, but Chanshan suddenly became greatly enraged. Sengjin further reflected:
"It must simply be that my karmic obstacles have not yet been extinguished."

Thereupon, he exerted himself with single-minded diligence for three years, practicing both dhyāna and repentance. During his meditative absorption, Sengjin beheld Śākyamuni Buddha and various great bodhisattvas bestowing the precepts upon him. That evening, more than ten people staying together with him all experienced dreams identical to what Jin had seen.
As Jing was about to go to see Moksala to explain this to him, before he had even reached him by a few dozen paces, Moksala started up in surprise and cried out:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Since you have already received the precepts, I shall act as your witness.
He then proceeded to explain the characteristics of the precepts before the Buddha image.
At that time, the śramaṇa Daolang, whose reputation resounded throughout Guānxī, also had a dream on the very evening when [Hui]jin received the precepts.

He then lowered his own monastic seniority to seek the status of a junior dharma-brother; consequently, more than a thousand people followed him to receive the teachings. The transmission of this Dharma has continued down to the present day, all being the remaining legacy of [Dharmakṣema’s] prophecies.

Another record states that the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-saṃgraha-sūtra* was likely brought to this land by the Bodhisattva Iṣvara, and was later translated by Dharmakṣema; one suspects that Dharmakṣema may not have been an ordinary person.
Mongxun had a younger cousin, Juqu Anyanghou, who was strong-willed and broad-minded, having read extensively through the records and documents.

Following the prophecies, he entered Hexi and propagated the Buddha-dharma. Anyanghou then applied his mind to the inner scriptures and observed the five precepts; whatever sutras he read, he could immediately recite them from memory. He constantly maintained that diligent study and extensive learning were the magnificent undertakings of a Mahāsattva.

After a short time, seeking the Dharma, he crossed the shifting sands and reached Khotan. There, at the Great Temple of Gomati, he met the Indian Dharma Master Buddhasena and consulted him on the meaning of the Way.
Paramārtha originally studied the Mahāyāna; his natural genius was exceptionally brilliant, and he could recite fifty million verses while possessing a clear understanding of the methods of dhyāna.
Consequently, throughout the various kingdoms of the Western Regions, he was titled "The Lion Among Men."
An-yang received the *Cānmiyào zhìbìng jīng* (The Sutra on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna for Healing Illness) from him; based on its Sanskrit manuscript, he recited it fluently from memory.
Subsequently, he returned east to his home district in Gaochang.
He obtained one fascicle each of the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* and the *Maitreya-sūtra*.
Upon returning to Hexi, he immediately translated the *Canyao* (Essentials of Dhyāna) and rendered it into the Jin script.

When the pseudo-Wei state annexed Xiliang, he fled south to the Song dynasty; there, he concealed his ambitions and humbled himself, refusing to associate with worldly society. He frequently visited stupas and monasteries, spending the remainder of his life as a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*).
When the two *Sūtras on Contemplation*, those of Maitreya and Avalokiteśvara, were first published, Meng Yi, the Governor of Danyang, saw them and praised them;
he treated him with profound esteem and hospitality.

Later, the nun Huiyao of Zhuyuan Temple again requested that he produce a translation of the *Dhyāna-sūtra*. Since Dao’an had long been thoroughly practiced in its methods, his hand did not falter when he took up the brush; in seventeen days, he produced it in five fascicles.
Shortly thereafter, he also produced the *Buddhapitṛparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in one fascicle at Dinglin Monastery on Mount Zhong.

An Yang lived in seclusion from wife and children, having no desire for honor or profit; he moved with ease among his dharma companions, proclaiming and disseminating the True Dharma. For this reason, both monastics and laypeople alike revered and admired him, and he later passed away after falling ill.

The various sutras produced by the *chans* (prophecies) were not transmitted to Jianye until the Yuanjia period; at that time, the Dharma Master Huiguan of Daochang Monastery sought to recover the *Latter Part of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
He then petitioned Emperor Taizu of Song for provisions and dispatched the śramaṇa Daopu with ten clerks to travel westward in search of the scriptures.
Upon reaching Changguang Commandery, their ship was wrecked and Daopu injured his foot; he subsequently passed away due to illness.
As he drew his last breath, Daopu sighed and said, "The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (specifically its latter portion) has no karmic affinity with the land of Song!"

Pubo was originally a native of Gaochang. Having traveled through the Western Regions and journeyed across all the kingdoms, he made offerings to the sacred images, carried the Buddha’s almsbowl upon his head, and beheld everything from the four stupas and the Bodhi tree to the footprints and statues, leaving none unseen.
He was proficient in Brahmi script and well-versed in the languages of various nations; his travels through foreign lands have been recorded in a separate major biography.
At that time, there was also the śramaṇa Fasheng of Gaochang, who likewise traveled abroad and composed a biography in four fascicles.
Furthermore, there were Zhu Fawei and Shi Sengbiao, both of whom traveled to the Buddha-lands, and so forth.
*Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume Two;
*Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume Three.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huijiao of Jiaxiang Monastery in Kuaiji during the Liang Dynasty.
Section on Translators of Scriptures, Part Two:

1. Shi Faxian: His secular surname was Gong; he was a native of Wuyang in Pingyang. He had three elder brothers who all died while still in their childhood. Fearing that disaster might befall Faxian, his father ordained him as a śrāmaṇera at the age of three.
After living at home for several years, he fell gravely ill and was on the verge of death; consequently, he was sent back to the monastery, where he recovered after staying for two nights.
He refused to return home again, and his mother, unable to see him, later had a small hut built outside the gate to serve as a place for his coming and going.
At the age of ten, he encountered the sorrow of his father’s death. His uncle, fearing that his mother would remain unsupported as a widow, pressured him to return to secular life.

Hsian said, "It was not because I had a father that I left the household life; it was precisely because I wished to distance myself from the dust of the world and depart from secular customs that I entered the Way."
His uncle approved of his words and desisted.
Shortly thereafter, his mother passed away; his filial nature surpassed that of ordinary men, and once the funeral rites were completed, he immediately returned to the monastery.

Once, while he was harvesting rice in a field with several dozen fellow students, some starving bandits appeared intending to seize the grain. All the śrāmaṇeras fled, but Faxian alone remained behind and said to the bandits: "If you require grain, take as much as you wish.

However, because you failed to practice giving in the past, you have fallen into this state of hunger and poverty; if you continue to rob others now, I fear your plight will become even more severe in future lives. I, a poor monk, am already concerned for your sake."
Having finished speaking, he immediately returned; the bandits abandoned the grain and departed, and among the several hundred monks, there was none who did not sigh in admiration.

Upon receiving full ordination, his will and conduct were clear and keen, and his ritual observances were orderly and solemn. He often lamented that the sūtras and vinaya were incomplete or corrupted, and thus vowed to seek them out.
In the third year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, he set out from Chang’an together with his fellow students Huijing, Daozheng, Huiying, Huivei, and others.

They traveled west across the shifting sands; above there were no birds in flight, and below there were no beasts running. Looking out in all directions, the landscape was vast and desolate, and they could not discern their destination. They could only rely on the sun to determine east and west, and use human bones as markers to indicate the path ahead.

There were frequent hot winds and malevolent spirits; anyone encountering them would surely die. Xian entrusted himself to his circumstances and surrendered his life to fate, passing straight through the perils.

After a while, he reached the Pamir Mountains (Congling). The peaks were covered in perpetual snow throughout both winter and summer, and there were fierce dragons that spat poison, while wind and rain drove sand and gravel. The mountain paths were treacherous and perilous, with cliffs rising sheer for thousands of fathoms.
In the past, there were those who hewed stone to open roads, installing stairways alongside them at more than seven hundred locations.
Furthermore, they crossed rivers by treading upon suspended ropes at over several dozen places—sites that neither Zhang Qian nor Ganfu of the Han dynasty ever reached.
Next, they crossed the Lesser Snow Mountains, where a violent cold wind suddenly arose; Huìjǐng shivered with cold and could not move forward, saying to Xuǎnxiǎn, "I am about to die;
you should go on ahead so that we do not perish together."
As soon as he finished speaking, he passed away. Faxian comforted him and wept, saying, "Our original plan has not been realized; what can we do against fate?
He then exerted himself to travel alone and eventually crossed over mountainous险峻 (precipices), traversing a total of more than thirty kingdoms.
As he was about to reach India, more than thirty *li* from Rājagṛha, there was a monastery where he passed by at nightfall.
The next morning, as Faxian wished to go to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, the monks of the monastery cautioned him, saying:
"The road is extremely difficult and obstructed; moreover, there are many black lions that frequently devour people. How could you possibly get there?"
Faxian said:

"I have traveled tens of thousands of li from afar, vowing to reach Vulture Peak; I do not expect to preserve my life, nor can I guarantee that my next breath will remain. How could I allow the sincerity cultivated over many years to be abandoned now that I have finally arrived?"
"Though there be peril and hardship, I am not afraid.
As none could stop him, he was sent off with two monks.
Once Xian had reached the mountain, the sun was setting; wishing to stay the night, the two monks became fearful and abandoned him to return home.
Xuán remained alone in the mountains, burning incense and prostrating himself; he was so moved by the ancient traces that it was as if he were beholding the actual presence of the Sage.
At night, three black lions came and crouched before Xuán, licking their lips and wagging their tails; yet Xuán did not cease reciting the sutras, maintaining single-minded devotion to the Buddha.
The lion then lowered its head and tucked its tail, crouching before Xian’s feet; Xian stroked it with his hand and recited a spell, saying:
"If you wish to harm me, wait until I have finished my recitation; if you merely wish to test me, you may withdraw at once."
After a long while, Siṃha departed.

Returning the following morning, he found the path leading back to be remote and overgrown, with only a single track for passage. Before he had traveled more than a *li*, he suddenly encountered a practitioner who appeared to be ninety years old; his appearance and clothing were coarse and simple, yet his spirit was noble and far-reaching.
Although Sengxian perceived that his tone was lofty, he did not realize he was a divine being.
Later, he encountered another young monk and asked,
"Who was that venerable elder just now?"
He replied, "He is the great disciple Dhūtakāśyapa.
Xian was then filled with profound regret and resentment.
He pursued them further to the mountain site, where a large horizontal rock blocked the entrance to the cave; thus unable to enter, Faxian departed with tears flowing.

He proceeded to the kingdom of Kāśī, where there was a white-eared dragon that regularly made covenants with the assembly of monks to ensure the country’s harvests were bountiful, which proved to be consistently effective.

The śramaṇas built a dwelling for the dragon and provided offerings of merit-food. Whenever the summer retreat concluded, the dragon would invariably transform into a small snake with both ears entirely white; everyone recognized it as the dragon. They placed curdled milk in a bronze bowl and set the dragon inside it, passing it around from the senior monk to the junior monks until it had gone through the entire assembly, whereupon it would vanish. It appeared once every year, and Daoxian personally witnessed this.

Later, he arrived in Central India and, at the Deva Temple south of the Aśoka Stūpa in the city of Pāṭaliputra in Magadha, obtained the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, as well as the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha*, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, and the *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Xuánliú remained for three years, studying the Sanskrit language and script, after which he personally transcribed the texts; he then took the scriptures and images and entrusted them to merchants, arriving in the Kingdom of Siṃhala.

He observed that of the dozen or so fellow travelers, some had remained while others had perished; looking at his own reflection, he was alone. He constantly harbored feelings of sorrow and lamentation.

Suddenly, before the jade image, he saw a merchant offering a white circular silk fan from the land of Jin as an act of devotion; he could not help but feel a profound sense of melancholy and shed tears.

After staying for two years, he further obtained the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the *Dīrgha-āgama* and *Saṃyukta-āgama*, as well as the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*; these were all texts that had not previously existed in the land of Han.
Shortly thereafter, he boarded a large merchant vessel and returned by way of the sea.

There were some two hundred people on board; encountering a violent storm, water flooded into the ship, and everyone was struck with terror, immediately taking miscellaneous goods and casting them overboard.

Fearing that they might abandon their scriptures and images, Xian single-mindedly recited the name of Avalokiteśvara and took refuge in the Sangha of the land of Han; thus, the ship was carried by the wind and reached its destination without damage or destruction.

After more than ten days, he arrived at the kingdom of Yavadvīpa and stayed there for five months. He then joined another merchant caravan and traveled east to Guangzhou. After sailing for over twenty days, a great wind suddenly arose at night; the entire ship was struck with terror, and the multitude all deliberated, saying:
"It is because we carried this śramaṇa that we have been brought to such distress. We cannot allow the whole company to perish for the sake of one man."
As they were about to push him down, Faxian’s lay patron rebuked the merchants with a stern voice, saying:
"If you would cast this śramaṇa down, you should likewise cast me down; otherwise, you shall be put to death."
"The emperors of the land of Han revere the Buddha and honor the Sangha; when I arrive there, I shall certainly accuse you to the King.
The merchants looked at one another, their faces turning pale with fear, and they reluctantly desisted.

Since the water was exhausted and provisions were depleted, they could only rely on the wind to carry them with the current; suddenly reaching a shore, they saw that the weeds and vegetables remained as before and knew it was Chinese territory, yet they did not know which region it was, so they immediately took their boat into a creek to seek out a village.
Seeing two hunters, Xian asked,
"What place is this? The hunters replied:
"This is the southern shore of Mount Lao in Changguang Commandery, Qingzhou.

When the hunter returned, he informed the Governor, Li Yi. Li Yi, who had long been devoted to the faith, suddenly hearing that a śramaṇa had arrived from afar, went in person to welcome and greet him.
Faxian returned with the scriptures and images he had carried.
Shortly thereafter, as he wished to return south, the Governor of Qingzhou requested that he remain for the winter.
Faxian replied, "I have cast myself into a land from which there is no returning; my resolve is to propagate the Dharma. As long as my purpose remains unfulfilled, I cannot stay for long."

He then traveled south to the capital, where he approached the foreign meditation master Buddhabhadra at Daochang Temple to translate the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Vaipulya-nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, totaling more than one million words.
After Huiyan had produced the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, he circulated it for the purpose of teaching and transforming others, so that all might see and hear it.

There was a family whose names have been lost, living near the Zhuque Gate, who had followed the True Teaching for generations. They transcribed a copy for themselves, reciting and making offerings to it; however, they had no separate scripture room, as the text was kept in the same house as their miscellaneous books.

Later, wind and fire suddenly broke out, spreading to his house; all his possessions were utterly consumed, yet only the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* remained intact. Unharmed by the embers and ashes, the color of the scrolls did not change. This was circulated throughout the capital, and everyone marveled at its divine mystery.
Other sūtras and vinayas remained untranslated.
Later, he arrived in Jingzhou and passed away at Xin Temple at the age of eighty-six; the assembly all mourned him with deep regret.
There exists a separate, extensive biography concerning his travels through various kingdoms.
2. Shi Tanwujie (釋曇無竭). Shi Tanwujie, translated here as Fayong (法勇), was surnamed Li and was a native of Huanglong in Youzhou.
From his youth, he served as a śrāmaṇera and practiced asceticism; he observed the precepts and recited the sūtras, earning the high esteem of his teachers and fellow monks.
Having heard that Faxian and others had personally traveled to the Buddha-land, he was moved by a profound sense of resolve and made a vow to sacrifice his own life.

Consequently, in the first year of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, he gathered twenty-five fellow śramaṇas, including Sengmeng and Tanlang, and together they took up banners, canopies, and various articles for offering. Setting out from the northern lands, they journeyed far toward the Western Regions.
Upon first arriving in the kingdom of Henan, he continued westward through Haixi Commandery and entered the shifting sands, eventually reaching Gaochang Commandery.

He passed through various kingdoms such as Kucha and Kashgar, ascended the Pamir Mountains, and crossed the Snow Mountains. There, obstructing mists lay in a thousand layers and tiered ice extended for ten thousand li; below was a great river whose current flowed as swiftly as an arrow.
On the flanks of the eastern and western mountains, they tied ropes to form bridges.

Ten people would cross at a time; once they had reached the opposite shore, they would raise smoke as a signal. Seeing the smoke, those behind knew that the preceding group had already crossed and could then proceed further.
When smoke was not seen for a long time, he knew that a violent wind had blown the rope away and the man had fallen into the river.

After traveling for three days, they again crossed the Great Snow Mountains; there were precipitous cliffs standing sheer with no place to set foot, yet upon the stone walls there were old holes for wooden stakes, facing one another at every turn.

Each person held four stakes; first pulling out the lower stake, they grasped the upper one with their hands, passing from one to another by climbing over them, and it was only after many days that they reached the level ground.
There, they waited for one another and accounted for their companions, finding that twelve people were missing.
He proceeded to the kingdom of Kaśmīra and paid homage to the Buddha’s almsbowl.

He stayed for over a year, studying the Brahmi script and the Sanskrit language, during which time he obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*. Continuing westward, he reached the Indus River (known in Chinese as the Siṃhamukha), followed its course upstream into the country of the Yuezhi, where he paid homage to the Buddha’s *uṣṇīṣa* bone and beheld a wooden boat that floats by itself.

Later, he arrived at Shiliu Temple on the southern side of Mount Dantaka; there were over three hundred resident monks who studied the various teachings of the Three Vehicles. Wujie stayed at this temple to receive the full ordination.

The Indian Dhyāna Master Buddhatara—translated here as "Awakening Savior"—was universally regarded in that land as one who had already realized the fruits of the path. Wujie requested him to serve as his Upādhyāya, while the Chinese śramaṇa Zhiding served as his Ācārya. They stayed for three months during the summer retreat, after which they set out again toward the realm of Central India. As the road was vast and desolate, they carried only rock honey as their provisions; although there were originally thirteen companions, eight perished along the way, leaving five remaining to travel together.
Although Wujie encountered numerous perils and hardships, he never for a moment ceased his focused mindfulness on the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* he carried with him.

Upon reaching the vicinity of Śrāvastī, he encountered a herd of wild elephants in the wilderness; as Wujie invoked the name [of the Bodhisattva] and took refuge, a lion immediately emerged from the forest, causing the elephants to flee in terror.

Later, while crossing the Ganges, he encountered a herd of wild oxen that came bellowing toward him, intending to harm him. As before, Wujie took refuge in the Buddha; immediately, a great vulture flew down, and the wild oxen scattered in terror, whereby he was able to escape.
That his sincere devotion moved the divine so that he was delivered from peril was entirely of this nature.
Later, he traveled by ship across the sea to Guangzhou from South India; the accounts of his various experiences are recorded separately in other biographies.
The *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* translated by him is still transmitted in the capital.
His ultimate end is unknown. 3. Buddhayaśas:
Buddhayaśas means "Awakened Life" (Jue-shou) in this language; he was a native of Jibin.

In his youth, he studied under the monks of the Mahīśāsaka school; he specialized in the Vinaya-piṭaka while also attaining mastery in the essentials of dhyāna. In the seventh month of the first year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty, he arrived in Yangzhou.

Previously, the śramaṇa Faxian had obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* in the Kingdom of Siṃhala; however, before it could be translated, Faxian passed away. When the monks in the capital heard that Kumārajīva was well-versed in this field of study, they requested him to produce a translation.
In the eleventh month of the winter of that year, they gathered at Longguang Temple and translated it into thirty-four fascicles, titled the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.

Kumārajīva held the Sanskrit manuscript while the Khotanese śramaṇa Zhisheng acted as the primary translator; Longsheng of Longguang and Huiyan of Dong’an assisted by holding the brush to verify the text. Wang Lian of Langya, the State Councilor of the Song dynasty, served as the patron (*dānapati*). The work was finally completed in the fourth month of the following year.
He further extracted the *Śīlacitta* (Essence of the Precepts) and the *Karmavācanā* texts from the extensive Vinaya collection, both of which circulated in the world.
After Kumārajīva’s death, nothing further is known of his final destination.
4. Buddhabhadra: Buddhabhadra, translated here as "Awakened Armor" (*Juekai*), was a native of the Western Regions.

From childhood, his conduct was upright and his character clear; he possessed a brilliance that surpassed his peers. He studied the Tripiṭaka and was particularly adept at the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which he constantly recited and upheld as the essential core of his heart.
During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, [the *Vibhāṣā*] reached Xiliang.

Previously, there was the śramaṇa Daotai, who was resolute and determined in his character; having traveled young to the region east of the Pamirs, he journeyed through various kingdoms and obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Vibhāṣā* consisting of one hundred thousand verses. Upon returning to Guzang, he sat with humble posture and an open mind, eagerly awaiting a master of the Dharma. Hearing that Guṇavarman had set his heart upon this treatise, he requested him to translate it.

At that time, Juqu Mengxun had already passed away, and his son Maoqian succeeded to the throne. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the fifth year of Chenghe (the *dingchou* year), corresponding to the fourteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he invited Guṇavarman to perform the translation within the Xianyu Palace in the city of Liangzhou.

Tai himself acted as the scribe; the śramaṇas Huìsōng and Dàolǎng, along with more than three hundred monks specializing in doctrinal studies, collated and verified the textual meanings, completing the work after two full cycles. The entire collection consists of one hundred fascicles, for which the śramaṇa Dàoyǐn composed a preface.

After some time, the Wei chieftain Tuoba Tao launched a western campaign against Guzang; the territory of Liang collapsed into chaos, and the scriptures and personal effects were all consumed by fire and swept away. Consequently, forty fascicles were lost, and only sixty remain today.
Guṇavarman fled westward to escape the chaos, and his final whereabouts remain unknown.

5. Shi Zhiyan: Shi Zhiyan was a native of Xiliangzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of twenty and soon became renowned for his diligent application. He wore patched robes, sat in meditation, and spent his years on a vegetarian diet. As his homeland lay in ruins, he resolved to travel extensively to serve famous masters and seek out the vast array of scriptures and teachings.

He then traveled extensively through the Western Regions until he reached Kaśmīra, where he entered the Madhyāntika Monastery. There, he received instruction in the methods of dhyāna from the bhikṣu Buddhasena. He practiced for three years until his realization was profound, such that his achievement surpassed ten years of study. Seeing that his meditative contemplation had reached its full potential, Buddhasena held him in particularly high esteem and regarded him as extraordinary.
When the clergy and laity there heard of this, they sighed in admiration, saying,
"In the land of Qin, there are indeed śramaṇas who seek the Way.
Only then did they cease their disregard for those of Qin and began to receive foreigners with respect.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Buddhabhadra, who was also a master of dhyāna in that country. Daoyan earnestly invited him to return to the East, wishing to transmit the Dharma to the Central Land. Buddhabhadra, admiring his sincerity, subsequently traveled east with him.
Thereupon, crossing deserts and traversing perilous terrain, he reached Guanzhong.
He constantly followed Guṇabhadra and resided at the Great Monastery in Chang’an.

Shortly thereafter, Guṇabhadra was unjustly expelled by the monks of Qin, and Sengyan also dispersed from him, taking up residence in a vihāra on the east of the mountains. There he sat in meditation and recited the sūtras, applying himself with great diligence to his studies and cultivation.

In the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, when Emperor Wu of the Song was returning from his successful western campaign against Chang’an, his banners passed through the region east of the mountains.

At that time, Wang Huai, the Duke of Shixing, accompanied the imperial carriage on an excursion to view the mountains and rivers. Upon arriving at the Yan Monastery, he saw three monks residing there, each sitting upon a rope-cot, their meditative concentration profound and serene. When Huai arrived, they remained unaware of him for a long while; he then snapped his fingers, whereupon the three opened their eyes, but they closed them again shortly after and did not speak a word in response to his inquiries.

Huihui was struck with admiration for their extraordinary character and inquired of the local elders, all of whom said, "These three monks are high-minded practitioners who dwell in seclusion to pursue their aspirations; they are masters of lofty purity.
Huihui immediately petitioned Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty to invite them back to the capital, but none of them were willing to go.
Since his repeated requests had been so earnest, the two men recommended Daoyan to accompany him.
Daohui, whose devotion to the Way had long been profound, attended to him with great reverence; upon returning to the capital, he immediately took up residence at Shixing Temple.

Yan Xing loved tranquility and stillness, and his will was set on avoiding the clamor and dust of the world; thus, Huihuai constructed a vihāra on the outskirts of the eastern suburbs, which is the present-day Zhiyuan Temple.

Previously, Yan had obtained various Sanskrit manuscripts of the sūtras in the Western Regions, but had not yet had time to translate or copy them. Upon arriving in the fourth year of the Yuanjia era, he then translated the *Lalitavistara*, the *Vaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka*, and the *Caturmahārājakāyika* together with the śramaṇa Baoyun.

Sengyan stayed at the monastery and did not accept private invitations; he constantly supported himself by wandering for alms. As his spiritual transformation reached both the hidden and the manifest worlds, all submitted to his influence.
A person who could see ghosts reported that he had seen the spirits among the Grand Sacrificial Altars of Xizhou conversing with one another:
"When Master Yan arrives, we must yield our way."
This man did not yet understand him.
Shortly thereafter, Yan arrived; he casually inquired after his name and surname, which was indeed "Zhiyan. He silently took note of this and treated him with secret respect and distinction.

Lady Liu, the wife of Xiao Si-hua, who held the rank of Yitong of Lanling, was suffering from an illness during which she constantly saw ghosts appear; it was truly terrifying. At that time, he invited Yan to preach the Dharma. As soon as Yan arrived at the outer hall, Lady Liu saw the host of ghosts scatter in all directions. Once Yan had entered and preached the sutras for the lady, her illness was cured. Consequently, she received the five precepts, and the entire family came to revere him.

Yan Qing was pure and simple, possessing few desires; he gave away whatever he received as soon as it came to him. Having traveled to various regions since his youth, he remained free from attachment or obstruction.
By nature humble and retiring, he did not speak of himself; thus, although his virtuous deeds were many, none could be fully recorded by the world.

In the past, before he had left the household life, Yan had received the five precepts; however, having committed violations of them, he later entered the Way and received full ordination. He constantly doubted whether he had obtained the precepts and was always filled with fear on this account.

Having practiced meditative contemplation for many years without being able to resolve his doubts, he subsequently traveled across the sea once more to reach India, where he consulted various enlightened masters.

There he encountered an arhat bhikṣu, to whom he related his situation in full; however, the arhat did not dare to provide a definitive judgment. He then entered a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and went to the Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya, who replied:
"He has obtained the precepts."
Huiyan was greatly delighted and returned on foot.

Upon reaching Jibin, he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-eight. According to the custom of that country, both ordinary monks and sages were cremated in separate locations. Although Huiyan’s observance of the precepts was lofty and brilliant, his practice had not yet reached full realization; thus, when they first moved his corpse toward the cemetery for ordinary monks, the body was so heavy that it could not be lifted.
When they turned toward the Holy Tomb, they felt a sense of lightness as if floating away.
His disciples Zhiyu and Zhiyuan had previously come from the West to report these auspicious signs, and both have now returned to their foreign lands.
Inferring from this, Xian certainly was one who had attained the Way; it is simply unknown whether his realization was deep or shallow at various stages between the fruition and the path.
6. Shi Baoyun: Shi Baoyun’s clan and lineage are not well known; according to tradition:

A native of Liangzhou, he left home to become a monk in his youth. He was diligent and possessed both learning and virtuous conduct; his aspirations and character were firm and pure, and he did not conform to the ways of the world. Thus, from his youth, he was renowned for his integrity, straightforwardness, and simple purity.

Seeking the Dharma with such earnest sincerity that he was prepared to sacrifice his life for the sake of the Way, he resolved to personally behold sacred sites and extensively seek out the essentials of the scriptures.

Consequently, at the beginning of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled far to the Western Regions, accompanying Faxian and Zhiyan in succession. They traversed the shifting sands and scaled the Snowy Mountains; though they endured toil, hardship, and peril, they regarded them as no difficulty.
He then traveled through the kingdoms of Khotan and India, witnessing numerous miraculous wonders.
Passing through the wilderness of the Rākṣasas, he heard the sound of celestial drums and paid homage at many sites associated with the traces of Śākyamuni’s presence.
Yun traveled abroad to study the Brahmi script extensively.
He fully mastered the phonology, characters, and glossaries of all the various kingdoms of India.
Later, he returned to Chang’an, where he followed the Dhyāna Master Buddhabhadra to practice meditation and advance on the Path.
Shortly thereafter, the Dhyāna Master was unjustly expelled by a monk from the Qin court; his disciples were all implicated in the fault, and Huiyun also fled in dispersal.

It happened that Shi Huiyuan of Mount Lu resolved the matter of the expulsion, and they returned together to the capital, settling at Daochang Temple. Because Huiyun’s resolve and vigor were firm and fierce, and because he had propagated the Way in remote regions, there was no one among the assembly of monks who did not open their hearts to consult him, regarding him with both reverence and affection.
Kumārajīva translated the *New Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and many other scriptures produced during his later years; most were edited and finalized by him.
Being proficient in both Chinese and foreign languages, his phonology and glosses were highly accurate. All people were convinced and submitted to what he established.
Initially, the śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Guanzhong was skilled at oral translation; during the two reigns of Fu Jian and Yao Xing, he manifested and produced numerous sūtras.

As for the translation of Sanskrit texts in Jiangzuo, none surpassed Kumārajīva; thus, during the transition between the Jin and Song dynasties, he propagated the Dharma-treasury, and śramaṇas such as Huiguan all befriended and esteemed him.
Huiyun’s character favored dwelling in seclusion to preserve his leisure and tranquility; he subsequently retired to a monastery on Mount Liuhe, where he translated the *Buddhacarita-kāvya*.

As the mountain was populated by many wild folk whose customs inclined toward petty theft, Huiyun preached the Dharma to instruct and transform them. Many underwent reform, and among ten households, eight performed rites of worship and made offerings.

Shortly thereafter, as Huiguan of Daochang Monastery was approaching death, he requested that Huiyun return to the capital to take overall charge of the monastery’s affairs; having no choice, Huiyun returned.
He resided at Daochang for about a year before returning once more to Heluo, where he passed away at his mountain temple in the twenty-sixth year of the Yuanjia era at the age of seventy-four.
His travels abroad are recorded in a separate biography. 7.
Guṇavarman: Guṇavarman, which translates as "Armor of Merit," was originally of the Kṣatriya caste; for generations his family had been kings, and they ruled in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
His grandfather was Haribhadra, which means "Lion-Worthy," who was exiled due to his upright integrity.
His father was Saṃghananda, which means "Joy of the Assembly," who lived in seclusion within the mountains and marshes.

At the age of fourteen, Guṇavarman was already exceptionally perceptive and brilliant; he possessed profound foresight, was broad-minded in his benevolence, and revered virtue while striving for goodness.
Once, when his mother required some wild meat, she ordered Guṇavarman to procure it.
Guṇavarman replied, "Among all living beings, there is none that does not cherish life. To take the life of another is not the act of a benevolent person."
His mother said angrily, "Even if you should incur guilt, I shall take your place.
On another day, while Varma was boiling oil, he accidentally spilled it on his finger; thereupon, he said to his mother:
"I will endure the pain on your behalf.
The mother said, "The pain is in your own body; how could I possibly endure it for you?"
Bamó said, "If one cannot even substitute for the suffering before one's eyes, how much less can one do so for the three miserable realms! Thereupon,
her mother repented and awakened, vowing to abstain from killing for the rest of her life.
When he reached the age of eighteen, a physiognomist saw him and said:
"At the age of thirty, you shall govern a great state and face south as a sovereign.
If you do not delight in worldly glory, you shall attain the fruit of sainthood."

When he reached the age of twenty, he left the household life and received the precepts. He thoroughly mastered the nine divisions of the scriptures and was widely learned in the four Āgamas. He recited over a million words of sutras, attained a profound understanding of the Vinaya categories, and wondrously entered the essentials of dhyāna; at that time, he was titled the "Dharma Master of the Tripiṭaka."
When he reached the age of thirty, the King of Kaśmīra passed away without any heir. The assembly all deliberated, saying:
"Guṇavarman is a scion of the royal house, and moreover, his talent is eminent and his virtue is profound. We should request that he return to secular life so that he may succeed to the throne."
Several hundred ministers repeatedly and earnestly entreated him, but Guṇavarman would not accept their plea.

He then took leave of his teacher and went against the crowd, dwelling among the forests and drinking from the valleys; he traveled alone through the mountains and wilds, concealing his traces from the world of men.

Later, he arrived in the Kingdom of Siṃhala to observe local customs and propagate the teachings; those among the assembly who recognized the truth all claimed they had attained the first fruit of the path.
His dignified demeanor moved all things, and those who beheld him were inspired to resolve their minds upon enlightenment.

Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Śrīvijaya. One day before his arrival, the mother of the King of Śrīvijaya dreamed at night that a Daoist was flying a ship into the country; the following morning, it turned out that Guṇavarman had indeed arrived.
The Queen Mother respectfully received the five precepts according to the sacred rites.
She then exhorted the King, saying:

"Through karmic conditions from past lives, we have become mother and son. I have already received the precepts, yet you do not believe; I fear that the causes for future births will forever sever the fruits of the present."
The king, constrained by his mother’s command, immediately accepted the precepts. As time passed, his devotion gradually deepened.
Shortly thereafter, the troops of a neighboring state invaded the border.

The king said to Guṇavarman, “The foreign enemies rely on their strength and wish to commit acts of aggression and insult. If we engage them in battle, many will surely be wounded or killed; yet if we do not resist, our ruin is imminent. Now I can only take refuge in you, my venerable teacher; I know not what plan to adopt.”

Guṇavarman said, "When violent rebels attack one another, it is necessary to defend against them; however, you should simply give rise to a mind of compassion and refrain from harboring thoughts of harm.
The king personally led his troops to confront them; as soon as the banners and drums met, the rebels immediately retreated and dispersed.
The king was struck by a stray arrow and wounded his foot; Guṇavarman performed a consecration with water to wash it, and after two nights, he was fully recovered.
The king’s devout faith grew increasingly earnest, and he desired to leave the household life to cultivate the Way. He then addressed his ministers, saying:
"I wish to personally take refuge in the Dharma-gate; you may choose another wise sovereign."
The ministers all prostrated themselves and entreated him, saying:

"If Your Majesty abandons the kingdom, the subjects will have no one to rely upon. Moreover, our enemy is fierce and powerful, holding us at bay with their natural defenses; if we lose your protective grace, where shall the common people find refuge?"
"Great King, your heavenly compassion—could you not take pity on me? I venture to entreat you with my very life to express my sincere devotion.
The King, unable to bear a firm refusal, then approached his ministers and requested three wishes; if they were granted, he would remain to govern the kingdom.
First, I vow that all within my royal domain shall together revere the Upādhyāya;
second, I vow that throughout the entire territory under my governance, all killing shall be abolished;
third, I vow that all accumulated wealth shall be distributed to relieve the poor and the sick.
The ministers were filled with joy and all respectfully agreed; thus, the entire kingdom followed suit and received the precepts.

Later, the King built a vihāra for Guṇavarman and personally hauled timber, during which he injured his toe. Guṇavarman again performed a mantra-ritual to treat it, and after a short while, it was restored to health.
The sound of his guidance and transformation spread both far and near; hearing of his reputation, neighboring countries all dispatched envoys to request his presence.

At that time, renowned and virtuous śramaṇas in the capital, such as Huiguan and Huicong, held his character and conduct in high esteem and desired to receive his instruction. Consequently, in the ninth month of the first year of the Yuanjia era, they presented a petition in person to Emperor Wen, requesting that Guṇavarman be invited. The Emperor immediately issued an edict to the Governor of Jiaozhou, ordering him to dispatch a ship to welcome and escort him.

Furthermore, Guān and others dispatched the śramaṇas Fǎcháng, Dàochōng, Dàojùn, and others to that region to offer prayers and petitions, while also sending letters to Guṇavarman and King Puṣyavarman of Śrīvijaya, earnestly hoping that they would deign to visit the borders of the Song realm to propagate the Way of the Buddha.
Guṇavarman, believing that the holy transformation should be widely propagated, did not hesitate to travel abroad.

He had previously traveled by sea on the merchant Zhu Nanti’s ship, intending to head for a small kingdom; however, encountering a favorable wind, he eventually arrived at Guangzhou. Thus, his own writings state:
"Driven by the winds of karmic action, I have thus reached the borders of Song."
This is what is meant by that.

Emperor Wen, knowing that Guṇavarman had already arrived in Nanhai, subsequently issued an edict to the provincial and commandery authorities ordering them to provide the necessary provisions for his journey to the capital.

On the way, he passed through Shixing, where he stayed for about a year. In Shixing there was Mount Hushi, its form towering and solitary, with peaks and ridges reaching high into the sky. Guṇavarman, deeming it to resemble Gṛdhrakūṭa, renamed it Lingjiu (Vulture Peak).

Outside the mountain monastery, he established a separate meditation hall several *li* away from the temple, where the sound of the *qing* gong could not be heard; yet every time the mallet was struck for the assembly, Guṇavarman had already arrived. At times he would encounter rain without being wetted, or tread through mud without getting his feet dampened; thus, among the monks and laypeople of the community, there were none who did not feel a profound sense of awe and increased reverence.

The monastery had a Baoyue Hall (Jewel Moon Hall), where Guṇavarman personally painted an image of Rāhula on the northern wall of the hall, as well as the scene of Dīpaṃkara and the youth Megha offering his hair. After the images were completed, they emitted light every evening, which eventually ceased after some time.

Cai Mozhi, the Governor of Shixing, held him in profound reverence. Later, when Mozhi was about to die, Guṇavarman went to visit him in person, preaching the Dharma to comfort him. Subsequently, Mozhi’s family members dreamed that he was in the monastery lecturing on the Dharma with the assembly of monks; this was truly due to the power of Guṇavarman’s transformative guidance.

This mountain was originally plagued by many tigers; however, since Guṇavarman resided there, he would travel by day and return at night. On occasion, if he encountered a tiger, he would press its head with his staff, toy with it, and depart. Consequently, travelers on the mountains and visitors by the waters passed to and fro without obstruction; those who were moved by his virtue and converted to his way numbered seven or eight out of ten.

Guṇavarman once entered meditative absorption in a separate chamber and did not emerge for several days. A monk from the monastery sent a novice to check on him; the novice saw a white lion climbing up a pillar, with blue lotus flowers blooming and spreading throughout the air. Startled and terrified, the novice cried out and went to chase the lion, but suddenly nothing was to be seen.
His spiritual manifestations were boundless, and instances such as these were numerous.
Later, Emperor Wen again issued a formal decree, earnestly inviting him once more; he then set sail for the capital, arriving at Jianye in the first month of the eighth year of the Yuanjia era.
Emperor Wen summoned him for an audience and questioned him with great earnestness, further saying:
"I, your disciple, have long desired to observe the fasts and refrain from killing; however, being constrained by the necessity of serving the state, I am unable to follow this aspiration."
"Since the Dharma Master has traveled ten thousand li from afar to transform this kingdom, with what will you instruct us?
Guṇavarman replied, "The Way resides in the mind, not in external affairs; the Dharma arises from oneself, not from others."

Moreover, the cultivation practiced by emperors and kings differs from that of the commoner; for the commoner is of humble station and inferior renown, and his words lack authority. If he does not discipline himself and subject his body to hardship, what purpose will he serve?

The Emperor takes the four seas as his home and the myriad people as his children; when he utters a single virtuous word, both men and women rejoice, and when he implements a single benevolent policy, both humans and spirits are brought into harmony.

When punishments do not cause untimely deaths and labor does not exhaust the people's strength, then wind and rain will arrive at their proper times, cold and warmth will correspond to the seasons, the hundred grains will flourish in abundance, and mulberry trees and hemp will grow lush and dense.
If one observes the fast in this manner, the merit of the fast is indeed great; if one refrains from killing in this manner, the virtue thereof is likewise manifold.
Is it not better to forgo half a day’s meal in order to preserve the life of a single bird, thereby achieving true and vast salvation?
The Emperor then leaned forward on his desk and sighed, saying:
"Ordinary people are deluded by profound principles, while śramaṇas are hindered by proximate teachings. Those deluded by profound principles claim that the Ultimate Way is mere empty talk;
those hindered by proximate teachings remain bound and attached to written texts."
"As for what the Dharma Master has said, it is truly an awakening of profound insight; he is one with whom one may discuss the boundaries between the divine and the human.

Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued for him to reside at Jetavana Monastery, where he was provided with generous and abundant support; among the princes, dukes, and eminent scholars, there were none who did not revere and follow him.

Shortly thereafter, he began lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* at the monastery. On the days of these dharma assemblies, carriages and canopies filled the streets; as people came and went to observe the teachings, they followed one another shoulder to shoulder and heel to heel.

Guṇavarman’s spiritual treasury was naturally profound and his wondrous eloquence was transcendent; at times, he would employ a translator, yet the exchange of ideas was understood with immediate insight. Later, Huiyi of the Jetavana Monastery requested that he translate the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*.

Initially, twenty-eight chapters were produced, and later his disciples continued the work by translating two more chapters, completing thirty chapters. Before these could be transcribed, the "Chapter on the Sequence" (*Anukrama-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on the Precepts" (*Śīla-parivarta*) were lost. Consequently, there are still two extant versions today, one of which is titled the *Bodhisattva-śīla-bhūmi*.

In the third year of the Yuanjia era, Wang Zhongde, the Regional Inspector of Xuzhou, invited the foreigner Saṃghavarman (Iye Poluo) at Pengcheng to translate the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*. However, when they reached the chapter on "Selection" (*Vibhaṅga*), obstacles arose and the work was consequently discontinued.

At this time, he further requested Guṇavarman to translate the subsequent chapters, completing the work in thirteen fascicles. Together with the previously translated *Caturvargika-karman*, the *Upāsaka-pañcaśīla-saṃkṣepa-śāstra*, and the *Upāsaka-dvāviṃśati-śīla*, there were twenty-six fascicles in total; all were detailed and accurate in both wording and meaning, with no discrepancy between the Sanskrit original and the Chinese translation.
At that time, the nuns Huiguo and Jingyin of Yingfu Temple jointly requested Guṇavarman, saying:

"Six years ago, eight nuns from the Kingdom of Siṃhala arrived in the capital and stated that there had never previously been nuns in the land of Song. How, then, could the two assemblies have conferred the precepts? We fear that the integrity of the precept-body is incomplete."

Bamó said: "The dharma of the precepts fundamentally originates from the great assembly of monks; even if one does not serve as a formal preceptor, there is no obstacle to receiving the precepts, as was the case with Mahāprajāpatī."
The nuns were again afraid that the years and months [of their ordination] would not be complete, and they earnestly desired to receive it once more. Guṇavarman declared, "Excellent!
If you truly wish to increase your clarity, I shall greatly rejoice in your endeavor."

"However, since the nuns from the Western Regions have not yet reached the required seniority and do not number ten, let them first study the Song language; meanwhile, we shall separately request foreign nuns to come through a lay devotee from the Western Regions so that the number of ten may be fulfilled."
In the summer of that year, he entered the retreat at the Lower Dinglin Temple.

At that time, there was a lay devotee who gathered flowers to spread over the seats; however, the flowers upon the seat where Guṇavarman sat were even more vibrant and fresh than the others. The assembly all revered him with saintly rites, and when the summer retreat concluded, he returned to Jetavana.

On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month of that year, before his midday meal was finished, he rose first and returned to his chamber; his disciple arrived later and found that he had already passed away, at the age of sixty-five.
Before his passing, he composed thirty-six lines of a posthumous verse in advance, explaining his own karmic conditions and stating that he had already realized the second fruit of the path.
He sealed it with his own hand and entrusted it to his disciple Āśāla, saying:
"After my death, you may present this text to the monks of India, and you may also show it to the monks of this region."
After he had passed away, they immediately helped him sit upon a rope-bench; his countenance was no different from before, appearing as if he were in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

More than a thousand people, both monastics and laymen, who gathered there all smelled a pungent and fragrant aroma and all saw an object resembling a dragon or a snake, about one *pí* in length, which rose from the side of the corpse and soared straight up toward heaven; none were able to identify it.
Thereupon, before the ordination platform in the Southern Forest, he was cremated according to the foreign rites.

The fourfold assembly gathered like scales; fragrant wood was piled into a pyre, drenched with scented oil to consume the remains. Five-colored flames rose up, their swirling vapors beautifying the sky.
At that time, the sky was clear and bright; both monastics and laypeople sighed in lamentation and subsequently erected a white stupa at that very spot.
The nuns who wished to receive the precepts once more wept bitterly, their hopes severed, unable to restrain themselves.

When Guṇavarman first arrived at the capital, Emperor Wen wished to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from him; however, as the northern barbarians were invading the borders, he had not yet had the opportunity to consult with him when the Emperor suddenly passed away.
Because his original intention had not been fulfilled, his grief and resentment grew ever deeper; he then ordered the assembly of monks to translate his final writings as follows:
First, I prostrate before the Triple Gem and the venerable elders of pure precepts.
In this defiled age, there is much flattery and crookedness; People are hypocritical and lack sincerity and trustworthiness.
Deluded by folly, they do not recognize the truth, And harboring envy, they disparage those with virtue.
For this reason, the various sages and saints Cause their traces to vanish from view in this world.
I, Guṇavarma, as the time for the end of my life has arrived,
shall now speak truthfully of the wholesome merits I have attained.
Without a mind of flattery or crookedness, nor with any hope of seeking fame or profit, I shall declare them.
To exhort those who are indolent and to increase all Buddha-dharmas, the power of the Great Dharma is such as this;
O virtuous ones, listen all with close attention.
In the past, amidst the wilderness, I first contemplated a corpse.
Swollen, bloated, and putridly decayed, with foul-smelling pus and blood flowing;
fix the mind upon such a state, for the nature of this body is thus.
Constantly beholding these characteristics of the body, the moth of craving knows no fear of the fire.
In this way, through countless varieties, he practiced the contemplation of the corpse;
having set aside other study and reflection, he took refuge among the forest trees.
That night, with focused diligence, he maintained right contemplation without ever forgetting it.
The objective realm is ever before me, as if facing a clear mirror.
As it is with that, so it is with me; by this, the mind becomes tranquil and still.
The body feels light and exceedingly pure; this coolness of mind is true bliss.
Increasing great joy, one then gives rise to a mind free from attachment.
It transforms into the appearance of a skeleton; white bones manifest before one.
The limbs decay and fall apart, until the white bones are entirely extinguished.
Stainless wisdom blazes forth; having tamed my thoughts regarding the characteristics of phenomena, I then attained such a state that my body was peaceful and exceedingly supple.
Through practicing with such skillful means, my excellence increased and grew ever further.
Atoms perish moment by moment; the dharma of right mindfulness destroys [the perception of] form.
This is the ultimate nature of the body—by what cause, then, would one give rise to craving?
Know that birth arises from various sensations, like a fish greedily biting at the bait on a hook.
Those sensations undergo immeasurable destruction; moment by moment, one contemplates their dissolution.
Knowing their basis, one realizes they arise from the monkey-like mind.
Karma and its karmic retribution depend on conditions and perish moment by moment.
The various things known by the mind are called phenomena with distinct characteristics (*svalakṣaṇadharma*).

This is the mindfulness of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayīprajñā*); through successive fulfillment of cultivation, one contemplates the various characteristics of phenomena, and the mind becomes increasingly clear and lucid.
Within the sphere of all phenomena, I clearly perceive the four foundations of mindfulness;
from this, my disciplined conduct is perfected, and I dwell with a concentrated mind focused upon its objects.
Suffering is like a blazing sword, arising from the turning of craving.
With craving extinguished, one attains parinirvāṇa, seeing clearly through all three realms.
Though scorched by the flames of death and the body becoming exceedingly emaciated,
through the joy of resting in skillful means, the body gradually becomes full once more.
The marks of a supreme and wondrous being, as well as the patience of the crown of the head, arise from within my own mind; this is the true and correct expedient means.
Gradually narrowing the sphere of objects, the joy of quiescence increases.
Attaining the Supreme Mundane Dharma, one contemplates the True Reality in a single thought-moment.
From this, the sequential patience regarding the Dharma arises; this is called the untainted path.
All conceptual constructions and their objects, as well as names and designations, are entirely transcended.
The meaning of the ultimate truth of the objective realm Eliminates affliction and attains refreshing clarity;
It achieves the fruit of samādhi, A condition for stainless purity and coolness.
Neither surging nor sinking, Pure wisdom is like the bright moon.
Tranquil and perfectly abiding, it is the singular mark of quiescence.
It is not that which I proclaim; only a Buddha can realize and know it.
In the *Nāpābhidharma*, five causal conditions for the fruit are taught.
The practice of knowing the ultimate reality cannot be seen by those who rely on names;
while various treatises present divergent ends, the principle of practice is non-dual.
Those who cling to partiality find right and wrong, but the one who has attained realization is free from conflict.
I shall not now proclaim the various wondrous marks cultivated through practice,
for I fear that people will give rise to false conceptions and thereby delude the world.
Regarding those marks of cultivated excellence, I have already explained a small portion.
If that wise one well understands this dependent origination,
he shall first attain the fruit of the noble ones within the borders of the kingdom of Mālava.
In a mountain hermitage in the forest, he shall cultivate the path of detachment.
Later, in the Lion Kingdom (Sīhaladvīpa), in a village named Kapila, he advanced in his practice and attained the second fruit; this is called the Sakṛdāgāmin.
From that time on, many obstacles arose, hindering his cultivation of the path to the abandonment of desire.
Seeing me practicing seclusion and knowing this place to be empty and quiet,
all developed a sense of rare wonder, and offerings and gain gathered there in competition.
Seeing these as like fire or poison, my heart gave rise to great wearying detachment.
Fleeing the chaos, he drifted upon the sea to Śrīvijaya and Lâm Ấp;
driven by the winds of karma, he followed his conditions to the borders of Song.
Thereupon, among these various kingdoms, he promoted the Buddha-dharma according to his capacity.
Without asking what should be asked, he contemplated with truth and reality;
now this body is extinguished, as tranquil as a lamp that has gone out. 8.
Saṃghavarman: "Saṃghavarman" means "Armor of the Multitude. He was a native of India.

Having renounced worldly life in his youth, he was pure and austere, possessing the virtue of the precepts; he was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and especially proficient in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he departed from Liusha and arrived at the capital.
His demeanor was grand and solemn; both monastics and laypeople revered him as extraordinary and all took him as their teacher, calling him the "Dharma Master of the Tripiṭaka.

Initially, in the first year of the Jingping era, Xu Sang, the Magistrate of Pinglu, donated his residence to establish a monastery, which was thus named Pinglu Temple. Later, Huiguan of Daochang Temple, recognizing that Guṇavarman’s spiritual conduct was pure and complete, invited him to reside at this temple.
They honored him with offerings to manifest his virtue.
Guṇavarman and others together oversaw the addition of three stories to the stupa; this is the present Fencheng Stupa.
Guṇavarman practiced the Way and recited scriptures day and night without ceasing; the monastic community gathered around him, and his spiritual transformation spread far and wide.

The Tripiṭaka Master, who was profoundly learned in the categories of the precepts, was about to administer the full ordination again to the nun Huìguǒ and others at Yǐngfú Monastery; however, at that time, the two assemblies were not yet complete when the Tripiṭaka Master passed away.

Shortly thereafter, the Bhikṣuṇīs Tiṣyā and others from Siṃhala arrived at the capital, whereupon the assembly collectively requested Guṇavarman to serve as their preceptor to continue the tradition of the Tripiṭaka masters.

Meanwhile, Huiyi of Jetavana was prominent in the imperial city; considering Guṇavarman’s approach to be eccentric, he held a different set of convictions and personally engaged in a series of confrontational debates with him.

Guṇavarman established the fundamental tenets and elucidated the Dharma; his reasoning was so clear, lucid, and convincing that, as his virtue found its rightful source, the lay official eventually softened his rigid disposition.
