He humbly submitted and yielded, ordering his disciple Huiji and others to receive him with devotion and serve him, while several hundred monks and nuns likewise accepted his teachings.

Prince Yikang of Pengcheng of the Song dynasty revered his precepts and models, extensively providing offerings for vegetarian feasts; the fourfold assembly gathered in great numbers, drawing crowds from throughout the capital.

Because Guṇavarman possessed a profound understanding of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* and could recite it with complete fluency, and because the previous Tripiṭaka master had translated it but not yet completed the transcription, Huiguan and others convened scholars at Changgan Monastery in the ninth month of that year to request another translation.
Baoyun translated the oral recitation, while Guanzi transcribed it by hand; after a thorough examination, collation, and verification, the work was completed in one cycle.
Subsequently, he produced the *Mātṛkā*, the *Vibhaṅga-karmavipāka*, the *Saṃkṣipta-rāja-prabodhana-gāthā*, and the *Ārādhana-āryasaṃgha-snāna-vākya*, among others.

Guṇavarman’s ambition was to travel and transform others, never remaining fixed in a single location. Once he had finished transmitting the scriptures, he took his leave to return to his native country; although the assembly all entreated him to stay, none were able to detain him.
In the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he returned to his native country on a merchant ship from the Western Regions; his ultimate fate is unknown.
9. Dharmamitra: Dharmamitra is translated here as Fashou (Dharma-Excellence). He was a native of Jibin.

When he reached the age of seven, his spiritual intelligence was clear and upright; whenever he witnessed Buddhist rites, he would spontaneously leap with joy. His parents loved him and marveled at this, so they eventually allowed him to leave the household life.

In Kaśmīra, many sages and realized ones have appeared; having repeatedly encountered enlightened masters, they have extensively mastered the various scriptures and possess particularly profound mastery of the methods of dhyāna. The gateways they have attained are exceedingly subtle and profound.

He was a man of profound depth and great wisdom, whose conduct and rituals were meticulous and correct. He was born with joined eyebrows, and thus he was known in the world as "The Master of Joined Eyebrows.

From his youth, he delighted in traveling abroad, vowing to propagate the teachings; he journeyed through various kingdoms and eventually reached Kucha. One day before his arrival, the King dreamed that a deity told him:
"A person of great merit and virtue shall enter this country tomorrow; you should provide him with offerings."
At dawn the following day, he immediately issued an edict to the outer officials, commanding that should any extraordinary person enter the borders, they must be dispatched to report it to him.

Shortly thereafter, Mātṛceṭa indeed arrived; the King went out to the outskirts of the city to welcome him in person, invited him into the palace, and subsequently received the precepts from him, performing all four types of ritual services.
Mita remained settled yet was able to move on; unconstrained by gain or offerings, he lived there for several years until he developed the intention to depart.
The deity again descended in a dream and said:
"A person of merit is leaving the King."
The king was startled awake by this; subsequently, although the sovereign and his ministers earnestly sought to detain him, none were able to stop him.
He then crossed the shifting sands and proceeded to Dunhuang, where he established a vihāra on a spacious and open site.
He planted a thousand peach trees and established a garden of one hundred mu; its halls, pavilions, ponds, and marshes were exceedingly solemn and pure.

Shortly thereafter, he traveled again to Liangzhou, where he renovated the hall and chambers at the former temple of the government office. His disciples gathered in great numbers, and his practice of Chan meditation flourished most vibrantly.

Constantly intending to transmit the Dharma to the royal capital on the left bank of the Yangtze River, he traveled by circuitous routes until reaching Shu in the first year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. Shortly thereafter, he emerged from the Gorges and settled in Jingzhou, where he constructed a meditation pavilion at Changsha Temple; with sincere and earnest devotion, he prayed for the appearance of śarīra relics.

After more than ten days, a single [fruit] was finally produced; it struck the vessel with a sound and emitted light that filled the room. Among the disciples, both monastics and laypeople, there was none who did not further increase their vigor and resolve, each redoubling their efforts.
Shortly thereafter, he traveled eastward down the river until he reached the capital.

Initially, he stayed at Zhongxing Temple, later resting at Zhihuan Temple. Since Samghamitra’s reputation for the Way had long been established and his transformative influence had permeated the surrounding regions, as soon as he arrived in the capital, the entire city turned out to pay their respects and inquire after him.

From Empress Yuan of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, through the Crown Prince and the Princesses, there were none who did not hold vegetarian fasts in the Gui Palace and request the precepts for the ladies of the inner court; messengers bearing inquiries followed one another every ten days.
Thereupon, at the Jetavana Monastery, he translated the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, the *Essentials of Dhyāna Methods*, the *Universal Worthy Contemplation*, the *Ākāśagarbha Contemplation*, and others.
He constantly taught the path of dhyāna; those who came from as far as a thousand *li* to seek his instruction—monks and laypeople alike from near and far—all hailed him as the "Great Dhyāna Master.

Meng Yi of Pingchang, the Governor of Kuaiji, held the True Dharma in deep faith and took the Three Jewels as his personal responsibility. Having long delighted in the flavor of meditation and possessed a profound sense of reverence, when he arrived in the region south of the Zhe River, he invited [Huiyi] to travel with him and subsequently established a stupa and monastery on the mountain at Maoshan.

In the ancient customs of the eastern borders, people mostly resorted to shamans and sorcerers; however, once transformed by this wondrous edification, every household returned to the orthodox path. From west to east, there was none who did not submit with sincere conviction.
In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era, he returned to the capital and resided at Dinglin Xia Temple on Mount Zhong.

Guṇabhadra was by nature serene and tranquil, possessing a refined love for mountains and rivers; he considered Mount Zhong to be a presiding peak whose beauty rivaled that of Mount Song and Mount Hua. He often lamented that the foundations and structures of Xia Temple were situated low and sloping toward a mountain stream.

Thereupon, he ascended a high point to survey the terrain and measured the topography of the mountain range. In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, he cleared away stones and felled trees to establish the Upper Monastery. The local officials and commoners, moved by his reputation, made offerings in such abundance that meditation halls and temple buildings rose up in tiered splendor. Consequently, a multitude of those who had renounced worldly desires gathered from ten thousand *li* away; they chanted the scriptures with solemn harmony, and their conduct transformed the region through the mere influence of his presence.

Dinglin Da Chan Master was a disciple endowed with supernormal powers; he propagated the teachings and his reputation resounded among both the clergy and the laity. Consequently, he was able to purify the community such that it remained unchanged for a long time, and his meritorious deeds were so lofty that they never faltered—this was truly the enduring legacy of Matanga.
From the Western Regions down to the southern lands, wherever he traveled, he established assemblies for almsgiving (*dāna*) and expounded the teachings without exception.

Initially, when Guṇamati departed from Kaśmīra, the divine king Kapiśa escorted him; they eventually reached Kucha, but midway on the journey, the king wished to return and manifested his form to bid farewell to Guṇamati, saying:
"Your supernatural powers and transformations allow you to travel everywhere with ease; I shall not accompany you further as we proceed to the south."
Having finished speaking, she immediately withdrew her shadow so that it was no longer visible.

He then followed her from afar to the capital, where she had an image painted upon the wall of the Upper Temple. To this day, there are still manifestations of her voice and shadow; those who pray with pure sincerity for blessings do not fail to have their wishes fulfilled.
He passed away at Shangsi Temple on the sixth day of the seventh month in the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era, at the age of eighty-seven.
The fourfold assembly of monastics and laypeople followed him with wailing and lamentation; he was subsequently buried in front of Songxi Temple on Mount Zhong.
10. Shi Zhimeng. Shi Zhimeng was a native of Xinfeng in Jingzhao, Yongzhou. By nature he was upright and intelligent;

he was diligent in his conduct and pure in his character. Having donned the dharma robes at a young age, he devoted himself single-mindedly to his studies, the sound of his recitation continuing from night into day.

Whenever I heard foreign monks speak of the land of India, where the traces of Śākyamuni’s legacy and the various Mahāyāna sūtras were preserved, I was constantly moved by a profound sense of longing. My mind yearned for those distant realms, and I considered ten thousand li to be but a few inches, believing that even a millennium could be bridged.

Thereupon, in the year Jiachen, the sixth year of the Hongshi era of the pseudo-Qin dynasty, he gathered fifteen fellow śramaṇas of like mind and set out from Chang’an. Crossing thirty-six rivers and valleys, they reached the city of Liangzhou.
Departing from Yangguan Pass and heading west into the shifting sands, he traversed perilous heights and treacherous terrain, surpassing all accounts in previous records.
He subsequently journeyed through the kingdoms of Shanshan, Kucha, and Khotan, observing their customs and culture in full detail.

Traveling two thousand li southwest from Khotan, they first ascended the Onion Range (Pamir), where nine of the men turned back; Mǎng and his remaining companions proceeded another seventeen hundred li and reached the kingdom of Bolor.
His fellow traveler, Zhu Daosong, also passed away; as they were about to perform the cremation, the corpse suddenly vanished from its place.
Filled with grief and struck by this marvel, Sengmeng exerted his strength and moved forward.
Accompanied by four others, he crossed the Snow Mountains and the Indus River, arriving at the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
There were five hundred arhats in that country who constantly traveled to and from Lake Anavatapta; upon seeing Meng, a great virtuous arhat was filled with joy.
Fameng inquired about the local regions, and [the king] recounted for him the affairs of the four deva-kings, as recorded in full in Fameng’s *Biography*.

In the kingdom of Qiśā, Fameng saw a stone spittle-pot of the Buddha; furthermore, in this same kingdom, he saw the Buddha’s almsbowl, its luster being a deep violet-blue, uniform throughout its four edges.
He made offerings of fragrant flowers with great vigor and, holding [the bowl] upon his head, made a vow.
If the bowl was appropriate for him, he could lift it lightly or carry it heavily.

After a while, it became increasingly heavy until his strength could no longer sustain it; yet when he set it down on the table, he again perceived no weight. Such is the manifestation of his resolute mind (*bodhicitta*).

Traveling again one thousand three hundred li to the southwest, he reached the kingdom of Kapilavastu, where he beheld the Buddha’s hair, his tooth, and the bone of his *uṣṇīṣa*, as well as the Buddha’s shadow and footprints, all of which remained vividly intact.

Furthermore, beholding the forest of the firm Nirvana and the Bodhi tree where Māra was subdued, his heart was filled with fierce joy; he made offerings for one day, using precious canopies and great robes to cover the image of the Subduer of Māra.
In the places he traveled and visited, he thoroughly observed spiritual transformations; the accounts of the Heavenly Ladder and the Dragon Pond are beyond counting.

Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, the former capital of King Aśoka, where there was a Brahmin of great wisdom named Rāyagṛha. His entire clan propagated the Dharma, and he was held in high esteem by the king, who had constructed a pure silver stupa thirty feet high.
Having seen that Daomeng had arrived, he asked,
"Is there the study of the Mahāyāna in the land of Qin? Meng replied:
"All have studied the Mahāyāna.
Rājagṛha was struck with wonder and exclaimed, "How rare!
How rare! Could it not be that a Bodhisattva has gone there to transform them?"

In his home, Meng obtained one copy of the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, as well as one copy of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other Sanskrit manuscripts of various sūtras; vowing to circulate them, he then returned.
Setting out from India in the year of Jiǎzǐ, he was accompanied by three companions; however, they met with death along the way, leaving only Fǔměng and Tánzuàn to return together.
In Liangzhou, they produced a version of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, obtaining twenty fascicles.
In the fourteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he entered Shu; in the seventh month of the sixteenth year, he composed the *Biography* (*zhuan*) to record his travels.
At the end of the Yuanjia era, he passed away in Chengdu.
I have extensively sought out itinerant śramaṇas and recorded their accounts of the routes; these often differ from one another.

As for the locations of the Buddha’s alms bowl and cranial bone, they likewise vary; this suggests that those traveling to India did not follow only a single path, and that the sacred relics of the cranial bone and the bowl were transferred to different lands at different times.
Therefore, it is difficult to establish a precedent based on the accounts of what has been seen and heard. 11.
*Kang-lyang-ye-she* (畺良耶舍): This is translated as "Renowned in His Time. He was a native of the Western Regions.

By nature he was upright and straightforward, with few worldly desires. He was skilled at reciting the *Abhidharma* and had extensively studied the Vinaya sections; as for the other various sūtras, he had mastered a great many. Although he was proficient in all three piṭakas, he specialized professionally in the gates of meditation (*dhyāna*).

During each period of contemplative wandering, he would sometimes remain without rising for seven days, constantly dwelling in the correct reception of samādhi as he traveled to convert various kingdoms.
At the beginning of the Yuanjia era, he braved the perilous desert sands to arrive at the capital, where Emperor Taizu Wenhuang deeply marveled at his extraordinary qualities.

Initially, he resided at Daolin Monastery on Mount Zhong; the śramaṇa Baozhi revered his methods of dhyāna, and the śramaṇa Senghan requested him to translate the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-vyūha* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna*, which Senghan then took down in writing.

Since these two sutras are the secret arts for transforming obstacles and the great causes for attaining the Pure Land, he pondered them deeply and relished their meaning, subsequently circulating them throughout the Song dynasty.

Meng Yi of Pingchang, who had long admired and revered his teachings, provided him with abundant support; when Yi was appointed as the Governor of Kuaiji, he earnestly requested that [Huiyuan] not depart, but later moved to reside in Jiangling.

In the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he traveled west to the regions of Min and Shu, propagating the Way everywhere; students of Chan practice gathered in great numbers around him. Later, he returned and passed away in Jiangling at the age of sixty.
At that time, there were also the Indian śramaṇas Saṃghadatta and Saṃgharāta, both of whom were profoundly learned in the study of dhyāna, who came to travel within the borders of the Song dynasty.

Once, while Saṃghadatta was practicing seated meditation in the mountains, as the time for his midday meal approached and he thought of fasting, a flock of birds flew in carrying fruits and presented them to him.

Upatiṣya reflected that since the Buddha had accepted and eaten the honey offered by the monkey, why should he not accept the food now offered by the bird? Thereupon, he accepted it and partook of it.
In the summer of the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he accepted an invitation from the Prince of Linchuan, the Kang Wang, and settled at Guangling; later, he passed away in Jianye.
Saṃgharāta—translated into Chinese as Zhòngjì (Savior of the Multitude)—arrived at the capital toward the end of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty.
He begged for alms among the people and sat in meditation beneath the forest trees, nourishing his simple nature in secluded leisure and remaining uninvolved with the affairs of the age.
In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era, he chose a site on the southern slope of Mount Zhong, cleared away thorns and brambles, and constructed a vihāra; this was the present-day Songxi Temple.
12. Guṇabhadra: Guṇabhadra means "Virtuous Merit" (Guṇakalyāṇa) in this language. He was a native of Central India; because he studied the Mahāyāna, he was known in the world as Mahāyāna.

Originally of Brahmin descent, he studied the various treatises on the five sciences from his youth; there was nothing among astronomy, writing, mathematics, medicine, or incantations that he did not master extensively.
Later, upon encountering the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, he read it with great astonishment and realization, thereafter deeply venerating the Buddha-dharma.

His family followed the way of the worldlings and prohibited him from associating with śramaṇas; consequently, he left his home and went into hiding, traveling far to seek teachers and friends. Thereupon, he cast off his hairpin and discarded his finery, dedicating himself with focused resolve to study.
Upon receiving full ordination, he became widely versed in the Tripiṭaka. He was compassionate, harmonious, respectful, and diligent by nature, serving his teacher with the utmost propriety.
After some time, he took leave of his teacher of the Hīnayāna and advanced to study the Mahāyāna.

The Mahayana master tested him by having him reach into a case of scriptures; he immediately drew out the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. The master praised him and sighed, saying:
"You have a profound karmic affinity with the Mahayana."
Thereupon, he recited and expounded [the scriptures], such that no one could challenge or oppose him; he then proceeded to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
He subsequently sent a letter to his parents, urging them to return to the True Dharma, saying:
"If you persist solely in following non-Buddhist paths, then even if you return, it will be of no benefit; however, if you place your faith in the Triple Gem, then we shall see each other forever."
His father, moved by the sincerity of these words, subsequently abandoned heterodoxy and followed the orthodox path.

Guṇabhadra proceeded to various kingdoms of the Lion Country (Siṃhala), where he was provided with all necessary provisions and offerings. Having established a karmic connection with the East, he then boarded a merchant vessel and set sail across the sea.
Midway, the wind ceased and the fresh water was exhausted; the entire ship's company was filled with anxiety and fear.
Guṇabhadra said, "We should unite our hearts and exert our strength to mind the Buddhas of the ten directions and invoke Avalokiteśvara; there is nowhere he will not respond."
He then secretly recited the dharani sutras and performed prostrations and repentance with utmost sincerity.

Suddenly, a favorable wind arose in a gale and dark clouds brought rain, whereby his entire ship was saved. Such was the power of his sincere devotion; in the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, he arrived at Guangzhou, where the Provincial Governor Che Lang reported his arrival to the throne, and Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty sent envoys to welcome him.

Upon his arrival in the capital, the Emperor issued an edict for the eminent monks Huìyán and Huìguān to welcome him at Xīntíng. Seeing that his spirit was clear and penetrating, all were filled with reverent admiration; although they conversed through an interpreter during the translation, they felt as much joy as if meeting a long-lost friend under a roadside tree.
At first he resided at Jetavana Monastery; shortly thereafter, the Great Ancestor (Emperor Wen) invited him and accorded him profound reverence.

Yan Yanzhi of Langya, a man of versatile talent and vast learning, came to his door with his belt fastened in formal attire. Consequently, from near and far throughout the capital, carriages and canopies followed one after another; both the Generalissimo, Prince Yi Kang of Pengcheng, and the Chancellor, Prince Yi Xuan of Nanqiao, served as his disciples.

Shortly thereafter, the assembly of monks collectively requested that he produce a translation of the scriptures. At Jihuan Temple, he assembled various monks specializing in doctrinal studies to translate the *Saṃyuktāgama*. At Dong’an Temple, he produced the *Dharmabherī-sūtra*. Later, at Danyang Commandery, he translated the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. With more than seven hundred followers, Baoyun acted as the oral translator while Huiguan took up the brush; through their repeated consultation and analysis, they captured the profound essence of the original texts with great precision.
Later, when the Prince of Qiao was stationed in Jingzhou, he invited Kumārajīva to accompany him. They settled at Xinsi Temple, where new halls and chambers were constructed.

There, at Xinsi Temple, Kumārajīva produced translations of the *Rāstrapālaparipṛcchā*, one fascicle of the *Past and Present Causes and Effects Sūtra*, one fascicle of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, the *Aṅgulimālīya*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-pāramitā-nītārtha*, the three-fascicle *Buddhanāmasūtra*, the *Paramārtha-pañcalakṣaṇasaṃkṣepa*, the *Aṣṭamaṅgalika*, and other various sūtras. Together with his previous works, these totaled over one hundred fascicles. He constantly had his disciple Fayong transmit the translations and provide the oral interpretation.

The Prince of Qiao wished to invite [Bodhiruci] to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras; however, Bodhiruci reflected that he was not yet proficient in the Song language and felt a sense of shame and regret. He immediately performed prostrations and repentance rites morning and evening, invoking Avalokiteśvara and praying for a hidden response.
He then dreamed of a person dressed in white garments holding a sword, who brought a human head before him and asked,
"Why are you grieving?
Guṇabhadra related the matter in detail, to which the figure replied:
"Do not grieve excessively.
He then exchanged his head for that of the sword, replacing it with the new one.
He spoke to him, commanding him to turn back, saying:
"Are you free from pain?
He replied, "I am not in pain."
Suddenly he was awakened and his mind became joyful and serene.
Rising at dawn, he fully understood the meaning of the words in the Song language and subsequently began to lecture upon them.
Toward the end of the Yuanjia era, Prince Xiao of Qiao repeatedly had strange dreams; Guṇabhadra replied to him as follows:
“Calamity and disorder shall befall the capital of Kyoto. Less than a year later, the primary culprit plotted a rebellion.

At the beginning of the Xiaojian era, Prince Xiao Qiao secretly conspired toward treasonous intent; Guṇabhadra’s countenance became grave and sorrowful. Before he could speak, Prince Qiao asked him the reason for his distress. Guṇabhadra admonished and remonstrated with such earnestness that he departed in tears, saying: [The following text continues from here.]
"I have no expectations whatsoever; I cannot allow myself to be accompanied by attendants.
Because the Prince of Qiao was someone whom the people trusted, he nevertheless pressured him to go down with him.

At the defeat at Liangshan, the great ships were driven in close pursuit and the distance from the shore was vast, making total escape impossible. With single-minded devotion, he invoked Avalokiteśvara, grasped an *qióngzhú* staff in his hand, and threw himself into the river. The water reached only to his knees; as he prodded the water with his staff, the current flowed deep and swift. He saw a young boy following after him, who took him by the hand. Looking back, he said to the boy:
"How could you, a mere child, deliver me?

In a daze, he suddenly found himself having walked some ten paces and had already reached the shore. He immediately removed his inner robe, intending to repay the boy, but when he looked around for him, he was nowhere to be seen. His hair stood on end with terror, and only then did he realize it was the power of a divine spirit.
At that time, General Xuanmu was commanding the troops at Liangshan; Emperor Shizu issued an edict to the army, stating:
"If you capture Mahāyāna, treat him with great care and send him to the Imperial Court by express courier."
Shortly thereafter, he was found and sent to the capital by boat. Emperor Shizu immediately granted him an audience and questioned him in detail, saying:
"I have long looked forward to this; only now do we finally meet."
Bhadra said, “Since I have been stained by wickedness, I deserve to be reduced to ashes; that I may now have the honor of an audience is a profound gift from Your Majesty.

When the Emperor asked who had acted as his accomplices in the rebellion, he replied, “As one who has left the household life, I was not involved in military affairs; however, Zhang Chang, Zong Lingxiu, and others were all driven and coerced into it.”
"What I have clarified, O Poor Monk, was not intended for such a karmic connection as this.
The Emperor said,
"I have nothing to fear."
On that day, he was commanded to reside in the Rear Hall; robes and provisions were bestowed upon him, and he was provided with a carriage and attendants.
Previously, while Guṇabhadra had been in Jingzhou for ten years, every letter and correspondence he exchanged with Prince Qiao was recorded.
When the army was defeated and the records were examined, not a single word concerning military affairs could be found.
Emperor Shizu, recognizing his purity and prudence, treated him with even greater courtesy.
Later, during a casual conversation, the Emperor jokingly asked him:
"Do you remember the Chancellor?
He replied, "I have received his offerings for ten years; how could I forget his virtue?"
"I now beg a boon from Your Majesty: I wish to burn incense for the Chancellor for three years.
The Emperor’s countenance grew somber with sorrow, and out of a sense of righteousness, he granted his request.
When Zhongxing Temple was completed, the Emperor issued an edict ordering him to move there and provided him with three rooms.

Later, at a banquet held in the Eastern Palace where princes and dukes had all assembled, the Emperor issued an edict to have Guṇabhadra appear before him. At that time, he had not yet undergone the tonsure ceremony, and his hair was white and gleaming. From afar, Emperor Shizu gazed at him and turned to address the Minister of Personnel, Xie Zhuang, saying:
"Mahāyāna is brilliant and possesses keen intellectual acumen; however, old age has already arrived for him. Let me question him; he will surely be able to discern the intentions of men."
Bhadra ascended the steps and, greeting him, said:
"The Mahāyāna does not fail the purpose of your journey from afar; however, there is but one remaining.
He immediately replied in kind:

"I, this poor monk, have returned from afar to the imperial capital for nearly thirty years; the Emperor's gracious favor has filled me with boundless gratitude. Yet, being seventy years old and afflicted by illness, death alone remains before me."
The Emperor praised his quick wit and eloquence, issuing an edict for him to sit near the imperial presence, while the entire court turned their eyes toward him.

Later, he established a monastery west of the Phoenix Pavilion in the borders of Moling; every time it reached midnight, there would suddenly be someone knocking at the door and calling out, yet when they looked, no one was there. This occurred repeatedly, causing the community to be plagued by such experiences.
Bhadra burned incense and made this prayer:
"Your karmic affinity lies here; as I now establish this monastery, I shall constantly perform the Way, prostrations, and repentance for your sake."
"If they remain, they shall serve as guardian deities of the monastery;
if they cannot remain, let each go wherever they find rest.

Subsequently, more than ten monastics and laypeople alike dreamed that very night of thousands of ghosts and spirits all carrying their belongings away on their shoulders. Thereupon, the community of the monastery became peaceful.
The White Pagoda Temple at Houzhu on the banks of the Tao River today is that very site.
In the sixth year of the Daming era, a severe drought prevailed throughout the land; prayers were offered to the mountains and rivers for many months without result.
The Emperor requested that he perform a rain prayer, stipulating that it must produce a response; he added that if no results were obtained, they need not meet again.
Guṇabhadra said, "I look up to the Triple Gem and rely upon Your Majesty’s celestial majesty, hoping that the rains will surely descend."
"If I do not obtain it, I shall never see it again.

He then went to the Fishing Platform at the Northern Lake to burn incense and offer prayers; he abstained from food and drink, silently recited the sutras, and secretly added the invocation of esoteric mantras.

The following day at the hour of *pūṣa* (the afternoon), clouds rose from the northwest like a canopy; as the sun hung low over the mulberry trees, a wind shook the earth and the clouds gathered, raining continuously for several days.

On the following morning, the high officials entered to offer congratulations. By imperial decree, he was granted an audience and comforted with kind words, and gifts and offerings were bestowed upon him in succession.
From his childhood until the end of his life, Bhadra maintained a vegetarian diet; he constantly held a censer in his hand, never letting it fall from his grasp.
Whenever he finished a meal, he would invariably share some with the birds, which would gather around his hands to take the food.
During the reign of Emperor Taizong, the offerings of ritual respect became increasingly grand.
In the first month of the fourth year of the Dashi era, Daohui’s health declined;
he then took his leave of Emperor Taizong, the high officials, and others.
On the day of his death, he stood waiting expectantly as he looked toward [the west].
He beheld celestial flowers and sacred images, and passed away at the hour of Youzhong (between 8:00 and 10:00 AM). He was seventy-five years of age.
Emperor Taizong deeply mourned him and provided exceptionally generous consolations and funeral expenses; high officials assembled for the burial, and both honor and sorrow were fully manifest.
At that time, there was also the śramaṇa Baoyi, whose Sanskrit name was Anamati. His original surname was Kang, and he was a native of Kangju, though his family had resided in India for generations.

During the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty, he came to reside at the Waguan Chan Hall in the capital. He frequently practiced seated meditation beneath the trees within the monastery and was also well-versed in the Sūtras and Vinaya; thus, his contemporaries also referred to him as a "Tripitaka Master."
He would constantly roll several hundred cowrie shells, and by doing so, he could immediately discern whether an event would be auspicious or ominous.
He was highly skilled in divine incantations; by applying fragrant paste to his palms, he could also perceive the past events of others.
During the reign of Emperor Shizu of the Song dynasty, he was presented with a bronze spittoon about two feet high, which he kept constantly before his bed; suddenly, someone stole it.

Yi took a single mat, folded it empty, and recited incantations over it several times; after three nights had passed, the spittoon was found back inside the mat, and no one could fathom how this came to be.
Consequently, monastics and laypeople from all directions alike revered him and marveled at his excellence.
Emperor Wenhui, Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty, and Taizhu of the Liang dynasty all honored him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
At the end of the Yongming era, he passed away at his residence.
13. Guṇavidi: Guṇavidi is translated here as "Peaceful Progress" (Anjin). He was originally a native of Central India.

In his youth, he followed the Way and served as a disciple of the Mahayana Dharma Master Saṃghasena from India. He was intelligent and possessed a powerful memory; he applied himself diligently to recitation and had thoroughly mastered both the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings, totaling some two hundred thousand words.
He also studied non-Buddhist texts and was clearly versed in the principles of yin and yang; his prognostications regarding time and verification of events were manifold.

At the beginning of the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty, he arrived at the capital and stayed at Vairāṭya Monastery. Carrying his mendicant’s staff and followed by his disciples, his deportment was dignified and solemn; kings, dukes, and the nobility vied with one another to provide him with offerings and invitations.
Initially, Saṃghasena, while in the kingdom of India, excerpted essential parables from the Sūtra-piṭaka and compiled them into a single work containing one hundred items to instruct beginners.

He was thoroughly proficient in both the Indic languages and well-versed in their underlying meanings; in the autumn of the tenth year of the Yongming era, he translated [the text] into the Qi vernacular, totaling ten fascicles, known as the *Śatākavavadāna-sūtra* (The Sutra of One Hundred Parables).
He further produced one scroll each of the *Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* and the *Sūtra of the Elder Sudatta*.
Since the Great Ming dynasty, the translation of scriptures had almost ceased; yet when these were circulated, everyone praised them.

Vidhi was broad-minded and magnanimous; thus, people gathered from ten thousand *li* away, and merchants from the South Sea all took him as their master. He accepted all their offerings and provided for them entirely according to the Dharma.

On the banks of the Huai River in Jianye, he established and resided at Zhengguan Temple; its multi-storied pavilions and tiered gates were magnificent, and its halls and chambers were elegantly adorned.
In the winter of the second year of the Zhongxing era, he passed away at his residence.
At the beginning of the Liang dynasty, there was a monk named Saṃghavarman, also a foreign scholar-monk of dignified and pure appearance who excelled in debate.

Upon arriving at the capital, he also resided at Zhengguan Temple; the reigning Emperor treated him with great courtesy and honor, issuing an imperial decree for him to translate the *Mahārājakaniskalekha-sūtra* (The Great Sūtra of the King’s Instructions), the *Vimuktimārga-śāstra* (Treatise on the Path to Liberation), and other works at Zhengguan Temple and within the Zhanyun Hall of Shouguang Palace. Shi Baochang, Yuan Tanyun, and others served as scribes to receive his oral explanations.
The Treatise states:
The merit of those who transmitted and translated [the scriptures] is venerable; indeed, it is beyond words of praise.

Long ago, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Elder Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Madhyāntika, and others, all fully maintained the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma. They propagated the Way and saved sentient beings, their achievements being most extensive. The sunlight of their holy wisdom has not yet faded from its lingering radiance.

Thereafter, Kātyāyanīputra, Dharmatrāta, Dharmasiri, and others extensively investigated divergent doctrines and each composed their own expositions; yet they all traced their origins to the four Āgamas and took the Tripiṭaka as their fundamental authority.
As for Nāgārjuna, Aśvaghoṣa, and Vasubandhu, they grasped the essential pivot of the profound Vaipulya sūtras.

Their source originated from the Prajñāpāramitā and their stream flowed through the Twin Trees; though it is said that their transformations harmonized both the lowlands and the highlands, they likewise each attained its true nature.

Thus, the Three Jewels have been transmitted through the ages and the Wheel of Dharma has not ceased; for this reason, during the five hundred years [following the Buddha’s passing], it was still said that the True Dharma remained in the world.

Indeed, wherever divine transformations reach, they extend both far and near: a single sound or a single ray of light immediately shakes other lands, while a single platform or a single canopy moves to cover the entire land of *Heng* (the Sahā world).

Although the land of China and the realm of Kapilavastu are separated by the Pamirs and the Indus River, with tens of thousands of *li* between them, if one considers the divine power of the Sage, they are as close as a single step; that our hearing and seeing are thus obstructed and separated—could this not be due to the influence of the times?

When the conditions and destiny for its reception were about to be realized and the teachings of the Name (the Confucian tradition) were subtly permeating the land, some referred to him as the Master of the Fútú, while others hailed him as the Great Deity of the Western Regions.
Thus, Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty issued an edict to Prince Ying of Chu, saying:
"The Prince recites the subtle words of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi, and honors the benevolent sacrifices of the Fútú."
Following the dream of the golden man, he dispatched envoys to the Western Regions, whereupon Śrīmitra and Dharmaratna, harboring the Way, came to convert the people.

They joined forces for a solitary journey, determined to reach their destination despite all hardships; they skirted steep cliffs while gazing down into the abyss and stepped upon flying ropes to cross perilous passes.

He sacrificed his body for the sake of sentient beings, remaining equanimous even amidst hardships; he transmitted the Dharma and proclaimed the sutras, first bringing transformation to the Eastern Land. That later students have heard [the teachings] is surely due to his power.

From this point on, An Qing, Zhi Chen, Kang Senghui, Zhu Fahu, and others—appearing both across different eras and at the same time—successively followed one another’s footsteps to propagate and extol [the teachings].

However, as the customs of the barbarians and the Chinese differ and their phonetic systems are vastly separated, it is truly difficult to grasp the meaning unless one meticulously compiles glosses and explanations.

During this period, there were Zhi Qian, Nie Chengyuan, Zhu Fonian, Shi Baoyun, Zhu Shulan, and Mokṣala; all of them were exquisitely proficient in both Sanskrit and Chinese phonology, and were thus able to fully realize the essence of translation.
Each word was repeated three times until its meaning and intent were clear; only then were the musical scales of this land employed to refine and complete the composition.
The Treatise states:
"By employing the vernacular language of each region, one can demonstrate the correct principle; within that correct principle, one places words that follow the specific circumstances."
This is precisely what is meant by that.

Subsequently, Kumārajīva, a man of profound learning who plumbed the depths of the sublime and possessed a divine insight into the most remote mysteries, traveled extensively throughout the Central Lands and became thoroughly conversant with all local dialects.

Furthermore, he lamented that the translations by Zhi and Zhu were archaic and austere in their literary style, failing to fully capture excellence and beauty; he therefore consulted the Sanskrit original once more and retranslated it, so that the two versions—the ancient and the modern—differ in expression but are identical in meaning.

At that time, there were Daosheng, Daorong, Faying, Huiyi, Huayan, Daoguan, Daoheng, and Sengzhao; all of them had attained realization prior to words, their phrasing was as lustrous as pearls and jade, and they took up the pen to receive his instructions. As the responsibility rested with these individuals, the translations produced in Chang’an became preeminent and unsurpassed.
At that time, Yao Xing usurped the title of Emperor and held sway over the imperial capital; he revered and loved the Triple Gem, thereby upholding the legacy of the Dharma.

He caused those who aspired to the Way to come and attend his court, so that people from near and far gathered like clouds. Within the gateway of the Tripiṭaka, all who possessed the karmic affinity were able to behold it; since the eastward migration of the Buddhist era, its prosperity has reached its peak here.

The *Avataṃsaka* in its extensive version translated by the Bhikṣu Xian in Jiangdong; the wondrous teachings of the *Nirvāṇa* translated by Dharmakṣema in Hexi; and the four Āgamas, the five sections, the Khandakas, and the Vibhāṣā produced by various masters—all of these accord with the fundamental Dharma and satisfy the three seals of the Dharma.

Yet Kumārajīva incurred the fault of having a separate residence, and Buddhabhadra left behind the record of being expelled; examining these actual accounts, it is not easy to investigate them in detail.
Perhaps because the times were degenerate and the Way had perished, leading people to drift apart, what they perceived through their spiritual resonance reached such extremes as these.
If one seeks [the truth] by means of their recent traces, they were merely minor flaws upon a jade vessel.
Furthermore, there were An Shigao, Dharmakṣema, Fazu, Fazuo, and others.

Their principles were profound and their understanding comprehensive; their benevolence was like a pervasive mist. Yet none of them met a natural death. This must be because the retribution of karma is transmitted and felt, and righteousness allows for no evasion. Is it not so that even though the Arhats have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), they still suffered the calamity of having their skulls pierced; and though Bi Gan was loyal and exhausted his sincerity in remonstrance, he still encountered the disaster of being granted a sword? Could it be otherwise!

Among them was one named Zhu Fadu, who claimed to be exclusively devoted to the Hīnayāna, yet his practices diverged from the Tripiṭaka: he used a copper alms bowl, which is not permitted by the Vinaya, and he prostrated himself facing others, a practice that does not exist in the ritual of repentance.

Furthermore, Fadu was originally from Nankang and had never traveled to India; it was only late in life that he encountered Dhammayasas, yet even this teacher was not one exclusively devoted to the Hinayana. Fadu simply sought to fill the chasms of his own desires, and thus acted with such artificial eccentricity.

Nevertheless, the eminent gentlemen who had attained the measure of wisdom never turned their steps toward them; yet the nuns were easy to follow, and they were the first to receive their transformation.

Indeed, the principles and teachings for women are difficult to satisfy, while their conduct is easily reversed: when they hear of cause and effect, they remain indifferent and turn their backs; but when they see displays of miraculous arts, they rush forward and pour out their devotion. This is precisely what is meant by the principle of "falling into ruin" through following [false teachers].
I humbly reflect that the True Dharma is profound and vast, numbering as many as eight hundred million [teachings]. Yet, of those obtained through translation, there are but a mere thousand scrolls.

All of these resulted from crossing desert barriers and traversing perilous precipices; some crossed dangerous passes by sight of rising smoke, while others pressed forward by clinging to wooden pegs. Even when meeting and seeking them out, not one in ten remains—nine out of ten are lost.

Therefore, when Faxian, Zhimeng, Zhiyan, Fayong, and others set out on their journey, they traveled in groups with many companions; yet upon their return, they were left as solitary figures facing only their own shadows—how truly lamentable this is!

One should know that once this is realized, is it not as if one has been granted an extension of life? Yet, the students of recent generations merely aspire to pore over a single scripture, claiming that extensive reading leads to much confusion. This is surely the talk of those who have fallen away from learning; it is by no means the instruction for one who masters all quarters of knowledge.

Why is this? For one who wishes to investigate the flavor of principle and resolve the gates of the Dharma, how can they decide upon it solely from their own breast without extensively seeking among the various scriptures? Thus, they cause their laborious copying to remain forever hidden away in boxes and chests; the nectar-like true teaching is never sought out, and the unsurpassed jewel remains concealed and unused—is this not a pity!

If one can penetrate and extract the essence of Chan and Vinaya, and fuse the teachings of the Sutras and Shastras, then even though the shade of the Jetavana grove has ceased, the profound breeze still fans; and though the leaves of the Śāla trees have changed, the Buddha-nature remains manifest.
