His aspirations and conduct were upright and steadfast; neither encouragement nor dissuasion could alter his integrity.
From his youth, he harbored profound awakening and cast off the mundane world; after entering the monastic life, he devoted himself exclusively to the study of the scriptures.

Formerly, during the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, Zhu Foshuo translated the *Daoxing jing*, which is the original version of the *Xiaopin*. Its prose and phrasing were concise and brief, and its meaning was not yet fully comprehensive.

Shi Xing once lectured on the *Daoxing jing* in Luoyang; finding its phrasing obscure and its substance unrefined, he felt that certain aspects were not yet fully perfected. He frequently sighed, saying:
"This sutra contains the essentials of the Mahāyāna, yet the principles of its translation are incomplete."
Vowing to sacrifice his own body to seek out the original texts from afar, he set out from Yongzhou in the fifth year of the Ganlu era of the Wei dynasty and crossed the shifting sands to the west.

Upon reaching Khotan, he indeed obtained the authentic Sanskrit manuscripts consisting of ninety chapters in total; he then dispatched his disciple Buzhutan—which means "Dharmapriya" in the local language—to bring them back.
He was returning to Luoyang with the Sanskrit manuscripts of the sutras.
Before he had yet departed, the various followers of the Hīnayāna in Khotan went to inform the king, saying:
"The śramaṇas from the land of Han wish to use the books of the Brahmins to confuse and subvert the authentic scriptures."
"The King is the lord of the land; if you do not restrain him, he will sever the Great Dharma and leave the land of Han deaf and blind—this will be the King's fault.
The King then refused to allow the scriptures to be taken away.
Shixing harbored deep anguish in his heart and requested that the scriptures be burned as proof; the king immediately granted his request.
Thereupon, he piled firewood before the palace and set it ablaze with flames.
Shixing stood before the fire and made this vow:
"If the Great Dharma is destined to flow into the land of Han, these scriptures shall not be consumed by the flames; if there is no such protection, what is the use of my life!"

Having spoken thus, he cast the sutra into the fire; the flames were immediately extinguished, not a single character was damaged, and the parchment remained as it was originally. The great assembly was struck with awe and submission, all acclaiming it as a divine manifestation.
He was subsequently escorted to the South Temple on the Cangheng River in Chenliu.
At that time, there was the layman Zhu Shulan of Henan; originally a native of India, his father’s family had resided in Henan to escape political turmoil.
Lan was fond of hunting from his youth; later, he underwent a temporary death and witnessed the full retribution of his karmic deeds.
Consequently, he reformed himself with diligent devotion, deeply venerating the True Dharma, extensively investigating various languages, and becoming proficient in both Sanskrit and Chinese.

Furthermore, there was the monk Wuluocha, a master from the Western Regions who was deeply learned in ancient lore; he personally held the Sanskrit manuscript while Zhu Shulan translated it into the language of Jin, and it was titled the *Fàngguāng Bōrě* (The Radiant Prajñā).
The original manuscript on leather scrolls is currently located in Yuzhang.
In the second year of the Taian era, Zhi Xiaolong transcribed five copies from Shu Lan at one time, which were then collated to form the definitive edition.
At that time, there were no yet established categories; the old edition consisted of fourteen bolts of silk, which he ordered to be transcribed as twenty fascicles.
Daosheng eventually passed away in Khotan at the age of eighty.

They cremated him according to the Western method; when the wood was exhausted and the fire extinguished, the corpse remained intact. The multitude were all struck with wonder and astonishment, and they uttered this incantation:
"If you have truly attained the Way, then the body ought to be destroyed."
At his voice, [the body] was shattered and dispersed; consequently, the bones were collected and a stupa was erected there.
Later, the disciple Fayi came from that country and personally transmitted this account; thus Sun Chuo’s "Treatise on the True and the Semblance" states:
"Shixing [Zhi Dun] dispersed his form at Khotan."
This is what that refers to.
Second is Zhī Xiàolóng, a native of Huáyáng. From his youth, he was esteemed for his refined bearing;
moreover, his spiritual brilliance was outstanding, and his lofty discourses were perfectly attuned to the times.
He constantly studied and savoring the *Prajñāpāramitā Hṛdaya Sūtra* (the *Xiǎopǐn*), regarding it as the essence of his heart.
Ruan Zhan of Chenliu and Yu Hui of Yingchuan both formed friendships with him based on mutual musical appreciation; people of the world called them the "Eight Talents" (*bādá*).
At times, some would mock him, saying:

"The Great Jin has risen like a dragon, and the world is now our common home. Why do you śramaṇas not preserve the integrity of your hair and skin, discard your kāṣāya robes, cast off these barbarian garments, and instead don fine silks and brocades?"
The dragon said:
"Embrace the One to roam in leisure; through stillness alone, one attains sincerity.
To shave the hair and alter the appearance, to change the robes and transform the form—others call this humiliation, but I cast aside their notion of glory."
"Therefore, by having no mind for nobility, one becomes increasingly noble;
by having no mind for sufficiency, one becomes increasingly sufficient.
His witty and eloquent responses suited the occasion, all of which were of this kind.

At that time, Zhu Shulan had recently translated the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* (Fàngguāng jīng). Since Dao Long had long delighted in the signless (*animitta*), he obtained the text and began reading it; after more than ten days, he proceeded to give a public lecture on it.
His ultimate end was unknown thereafter.
Sun Chuo composed a eulogy for him, saying:
"The small square is easy to model; the great vessel is difficult to image. Resolute and steadfast was Xiaolong, who strove to surpass the lofty and expansive."
"Things compete to find their ultimate source, and people long to emulate and look up to him; clouds and springs overflow, and the fragrance of orchids wafts afar. 3.
Kang Sengyuan: Kang Sengyuan was originally a man from the Western Regions who was born in Chang'an.

Although his appearance was that of a Brahmin, his speech was actually that of the Middle Kingdom; his deportment was dignified and correct, and his aspirations and practices were vast and profound. He recited the two versions of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, namely the *Prakāśaprabhāsa* and the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, which correspond to the "Large" and "Small" *Prajñāpāramitās*.
During the reign of Emperor Cheng of the Jin dynasty, he crossed the Yangtze River together with Kang Fachang, Zhi Mindu, and others.
Fachang was also possessed of talent and ingenuity; he excelled at debate and composed works such as the "Treatise on the Original Meaning of Human Figures."
Zhu Fanchang constantly carried a fly-whisk (*chūwei*). Whenever he encountered a renowned guest on his travels, he would invariably engage in refined conversation until the day was done.
Yu Yuan gui remarked to Fanchang, "Why is this fly-whisk always with you?"
Chang said, "The honest do not take, and the greedy do not give; therefore, one attains eternal constancy.
Mindu was likewise wise and renowned; he composed the *Yijing lu* (Record of Translated Scriptures), which circulates in the world today.

Although Huiyuan’s virtue surpassed that of Daoyu, he distinguished himself by living in purity and austerity; he often supported himself by begging for alms, and people did not yet recognize his worth.

Later, while on his rounds for alms, he encountered Yin Hao of Chenjun. Hao first inquired about the profound and far-reaching principles of Buddhist scriptures, but when Yuan instead debated the nature and meaning of secular texts, Hao was unable to best him from morning until dusk. It was through this that Hao changed his perspective.
Wang Maohong of Langya mocked him for having a high nose and deep-set eyes, to which Yuan replied:
"The nose is the mountain of the face, and the eyes are the abyss of the face; if the mountain is not high, it lacks spirit, and if the abyss is not deep, it lacks clarity."
At that time, people took this as his formal reply.
Later, he established a monastery on Mount Yuzhang, some several dozen *li* from the city.
It was situated along a river and beside a ridge, where the forests and bamboos grew lush and dense; renowned monks and eminent masters flocked there in great numbers, like echoes following a sound.

Because the principle of emptiness in the *Cittavajra-brahma-sūtra* was profound and far-reaching, he specifically devoted himself to its exposition; consequently, students seeking learning flocked to him from all directions.
Later, he passed away at the monastery.

4. Zhu Fayā: A native of Hejian, Fayā was steadfast and upright, possessing great personal dignity and capacity. In his youth, he was proficient in non-Buddhist studies; as he grew older, he mastered Buddhist doctrine. Consequently, the gentry and scholar-officials all sought him out to consult and receive instruction.

At that time, the disciples were all proficient in secular classics but had not yet mastered Buddhist principles. Daoyaya, together with Kang Falang and others, used the categories and numerical lists found in the sutras to correlate them with external (non-Buddhist) texts, establishing a method for generating understanding which they called "Ge-yi" (Matching Meanings).
These included Pifu, Xiangtan, and others.
They also expounded upon the "matching meanings" (gēyì) to instruct their disciples.
Their refined bearing was elegant and unencumbered, and they were adept at the essential points of discourse.
He lectured on both non-Buddhist classics and Buddhist sutras, alternating between them.
Together with Dao’an and Fatai, he frequently examined and interpreted difficult passages, striving collectively to exhaust the essential meanings of the scriptures.
Later, he established a monastery at Gaoyi; with more than a hundred monks, he tirelessly instructed and exhorted them.
Ya’s disciple, Tanxi, followed in the footsteps of his former master and was skilled in discourse.
It is said that he was held in high esteem by Shi Xuan, the Crown Prince of the puppet state of Zhao. 5.
Kang Falang: Kang Falang was a native of Zhongshan. He left home to become a monk in his youth and was renowned for his mastery of the precepts and ascetic discipline.
Once, while reading the scriptures, I saw the sites of the twin śāla trees and the Deer Park; sighing deeply, I said:
"I have already failed to meet the Sage in person; how could I not at least behold the places where he dwelt?"
Thereupon, he vowed to travel to Kāśī to gaze upon the sacred remains.
He then set out from Zhangye with four fellow students and crossed the shifting sands to the west.

After traveling for three days, the path was deserted of human trace; suddenly, he saw an old temple by the roadside, overgrown with weeds and grass reaching above the men's heads. Inside were two dilapidated rooms, each occupied by a person: one was reciting a sutra, while the other suffered from dysentery. The two shared a room but did not attend to one another; excrement and urine were strewn about, and the entire room reeked of filth.

Faluang said to his followers, "Those who have left the household life share the same Way; we take the Dharma as our kin. If we do not see them, that is one thing, but how could we see them and yet abandon them?
Faluang then stayed for six days, providing them with washing services and offerings.
On the seventh day, he saw that this room was entirely filled with fragrant flowers and realized it was a divine being.
He then said to Lang, "This room belongs to my Upādhyāya, who has already attained the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa); you may go to pay him your respects."
Lang went to pay his respects and, taking the opportunity, said to him:

"Your companions are truly bound by a spiritual affinity; all of you shall surely enter the Way. There is no need for you to travel far to various countries, as it will be of no benefit to your practice."
"You must simply exert yourself to practice the Way and not let this opportunity pass.
However, your meritorious achievements are still slight and not yet pure; you have not yet attained your aspiration. You should return to the land of Zhendan to serve as a Great Dharma Master."
Thereupon, the four men no longer traveled westward, but remained there to apply themselves with single-minded diligence to the path of practice.
Only Daolang continued his travels through various kingdoms to investigate and seek out the sūtras and śāstras.
Later, he returned to Zhongshan, where several hundred disciples followed him as he lectured on the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Characteristics of Dharmas) in continuous succession.
His final destination is unknown.
Sun Chuo composed a eulogy for him, which says:
As the saying goes: "A person may have flaws that are not hidden. Master Lang is brilliantly radiant, yet he is able to conceal his brilliance.
He honors the end while being cautious at the beginning; he investigates the subtle and distinguishes the manifest. How does he provide proof? By observing the hoarfrost to know the ice is firm.
Lang’s disciple Lingshao was originally from Yanmen; his surname was Lü. In his youth he was a hunter, but later he resolved to leave the household life and served Lang as his teacher.

He applied himself diligently to his studies and was particularly adept at dhyāna and the counting of breaths (*gaṇanā*). Whenever he entered meditative absorption, he would sometimes remain seated for several days without arising.
Later, he moved to Mount Liuchuan, where he carved out a cave to sit in silent meditation.
After Lang’s death, a wooden image was carved of him, which was worshipped morning and evening.
Sun Chuo’s “Treatise on the Correct Image” states:
“Lü Shao concentrated his spirit at Zhongshan.”
"He is that very person. 6. Zhu Fasheng: It is not clearly known who he was.

From childhood, his spiritual insight was transcendent and his prescient discernment surpassed that of others. He became a śrāmaṇera under Zhu Fahu; he was pure and sincere, possessed of noble ambition, and Fahu held him in high esteem.

Since Kumārajīva’s teachings had already spread throughout Guanzhong and his resources were abundant, a prominent family in Chang’an who wished to support the Great Dharma sought to test his spiritual virtue. They feigned an urgent plea for help, requesting two hundred thousand coins.
Before Hu had replied, Sengcheng, who was thirteen years old and attending by his master’s side, immediately said,
"The Upādhyāya has already given his consent.
After the guest had withdrawn, Sengcheng said:
"Judging by this man's expression and demeanor, he does not truly seek money; he has come merely to observe what kind of spiritual virtue his Venerable Master possesses.
Dharmagupta said, "I also think so."

The next day, this guest led his entire clan, numbering over a hundred members, to visit Hu to request the full set of precepts; they then expressed their gratitude for his refusal of their offer of money, whereupon the fame of this teacher and his disciples spread far and wide.
Faxian subsequently traveled west to Dunhuang, where he established monasteries to welcome students. He dedicated himself to the Way, teaching without weariness.

That even the maned wolves and wolves have reformed their hearts and the Rong and Di tribes come to know propriety—such that the Great Transformation has spread to the West—is due to Faxian’s efforts.
Later, he passed away at his residence.
In Sun Chuo’s “Discourse on the Virtuous Sages,” Faxing is compared to Wang Junchong; the discourse states:
"Faxing and Anfeng possessed a keen discernment from their youth. Although the monastic and the secular differ in their conduct, their paths may be measured against one another."
The eminent scholar Ji Yong composed a biographical eulogy for him.
His fellow students, Zhu Faxing and Zhu Facun, both lived as hermits in the mountains practicing their ascetic conduct, and were renowned throughout the world.
7. Zhu Qian Shen: Zhu Qian, courtesy name Fashen, was surnamed Wang and was a native of Langya. He was the younger brother of Wang Dun, the Chancellor of Jin and Duke of Wuchang Commandery.
At the age of eighteen, he left the household life and served Liu Yuanzhen of Zhongzhou as his teacher.
Yuanzhen had long enjoyed a reputation for his talent and understanding; thus Sun Chuo praised him, saying:
"How desolate is the empty breast, how obscured is the quiet serenity! Who could embody these qualities? It is our Master Liu."
His discourse was capable of refined embellishment, and his illumination was sufficient to dispel ignorance; within his breast, all things were ever expansively harmonized.

After Huiqian took him under his tutelage, he discarded superficiality and flourished, honoring the fundamental and devoting himself to study. His subtle words promoted transformation, and his reputation spread throughout the Western Capital. His bearing and appearance were truly magnificent and imposing.

By the age of twenty-four, he was lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Possessing profound understanding and being further able to expound them skillfully, those who came to observe his demeanor and savor the flavor of the Dharma constantly numbered no fewer than five hundred.
At the beginning of the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty, he crossed the Yangtze River to escape the chaos.
Emperor Yuan (the Zhongzong), Emperor Ming (the Suzu), Chancellor Wang Maohong, and Grand Marshal Yu Yuangui all admired his character and virtue, befriending him with great respect.
During the Jianwu and Taining eras, Huiqian often went into the palace wearing wooden clogs; those of his time all regarded him as a man beyond the mundane world because of the gravity of his virtue.
When Emperor Xiaowu (Zhongzong) and Emperor Xiaowen (Suzu) passed away, and the dukes Wang and Yu also died, he then withdrew from public view at Mount Shan to avoid the affairs of the age.
Those who sought him out followed him back to the mountain gate, where he once again gathered his followers.
For over thirty years, he lived in leisurely seclusion within the lecture hall, at times expounding upon the Vaipulya sutras and at other times interpreting the *Laozi* and *Zhuangzi*.
Among those who turned northward to him, there were none whose inner and outer needs were not fully satisfied.

When Emperor Ai took a deep interest in the Buddha-dharma, he repeatedly dispatched two envoys with earnest invitations. Taking advantage of the gravity of the imperial decree, [Dao'an] visited the palace for a short time and delivered a lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* at the imperial banquet; both the Emperor and the court officials praised his excellence.

At that time, Emperor Jianwen served as Chancellor; both the court and the commonalty regarded him as one of supreme virtue. Because Huiqian was a preeminent leader among both the monastic and lay communities, and had been a friend and object of respect during the previous reign, the Emperor held him in profound esteem and deference, honoring him with constant devotion. This continued until his accession to the throne, when his reverent service became even more earnest.
Once, while at the residence of Emperor Jianwen, Huiquan encountered Liu Tan of Pei-guo, who mocked him, saying:
"Daoist, why do you frequent the gates of the crimson palace?
Huiquan replied:
"You behold its vermilion gates, while this poor monk sees it as a thatched door.

Sire He Cidao was of pure and simple virtue and possessed profound faith in the scriptures; he always treated [the Master] with the utmost reverence, honoring him with the respect due to a teacher, frequently inviting him and repeatedly sponsoring dharma assemblies.

Although Qian followed the currents of fortune east and west, his innate disposition was one of discontent; he therefore petitioned for leave to return to Mount Yang in Shan County to fulfill his long-held aspiration, whereupon he lived in leisure among the woods and hills to spend the remainder of his years.
Zhi Dun sent a messenger to request the purchase of a small ridge at Wozhou, beside Mount Yang, desiring it as a place for secluded retirement. Huiqian replied:
"If you wish to come, I shall provide it immediately; have you ever heard of Chao Fu or You Yu buying a mountain to hide away?"
Later, Zhu Dun wrote in a letter to a monk from Goguryeo:
"The Venerable Zhu Fashen is a disciple of Lord Liu of the Central Plains; his virtuous character stands firm and upright, and he is a master who weaves together both the monastic and the secular."
Formerly, while in the capital city, he maintained the framework of the Dharma.
Respected by all within and without as a master who propagated the Way, he has recently sought to bring peace through his spiritual practice;
finding the secular world intolerable, he built a dwelling in the mountains and marshes to cultivate virtue and pursue seclusion.

He is now at Mount Yang in Shan County, where he leads his fellow travelers in discussing the Way and expounding upon its principles; dwelling in lofty seclusion with radiant purity, he is celebrated in verse by those both near and far.
He passed away in a mountain lodge in the second year of the Ningkang era of the Jin dynasty at the age of eighty-nine.
Emperor Xiaowu of the Liezong era issued an edict stating:

"Master Shen has attained a profound and far-reaching realization of the principles; his character is pure and upright. He has renounced the glory of the position of Chancellor to don the simple garb of a monk."
Dwelling among the mountains beyond the reach of worldly men, he was steadfast and diligent without slackening; we were just relying on him to proclaim the Way in order to save all living beings.
That he has suddenly passed away brings deep sorrow to our hearts.
"You may provide a funeral subsidy of one hundred thousand coins and send it by express courier.
Sun Chuo compared Daoxin to Liu Bo-lun, stating in his commentary:
"The Honorable Daoxin was by nature profound and grave, possessing a capacity for great and far-reaching aims;..."
Liu Ling gave rein to his unrestrained indulgence, regarding the universe as small.
Although his practice of lofty seclusion was something Liu could not match, their expansive spirit was identical.

At that time, there was also Zhu Fayou of Yangshan, whose aspirations and conduct were firm and upright, and who was widely learned in the various scriptures; he once studied the *Abhidharma* under Dao-shen and could recite it from memory after staying for only one night.
Sengshen said:
"To memorize a scripture upon merely seeing it is a feat praised by people of old; if you can cause the Great Jin to flourish once more, I shall surely take you as one of the five hundred arhats."
At the age of twenty-four, he was already able to lecture and explain the scriptures.
Later, he established NanTai Temple south of the city of Shan County.
Zhu Fayun possessed profound insight and understanding that reached the profound mysteries; he was especially skilled in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* (Fàngguāng Bōrě).
Kang Fashi also possessed merit in the study of doctrine, yet he was renowned for his cursive and clerical scripts.

He once encountered Kang Xin, who claimed that his own calligraphic skill surpassed that of Fashi. Fashi and Xin each composed a cursive draft of Wang Xizhi’s style; bystanders secretly purchased them as merchandise, unable to distinguish between the two.
Furthermore, he transcribed various scriptures and was held in high esteem.
Zhu Faji, who possessed literary talent from his youth, composed the *Biographies of Eminent and Recluse Śramaṇas*.
As for all these individuals, they were all hidden "feet of the gods" (arhats); Sun Chuo composed eulogies for each of them, which I shall not transcribe in full here.
8. Zhidao Lin (Zhi Dun), whose courtesy name was Daolin, was originally surnamed Guan and was a native of Chenliu; some say he was from Linlü in Hedong.
From childhood, he possessed a divine intelligence and was exceptionally brilliant and perceptive.
Upon his first arrival in the capital, Wang Meng of Taiyuan held him in high esteem, saying:
"His achievement in penetrating the subtle does not fall short of that of [Xi] Fusi.
Yin Rong of Chenjun had once been acquainted with Wei Jie and remarked that his spirit and expression were so brilliant and penetrating that none among the younger generation could succeed him.
Upon meeting Zhi Dun, he sighed in admiration, feeling as though he were seeing such a person once again.
His family had served the Buddha for generations, and he had early on awakened to the principle of impermanence.

He lived in seclusion on Mount Yuhang, where he deeply contemplated the chapters of the *Daoxing* [Prajñāpāramitā] and thoroughly investigated the *Huiyin* [Jñānamudrā] Sūtra; his insights were preeminent and solitary, having attained direct inspiration from the Heavenly Mind.

At the age of twenty-five, he left the household life; whenever he attended a lecture hall, he was adept at identifying the core principles and their convergence, yet he occasionally omitted certain phrases and passages, for which reason he was sometimes disparaged by those who adhered strictly to the literal text.
When Xie An heard of this, he approved it, saying:
"This is like Jiu Fangyin’s appraisal of horses; he disregards their black and yellow markings and values only their noble spirit and swiftness."

Wang Xia, Liu Hui, Yin Hao, Xu Xun, Xi Chao, Sun Chuo, Huan Yanbiao, Wang Jingren, He Cidao, Wang Wendu, Xie Changxia, Yuan Yanbo, and others were all renowned figures of their generation, yet they all maintained intimate friendships with those beyond the mundane world.
Once, while Huì was at Baima Monastery,
he was discussing the "Xiaoyao" chapter of the *Zhuangzi* with Liu Xizhi and others, saying:
"Each adapts to their own nature to achieve *xiao-yao* (carefree wandering).
Hui Tui replied, "Not so.
Now, Jie and Zhi took cruelty and harm as their nature; if adapting to one's nature constitutes attaining [the Dao], then they too would have achieved *xiao-yao*."
Thereupon, he retired to compose his commentary on the "Xiaoyao" chapter.
Among the various Confucian scholars and those of established learning, there were none who did not express admiration and submission.
Later, he returned to Wu and established Zhishan Temple.
In the evening, he wished to enter Shan County; Xie An, who was then the Governor of Wuxing, wrote a letter to Huida saying:
"My longing for you grows day by day, and my impatience increases with each passing hour. Knowing that you intend to return to Shan to cultivate yourself, I feel nothing but deep regret."
Human life is but a temporary lodging; those recent affairs of elegance and success have almost entirely vanished.

All day long I am filled with sorrow, feeling despondent at every turn. I only look forward to your arrival so that we may converse and dispel these feelings, for a single day would then be equal to a thousand years.

This district of Many Mountains is secluded and tranquil, quite suitable for recuperating from illness; its conditions are not unlike those of Shan, yet the medical provisions differ. You must consider these circumstances so as to fulfill your long-cherished aspirations.
At that time, Wang Xizhi was in Kuaiji and had long heard of Zhi Dun’s reputation.
Not yet believing it, he said to others, "He is merely someone with a fleeting spirit; what is there to say of him?"
Later, after Huida returned to Shan, he passed through Yu County. Wang went to visit Huida specifically to observe his spiritual power.
Upon arrival, Wang said to Huida, "May I hear the 'Pian on Wandering at Ease'?"

Daoxun then composed several thousand words, setting forth novel principles with such extraordinary brilliance that Wang was moved to open his breast and loosen his girdle, lingering in admiration without end.
He continued to reside at Lingjiasi, intending to remain in close proximity [to his teacher].

Shortly thereafter, he again set out for Mount Shan, where he established a monastery on the Small Ridge of Wozhou to practice the Way; more than a hundred monks constantly followed him there to receive instruction.
At that time, there were some who fell into negligence, so Tao Dun composed the "Epitaph for the Seat" (Zuo-you-ming) to exhort them, saying:
"Be diligent! Be diligent! The Ultimate Way is not far off; why do you linger and delay?"
The wondrous and marvelous has been lost in weakness.
Vast and boundless are the three realms; remote and far-reaching is the long night. External vexations converge upon one, while the darkened mind races within.

One pursues and hastens toward them with thirsty longing, forgetting fatigue as they recede into the distance. A human life in this world is but a fleeting drop like dew hanging from a blade of grass.
This body of mine is not the self; who, then, is it that gives? The man of realization cherishes virtue, knowing that security is inevitably followed by peril.
He rises in solitary purity, washing away defilements in the pool of dhyāna; he reverently observes the clear prohibitions and elegantly contemplates the profound rules.
He settled his spirit in the Way of the Mind and raised his will toward non-action; he cleared away the three obscurations and melted away the six defects.
He made the five aggregates empty and uniform and opened up the four limbs to emptiness; though not using a finger to point at a finger, he transcended all yet remained inseparable from it.

Once the wondrous awakening has been set forth, its knowledge becomes even more profound and mysterious; moving with graceful flexibility and remaining equanimous and natural, it shifts and transforms along with all things. Beyond this point, one need neither contemplate nor deliberate.
"His awakening is that of a mature father, yet his aspirations remain those of an infant.

At that time, public opinion held that although Sengrui’s talent was fit for composing scriptural commentaries, his practice of purifying himself and distancing himself from the world violated the Way of Universal Salvation. Consequently, Sengrui composed the "Treatise on Dispelling Ignorance" (*Shimōng lùn*).
In the evening, he moved to Mount Shicheng and established Qiguang Monastery there.

He sat in meditation at the mountain gate and let his mind roam within the garden of Chan, subsisting on forest fruits and drinking from mountain streams, while setting his aspirations upon the state of non-arising.

He then annotated various sutras such as the *Ānāpāna* and the *Catvāri Dhyānāni*, as well as treatises including the "Discourse on Roaming the Profound through the Nature of Form," the "Discourse on the Sage Not Discerning Knowledge," the "Purport of the Practice of the Way," and the "Admonitions for Studying the Way."
He followed in the footsteps of Aśvaghoṣa and traced the shadow of Nāgārjuna; his principles accorded with the fundamental Dharma and did not deviate from the true nature (*dharmatā*).

Later, he went to Shanyin to lecture on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*. Zhu Fadu served as the Master of Dharma, while Xu Xun served as the Recitation Master. Whenever Fadu elucidated a point, the assembly all said that Xu Xun had no way to pose a challenge; whenever Xu Xun proposed a difficulty, they likewise said that Fadu could no longer resolve it. Thus it continued until the end, and neither side was exhausted.

All those who heard him were convinced that he had thoroughly grasped the essence of Zhu Fonian’s teachings; they urged him to explain them himself, yet after two or three turns of discourse, he would become confused.

When Emperor Ai of the Jin dynasty ascended the throne, he repeatedly dispatched two envoys to invite him to the capital, where he resided at Dong’an Temple and lectured on the *Daoxing Banruo*. Both monastics and laypeople revered him, and both the court and the commonalty were won over by his influence.
Wang Meng of Taiyuan had long cultivated refined principles and composed his own eloquent prose; he went to visit Zhu Fonian, speaking several hundred words, believing that none could withstand him.
Tun then said slowly,
"I have been separated from you for many years, yet your speech has not improved at all.
Meng withdrew in shame and sighed, saying:
"What indeed is the king of those with black alms-bowls?
Xi Chao asked Xie An:
"How does Master Lin’s discourse compare to that of Ji Zhongxian?"
An said, "Xi has managed to get away by exerting himself.
He asked again:
"How does Yin Hao compare?
Dao'an replied, "In terms of continuous debate, I fear Yin would best Shi; however, in terms of transcendent excellence and direct ascent to the profound source, Hao truly has cause for shame."
Later, Xi Chao wrote in a letter to his relatives and friends:
"Dharma Master Lin’s spirit and principle are in perfect accord; he is profoundly transcendent and uniquely enlightened.
Truly, for several hundred years, he is the only one who has propagated and clarified the Great Dharma, ensuring that the True Principle does not perish."
Tun remained in the capital for nearly three years before returning to the Eastern Mountains.
He submitted a letter of farewell, stating:
"Tun bows his head and says:..."

Venturing to rely on my own lack of talent, I have sought to emulate the spirit beyond the mundane world; yet, failing to spur myself forward, I have fallen short in responding to the transformation of the numinous.
For the meaning of the śramaṇa arises from the Buddha, the Sage; it carves away artifice to return to simplicity, and cuts off desire to revert to the ultimate source.
They roam the marketplace of the profound and the mysterious, uphold the principles of the inner sages, wear the integrity of the five precepts, and assist the transformations of the external kings.
They harmonize the music of the unmanifest, taking self-realization as their concordance.
Practicing the filial piety of profound compassion, one does not harm even the crawling insects;
harboring a grief that knows no respite, one perpetually laments unrighteousness.
Upholding a compliance that precedes the manifestation of signs, one guards against the dictates of fatalism from afar.
Drawing upon the principles of those who hold no official rank, they tread the path of the "Exalted" without regret.

Thus, when wise kings preside over the heavy responsibilities of the southern-facing throne, there are none who do not revere their noble character and find peace in their tranquil course; they explore the underlying harmony of their hearts and simplify outward formalities, ensuring that these traditions become ever more renewed through successive generations.

Your Majesty has been endowed by Heaven with sagely virtue; you take sublime pleasure in your pursuits without weariness, wandering in the Way through spiritual models until the sun declines, forgetting even to attend to your meals. It may truly be said that you have struck the bells and drums at the celestial pole, and your fame resounds throughout the world.
Now that the pure wind has prevailed, there is no one who does not consider this most fortunate.

We pray, Your Majesty, that you may equal the longevity of the two polarities and widely propagate the ultimate transformation: cast aside the demonic deceptions of the old faiths, seek out the grand principles of the sages’ prayers, sever the muddy paths of minor doctrines, and gallop the great chariot upon the level road.
If this is so, Mount Tai did not require the seasonal sacrifices of the Ji clan to become a numinous spirit; it attained this by attaining the One.
A sovereign does not perform the *yin* sacrifice on the Round Mound; he achieves eternal rectitude by attaining the One.

If the upright spirit and the individual are each distinct, such that man and the divine forget one another; if every ruler acts without partiality toward those below, and every spirit responds without the need for incantations to bestow its power; if the profound virtue of the Way is shared universally and the people receive hidden blessings, then the vast six realms will become a dwelling place of auspiciousness, and the expansive Great Jin will become a realm of ultimate prosperity.

By remaining eternally non-active, the myriad things return to their source; by grasping the Great Image, all under heaven spontaneously follow. When the state’s statutes involve execution, it is the officials who carry them out; if life is granted without partiality, then those who receive rewards do so of their own accord.
If execution is carried out without anger, then those who are punished undergo their sentence naturally.
Master Hong has broadened his capacity to satisfy the divine will and held the scales of judgment to fathom the profoundest measures.
As it is said, "What does Heaven say? Yet the four seasons proceed.

This humble monk has lived in rustic seclusion on the Eastern Mountain, differing from the world in its honors; I have grown vegetables upon the heights and rinsed my mouth with clear streams, intending to spend my life in such simplicity, forever cutting off all hope of beholding the imperial steps.

Failing to realize that the brilliant light of the imperial favor had so humbly reached my thatched cottage, I have repeatedly received Your Majesty’s clear edict commanding me to proceed to the capital; thus, whether advancing or retreating, I am in a state of distress, not knowing where to place myself.
Since arriving at the Heavenly Way, I have repeatedly been granted audiences, treated with the courtesy due to a guest, and exhorted with profound words.

I am constantly ashamed that my talent cannot extricate me from stagnation and my principles lack the capacity to embrace the new; thus, I am insufficient to proclaim the sublime model and satisfy the imperial gaze and hearing. As I attend upon Your Majesty in trepidation, sweat flows down upon my seat.
In the past, Nan-si-weng went to the Han court and Gan-mu flourished under Wei; both emerged or withdrew at the appropriate times, and their silence or speech was perfectly suited to the occasion.

Today, your virtue is not that of those ancients, and your movements and stillness contradict the requirements of the age. With your wandering soul confined within the palace precincts, you drum your words by the Emperor’s side; since you will be constrained by an improper position, how can you achieve anything?

Moreover, as the months and years press on, I am moved by such sighs; how much more so when those of like mind dwell in seclusion, their studies falling into neglect? Raising my head and gazing toward the east, who could remain without longing?
I further pray that Your Majesty will, at this time, grant me leave to depart for the forest thickets, where I may be nourished by birds as a bird; such a favor would be most gracious.
I hereby submit this informal memorial to inform Your Majesty, expressing my humble thoughts; with provisions packed, I await your compassionate decree upon the road.

The imperial decree granted his request immediately; he was provided with generous provisions for his departure, and every detail was handled with great magnificence. The famous figures of the time all saw him off at Zhenlu.
Cai Zishu arrived first and sat down close to Hui Dun. Xie Wanshi arrived later and, finding Cai momentarily away, simply moved over to take his place.
When Cai returned, he gathered his mat and lifted Xie up, throwing him to the ground; yet Xie did not take it to heart.
Such was the way he was admired by the worthies of his time.
Subsequently, he withdrew from public life to Mount Shan, spending the remainder of his days in the forests and marshes.

Once, someone gave a horse to Huida; Huida loved it and raised it. At times, there were those who mocked him, to which Huida replied, "I cherish its divine spirit and fine form, so I am merely keeping it for that reason."
Later, when someone brought food for the cranes, Huidun said to them, "You are creatures that soar toward the heavens;
how could you be mere objects for the amusement of the eyes and ears?
He then released them.

When Huìdùn was young, he once engaged in a discussion on the nature of things with his teacher, asserting that using a chicken egg for consumption did not yet constitute killing; his teacher could not refute him.

Shortly thereafter, the teacher passed away and suddenly appeared in a vision to Huìdùn, throwing an egg to the ground. As the shell broke open, a chick emerged and walked about; after a moment, both vanished. Huìdùn was then profoundly enlightened by this, and from then on he maintained a vegetarian diet for the rest of his life.

Huidun previously stayed in the mountains of Yuyao Wushan; even when it was time for him to return to the capital, he would still go back to the valley. Someone asked him the reason for this, and he replied:

"In the past, Xie An came to visit me several times, and each time we would stay together for ten days or more. Now, whenever my feelings are stirred or my eyes meet with something, I cannot help but be moved by memories of him."

Later, his illness becoming severe, he moved back to the walled enclosure; he passed away at his residence on the fourth day of the intercalary fourth month in the first year of the Taihe era of the Jin dynasty, at the age of fifty-three.
He was immediately interred in the Wū area, and his tomb remains there.
Some say he died in Shàn, though this is not certain.
Xí Chāo composed a preface and biography for him, Yuán Hóng wrote an inscription and eulogy, and Zhōu Tánbǎo composed a funeral oration.
In his "Discourse on the Worthies of the Way" (*Daoxian lun*), Sun Chuo compares Zhi Dun to Xiang Xiu; the discourse states:
"Zhi Dun and Xiang Xiu both held the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi* in high esteem."
"At different times, the two sons shared the same profound fondness for the Mysterious.
Furthermore, the "Discourse on the Metaphor of the Way" states:
"As for Zhi Daolin..."
Consciousness is pure and its substance is compliant, yet it does not obstruct objects.
The profound Way is empty and all-sustaining, functioning in concert with the spirit and emotions.
This is why those of the distant tradition return to this ultimate source, while the common folk remain unenlightened.
Later, when the eminent scholar Dai Kui passed by Zhi Dun’s tomb, he sighed and said:

"The virtuous reputation has not yet faded, yet the trees around the grave have already grown thick; I hope that the divine principle remains continuous and does not perish along with the movement of the vital breath."
Tun had a fellow student named Faqian, who was so refined in principle and profound in realization that he surpassed even Tun; Faqian passed away before him.
Tun sighed and said:

"In the past, Jang Shi set aside his chisel because of the people of Ying, and Ya Sheng stopped plucking his strings for the sake of Zhong Zi. Inferring from myself to seek others, this is truly not in vain."
"Now that the Precious Seal has vanished and my words find no one to appreciate them, my inner heart is bound with grief; I shall surely perish.
He then composed the "Chapter on Utter Awakening," completing it as death approached, and passed away the moment he set down his pen.
In total, the collected writings produced by Huidun comprise ten fascicles that were widely circulated in the world.
At that time, there was also Zhu Fayang in the eastern lands, whose profound understanding and wisdom brought him renown and earned him the high esteem of Wang Tanshi.
After his passing, he was still seen appearing before the King, exhorting him with regard to religious practice and conduct. 9.
Yufa Lan: Yufa Lan was a native of Gaoyang; from his youth, he possessed extraordinary character.

At fifteen, he left the household life and made diligent application his primary vocation; he studied and recited the scriptures day and night, seeking the Dharma and inquiring about the Way, always taking the lead among the assembly.
By the time he reached the age of capping, his character and spirit were exceptionally refined; his Way resounded throughout the Three Rivers, and his fame spread far and wide.
By nature he loved mountain springs and frequently dwelt among crags and grottoes.

Once, while he was staying in the mountains during the winter months when the ice and snow were most severe, a tiger came into Lan’s chamber. Lan’s expression showed no sign of alarm, and the tiger was likewise very docile; it departed the following morning once the snow had ceased.
The deities of the mountains often came to receive the Dharma from him; that his virtue permeated even the spirits was of this nature.

Later, hearing that the mountains and waters of Jiangdong were renowned for their wonders, particularly those of Shan County, he traveled leisurely to Dong’ou and gazed afar at the Yang and Sheng peaks. He settled at the foot of Mount Shicheng, which is the present-day Yuanhua Temple.
People of the time compared his intellectual power to that of Yu Yuangui; Sun Chuo’s "Discourse on the Worthies of the Way" compared him to Ruan Sizong, stating:
"Master Lan cast aside his person and pursued lofty and wondrous traces, approaching the rank of a Perfected Man;
Ruan the Infantry Officer was haughty and solitary, not conforming to the crowd—he too was a peer of Lan."
After residing in Shan for a short time, he suddenly sighed and said:

"Although the Great Dharma has flourished, there are many deficiencies in the transmission of the sutras and the Way. If I could but hear the Perfect Teaching once, I would be content to die this very evening."
He then traveled far to the Western Regions, desiring to seek out extraordinary teachings; upon reaching Jiaozhou, he fell ill and passed away at Xianglin.
The śramaṇa Zhi Dun composed a eulogy for his statue, saying:
"The Yu family transcended the world, comprehending the profound essence of the mysteries; they delighted in seclusion among mountains and marshes, taming even tigers and rhinoceroses."
The *Biézhuan* states:
"Lan was also moved by a dried-up spring to rinse his mouth with water;
this incident is the same as that of Zhu Fahu."
The details are unknown.

Furthermore, there were Zhu Faxing, Zhi Fayuan, and Yu Fadao, who were contemporaries of Lan and whose virtues were comparable to his. Faxing was renowned for his extensive learning; Fayuan was celebrated for his literary talent; and Fadao was famous for his skill in interpreting the meaning of the scriptures.
10. Regarding Fayuan: Fayuan was a man of unknown origins. He served Master Lan as his disciple;

he reflected deeply and with independent insight, perceiving meanings beyond the literal expression of words. He was proficient in the *Prajñāpāramitā in Eight Thousand Lines* (*Fàngguāng*) and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (*Fǎhuá*), and furthermore, following the tradition of Jīvaka, he was exquisitely skilled in medical arts.

Once, while begging for alms, he entered the home of a host where a woman was in critical condition in her chamber. The family had tried various treatments without success and were all in a state of anxious turmoil.
Daosheng said, "This is easily cured."

The host was then slaughtering a sheep, intending to perform a licentious sacrifice. He told An Shigao to first take a small amount of meat to make a broth. Once it had been served and finished, he applied the needle to the sheep's vital point; in a short while, a lamb wrapped in its own placenta emerged.

In the fifth year of the Shengping era, Emperor Xiaozong fell ill. When [Wang] Keng was summoned to examine his pulse, he knew the Emperor would not recover and refused to re-enter. Empress Dowager Kangxian issued an order: "The Emperor is slightly unwell;

yesterday he summoned Master Yu to examine his pulse, yet Keng reached the gate and did not proceed, making all manner of excuses and showing reluctance. He should be arrested and handed over to the Court of Judicial Review."
Shortly thereafter, the Emperor passed away, and he was spared from [punishment].
He returned to Shicheng in Shan County and continued the reconstruction of Yuanhua Temple; later, he moved to Lingjiu Temple on Mount Bai.

He frequently debated the meaning of "form is emptiness" with Zhi Daolin; He Mo of Lujiang clarified and defended Sengzhao’s refutations, while Xi Chao of Gaoping expounded upon Zhi Dun’s interpretations, both of which were transmitted to the world.
Kai had a disciple named Fawei, who was pure and enlightened, possessing a pivotal eloquence; thus Sun Chuo composed a eulogy for him, saying:
"The *I Ching* speaks of the white feathers; the *Shi Jing* praises the pondweed and duckweed."
Their brilliance was like that of the morning sun appearing from behind the clouds, and their fragrance like clear water settling after a rainstorm.
Yu and Wei were resolute in their awakening, pursuing the Way with steadfast determination.
They purified their names and remained free from any sense of shame within their hearts.
Later, when Zhu Fakuang sent Wei out to the capital, they passed through Shanyin.
At that time, Zhi Dun was lecturing on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in Eight Thousand Lines* (*Xiǎopǐn*). Kuang said to Wei:
"Dao Lin will deliver his lecture; by the time you arrive, it shall have reached a certain chapter.
He presented several dozen rounds of challenging arguments, saying, "These points have long been difficult to resolve."

When Wei arrived at the commandery, he happened upon Hui Dun giving a lecture; it was exactly as Dao’an had said. After several rounds of debate, Hui Dun was ultimately defeated, whereupon he said in a stern voice:
"How can you be worthy enough to have been carried here by others!"
Thus, the saying of Mount Dongshan goes:
"Deep in measure, opening the mind; in the forest, discourse and remembrance.

During the reign of Emperor Ai, he was repeatedly summoned by imperial decree and subsequently left the capital to lecture on the *Prabhāvatī-sūtra* (Fàngguāng jīng). Among those of the old school who harbored doubts, there were none who did not have them resolved through him. Upon concluding his lectures, he took his leave and returned to Mount Dongshan.
The Emperor, deeply attached to his virtue, generously bestowed upon him money, silk, a palanquin, and clothing for both winter and summer; Xie An and Wang Wendu were both his close friends.
Someone asked:
"The Dharma Master is lofty, brilliant, firm, and simple; why do you keep medical arts in your heart? He replied:

"To clarify the six perfections in order to eliminate the maladies of the four māras, and to regulate the nine pulses in order to treat the ailments of wind and cold—is it not fitting that one should thus benefit oneself and others?"
At the age of sixty, he passed away at the mountain monastery. Sun Chuo composed a critical appraisal for him, saying:
"His talent and eloquence were unrestrained; he propagated the teachings through the arts of calculation and divination. Is this not truly the Master Kāi?"
11. Dao Sui of Dunhuang lost his parents at a young age; his paternal uncle raised him. Sui served his uncle with such sincerity and filial piety that he treated him as if he were his own mother.
At the age of sixteen, he left home to become a monk, serving Master Lan as his disciple.

His learning was brilliant and lofty; he had mastered both Buddhist and secular classics. He was skilled in medical prescriptions and medicines, possessed a fine hand for calligraphy, had a profound understanding of foreign customs, and was particularly adept at discourse and debate.

Master Hu often praised Sui for his lofty, simple, and elegant character, noting that he possessed the style of the ancients; he remarked that if not for him, there would have been no one to serve as a pillar and beam for the Great Dharma.
Later, he and Master Jian both crossed the Yangtze River together, where they were highly esteemed by Xie Qingxu.
By nature he loved mountains and marshes; while in the East, he frequently traveled to renowned peaks.
As a man, he was indifferent to defamation or praise, and never allowed worldly affairs to interfere with his sacred studies.
Later, he accompanied Falan to the Western Regions, where he contracted an illness and passed away in Jiaozhi at the age of thirty-one.
Xi Chao painted his likeness, and Zhi Dun composed an inscription in praise, saying:
"The eminent monk is brilliant; his insight penetrates and his mind is pure.
His radiant nature is as translucent as jade, and his virtuous reputation is as fragrant as orchids."

Sun Chuo compared Sui to Ruan Xian; someone remarked, "Ruan Xian was subject to the criticism of being 'ridden by a succession of horses,' whereas Sui enjoyed a reputation for 'pure coolness. How can they be matched?"
Sun Chuo said: "Although their outward traces may vary between low and high, their lofty spirit is one and the same.
The *Yudao lun* (Treatise on Illustrating the Way) states:
"In the vicinity of the capital there is Zhu Faxing, whom critics compare to Yue Ling;
in Jiangnan there is Yu Daosui, whom the wise regard as a peer to Shengliu."
"All of this was witnessed and heard by everyone at that time; it is not a private eulogy from a partisan.
12. Zhu Fachong: It is unclear who Zhu Fachong was.

Having entered the Way at a young age, he was renowned for his disciplined observance of the precepts; moreover, being quick-witted and fond of learning, he was deeply devoted to the scriptures and records, and was particularly proficient in the teachings of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Once, while traveling to Lushan in Xiangzhou, a mountain spirit transformed into a lady and came to Huichong to request the precepts; she then offered the mountain where she resided to be established as a monastery, which Huichong occupied for a short time.
His transformative influence permeated the land of Xiang.

Later, he returned to Gexian Mountain in Shan, where he lived in a thatched hut and drank from mountain streams, finding joy in meditative wisdom; scholars from Dong’ou vied with one another to flock to him there.

He met with the hermit Kong Chunzhi of the state of Lu; whenever they went out for excursions until the day was spent, they would invariably stay for two or three nights, forgetting to return. They opened their hearts to one another with immediate resonance, each considering the other a companion with whom he shared a profound mutual understanding.
Sengchong then sighed and said, "I have contemplated the world beyond for more than thirty years; meeting you here today, I am unaware that old age is fast approaching.
Later, when Hui-chun departed on a journey, Sengchong recited this verse:
"The spirit of his brilliant clarity still lingers in my mind’s eye; those scholars of the mountains and forests who have gone forth will not return.
Is he not the very person one would describe as such?
Later, Hui-chong passed away in the mountains, having authored the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra* in four fascicles.

At that time, on Mount Yang in eastern Shan, there was another named Shi Daobao, whose original surname was Wang and who was a native of Langya; he was the younger brother of Wang Dao, the Chancellor of the Jin dynasty.

From his youth, he possessed faith and awakening, and he sought to withdraw from the world and renounce glory. Although his relatives and old friends urged him to desist, none were able to restrain him.
Having bathed in fragrant water and prepared for the tonsure ceremony, he then recited:
"Who would have known that ten thousand li of water began its course from a mere trickle?
Later, he became renowned for his learning and conduct.
13. Zhu Fayi. It is not clearly known where Zhu Fayi was from.
At the age of thirteen, he encountered Master Dao’an (Shen Gong), who immediately asked him:
“Beneficence and profit are what the gentleman practices; for what reason did Confucius rarely speak of them?”
Daoshen said, "Few are those who can truly practice; for this reason, I rarely speak of it.
Seeing that he was precocious and possessed of keen insight from a young age, Daoshen encouraged him to leave the household life.
Thereupon, he settled his aspirations upon the Dharma-gates and studied under Dao-shen.
He moved with ease through the various scriptures and was particularly proficient in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Later, he took leave of Dao-shen and departed for the capital, where he once again opened a great lecture hall; Wang Dao and Kong Fu both received his influence and revered him as a friend.
During the Xingning era of the Jin dynasty, he returned once more to Jiangzuo and stayed at Baoshan in Shining, where he constantly had over a hundred disciples receiving instruction from him.

In the second year of the Xian’an era, he suddenly suffered from a heart ailment; he habitually maintained mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara and subsequently dreamed of a person who cut open his abdomen and washed his intestines. Upon waking, his illness was immediately cured.
Fu Liang often remarked:
"Whenever my late father associated with Master Yi and heard him speak of the divine wonders of Avalokiteśvara, everyone, regardless of their status, was moved to solemn reverence."

In the third year of the Ningkang era of the Jin dynasty, Emperor Xiaowu dispatched an envoy to invite him to the capital to lecture and expound the teachings. He passed away in the capital in the fifth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty at the age of seventy-four.

The Emperor purchased Xinting Hill for one hundred thousand coins to serve as his burial site and erected a three-storied pagoda there. His dharma-son Tanshuang established a monastery at the site of the tomb, which was consequently named the Xinting Vihāra.
Later, when Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty marched south to punish the rebels, his imperial banners arrived and he visited this monastery.
Upon ascending the throne, he again visited the Chan Hall and expanded its grounds, renaming it "Zhongxing" (Restoration).
Therefore, at the end of the Yuanjia era, a children’s rhyme said:
“A Son of Heaven emerges from Qiantang. This refers to Chantang.
Therefore, in the Chan quarters of Zhongxing Temple, there still remains the Longfei Hall, which is the present-day Tian'an Hall.
14. Zhu Sengdu: Zhu Sengdu, surnamed Wang, named Xi, with the courtesy name Xuangong, was a native of Dongguan.
Although he came from a humble and obscure background in his youth, his natural endowment was exceptionally brilliant.
By the age of sixteen, his spirit was clear and transcendent, standing out as a man of extraordinary character; his temperament was gentle and mild, earning him the admiration of his neighbors.
At that time, he lived alone with his mother, serving her with filial piety and performing all rites with due propriety.

He sought the daughter of Yang De-shen from the same commandery; she was also from a family of scholar-officials. The girl’s name was Tiao-hua; she was of upright appearance and proficient in the classics and histories. As she was of the same age as Sengdu, on the day the marriage was proposed, it was immediately granted.
Before the wedding rites could be completed, Tiaohua’s mother passed away; shortly thereafter, Tiaohua’s father also died, and her stepmother likewise perished.

Sengdu, witnessing thus the impermanence of the world across successive generations, was suddenly awakened to its truth. He consequently renounced secular life to become a monk, changing his name to Sengdu.
His conduct stood aloof from the dust of the mundane world, as he traveled and studied to seek refuge elsewhere.

Once his mourning for Tiāohuá was completed, he reflected upon the duty of following one’s kin and realized there was no path for independent existence; he thus wrote a letter to Fǎdù, stating: "The hair and skin must not be injured or defiled, and the ancestral sacrifices must not be abruptly abandoned. He urged her to "heed worldly teachings and alter her far-reaching ambitions, so that her brilliant and radiant form might shine within this flourishing and enlightened age, thereby honoring the spirits of her ancestors afar and comforting the wishes of human sentiment nearby."
He also presented five poems, one of which read:
"The Great Way is naturally inexhaustible; heaven and earth are long and enduring.
A massive boulder remains difficult to erode, and even mustard seeds are hard to count."
A human life spent within this world passes as fleetingly as a breath through a window.
How lush may its splendor be, yet by evening it falls into decay and ruin.
On the riverbank there is lingering song; as the sun slants, one thinks to beat the jar.
Pure sounds can delight the ear; exquisite flavors can satisfy the palate; fine silks can adorn the body; and ornate crowns can illuminate the head.
Why then do you subject yourself to self-mutilation, indulging in emptiness to the detriment of existence?
"I do not say that my humble efforts are of no account; I only wish for you to provide for those who come after.
Du replied in a letter:
"In serving a ruler to govern a single state, one does not compare to propagating the Way to bring salvation to the myriad realms."
To bring peace to one's parents and complete the welfare of a single family is not equal to propagating the Way to rescue all beings within the three realms.
That the hair and skin should not be mutilated is merely a conventional, worldly maxim.
However, my virtue does not extend far enough to encompass all; for this, I feel ashamed.
Nevertheless, just as a mountain is formed by the accumulation of baskets of earth, I also hope to achieve the manifest through the minute.
Moreover, donning the kāṣāya and shaking the śikya-staff, I drink from clear streams and chant the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Although one may possess the robes of a high noble, the delicacies of the eight treasures, the resonance of tinkling sounds, and the brilliance of radiant colors, I would not exchange them for these worldly things.
If one can achieve a profound resonance with the truth, then we shall be equal in reaching Nirvana.
Moreover, human minds differ as much as their faces; your lack of delight in the Way is just as my lack of longing for the mundane world.
Mr. Yang, we shall part forever!
The karmic conditions for ten thousand generations have now been severed!

The year draws to a close; time does not wait for us. Those who study the Way should take "daily diminution" as their resolve; those who dwell in the world should take "timeliness" as their primary task.

"You, my lord, possess both mature years and great virtue; you ought to find a worthy object of devotion quickly. Do not let your mind remain fixed on the Way of the Daoists, lest you sit idly by and lose the prime of your life.
He further sent five poems in reply, one of which said:
"The movement of destiny knows no pause; in a flash, the years and seasons pass away."
The great boulders shall eventually be exhausted; how could the mustard seeds be called many?
It is precisely because one departs without ceasing that they evoke sighs by the riverbank.
Have you not heard of Rong Qiqi, who sang a pure song with his hair white as snow?
Coarse cloth can warm the body; who needs to discuss the adornment of silk and brocade?
Though this life may be said to be pleasant, what can one do for future lives?
Sin and merit truly depend on oneself; how can one say that one is merely pitying others?
Since Sengdu’s resolve was as unyielding as a rock and could not be turned back, Tiaohua was moved to realization and likewise gave rise to deep faith.

Thereupon, Sengdu devoted himself single-mindedly to the Buddha-dharma, delving into and savoring the various scriptures; he also composed the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra-tattvārtha*, which circulated in the world. His final whereabouts remain unknown.

At that time, there was another named Zhu Huichao in Henei, whose practice and understanding were both eminent. He was a close friend of the eminent scholar Zhou Xuzhi of Yanmen and annotated the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huijiao of Jiaxiang Temple in Kuaiji during the Liang Dynasty.
The two [masters] Shi Dao’an (1) and Shi Fahe (2); Zhu Senglang (3); Zhu Fatai (4);

Shi Sengxian (5); Zhu Sengfu (6); Zhu Sengfu (7); Shi Tanyi (8); Shi Fayu (9); Shi Tanhui (10); Shi Daoli (11); Shi Tanjie (12); Zhu Fakang (13); Shi Daoyi (14); Shi Huiqian (15). 1. Shi Dao’an: His secular surname was Wei, and he was a native of Fuliu in Changshan.
His family had been a lineage of eminent scholars, but he lost his parents early and was raised by his maternal uncle, the Kong family.
At the age of seven, he began reading; he could recite a text after reading it only once, which drew the admiration and astonishment of his neighbors.
At the age of twelve, he left the household life.
His spiritual wisdom was sharp and acute, yet his physical appearance was extremely unprepossessing; consequently, he was not held in high regard by his teacher.

For three years, he was driven to labor in the fields; though he performed his duties with diligence and underwent such toil, he never showed a trace of resentment. By nature steadfast and diligent, he observed the fasts and precepts without fail.

After several years, he finally approached his teacher to request scriptures. The teacher gave him one fascicle of the *Bianyi jing* (Sūtra on Resolving Doubts), consisting of approximately five thousand words.
Dao’an took the scripture with him into the fields; while resting there, he began to read it. Returning home at dusk, he returned the scripture to his teacher and requested another.
The teacher said, "You have not finished reading yesterday’s scripture, yet you are already asking for more?"
He replied, "I have already recited it from memory.
Although the master marveled at this, he did not yet believe him.
He was further given one scroll of the *Sūtra on the Radiance of Accomplishment*, consisting of slightly less than ten thousand words.
He carried it with him as before and returned to his teacher at dusk.
