Daolang then established a separate vihāra in the Kunlun Mountains of Jinyu Valley; this was a cliff to the northwest of Mount Tai.
The peaks and gorges were lofty and precipitous, while the waters and rocks were grand and imposing.
Senglang constructed chambers and halls, exhausting the natural beauty of the mountains; there were more than several dozen buildings both inside and out.
More than one hundred people came to him upon hearing his reputation; Hui-lang tirelessly instructed and exhorted them, never complaining of fatigue despite his labors.
Fu Jian, the ruler of Qin, admired his long-standing virtue and sent an envoy to invite him, but Lang declined on the grounds of old age and illness, and thus the matter was dropped.
Thereupon, [Hui]jian sent letters and gifts every month.
Later, when Jian purged the monastic community, he issued a separate edict stating:
"Dharma Master Lang’s preceptual virtue is as pure as ice and frost, and his disciples are refined and elegant; this entire mountain of Kunlun shall not be subject to the search."
Later, Yao Xing of the Later Qin also marveled at and highly esteemed him.

Murong De, the Prince of Yan, admired Daolang’s reputation and conduct; he granted him the title of King of Dongqi and provided him with the tax revenues of two counties. Daolang declined the kingship but accepted the tax revenues to cultivate meritorious karma.
Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty sent him a letter and gifts, and Tuoba Gui, the ruler of Wei, likewise sent a letter and presents; such was the respect he commanded from his contemporaries.

Previously, this valley had suffered frequent tiger disasters, and travelers would always have to travel in groups while carrying weapons. However, once Hui-lang resided there, the fierce beasts submitted and retreated; whether traveling by day or night, both monastics and laypeople encountered no obstacles. The common people sighed in admiration, praising him boundlessly, and thus the title "Fenggaoren" (The Man of High Virtue) remains to this day.
Thus, Jinyu Valley was called Lang Gong Valley.
Whenever anyone came to visit Lang, no matter how many people there were, he would invariably know their number in advance, even before they had arrived on the day of their arrival.
He instructed his disciples to prepare food and drink, and as he had predicted, they arrived exactly as he had said; there were none who did not marvel at his prescient insight.
Later, he passed away in the mountains at the age of eighty-five.
At that time, there was also Zhi Sengduan of Taishan; originally a native of Jizhou, he traveled through Qianlong during his youth and spent his adulthood in Jingzhou and Yongzhou.
He was profoundly versed in the Mahāyāna and was also skilled in the Abhidharma-śāstra and the Nyāya-śāstra.
He authored the *Treatise on the Original Meaning of Human Figures*, which also circulated in the world.
4. Zhu Fatai was a native of Dongguan. In his youth, he studied together with Dao’an;
although his talent and eloquence did not equal his teacher’s, his physical appearance surpassed him.
While fleeing from the dangers together with Dao’an, they traveled as far as Xinye. Dao’an divided his disciples, commanding Tái to proceed to the capital.

As they parted, he said to Dao’an, “The Master shall establish the ritual standards in the northwest, while I shall propagate the teachings in the southeast; thus our paths in the rivers and lakes shall remain within sight of one another.”
"As for the sublime assembly and pure causes, we shall await them through the cold of the coming years.
Thereupon they parted ways, bidding farewell with tears.
He then traveled eastward along the river with over forty disciples, including Tanyi and Tange, but encountered illness and halted at Yangkou.
At that time, Huan Wen was stationed in Jingzhou and sent an envoy to invite him, providing him with medical supplies and medicine;
Master Dao’an also dispatched his disciple Huiyuan to go down to Jingzhou to inquire after his illness, and Daotai’s condition improved slightly.

He went to see Sengwen; Wen wished to engage in a long conversation with Sengtai, but while he was still addressing his guests, he had not yet reached Tai. Since Tai’s illness had not yet abated, he could not endure sitting for long, so he mounted a carriage, passed through the corridors, and departed.
Xiang Wen said to Sengyuan, "A fit of wind-phlegm has suddenly arisen; I cannot endure speaking for long, so I shall come again later.
Sengyuan hurriedly rose and went out, escorting him back home.
Tài was eight chi tall; his bearing was elegant and worthy of admiration. He was refined and dignified in his speech, and his words were as fragrant as orchids.

At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Dàohéng, who possessed considerable talent and influence; he constantly upheld the doctrine of "Mind-Non-existence" (wúxīn), which was widely practiced throughout the Jing region.
Fatai said,
"This is a heterodox teaching and must be refuted.
He then assembled a great multitude of renowned monks and ordered his disciple Tanyi to challenge them with difficult questions.
Relying on scriptural citations and logical reasoning, he analyzed and refuted their various arguments.
Constantly relying on his verbal eloquence, he refused to yield; as the daylight faded, they gathered again the following morning.
Huiyuan took his seat and posed several rounds of difficult questions, his critical inquiries arising with sharp intensity.
Daoheng felt that the paths of their respective doctrines were diverging; his expression shifted slightly, and he tapped the desk with his fly-whisk, yet he did not immediately provide an answer.
Yuan said, "If one is swift without exerting effort, what need is there for the shuttle and loom?
Those present all laughed.
The meaning of "the non-existence of mind" finds its cessation here.

Daotai retired from the capital to reside at Waguan Temple; Emperor Jianwen, the second sovereign of the Jin dynasty, held him in profound esteem and requested that he lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Fangguang jing).
At the opening assembly, the Emperor personally attended, and the princes, dukes, and high officials all gathered there without exception.

Daotai’s physical bearing and spiritual liberation surpassed those of ordinary men, and his reputation had spread far and wide; on the day he began his lectures, both monastics and laypeople, men and women alike, assembled in great crowds to observe and listen.
He consulted with his disciples, who sat in rows one after another; from the Three Wu regions, thousands arrived carrying their bundles of books.

The Waguan Monastery was originally the site of the tomb of Shan Wan of Henei, used as a kiln for making pottery. During the Xingning era of the Jin dynasty, the śramaṇa Huili petitioned to have it converted into a monastery, at which time there were only a hall and a stupa.
When Dao-tai took up residence there, he further expanded the chambers and halls and established various monastic works; he also constructed a grand gatehouse to take advantage of the topography.

The residence of Sengzi Sima Zong, the heir apparent of Runan, was close to the temple, and he subsequently encroached upon and excavated the side of the monastery, causing the gatehouse to collapse and sink; yet Dao-tai did not take this to heart.
Zong was then moved to realization; he went in person to apologize for his transgressions. Daotai lay down to meet him, appearing as if no one else were present.
Wang Qia, General of the Household; Wang Xun of Dongting; and Xie An, Grand Preceptor—all held him in boundless reverence.
A few days before his death, he suddenly felt unwell and said to his disciples,
"I am about to depart.
He passed away in the twelfth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty at the age of sixty-eight.
Emperor Xiaowu of the Liezong era issued an edict, saying:
"The Dharma Master T'ai’s Way has spread throughout the eight directions, and his bounty flows down to future generations. That he has suddenly passed away pierces my heart with grief."
"You may provide a funeral subsidy of one hundred thousand coins; whatever is required for the funeral rites shall be prepared accordingly.
Sun Chuo composed a eulogy for him, saying:
"A chilling wind brushes the forest, and the sounding strings reflect upon the waves."
"Shuangshuang Fatai, when comparing our virtues, I have no cause for shame.

Fatai’s disciples, Tanyi and Tan’er, were both extensively trained in the meanings of the scriptures and were also skilled in the *Laozi* and the *Yijing*. Elegant in their refined tastes and pursuits, they were renowned as equals to Huiyuan.
When Tanyue died young, Fatai wept for him so bitterly that he exclaimed,
"Heaven has destroyed my Hui!
Fatai’s commentaries on the scriptures, as well as his letter to Xi Chao discussing the meaning of "original non-being" (benwu), both circulated throughout the world.
As for those who claim that Fatai was a disciple of Master Dao’an, this is incorrect. 5.
Zhu Sengxian: Sengxian was a native of Jizhou and a disciple of Master Yuan of Changshan.
By nature he was pure and abstemious, and possessed of steadfast integrity.

While he was still a śrāmaṇera, he encountered Dao’an at an inn; at that time, Dao’an had also not yet received full ordination, so they shared their aspirations and mutual admiration with such noble spirit and vigor.
As they were about to part, they said to one another, "When we have both grown up, let us not forget our shared journey.

After receiving the precepts, he practiced with diligent austerity; his mastery of the sutras and śāstras was profound. Encountering the chaos of the Shi clan, he went into hiding on Mount Feilong. There, he dwelt in contemplation among the crags and cliffs, attaining realization in the wisdom of dhyāna.
Later, Dao’an followed him again; they met with great joy, and Dao’an said:
"Since we first followed [the Master] according to our former vow, we have together examined the texts and applied our reflections, resulting in many new insights."
Dao’an said, “The old method of *geyi* (matching meanings) frequently deviates from the underlying principles.
Daosheng replied:
"Let us first set aside our leisurely contemplation; how can we permit ourselves to judge the right or wrong of our predecessors?

Dao'an said, "In propagating and extolling the principles of the teachings, one should ensure they are fully satisfying; when the Dharma drums resound in competition, what priority or sequence can there be?"
Previously, he had traveled south with Fatai and others to the Jinping region, where he lectured on the Way and propagated the teachings.
Later, upon returning to Xiangyang, he fell ill and passed away.
There was also the śramaṇa Daohu, likewise a native of Jizhou, who possessed pure integrity and profound insight; he too lived in seclusion at Feilong Mountain.
Upon meeting with Dao’an and the others, he spoke with them, saying:

"Dwelling in seclusion and having distanced ourselves from the secular world, we have always desired to rectify the Great Dharma; how can we merely walk alone within the mountain gates, allowing the turning of the Wheel of Dharma to come to a halt?"
"It is fitting that each of you, according to your own capacity, repay the Buddha's kindness.
The assembly all said,
"Excellent."
Thereupon, they each went forth to propagate the teachings.
Later, their final whereabouts remained unknown.
6. Zhu Sengfu: Zhu Sengfu was a native of Ye.

From his youth, he maintained the precepts and held fast to his resolve with austere integrity; his learning was thorough across all treatises, and he was additionally proficient in the sutras and the Dharma. His Way resounded throughout the Yi and Luo regions, and the capital’s populace revered him as their master.

Encountering the famine and turmoil of the Western Jin dynasty, Sengfu hid with Shi Dao’an and others at Huozhai, where he refined his studies and engaged in analytical inquiry until he thoroughly mastered the subtle and profound mysteries.

Later, while staying at Shangming Temple in Jingzhou, he lived frugally on simple vegetarian fare, performing rituals and repentances with diligent devotion, vowing to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven to gaze upon Maitreya.

At that time, Wang Teng, the Prince of Langya, served as the Governor of Jingzhou; admiring Xu Fu’s integrity and simplicity, he invited him to serve as his preceptor for the precepts, and the entire family followed his teachings with devotion.
Later, two days before his death, he suddenly said:
"I shall depart tomorrow."
Upon his death, a wondrous fragrance filled the room and the sounds of Brahma resounded in succession; both monastics and laypeople rushed there in droves, numbering in the tens of thousands.
In the afternoon of that day, he passed away peacefully without illness at the age of sixty. He was buried within the monastery, and the monks erected a stupa for him.
7. Zhu Sengfu: His clan and lineage are unknown.

He was thoroughly versed in the various sutras and was particularly skilled in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* (The Light-Emitting) and the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* (The Path-Practice).

During the turmoil at the end of the Western Jin dynasty, he moved to the region east of the Yangtze River and resided at Waguan Monastery in the capital. He established a flourishing seat for lectures, and among the veteran monks of Jianye, there was none who did not respect and submit to him.
At that time, the śramaṇa Daosong of the same monastery, whose talent and understanding were likewise of the highest order, wrote a letter to Dao’an, saying:
“Master Fu’s investigation of the subtle is brilliant and outstanding; it is beyond the reach of those such as us.”
At that time, the followers of the various heterodox schools all maintained that the mind and spirit possess form, though they are more subtle than the myriad things;
each, according to their own eloquence, sought to refute and suppress the others.

Fu then composed the "Discourse on the Formlessness of the Spirit" (*Shen Wuxing Lun*), arguing that whatever possesses form necessarily possesses number, and whatever possesses number is subject to exhaustion; since the spirit is inexhaustible, one knows it must be formless.

At that time, those who relied on mere sophistry were embroiled in a chaotic and contentious dispute; once the principles had found their proper resting place, they were satisfied and submitted with conviction.
Subsequently, he also composed commentaries (*yishu*) on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in Eight Thousand Lines* (*Fangguang*) and the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (*Daoying*).
Later, he passed away within the monastery at the age of over seventy.
Zhu Fatai wrote in a letter to Dao’an:

“Every time I recall the Venerable Fu’s presence with me, it seems as if it were only yesterday; yet since his passing, many years have already elapsed. On those days when we engaged in pure conversation, there was never a moment when I did not miss him.”
I had hoped to collaborate with you in further elucidating its excellence; I never imagined that one day we would be forever separated by death.
My grief and regret are so profound that how could I ever forget my feelings?
As for the principles realized and the labor spent in investigation, it is truly difficult to ever fully represent them.
Fatai sent letters to Dao’an, frequently recounting Sengfu’s exegesis; however, as I now search for them, I have lost the original texts, and their disappearance is lamentable.
8. Shi Tanyi: Shi Tanyi’s secular surname was Yao; he was a Qiang person, though some say he was from Jizhou.
At the age of sixteen, he left the household life and served Master Dao’an as his teacher.
From his youth, he was renowned for his observance of the Vinaya; his learning encompassed the Tripiṭaka, and he was highly esteemed by those within the school.
While traveling through Shu Commandery, the Provincial Governor Mao Qu held him in high esteem and prepared a midday meal for him, attending to his needs with his own hands.

Seeing a single grain of rice in the bowl, Sengyi picked it up first and ate it; Qu, observing this in secret, marveled at his extraordinary character and knew that he would surely not fail to honor the faithful offerings made to him.
He subsequently received a gift of one thousand hu of rice, which Sengyi accepted and distributed as alms.
Sengyi once accompanied Dao’an at Tanchi Temple; at that time, Teng Han, the Governor of Changsha under the Jin dynasty, donated his residence in Jiangling to establish a temple.

Hui'an requested one monk to serve as the leader, and Hui'an said to Sengyi, "The gentry and commoners of Jingzhou and Chu are beginning to seek a teacher; who other than you could bring their transformation to completion?"
Fayi then took up his staff and traveled south, where he constructed a monastery; this was the Changsha Monastery.

Later, when the Hu rebels broke out and plundered the region south of the Han River, the entire district of Jiangling fled to Shangming to seek refuge, and Fayi once again established a monastery there.
Once the rebel hordes had been dispersed, he returned to Jiangling and restored Changsha Temple.
Through his sincere and earnest prayers, he was moved to manifest śarīra relics; these he enshrined in a golden vase and placed upon the altar during the vegetarian feast.
Yi then prostrated himself and made a vow, saying:
"If this is truly the lingering radiance of Vajrapāṇi, may he release his light.
At midnight, five-colored splendors gradually emerged from the flask, illuminating the entire hall.
The entire assembly was struck with wonder and sighed in admiration;
there was none who did not feel a divine inspiration as if on the wings of faith. At that moment, even those such as Pūraṇa, upon seeing this, turned away from falsehood and returned to the truth.
Later, he entered Mount Jun near Baling to fell timber; this is the Mount Dongting mentioned in the *Shanhai jing*.
On the mountain there is a cavern that connects to Baoshan in Wu.

As the mountain was already renowned for its spiritual anomalies, people were deeply apprehensive of it. When Sengyi led his followers into the mountains, they encountered dozens of white snakes lying across the path to block their way. Sengyi retreated to his residence and, from afar, requested the mountain deity to perform rites of repentance on his behalf.
He then said to the deity, "I am felling timber to build a temple; I pray that you will join me in this meritorious deed.
That night, he immediately saw the deity in a dream, who told Xiyi:
"The Dharma Master has already granted his special approval for this timber to be used for the Three Jewels; you must simply ensure that no one else takes it by wrongful means.

The next day they went again, and the road was exceptionally clear and level. Thereupon they felled the wood and floated it downstream, though among those who felled the wood, some could not help but pilfer it privately.
Upon returning to the monastery, the construction materials had already been completed; those items that others had privately claimed were all confiscated by the authorities.
Such was the power of his sincerity.
Zhiyi often sighed that while the monastery was established and the monastic community sufficient, the sacred images were still too few.

The images and reliquaries commissioned by King Aśoka were numerous and possessed many divine wonders, yet they were distributed throughout all directions; how is it that there was no response, and none could be summoned?
Therefore, one must apply oneself with single-minded devotion and sincere compassion, so that a true response may be sought.

On the eighth day of the second month in the year of Jiawu, the nineteenth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, a statue suddenly appeared to the north of the city, its radiant form piercing the heavens. At that time, the monastic community of Baima Temple went out first to welcome it, but they were unable to move it.
Yi then went to pay his respects and said to the crowd, "This must be an image of King Aśoka, which has descended upon our Changsha Temple.

He immediately ordered three disciples to receive it with their hands; it rose up with a whirring motion, and they welcomed it back to their own temple. Monastics and laypeople rushed there in a great throng, the sound of carriages and horses filling the air.

Later, the Kasmirian meditation master Saṃghananda came down from Shu and entered the temple to pay his respects; seeing the Sanskrit characters upon the light above the image, he said, "This is an image of King Aśoka. When did it come here?"
Those who heard this at the time finally realized that his words were not mistaken.
He passed away at the age of eighty-two; on the day of his death, the halo around his image suddenly underwent a spiritual transformation, and no one knew where it had gone.
Both monastics and laypeople alike claimed that Huīzhī’s spiritual resonance was profound.

At that time, there was also the śramaṇa Sēngwèi at Chángshā Temple, whose scholarly achievements were highly esteemed and for whom Yīn Zhōngkān held great respect; he was particularly skilled in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and composed a commentary upon it.
9. Shi Fayu: It is unknown who Shi Fayu was.
From his youth, he was fond of learning and devoted himself earnestly to the ancient classics; however, he was by nature arrogant and boastful, acting as if there were no one else around him.
Later, he encountered Master Dao’an and was suddenly filled with faith and submission; he subsequently cast aside his hairpin to pledge himself to the Way, serving An as his teacher.
Having been bathed in this profound transformation, his realization became extraordinary; he subdued his original ambitions and cultivated virtue through humility.

Ruan Bao, the Governor of Yiyang, heard of his reputation and admired him from afar, establishing a bond of spiritual friendship with him. He sent letters to maintain friendly relations and provided him with continuous offerings.

Later, when Xiangyang was beset by invaders, Daoxu encountered the chaos and fled eastward, settling at Changsha Monastery in Jiangling, where he lectured on various sutras; more than four hundred people received his instruction.
At that time, a certain monk drank wine and neglected the evening incense offering; he encountered Daozhi, who punished him but did not dismiss him.

Master Hui’an heard of this from afar and placed a single willow switch inside a bamboo tube, which he personally sealed and addressed to Daozhi. When Daozhi opened the seal and saw the switch, he said:
"This is because of the monk who drank wine. I am negligent in my leadership and training, and have thus caused you to bestow your concern upon me from afar."

He immediately commanded the *karmadāna* to strike the gavel to assemble the community; he placed the staff-case upon the incense table, and once the incense offering was completed, Yu rose, stepped before the assembly, and paid his respects toward the case.
Thereupon, he prostrated himself on the ground; the *vina* was ordered to administer three strokes of the staff, which were then placed inside the staff-tube as he shed tears and reproached himself.
At that time, among the monastics and laypeople within the jurisdiction, there was none who did not sigh with emotion, and consequently, many were inspired to exert themselves in their practice.
Shortly thereafter, he wrote to Huiyuan, saying:

"I am a person of meager virtue, obscure and deficient, unable to lead the multitude. Although you, Venerable One, are separated from me by distant lands, you still graciously extend your compassionate concern; my transgressions are profound indeed."
Later, he passed away in Jiangling at the age of sixty.
10. Shi Tanhui. Shi Tanhui was a native of Henei. At the age of twelve, he entered the monastic order under Dao’an.

Dao’an, admiring his spiritual brilliance, first had him study secular texts; within two or three years, his learning encompassed both the Confucian classics and the histories. It was not until he was sixteen that Dao’an permitted him to have his head shaved.

Thereupon, he devoted himself exclusively to the principles of Buddhism, reflecting upon and fathoming its profound mysteries; before even reaching his twentieth year, he was already able to lecture and expound upon them.
Although his aspirations and achievements were lofty and pure from the start, he was held in high esteem for his humility and deference.
Later, he followed Dao’an to Xiangyang. When Fu Pi invaded the borders, he traveled east to Jingzhou and stayed at Shangming Temple.
Whenever the Dharma wheel was turned, both monastics and laypeople would rush there in haste.
Constantly mindful that there must be a source for this understanding, he then had a portrait of Dao’an painted, which he kept in mind and worshipped.
Thereupon, the men and women of Jiangling all turned westward to pay their respects to the Bodhisattva Yinshou.
Someone asked,
"Regarding the Dharma Master’s transformation through the Way, how does he compare to the Upādhyāya? Huī replied:
"The inner practice of my Preceptor is so profound that it is not easily fathomed;
as for the external conditions he brings to bear, there are many miraculous responses.
Compared to me, who am but a single drop, how could I possibly be likened to the rivers and seas!"
He passed away in the twentieth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty.
On the day of his death, his body was free from any ailment; he ascended to the hall to eat with the assembly and there took his leave.
Having finished his meal, he returned to his room and passed away while lying on his right side; he was seventy-three years of age.

He authored nine chapters of the *Liben lun* (Treatise on Establishing the Foundation) and twelve pieces titled *Lishi zhigui* (The Essential Return of the Six Consciousnesses), both of which circulated in the world.
11. Shi Daoli. Shi Daoli was a man of unknown origins.
He left home to become a monk in his youth and served Master Dao’an as his teacher; he was well-versed in the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* (Fàngguāng jīng).
Furthermore, as the "Three Mysteries" of the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi* subtly correspond to Buddhist principles, he also devoted considerable attention to them.
By nature, he was serene and pure, remaining aloof from the affairs of the contemporary world.
Later, he followed Dao’an into the Guanzhong region and lived in seclusion on Mount Fuzhou; dwelling among the crags alone, he accepted no offerings.
Whenever he immersed himself in contemplation and entered dhyāna, he would not rise for seven days, and this occurred several times.
Later, at the beginning of summer, he suddenly left the mountain and gathered the assembly of monks to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* himself.
When someone asked him the reason for this, he replied:
"I can only remain until autumn; I wish to bring my current undertakings to a rough conclusion."
A few days after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he indeed passed away without illness; those of the time remarked that he was one who knew his destiny. 12. Shi Tanjie (釋曇戒).

Shi Tanjie, also known as Huijing (慧精), was surnamed Zhuo (卓) and was a native of Nanyang (南陽). He was the younger brother of Zhuo Qian (卓潛), who served as the Commandant of Jiyang (棘陽) in the Ministry of External Military Affairs during the Jin dynasty.
Living in poverty, he devoted himself to study, immersing his mind in the ancient classics.

Later, hearing that Yu Fadao was lecturing on the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, he borrowed robes to attend a single session; thereupon, he gained a profound realization of Buddhist principles, abandoned secular life for the Way, and served Master Dao’an as his teacher.

He was extensively versed in the Tripiṭaka and could recite over five hundred thousand words of the sūtras. Every day he performed five hundred prostrations before the Buddha; the Prince of Linchuan of the Jin dynasty held him in high esteem.

Later, while suffering from a severe illness, he constantly recited the name of Maitreya Buddha without ceasing. His disciple Zhisheng attended to his illness and asked why he did not aspire to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
He instructed him, saying: "I and seven others, including Huishang, have made a common vow to be reborn in Tuṣita."
"The Upādhyāya, Daoyuan, and the others have all already attained rebirth in the Pure Land; as for me, I have not yet been able to go, which is why I made this vow.

Having finished speaking, light immediately shone upon his body and his countenance became even more serene. He then suddenly passed away at the age of seventy, and was buried to the right of An Gong’s tomb.

13. Shi Fakang (also known as Zhu Fakang): His surname was Gao, and he was a native of Xiapi. He resided in Wuxing and lost both parents at an early age; he served his stepmother with such filial piety that it became renowned.
His family was poor and had no savings; he constantly worked the fields by the embankments to provide for his mother’s material needs and nourishment.
When his mother passed away, he observed the funeral rites with full propriety. Upon completing the period of mourning, he left the household life and served the śramaṇa Zhu Tan-yin as his teacher.
Yin Mingyue possessed noble conduct and spiritual practice; Kuang served him with utmost sincerity until he received full ordination.
His character and discipline were lofty and stood out from the crowd; he lived in simplicity and remained settled in his vocation, his aspirations and conduct being profound and deep.

Once, when Sengyin was gravely ill and in a critical condition, Huikang prayed with utmost sincerity and performed ritual repentance for seven days and seven nights. On the seventh day, he suddenly saw five-colored light illuminating the door of Sengyin’s room; Sengyin felt as though someone were pressing on him with their hand, whereupon his ailment was immediately cured.
Later, he took leave of his teacher to travel afar, extensively seeking the essentials of the scriptures. Upon his return, he settled in a stone grotto on Mount Qing at Qian.

He consistently regarded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the principle for the convergence of the three vehicles and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* as the cause for rebirth in the Pure Land. He frequently chanted these two texts; when there was an assembly, he would lecture upon them, and when dwelling alone, he would recite them.

When Xie An was serving as the Governor of Wuxing, he went there to pay his respects; however, the mountain retreat was so secluded and remote that even carriage tracks could not reach it. Thereupon, he unharnessed his horses on the mountain ridge and proceeded on foot across the peaks.

Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty dispatched Qu Anyuan, the Governor of Tangyi, with an imperial decree to inquire after his health and to consult him regarding a malevolent star, requesting that He Kang exert his efforts [to avert it].
Kang replied to the decree:

"In the past, when Lord Jing of Song cultivated merit, the malevolent star shifted its position. Since Your Majesty has provided brilliant support, the administration and justice have been harmonious and settled. However, the Mandate of Heaven is heavy and the myriad affairs are numerous; to err by even a hair's breadth is to be off by a thousand li."

"You should simply diligently cultivate virtuous governance to compete with Heaven's retribution; I, a poor monk, shall surely respond with utmost sincerity, yet I fear I have the will but lack the power.
Thereupon, he and his disciples performed a fast and repentance ceremony, and after a short while, the calamity was extinguished.
During the Xingning era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled east to explore the Cave of Yu, gazing upon the mountains and waters.

He first cast himself into the solitary pool of Ruoye, intending to dwell among the crags and ridges to live in leisure and cultivate his aspirations; both Xi Chao and Xie Qingxu likewise formed a bond with him to reside beyond the mundane world.

At that time, the eastern regions were frequently afflicted by epidemics. Since Dao Kuang had studied the *Compassion Sūtra* (Cibei jian) in his youth and was skilled in divine incantations (*mantras*), he traveled through the villages to rescue those in urgent distress.
He subsequently left the city and stayed at Changyuan Temple; among the common people who were ill, many sought his prayers with great efficacy.
There was one who could see ghosts, who said that whenever Zhu Sengkuang walked or stayed, there were always several dozen spirits and deities guarding him from before and behind.
