Truly, I have not yet been able to knock at the wondrous gate of the ford and move the lingering spirits through my sincerity.
As for my empty bosom and forgotten covenant, there is not a day that I do not cherish them.
Indeed, when sandalwood is transplanted, it perfumes other things with its fragrance;
when the mani-jewel emits its radiance, various treasures gather of their own accord.

This is precisely the Way of harmonizing with the teachings: one departs empty-handed but returns with substance; how much more so for one who takes the formless One as the ultimate principle and responds without emotional attachment?
Therefore, those who shoulder the Great Dharma must take non-requital as their core intention;
those who gather friends through benevolence ensure that merit does not accrue to themselves alone.

If the Wheel of Dharma were made to cease its turning on the path of the Eightfold Noble Way, and the Three Jewels were allowed to stop their resonance at the end of the kalpa, then Sāramati’s fulfillment of his vows would not alone possess singular beauty across the ages, and Nāgārjuna would not be uniquely virtuous for following in the footsteps of those who came before.

I have now brought a garment tailored according to the rules of inference; I pray that you will ascend the high seat and don it, along with this vessel for straining water from the heavens. Since these are ritual objects, I offer them briefly as an expression of my devotion.
Kumārajīva replied in a letter, saying: "Kumārajīva bows in greeting.
Since we have not yet met in person and our written expressions are so vastly different, the path for guiding the mind is blocked and the conditions for attaining mutual understanding are severed."

I have received news through the postal relay and have roughly grasped the essence of your virtuous character; I hope you are well. One thorough understanding is sufficient to encompass a hundred details.
As the Sūtra says:
"In the final age, there shall be a Bodhisattva in the East who protects the Dharma."
Exert yourselves, O benevolent ones, and skillfully propagate this task.

Now, there are five requisites for wealth: merit, precepts, extensive learning, eloquence, and profound wisdom. Those who possess all of these will cause the Way to flourish; those who lack them will encounter doubt and stagnation.
Venerable sir, you have already prepared these matters.
As for entrusting my heart to maintain friendly relations and using a translator to convey my meaning, how could I possibly exhaust the matter? It is merely a rough response to your kind intentions.

Regarding the tailored robes you sent by courier, intended for me to wear when ascending the Dharma seat, they truly accord with the Tathāgata’s wishes; yet, as the person does not match the object, I feel only shame.
I now take this brass double-mouthed bathing pitcher, which I have used for a long time, to serve as one of my ritual implements; along with it, I leave behind a verse which says:
"Since you have already abandoned the pleasures of defilement, has your mind attained proper restraint?"
If one does not allow the mind to wander, does one enter deeply into the true mark?
Within the mark of ultimate emptiness, the mind finds nothing to delight in.
If one takes pleasure in dhyāna and wisdom, this is the non-illumination of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
"Deceptive things such as these lack reality and are not places where the mind may rest.
O Benevolent One, I pray that you will graciously show me the essentials of the Dharma you have attained.
Yuanzong again sent a letter to Kumārajīva, saying:
"The days have been cool; how have things been since then?
Last month, when the Dharma-knowing practitioner arrived, I heard that you intended to return to your native land, which left me with a sense of regret."

Previously, I heard that you were about to bring forth many Mahāyāna sūtras; therefore, I have come specifically to consult you. If this report is not false, the grievances of the multitude are beyond words.

I now briefly inquire about several dozen matters, hoping you might find the leisure to explain one or two of them. Although these are not the most difficult points within the sūtras, I wish to seek a definitive resolution from you.
He then sent back a verse, saying:
"From where does the root of all things ultimately arise? Its arising and ceasing span the limits of existence and non-existence.
A single atom, once it enters the realm of movement, creates this momentum like a crumbling mountain."
Delusive thoughts multiply one after another; upon encountering the Principle, they naturally give rise to stagnation.
Although causes and conditions have no master, the opening of the path does not occur in a single lifetime.
Since there is no enlightened master at this time, who will grasp the profound seal?
"Your coming to inquire has been long anticipated; let us together look forward to the final years.

Later, Puṇyatāra arrived in Guanzhong and recited the Sanskrit text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Kumārajīva translated it into the language of Jin, but when two-thirds of the work had been completed, Puṇyatāra passed away. Huiyuan constantly lamented that the text remained incomplete.

Upon hearing that Dharmaruci had entered the Qin territory and was moreover well-versed in reciting this section of the Vinaya, he dispatched his disciple Tanyong with a letter of entreaty, requesting that the remaining portions be translated once more in Guanzhong; thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong) was made complete and without omission.
The original texts were obtained in the territory of Jin and have been transmitted down to the present day.
These wondrous scriptures from beyond the Pamirs and the excellent expositions from Guanzhong were brought together in this land through the power of Huiyuan.

The monastic community of foreign lands all proclaimed that there were Mahāyāna practitioners in the land of Han; whenever they burned incense and prostrated, they would invariably bow their heads toward the east, offering their hearts to Mount Lu.
The traces of its divine principle are, therefore, as yet unfathomable.
Previously, in the Central Land, there had been no doctrine of *nirvāṇa* as eternal permanence; one spoke only of the longevity of life.
Huiyuan then sighed and said:
"The Buddha is the ultimate; that which is ultimate is unchanging.
How could the principle of the unchanging ever come to an end!"
Consequently, he composed the *Dharmatā-śāstra*, stating:
"The ultimate takes non-alteration as its nature; attaining this nature takes the embodiment of the ultimate as its principle.
When Kumārajīva saw this treatise, he sighed in admiration, saying:
“The people of this frontier land have not yet possessed the scriptures, yet they have spontaneously conformed to the principles; how marvelous!

Yao Xing, the ruler of Qin, admired his virtue and reputation and marveled at his talent and insight. He sent him letters with profound courtesy and a continuous stream of gifts and offerings. To express his sincere devotion, he presented him with a finely woven image of various transformations from the kingdom of Kucha, and further ordered Yao Song to offer him a pearl image.
When the new translation of the *Śāstra* was completed, Kumārajīva sent the treatise along with a letter, saying:

"The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* has been newly translated. Since this work was composed by Nāgārjuna and represents the ultimate purport of the Vaipulya sūtras, it is fitting that you compose a preface to express the author's intent."
However, these various Daoist masters all defer to one another and none dare to set hand to it; you, Dharma Master, might compose a preface for it to be bequeathed to future students.
Huiyuan replied in a letter, saying:
"I wish to have you compose a preface to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to express the author's intent.
I, this poor monk, have heard that..."
To harbor the great is not something a small vessel can contain; to draw from the deep is not something a short rope can fathom.

On the day I opened and examined [your letter], I felt ashamed that my words could not match your lofty command. Furthermore, as my body is frail and plagued by many ailments, I have been unable to attend to matters; it has been a long time since I last applied my mind to such things. Yet, because of the gravity of your communication, I have hastily jotted down these rough thoughts of what I hold in my heart.
"As for the beauty of scholarly research, one must further look to those of illustrious virtue.
Such was the loftiness of his reputation.

Daoyuan often remarked that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* was so voluminous and extensive that beginners found it difficult to navigate; he therefore excerpted its essential passages and compiled them into twenty fascicles.
The preface was profound and elegant, such that it allowed students to achieve more than half their intended merit with ease.
Later, when Huan Xuan campaigned against Yin Zhongkan, his army passed by Mount Lu; he summoned Huiyuan to emerge from Tiger Creek.
Huiyuan was far away and claimed he was too ill to endure it.
Daoyuan entered the mountains himself, and his attendants said to him, "In the past, Yin Zhongkan entered the mountains to pay his respects to Huiyuan; we pray that you do not show him such honor."
Xuan replied: "How could such a principle exist!
Zhongkan was originally nothing but a dead man."
When he arrived and saw Huiyuan, he could not help but pay his respects.
Huiyuan asked, "The precept states 'one must not dare to injure or damage [the body]'; why then have you shaved your hair?"
Yuan replied, "To establish oneself and practice the Way.
Xuan praised this as excellent; he did not dare speak further of the questions and difficulties he had harbored, and instead spoke of his intention regarding the military expedition.
Huiyuan did not answer.
Daoyuan asked again,
"How do you perceive your vows?"
Yuan said, "I pray that the donor may remain in peace and security, and that he too shall meet with no misfortune.
When Huiyan emerged from the mountains, he said to those around him:
"Truly, this is something I have never seen in my life.
Later, Huan, employing his influence as one whose power could rival the sovereign, earnestly sought to entice him with invitations; Xun then sent a letter to Shen, urging him to accept office.
Huiyuan’s reply was firm and upright, resolute and unshakable; his will surpassed that of red stone, and in the end, no one could turn him back.
Shortly thereafter, Huanxuan intended to purge the monastic community and instructed his subordinates, saying:

"Among the śramaṇas, those who can expound the scriptures and elucidate their principles, or whose conduct is disciplined and refined such that they are fit to propagate the Great Transformation—let all others who deviate from these standards be dismissed."
"Only Mount Lu is the abode of those who dwell in the Way and its Virtue; it is not subject to the rules of searching and selection.
Huiyuan wrote in a letter to Daoxuan:
"The Buddhist teaching has declined, and for a long time it has been defiled by impurities. Every time I reflect upon this, my heart is filled with lamentation and indignation."
I am constantly apprehensive that my destiny may take an unintended turn and that ruin may soon befall me.
I have observed the teachings of the various pure and serene practitioners, which truly accord with my own fundamental heart.
Indeed, when the Jing River is distinguished by the Wei, the clear and the turbid become distinct in their course.
If the crooked is rectified by means of the straight, then unkindness will naturally distance itself.

Once this mandate is implemented, the single principle will surely be attained; thereafter, those who adorn themselves with falsehood will be cut off from the path of deceptive communication, while those who cherish the truth will no longer suffer the reproach of being out of step with the world.
"The Way and the world shall flourish together, and the Three Jewels will once again prosper.
Thereupon, he extensively established regulations, which Xuán followed.
Formerly, when Emperor Cheng was young and immature, Yu Bing assisted in governance and maintained that śramaṇas should pay homage to the sovereign.

He Chong, Director of the Imperial Secretariat; Chu Yu, Vice President of the Department of State Affairs; and Zhuge Tan, among others, submitted a memorial stating that [the Emperor] should not pay respects. The official deliberations were entirely in agreement with Chong and his colleagues, yet the Gate Keepers (Mendǎ) followed the will of the Emperor (Chengbīng) to issue a rebuttal; thus, opinions on what was right or wrong were in great confusion, and in the end, no resolution could be reached.
When Xuán was in Gūshú, wishing to ensure that full reverence was rendered [to the throne], he wrote a letter to Huiyuǎn, saying:

"That śramaṇas do not pay homage to kings is something my feelings cannot yet comprehend, nor is it something my reasoning can yet understand. This is a momentous matter for the age; one must not allow its fundamental principle to be improper."
I have recently sent a letter to the Eight Ministers; I now present it to you for your inspection. You may explain therein the reasons for my lack of respect toward them.
I shall also set forth one or two matters regarding what is currently to be implemented, so that they may be fully detailed; I trust this will suffice to resolve their doubts.
Huiyuan replied in a letter, saying:
"What is it that one calls a śramaṇa?

It means one who can dispel the profound darkness of the ignorant world and open the mysterious path beyond conventional transformation; such a person is precisely one who, through the Way of 'forgetting both self and others,' proceeds together with all under heaven."
This will cause those who aspire to loftiness to draw from his lingering influence, and those who rinse their mouths with mountain streams to savor his remaining essence.
If this is so, then even though his great enterprise was not fully realized, by observing the traces of his transcendent strides, what is realized is already vast indeed.

Furthermore, the kāṣāya is not the garment for court audiences, and the alms bowl is not a vessel for the imperial court; as śramaṇas are men who dwell beyond the mundane world, they ought not to pay homage to the sovereign.

Although Daoxuan stubbornly clung to his former resolve and felt ashamed to immediately comply with the external authority, upon seeing the purport of Huiyuan’s words, he hesitated and could not decide.
After a short while, Daoxuan usurped the throne and issued an edict, stating:
"The Buddha-dharma is vast and sublime, beyond what can be fathomed; out of my sentiment of honoring my sovereign, I have therefore extended my reverence toward it."
"Now that the matter rests with me, I ought to manifest the full extent of my humility; let the various practitioners of the Way no longer offer me formal salutations.
Huìyuǎn then composed the "Treatise on Why Śramaṇas Do Not Pay Homage to Kings," consisting of five chapters in total.

The first is titled "The Layperson": this refers to those who dwell at home and revere the Dharma; they are subjects who follow the transformative influence of the teaching. While their inner sentiments have not yet changed from worldly customs, their outward traces remain within the secular realm. Consequently, they possess the love of kinship and observe the rites of serving a sovereign; as these rituals and respects have their foundation, they are thereby used to establish the teaching.
The second is titled "Leaving Home":
This means that those who leave home are able to withdraw from the world to pursue their aspirations and transform their secular ways to realize the Way.

Because they transform their secular ways, their dress and insignia must not conform to the rituals of worldly codes; because they withdraw from the world, they ought to elevate their conduct beyond the mundane.

By virtue of his great merit, he was able to rescue the drowning world from its submerged current and uproot the dark foundations of heavy kalpas; he reached far back to connect with the ferry of the Three Vehicles and drew near to open the path for humans and devas.

If a single man were to perfect his virtue, then the Way would permeate his six relations and its bounty would flow throughout the world; even though he does not occupy the rank of a prince or lord, he has already harmonized with the Imperial Ultimate and granted respite to the people.
Therefore, internally they violate the gravity of natural kinship yet do not oppose filial piety;
externally they lack the deference due to a sovereign yet do not lose their reverence.
The third [section] is titled "Seeking the Ultimate Source Without Following Transformation":
This means that those who return to the root and seek the ultimate do not allow life to burden their spirit;
those who transcend and cast off worldly constraints do not allow emotions to burden their life. When emotions do not burden life, then life can be extinguished;
when life does not burden the spirit, then the spirit can merge with the profound mystery.
The profound spirit reaches the ultimate limit; therefore, it is called Nirvana.

Thus, although the śramaṇa treats even the sovereign of ten thousand chariots with equal courtesy and holds his own vocation in high esteem, he does not accept rank from kings or lords, yet he partakes in their bounty.
The fourth is titled "The Ultimate Reality Does Not Admit Dualism":

It should be said that although the ultimate aims of the Tathāgata and those of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius differ, they secretly influence one another; though their modes of engagement with the world—whether emerging or withdrawing—are entirely distinct, their final goal is necessarily the same.
Therefore, although it is said that the paths differ, that to which they return is one.
As for those who do not respond universally, it is because beings are unable to receive [the teaching] universally.
The fifth chapter is titled "The Body Perishes but the Spirit is Not Extinct."
This means that consciousness and the spirit gallop about, following along as they move east or west.
This is the general purport of the treatise.
From this point on, the śramaṇa was able to maintain his status beyond the mundane world.
When Huan Xuan fled westward and Emperor An of the Jin dynasty returned from Jiangling to the capital, He Wujì of the Fuguō Commandery urged Huiyuan to go and pay his respects at court.
Huiyuan, however, cited illness as an excuse and did not go.
The Emperor sent an envoy to offer his greetings, and Huiyuan composed a letter in reply, saying:
"Huiyuan of the Shi clan bows his head.
As the spring months are mild and warm, I hope Your Majesty’s diet remains in good health."

This humble monk has long been afflicted by a grave illness, and as my years have declined, it has grown even more severe. Having unexpectedly received your compassionate decree, graciously bestowing its illuminating consolation, my profound sense of gratitude and trepidation truly fills my heart a hundredfold.
"I am fortunate to have encountered this auspicious occasion, yet my body cannot move of its own accord; these feelings and regrets are truly beyond description.
The Emperor replied in an edict:
"I am moved by your words and know that your ailment has not improved; your condition remains deeply concerning."
I departed from Jiangling last month; on the road, I encountered many unfavorable circumstances and my progress was slower than usual.

Originally, I had hoped to pass by and meet you, Master, but since you have long cultivated your purity in the mountain forests and your illness has not yet been cured, there is now no further possibility of such an encounter. This only increases my sighs and regrets.

Xie Lingyun of Chenjun was a man of exceptional talent who held himself in high esteem and looked down upon the common world; yet, upon meeting Huiyuan for the first time, he was struck with solemn reverence and submitted his heart to him.

Huiyuan was profoundly versed in Buddhist principles internally and skilled in various secular texts externally; among those who joined his circle of disciples, there were none who did not rely upon and emulate him.
At that time, Huiyuan was lecturing on the *Sangfu jing* (Classic of Mourning Rites), and Lei Cizong, Zong Bing, and others all held their scrolls to receive his instructions.
Later, Cizong composed a separate commentary (*yishu*), which he headed with the title "The Lei Family [Commentary]."
Zong Bing then sent him a letter in jest, saying:
"In the past, you and I received this teaching face-to-face together with Master Shi; how is it that you now place your own name at the head of the scroll, styling yourself 'Master Lei'?"
His transformations encompassed both the monastic and the secular; such instances were not limited to these alone.
Having chosen to reside on Mount Lu for over thirty years, his shadow never left the mountains and his traces never entered the mundane world.
Whenever he sent off guests for excursions, he always took the Tiger Brook as his boundary.

In the eighth month of the twelfth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, his illness began to spread; by the sixth day, he was critically ill. Virtuous elders and senior monks all prostrated themselves, entreating him to drink fermented soybean wine, but he refused;
they further requested that he drink rice gruel, but he refused again.

He further requested that honey be mixed with water to serve as a beverage, and then commanded the Vinaya Master to open the scrolls and search for the text to determine whether such a drink was permitted.
Before the scroll had even been half-finished, he passed away at the age of eighty-three.
The disciples wailed and lamented as if they had lost their own parents;
monastics and laypeople rushed to the site, following one another shoulder to shoulder and wheel to wheel.
Huiyuan, finding it difficult to sever his grief as an ordinary man, established a seven-day period for mourning, and left instructions that his remains be exposed beneath the pine trees.
Subsequently, his disciples collected his remains for burial; Ruan Bao, the Governor of Xunyang, excavated a tomb and opened a tunnel on the mountain ridge to the west.
Xie Lingyun composed an inscription for a stele to commemorate his enduring virtues.
Zong Bing of Nanyang also erected a stele at the temple gate.

Initially, Huiyuan was skilled in composing literary works; his diction and tone were elegant and refined, and his discourse during gatherings was characterized by profound meaning and concise expression.

Furthermore, his countenance and deportment were dignified and refined, and his bearing was elegant and spirited; thus, his likeness was enshrined in the temple for the veneration of those both near and far.
His collected works—including treatises, prefaces, inscriptions, eulogies, poems, and letters—comprise ten volumes and over fifty pieces, which are held in high esteem by the world.
2. Shi Huichi. As for Shi Huichi, he was the younger brother of Huiyuan.
He was profound, silent, and possessed great capacity.
At the age of fourteen, he began his studies; what he mastered in a single day equaled what others achieved in ten days.
He was skilled in literature and history, possessing refined talent and craftsmanship.
At the age of eighteen, he left the household life and, together with his elder brother, served under Dharma Master Dao’an.
He studied the various sutras extensively and wielded mastery over the Tripitaka.
When [Hui]an was stationed in Xiangyang, he sent Huiyuan down to the east, and Sengchi also accompanied him.
Initially, they rested at Shangming Temple in Jingzhou, and later they traveled to Mount Lu; in both places, they stayed together following Huiyuan.
Sengchi stood eight chi tall; his spirit was sharp and refined. He always wore leather sandals and a patched robe that reached halfway down his calves.
Among the disciples at Mount Lu, there were none who were not eminent and talented, yet among the three thousand who came and went, Sengchi was universally regarded as the foremost.
Sister Chi’s aunt was a nun named Daoyi, who resided in Jiangxia.
Hearing that the Buddha-dharma was flourishing in the capital, Daoyi wished to travel there to observe and transform others.
Chi then escorted his aunt to the capital, where she stayed at Dong’an Temple.
Wang Xun of Langya, the Jin General of the Guard, held him in high esteem.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa from the Western Regions named Saṃgharakṣa, who was skilled in reciting the four Āgamas; Wang Xun requested that he translate the *Madhyama Āgama*.
Sengchi then collated and edited the literary phrasing, conducting a thorough investigation and final determination before returning to the mountains.

Shortly thereafter, Fan Ning, the Governor of Yuzhang, invited him to lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Abhidharma*; consequently, disciples gathered from all directions like clouds, assembling from as far as a thousand li away.
Wang Xun wrote a letter to Fan Ning, asking:
"Which is superior, Master Huiyuan or Master Daohchi?
Fan replied in his letter:
"Truly, they are a pair of worthy brothers.
The King wrote again in reply:
"To have even one such as the elder brother is truly not easy to find; how much more so when the younger brother is also virtuous."
Wang Gong of Langya, the Regional Inspector of Yanzhou, sent a letter to the śramaṇa Sengjian, asking:
"How are the supreme virtues of the brothers Yuan and Chi? Jian replied:
"Yuan is my brother by adoption; he is so dignified and composed that he truly possesses the air of one who has attained the Way.
While Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong, he held [Daoan] in high esteem from afar, sending a letter to establish friendly relations and forming a bond as virtuous friends.

Holding this resolve, he later heard that the land of Chengdu was fertile and its people prosperous; he set his mind on traveling there to propagate the teachings and, furthermore, desired to behold Mount Emei. Thus, in the third year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, he took leave of his companions and entered Shu.
Huiyuan tried to detain him for a long time, but he would not stay.
Huiyuan sighed and said, "In human life, people cherish gathering together; you, however, delight in parting—how can this be?"
Dhṛti also said with compassion,
"If you were one whose emotions remained attached to worldly gatherings, you would not have left the household life in the first place.
Now that you have severed desire to seek the Way, you shall simply take the Western Land as your destination."
Thereupon, the brothers wiped away their tears and parted in sorrowful silence.
Upon arriving in Jingzhou, they were received with great courtesy and respect by the Regional Inspector, Yin Zhongkan.
At that time, Huan Xuan was also there.

Although Xuan’s scholarly pursuits have been superficial, his spirit has transcended them in a single stroke; seeing that your mastery of the Vinaya is nearly peerless and almost unique, I am especially moved by the fact that such a person is without equal from ancient times to the present, and I greatly desire to form a bond of friendship with you.
Daodchi, already suspecting their character, ultimately abandoned them and would not take them in.
Although Yin and Huan both earnestly wished to retain him, Daodchi became increasingly determined to leave.
As he was about to depart, he wrote a letter to Xuansheng, saying:

"Originally, I intended to dwell upon the peaks of Mount Emei and observe the transformations beyond the shifting sands; yet, unable to bear the burden of my initial resolve, I have already packed my bags and set out on the road."
Upon receiving the letter, Xuangde was filled with sorrow, realizing that he could not be dissuaded.

He subsequently traveled to Shu, where he stayed at Longyuan Monastery; there he extensively propagated the Buddha-dharma, and as his reputation spread throughout the four quarters, many came to admire his virtue and became his disciples.
The Regional Inspector Mao Qu held him in high esteem and deep respect.
At that time, there were the śramaṇas Huìyán and Sēnggōng, who had previously resided in Mǐn and Shū;
the local people there were so devoted to them that they would stop their carriages at the first meeting.
When Sengchi arrived and settled there, everyone was moved to submission upon merely hearing his reputation;
those who ascended to serve under him were all hailed as having "climbed the Dragon Gate.
Master Senggong possessed talent and insight from his youth and served as the *Sengzheng* (Chief Administrator) of Shu Commandery.
Master Yan was widely learned in both internal and external studies and had long been held in high esteem by Mao Qu.
Later, the Shu man Qiao Zong took advantage of the turmoil of war to attack and kill Mao Qu, seizing control of the land of Shu and styling himself the King of Chengdu.
He then assembled the monastic community and established a dharma assembly, urgently inviting Master Yan. Having no choice, Yan went.

Since Sengqu had long been his patron, the sudden injury and destruction of his temple filled him with grief; his sorrow was so manifest on his countenance that he was resented by Xiao Zong, who subsequently had him killed.
The entire district was thrown into turmoil, and both the monastics and the laity were filled with dread.
He took refuge from the danger at Zhongsi Temple in Pi County.
Although his nephew Daofu was present, he was even more wicked and rebellious; he led troops to Pi to carry out executions.
Returning to enter the monastery, his men and horses were covered in blood; the monks were greatly terrified and fled in a panic all at once.
Yet as he washed himself in front of his room, his countenance remained unperturbed.
Tao Fu followed Huzhi to the edge of the stream; as Huzhi snapped his fingers to strain the water, he remained composed and serene.
Tao Fu was filled with shame and remorse, sweating profusely; leaving the temple gate, he said to those around him, "This great man is truly different from the rest."

Later, when the realm was pacified, he returned to reside at Longyuan Temple. He lectured on the scriptures and performed rites of repentance with increasing devotion as he grew older. He passed away in the temple in the eighth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty at the age of seventy-six.
In his final testament, he was intent on exhorting them to observe the precepts, saying to his disciples:
"The Sūtras state:
'Precepts are like level ground; from them all virtues arise.'"
"In your walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, you must be diligent.
He entrusted the scriptures in the eastern chamber to his disciple Daohong,
and committed the dharma texts in the western chamber to his disciple Tamlan.
Hongyang’s conduct was pure and refined, while Huilang’s spiritual awakening was divinely inspired; both followed in the footsteps of their teacher. 3.
Shi Huiyong: Shi Huiyong’s secular surname was Pan, and he was a native of Henei.

At the age of twelve, he left home to become a monk and served the śramaṇa Zhu Tanxian as his teacher; later, he further devoted himself to the Venerable Dao’an. Having long shared an aspiration with Huiyuan, he desired to establish a dwelling on the peaks of Mount Luofu.
Since Huiyuan had already been detained by Dao’an, Huiyong intended to cross the Five Ridges first.
While traveling through Xunyang, Tao Fan, a local of the commandery, earnestly entreated him to stay; consequently, he halted for a time at Xilin Monastery on Mount Lu.
As his disciples gradually increased in number and Huiyuan had likewise built [the monastery], he eventually resolved to spend the remainder of his life there.

Yongzhen was naturally pure and simple; he purified his mind and disciplined himself, always smiling when speaking and never saying anything that would harm others. He was devoted to the scriptures and excelled at lecturing on them; he lived on vegetarian food and wore coarse cloth, maintaining this lifestyle throughout his years.
Furthermore, he established a separate thatched hut on the mountain ridge; whenever he wished to engage in meditative contemplation, he would go there to reside.
Whenever anyone entered the room, they all smelled the fragrance of a sublime incense.
In Yong’s house there was always a tiger; whenever anyone felt afraid, he would drive it up the mountain. After the people had left, the tiger would return and become tame once more.
Once, Yong went out of the town and returned to the mountain late in the evening, arriving at Wuqiao Bridge.
The commander of the Wujiao garrison was intoxicated; as he rode his horse across the road, he blocked [Seng]yong and would not let him pass.

As evening approached, Yong pointed his staff at the horse from afar, whereupon the horse bolted in alarm. The commander fell to the ground, and Yong supported and comforted him back to the garrison, after which the commander fell ill because of this.
The next morning, he went to the monastery to repent before Sengyong.
Yong said, "This was not my original intention; I suspect it was the work of the deity of the precepts."
When the white-robed and black-robed [monastics and laypeople] heard of this, those who turned their hearts toward him were numerous.
Later, when General-in-Chief of the South, He Wujī, was stationed at Xunyang, Tao Yuanming gathered them at Huxi and invited Huiyong and Huiyuan.

Having long maintained a reputation for his distance from worldly affairs, Yuan was also naturally endowed with refined talent and capability; his followers numbered over a hundred, all of whom were dignified and possessed a sense of propriety.
When he engaged in lofty speech and elegant discourse, his every movement was worthy of admiration.

Yong remained calm and proceeded alone; Shuai arrived later, wearing grass robes and straw sandals, holding a staff and carrying an alms bowl. His spirit remained composed and his demeanor tranquil and unassuming. The assembly all esteemed his integrity and simplicity, and instead of finding fault with him, they respected him even more.
Huiyuan held Huiyong in high esteem from his youth and, admiring his noble conduct, personally maintained a humble and reverent attitude in hopes of attaining blessings in the unseen realm.
Huiyong practiced asceticism with rigorous austerity, vowing to be reborn in the Western Paradise.

In the tenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he fell ill and his condition became grave; nevertheless, he remained devotedly observant of the precepts, and his resolve grew even more diligent. Although he bore the pain of his chronic illness, his countenance remained serene and joyful.
Before long, he suddenly adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and asked for his sandals, wishing to rise as if he had seen something.
The assembly all asked him in alarm, and he replied, "The Buddha has come."
Having finished speaking, he passed away at the age of eighty-three.
Both monastics and laypeople on the mountain perceived a wondrous fragrance that did not cease for seven days.
At that time, there was also the monk Shi Sengrong of Mount Lu; he too was one of austere discipline who attained spiritual communion, and it is said he could subdue ghosts and spirits.
4. Shi Sengji. Shi Sengji’s place of origin is unknown.
During the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, he came to Mount Lu and studied under Master Huiyuan.
Regarding the number of various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras as well as secular texts, he had thoroughly cultivated his mind through their study and mastered their profound essentials.
When he reached the age of forty, he left the village to open a lecture hall, where he successively served under the foremost masters of his time.
Huiyuan often said to him, "Are you not the very person with whom I shall propagate the Buddha-dharma?
Later, after staying at the mountain for a short time, he was suddenly stricken by a severe illness; consequently, he summoned Cheng from the Western Regions to visualize Amitābha.
Yuan sent a candle to Ji, saying:
"You may use this to establish your mind in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and compete with the passing of the water-clock.

Ji held the candle, leaned against his desk, and remained in meditative concentration without distraction; he further requested that the assembly of monks gather at night to recite the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* for him.
At the fifth watch of the night, Tanyao gave his candle to a fellow student and instructed him to pass it through the assembly of monks.

Thereupon, he lay down for a short while and dreamed that he was holding a candle himself, traveling through the void. He beheld Amitābha Buddha, who took him up in his palm and traveled throughout the ten directions. Suddenly, he awoke from the dream and related the experience in detail to those attending to his illness.
Feeling both sorrow and consolation, he reflected within himself that his four great elements were entirely free from ailment or suffering.
When the following evening arrived, he suddenly asked for his shoes, stood up, and gazed into the void as if seeing something there.
After a short while, he lay down again; his complexion became even more radiant, and he said to those beside him, "I am now departing.
Thereupon, turning onto his right side, his speech and breath ceased together at the age of forty-five.
5. Shi Fa’an: Shi Fa’an, also known as Ciqin, was a person of unknown origins and was a disciple of Master Huiyuan.

He was virtuous in his observance of the precepts and lectured on various sutras; he also practiced the discipline of dhyāna and was exceptionally skilled at enlightening the ignorant and leading those who followed heterodox paths back to the orthodox.
During the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, there was a tiger disaster in Xinyang County.
The county had a large sacred tree (dashu) beneath which a shrine had been built.
Hundreds of residents lived nearby, and every evening one or two people would be killed by tigers.
Dao’an once traveled through this county and stopped overnight at this village.
Fearing tigers, the villagers had closed their gates early;
Dao’an went directly beneath a tree and sat in meditation throughout the entire night.
At dawn, he heard that a tiger had arrived carrying a man and had thrown him to the north of the tree.
Upon seeing An, the tiger was both joyful and startled; it leaped down and prostrated itself before An.
An preached the Dharma and conferred the precepts upon it; the tiger remained crouched on the ground without moving, and after a short while, it departed.
At dawn, the villagers pursued the tiger to the foot of the tree and were greatly startled upon seeing An; they regarded him as a divine being.
Consequently, the news spread throughout the entire county, and both the gentry and the commoners venerated him.

The tiger disasters ceased from this point on, whereupon he renovated the shrine and established the Anli Temple; he donated all the surrounding fields and gardens as communal property for the assembly.
Later, wishing to create a painted image, he required copper green (cinnabar), but was unable to obtain it despite his efforts.
One night he dreamed of a man who walked before his bed and said,
"There is a bronze bell beneath this spot.
Upon waking, he immediately dug there and indeed found two bells, which he subsequently used to create images.
Later, he used his bronze to assist Master Yuan in casting a Buddha statue; one piece remained. Xiong Wuhuan, the Governor of Wuchang, borrowed it to inspect it and subsequently kept it.
Dao’an’s final whereabouts were unknown thereafter.
6. Shi Tanyong: Shi Tanyong’s surname was Yang, and he was a native of Guanzhong.
In his youth, he served the puppet state of Qin, rising to the rank of General of the Guards.
He stood eight chi tall and possessed a heroic and martial bearing that surpassed others.

In the eighth year of the Taiyuan era, he followed Fu Jian on a southern expedition; when they were defeated by the Jin army, he returned to Chang’an and subsequently left the household life under Master Daoan.
After Master Daoan had passed away, he traveled south to Mount Lu, where he served Master Huiyuan as his teacher.
He was extensively versed in both internal and external scriptures and was dedicated to propagating the Dharma, never shrinking from toil or hardship.

Later, he traveled far into the Guanzhong region to deliver a letter to Kumārajīva. For more than ten years, he served as an envoy, stirring up the prevailing trends and shaking the mountain peaks; steadfast and courageous, he handled diplomatic missions with such skill that he never brought disgrace upon his mission.

The monk Jìng from the monastic center in the capital admired Huiyǒng’s virtue and understanding, and invited him to return to Yangzhou; however, because Huiyǒng was advanced in years, he ultimately did not go.

Nevertheless, there were many among those who held Huìyuǎn in high esteem for his spiritual power and integrity; fearing that they might fail to show him due respect in the future, Huìyuǎn used a minor pretext to cast Huiyǒng out.

Having received this command, Daoyong emerged from the mountains without resentment or opposition; he then established a thatched hut to the southwest of the mountain and, together with his disciple Tanguo, applied himself to meditative contemplation within the gates of Chan.
Once, in a dream, Guo saw a mountain deity requesting to receive the five precepts. Guo said, "My master is here;
you may go to him to inquire about and receive them.
A short while later, Yong saw a man wearing a single-layered robe and a cap, with a refined and elegant bearing, accompanied by about twenty followers, who requested to receive the five precepts.
Faguang, taking the dream as a sign that he was a mountain deity, preached the Dharma and conferred the precepts upon him.
The deity presented him with a foreign-style spoon and chopsticks as an offering, prostrated himself, took his leave, and vanished in an instant.
When Huiyuan was on the verge of death, he rushed to his side, wailing and leaping in grief; his sorrow was as deep as that for a close kinsman.
Later, he went to Jingzhou and passed away at Zhulin Temple.
7. Shi Daozu. Shi Daozu was a native of Wuguo. He left home to become a monk in his youth and served as a disciple of Zhi Faqi at Tai Temple.
From childhood, he possessed talent and insight, and applied himself with diligence to his studies.

Later, together with his fellow practitioners Sengqian, Daoliu, and others, he entered Mount Lu for seven years; they all received ordination within the mountains and, each following their own areas of study, made daily progress.
Master Huiyuan often remarked that Daoshu and the others were quick to attain awakening, saying, "If all future generations are like these men, I shall no longer have cause for concern.
Daohui and Daoliu both died at the age of twenty-eight.

Master Huiyuan sighed and said, "These youths possessed such brilliant talent and virtue, and their pure insight was ever-renewing. That they should depart forever while still harboring such potential—how painful this is!"
Dao Liu had begun compiling a catalogue of various scriptures but had not yet completed it; the Master finished it for him, and it is still circulated in the world today.
Later, when the Master returned to the Waguan Monastery in the capital to lecture, Huan Xuan went there frequently to listen and remarked to others:
"Daokuang’s later emergence surpassed that of Master Yuan, though he does not quite reach him in the breadth of his Confucian scholarship."
When Xuanchao and Xuancheng wished to compel the śramaṇas to pay homage to the king, Sengzu declined and returned to Taisi Temple in Wu.
Shortly thereafter, Xuanchao ascended the throne and issued an edict for the commandery to escort Sengzu out of the capital.
The Patriarch cited illness as an excuse and did not go; thereupon, he withdrew from worldly affairs and spent his days lecturing on the Way.
He passed away in the first year of the Yuanxi era of the Jin dynasty at the age of seventy-two.
Huiyao, a disciple of Yuan, was also learned in the sutras and the vinaya, and was particularly gifted in ingenious ingenuity.

As there were no water clocks in the mountains, he erected twelve-leaf lotus flowers in a spring; by means of their rotation with the flowing waves, he determined the twelve hours, such that the measurement of time was without error.
He also once fashioned a wooden kite that flew for several hundred paces.
Huiyuan also had disciples named Tanshun and Tanzhen, both of whom were renowned for their mastery of Buddhist doctrine. Tanshun was originally from Huanglong;
he studied under Master Kumārajīva in his youth and later returned to serve as a disciple of Huiyuan. He maintained a vegetarian diet and was distinguished for his virtuous conduct.
Liu Zun, the Commandant of the Southern Barbarians, established Zhulin Monastery in Jiangling and invited Huiyuan to initiate its construction;
Huiyuan was subsequently dispatched there.
Daoshen was likewise refined and possessed a dignified bearing; he annotated the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* and authored works such as the "Treatise on Adversity and Success."

Furthermore, there were more than one hundred people, including Fa You, Dao Heng, and Dao Shou, who either possessed profound and clear understanding of the doctrines, or managed and rescued various affairs, or maintained pure and lofty conduct, or entered deeply into meditative contemplation; all of them established their reputations in their own time and have transmitted their legacy to the present day.
8. Shi Sengshao: Shi Sengshao’s secular surname was Fu; he was a native of Niyang in Beidi and the eldest son of Fu Xia, who served as the Langzhongling of Hejian during the Jin dynasty.
He left home to become a monk at a young age and resided at the Great Monastery in Chang’an as a disciple of Dharma Master Hongjue.
Hongjue was also a master of the Dharma of his time; [Dao]shao initially received his instruction from him and later traveled through the regions of Qing, Si, Fan, and Jin.
He was thoroughly versed in the Six Classics and the Tripitaka; his observance of the Vinaya was pure and meticulous, and he was capable of upholding and revitalizing the Buddha-dharma.
Yao Chang and Yao Xing had long admired his reputation and esteemed him from the outset; once they usurped power in Guanzhong, they held him in the deepest reverence.

Since Emperor Xing had developed profound faith in the Triple Gem and vigorously propagated the Great Transformation, he established assemblies and provided vegetarian feasts, with incense smoke rising in dense layers, such that among those who admired the Way and renounced secular life, half the households in every ten did so.
Since Kumārajīva entered the Pass, eminent monks had gathered once more; as the number of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs grew large, some committed transgressions.
Daoxing said, "How can those who have not yet studied the Dharma and have not yet attained the stage of *duḥkhakṣānti* (patience regarding suffering) be expected to be without fault?"
"Since faults have gone unrebuked, transgressions have consequently multiplied. It is fitting to establish a monastic head (Sengzhu) to purify the great reputation [of the Sangha].
Thereupon, he issued an edict stating:

"The Great Dharma has migrated eastward and now flourishes more than ever. As monks and nuns have already become numerous, there must be a governing authority to proclaim far-reaching regulations and rescue the failing traditions."
Dharma Master Sengshao has possessed superior learning since his youth and his virtue has flourished in his later years; he may serve as the National Preceptor.
Dharma Master Sengqian has cultivated both meditation and wisdom concurrently; he shall serve as the Director of the Assembly.
Faqin and Huibin jointly held the office of *Senglü* (Registrar of Monks).
They were granted carriages, attendants, and laborers.

Their stipends were equal to those of Palace Attendants (*Zhongzhong*), and they each had two attendants for transmitting imperial edicts and for their sheep-drawn carriages; Qian and the others likewise received generous provisions.

In his service, he was consistently frugal and upright, fully satisfying the expectations of his time; the five assemblies were strictly purified, and throughout the six periods of the day, he never grew weary.
In the seventh year of the Hongshi era, an imperial decree was issued granting him the privilege of a personal retinue, with thirty attendants each for both the inner and outer services.
The rise of the Sangzheng (Chief Monastic Officer) marked the beginning of the *tuo* (a monastic office).

The *tuo* personally traveled on foot, reserving carriages and litters only for the elderly and infirm; the offerings and provisions he received were always used to support the needs of the entire community.
Although he was already in the autumn of his years, he tirelessly exhorted the assembly through lectures on the sutras and vinaya.
At the end of the Hongshi era, he passed away at the Great Temple in Chang’an at the age of seventy.
9. Shi Daorong. Shi Daorong was a native of Linlü in Jiji Commandery; he left home life at the age of twelve.
His master, admiring his spiritual brilliance, first ordered him to study secular learning and sent him to a village to borrow the *Analects*.
He did not take the text back with him, having already memorized it there.

When his teacher borrowed the original text to verify his recitation, he failed to miss even a single character; the teacher marveled at this and was filled with wonder, whereupon he allowed him to travel freely for further study.
By the time he reached his twenties, his talent was already peerless; he had mastered the inner and outer scriptures through intuitive insight.
Hearing that Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong, he went there to seek instruction from him.
Upon seeing him, Kumārajīva marveled at his extraordinary nature and said to Yao Xing, "Yesterday I met Master Rong; he is another exceptionally brilliant and gifted monk.
Yao Xing invited him for an audience and praised him highly, issuing an edict for him to enter the Xiaoyao Garden to participate in the refinement and detailed translation of the scriptures.
He requested Kumārajīva to produce the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śīla-sūtra*, which is currently practiced in the world.

Later, when the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* was being translated and only two fascicles had been completed, Sengrong immediately began lecturing on it; he analyzed the words and phrases with such thoroughness that he already grasped the work from beginning to end.
Kumārajīva also commanded Daorong to lecture on the *New Lotus Sūtra*.
Kumārajīva listened to it himself and then sighed in admiration, saying:
"As for the flourishing of the Buddha-dharma, Daorong is truly the man for it."

Shortly thereafter, there was a brahmin from the Kingdom of Siṃhala who was intelligent, eloquent, and widely learned; there were few secular texts of the Western lands that he had not read and recited, and he served as the preeminent leader among the non-Buddhist outsiders of that country.
Hearing that Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong widely propagating the Buddha-dharma, he said to his disciples:
"How could we allow the teachings of Śākya to spread alone throughout China, while our own orthodox transformation fails to reach the Eastern lands?"
He then mounted a camel, carrying the scriptures, and entered Chang’an.
Upon seeing his sly and fawning manner, Emperor Yao Xing was somewhat deluded by him.
The Brahmin then addressed the Emperor, saying:

"The Ultimate Way has no fixed direction; each person honors their own practice. I now request to compete with the monks of Qin in the power of debate; whichever side proves superior shall propagate its teachings."
Xing immediately granted his permission.
At that time, the monastic community in Guanzhong looked upon one another with a sense of deficiency, and none dared to step forward.
Kumārajīva said to Daorong:

"Furthermore, these non-Buddhists are more intelligent than ordinary men; they will surely prevail in debate. It would be truly lamentable if the unsurpassed Great Way were to be defeated while remaining among our own followers."
"If it were allowed for the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) to gain the upper hand, the Wheel of the Dharma would be shattered;
how could such a thing be permitted? As I see it, the responsibility rests with you alone.

Daorong reflected that while his own talent and strength were not inferior, he had not yet finished reading all the scriptures of the non-Buddhists. He therefore secretly had someone copy the list of scriptures read by the Brahmins; upon seeing them once, he was able to recite them from memory.

Later, when the day for the debate was set, Yao Xing came in person, and the high officials all assembled at the palace gate; the monastic community from throughout Guanzhong gathered from far and near.
Daorong and the Brahmin engaged in a contest of mutual challenge, their sharp dialectics soaring into the profound mysteries, such that the other could not equal them.
The Brahmin knew that his arguments were already defeated, yet he still boasted of his extensive reading.
Daorong then listed the titles of the books he had read, along with the names and volumes of the classics and histories of the land of Qin, which were three times more numerous than the Brahmin’s.
Kumārajīva mocked him, saying, "Have you not heard that the Great Qin is a land of vast learning? Why have you so hastily come from afar?
The Brahmin felt ashamed and repentant; he prostrated at Daorong’s feet and departed after a few days.
That the Dharma-vehicle was revived once more was due to the power of Daorong.

After Daorong returned to Pengcheng, he constantly preached the teachings in continuous succession; those who came to seek the Way numbered more than a thousand, and the disciples following him exceeded three hundred.

By nature he did not frequent noisy crowds, but often ascended the tower to study and contemplate the scriptures. He was diligent in skillfully guiding others and dedicated his life to propagating the Dharma. Later, he passed away in Pengcheng at the age of seventy-four. His commentaries on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, *Daśabhūmika*, and *Vimalakīrti* sūtras all circulate in the world today.
10. Shi Tanying: Shi Tanying was sometimes said to be a person from the north, though it was unknown which commandery or county he hailed from.

By nature he was empty and tranquil, and did not socialize much; he lived simply and was dedicated to his studies. His deportment was careful and deliberate, appearing almost overly slow, yet his spirit was swift and agile—his will thus contrasted with his physical bearing.

He was able to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Prakāśapraṇidhāna-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; whenever he turned the wheel of the Dharma, there were always several thousand monastics and laypeople in attendance.
Later, he entered Guanzhong, where Yao Xing received him with great courtesy and honor.
When Kumārajīva arrived in Chang’an, Fotuoying went to follow him.
Kumārajīva said to Yao Xing, “Yesterday I saw Master Ying; he too is a monk of distinguished character and high reputation in this country.”
The Emperor summoned him to reside in the Xiaoyao Garden to assist Kumārajīva in translating the scriptures.
When the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* was first produced, all the debates, questions, and answers were conducted in successive exchanges.
Daoying regretted that his draft was fragmented, so he composed it in five sections and eventually presented it to Kumārajīva.
Kumārajīva said, "Excellent!
You have truly captured my intended meaning."

After Kumārajīva later produced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Daoying—since it was the very doctrine he had previously been commissioned to uphold—delved deeply into its meaning and subsequently composed the four-fascicle *Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus Sutra* (*Fahua yishu*), as well as a commentary on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
Later, he dwelt in seclusion on the back mountain, maintaining his integrity beyond the mundane world; he cultivated merit and established virtue, becoming increasingly steadfast as he grew older.
He passed away during the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty at the age of seventy.
11. Shi Sengrui. Shi Sengrui was a native of Changle in Wei Commandery.
From his youth, he delighted in the monastic life; at the age of eighteen, he finally fulfilled his aspiration and became a disciple under the Dharma Master Sengxian.
Humble in character and internally perceptive, he pursued his studies with a competitive diligence.
By the age of twenty-two, he had extensively mastered the sutras and śāstras.
Once, while listening to Dharma Master Senglang lecture on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he repeatedly posed critical questions and challenges.
Lang shared a bond with Xian, reminiscent of the friendship between the Duke of Huan and Yan Hui;
he said to Xian, "Regarding the difficult passages in the *Shuoyi*, I have contemplated them repeatedly yet cannot penetrate them. You may truly be called a 'virtuous disciple of a virtuous master.'"

At the age of twenty-four, he traveled through famous regions, preaching everywhere. Scholars who understood his teachings followed him in crowds with their bundles of books, and he would often sigh, saying:

"Although the sutras and dharmas are few, they are sufficient for understanding cause and effect; yet as the methods of Chan have not yet been transmitted, there is no ground upon which to settle the mind."

After Kumārajīva arrived at Guanzhong, he requested the translation of the *Cān fǎ yào* (Essentials of Dhyāna Methods) in three fascicles. Its beginning was composed by Kumāralāta, its end was spoken by Aśvaghoṣa, and the middle portion was jointly created by various sages of foreign lands; it is also titled the "Bodhisattva Dhyāna."

Once Yao Rui had obtained them, he practiced and cultivated them day and night; he eventually refined the five gates to perfection and skillfully entered the six purities, such that Yao Song, the Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, held him in profound esteem and respect.
Yao Xing asked Sengsong,
"What do you think of Master Rui?
Sengsong replied:
"He is truly the pine and cypress of Ye-wei.
Emperor Xing summoned him for an audience; the high officials all assembled, wishing to observe his talent and character.
Sengrui’s demeanor was flowing and refined, and his speech was elegant and brilliant.
Xing was greatly delighted and immediately issued an edict granting him a salary, provisions, administrative support, and a carriage.
Later, Xing said to Sōng, "You are a preeminent leader throughout the four seas; how could you be merely the pine and cypress of Ye and Wei?"
Thereupon, his excellent reputation spread far and wide, and people from near and far turned to him in reverence.
As for the sutras translated by Kumārajīva, Sengrui participated in verifying and correcting them all.
Previously, when Dharmarakṣa produced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Receiving Predictions," it said:
"Gods see humans, and humans see gods.
When Kumārajīva reached this passage in his translation of the sutra, he remarked:
"This statement accords with the meaning in the Western Regions (India), but it is somewhat excessive in its phrasing."
Sengyai said, "Is it not that humans and devas have met, so that both may see one another?
Kumārajīva replied with joy:
"It is indeed so.
His insights and expositions were all of this nature.
Later, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* was produced, and he had Huì lecture upon it.
Kumārajīva said to Sengrui:
"In this polemical treatise, there are seven points of transformation where the text refutes the *Abhidharma*, yet the arguments remain somewhat obscure.
If you can understand them without asking, you may truly be called a man of exceptional talent."

When Sengrui reached the subtle and profound depths of the teachings, he indeed attained a realization that accorded perfectly with the truth without consulting Kumārajīva. Kumārajīva sighed in admiration and said:
"In my translation of the sūtras and śāstras, it has truly been no regret for me to have encountered you."

He composed prefaces for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and other such works; he also wrote prefaces for the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* and *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* (the "Large" and "Small" *Prajñāpāramitās*), as well as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, and the *Ārya-vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-bodhisattva-caryā-sūtra*. All of these have been transmitted to the world.

Initially, Huikai was skilled at maintaining dignified deportment and widely propagated the sutras and the Dharma; he constantly dedicated these various karmic merits, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he never dared to turn his back directly toward the West.
Later, knowing his life was coming to an end, he suddenly assembled the Sangha to take his leave and said to the assembly:

"Throughout my life, my vow has been to be reborn in the Western Land. As I have perceived it, I may perhaps go there, yet I do not know for certain whether I shall be spared; I remain in doubt as to whether this will be achieved. However, my actions of body, speech, and mind may have been inconsistent with my vows; I pray that you will bestow upon me great compassion and be my companions in the Dharma for eternal kalpas."
Thereupon, he entered his room to bathe, burned incense, and prostrated. Returning to his bed, he faced westward, joined his palms, and passed away.
On that day, everyone in the monastery saw five-colored fragrant smoke issuing from En’s room; he was sixty-seven years of age.
At that time, there was also the śramaṇa Seng-kai,
who had studied under the same teacher as Master Rui and likewise possessed a high reputation.
12. Shi Daoheng. Shi Daoheng was a native of Lantian.
When he was nine years old, he was playing on the road when the hermit Zhang Zhong saw him and sighed, saying:

"This child has the appearance of one who transcends others; if he remains in secular life, he will surely have merit in assisting the administration of government; if he dwells in the Way, he will surely be able to bring glory and distinction to the Buddha-dharma."
"I regret that I am old and shall not live to see it.

Heng lost both his parents while young and served his stepmother with such filial piety that he became renowned for it. His family was poor and possessed no savings, so he would often paint with his own hands to provide for her support; furthermore, he was deeply devoted to the scriptures, studying them day and night.
When he reached the age of twenty, his stepmother also passed away; he observed the funeral rites with full propriety and, upon completing the period of mourning, entered the monastic order.

He moved with ease through the principles of Buddhism, mastering many fields of knowledge; his learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular texts, and his intellectual faculties were clear and敏捷 (nimble).
When Kumārajīva entered Guanzhong, Huigeng immediately went there to assist him.
Kumārajīva greatly admired him, and when various scriptures were being translated, Geng assisted in their detailed revision and verification.
At that time, there was also a fellow student named Daobiao, who likewise possessed refined talent and capability; he was renowned during his era and ranked second only to Geng.

The ruler of Qin, Yao Xing, considering that the two men, Heng and Biao, possessed brilliant spirits and the capacity to govern a state, issued an edict to the sham Minister of the Secretariat, Yao Xian, ordering him to urge Heng and Biao to renounce the monastic life and assist in consolidating the royal enterprise.
Furthermore, he issued a decree to Heng, Biao, and others, saying:

"Your pure and resolute integrity is truly praiseworthy; however, as you preside over the four seas, the governance of the realm urgently requires talent. I have now commanded Xian, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, to strip you of your dharma robes so that you may assist in supporting and stabilizing the current age."
"If one's mind dwells upon the flavor of the Way, how could it be bound by the distinction between white and black robes?
I hope you will understand this sentiment and not decline on account of maintaining your monastic vows.
Heng, Biao, and the others replied:

"Having received the imperial edict issued on the twentieth day of last month, ordering that Heng, Biao, and the others be stripped of their monastic robes, we have received this command with sorrowful hearts, our five emotions overwhelmed.

Heng and the others are of dull and inferior talent; our immersion in the Dharma has not been profound. Daosheng’s original surname was Wei; he was a native of Julu who resided in Pengcheng.
His family had been an official lineage for generations, and his father served as the Magistrate of Guangqi, being esteemed by his fellow villagers as a man of virtue.
From childhood, he was exceptionally brilliant and possessed a divine-like intelligence.

His father, recognizing that he was no ordinary vessel, cherished him with extraordinary affection. Later, meeting the śramaṇa Zhu Fatai, he renounced secular life to take refuge in the Dharma, humbly submitting to him as his teacher to receive instruction.
Having entered the gateway of the Dharma, his brilliant intellect was extraordinary; as he investigated and savoring the meanings of the texts, he attained spontaneous understanding.

Thus, while still at the age of *zhixue* (the age of formal study), he ascended the lecture seat. His expositions and responses to inquiries were as pure and refined as pearls and jade; even veteran monks of established reputation and renowned scholars of the day all feared their words would be defeated and exhausted, none daring to challenge or oppose him.
Upon reaching the age for full ordination, his capacity for discernment deepened daily; his character was alert and quick-witted, and his spirit was serene and dignified.
Having first entered Mount Lu, he lived in seclusion for seven years to pursue his aspirations.

Always regarding the essential means of entering the Way as being rooted in wisdom and understanding, he delved into and revered the various sutras and weighed the diverse treatises; he followed the Dharma across ten thousand miles, undaunted by weariness or hardship.

This temple was established by Empress Chu Gongsi of the Jin dynasty; it was originally a place where blue lotuses grew, and thus it took its name from them.
