"Although this is not what I wear, since it has been bestowed by Your Majesty, I shall simply use it accordingly."
Xie Lingyun of Chenjun was deeply devoted to Buddhist principles and possessed a remarkable understanding of foreign languages.

He consulted Fayue regarding various characters in the scriptures, as well as their diverse pronunciations and meanings; consequently, Fayue composed the "Preface to the Training in the Fourteen Vowels," which systematically lists the Sanskrit and Chinese correspondences so clearly that they are easily understood, providing a reliable basis for the written language.
Huiyi passed away during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty at the age of eighty-five. 3.
Shi Huiyan: Shi Huiyan’s secular surname was Fan; he was a native of Yuzhou.

At the age of twelve, he became a student (*zhusheng*), becoming extensively learned in the *Shijing* and *Shujing*. At sixteen, he left the household life and further refined his mastery of Buddhist principles.
By the time he reached his early twenties, his learning had penetrated all the various scriptures; his reputation spread far and wide, and his transformative influence reached distant lands.

Hearing that Master Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong, he went there once more to study under him, seeking to verify the phonology and meaning of the scriptures; thus he acquired much that was previously unknown.
Later, he returned to the capital and resided at Dong'an Temple.
Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty had long held him in high esteem.
Later, when Gaozu set out to campaign against Chang'an, he requested that Yan accompany him. Yan replied:
"Although your journey, O Patron, is for the purpose of punishing the guilty and consoling the people, I am a man beyond worldly affairs and dare not accept your command.
The Emperor pressed him earnestly, and he finally set out.
During Emperor Wen’s reign, their personal rapport became even more intimate; whenever he saw him, he would praise him and inquire about the Buddha-dharma.

Previously, the Emperor had not yet placed great stock in or faith in it, but by the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, Xiao Mozhi, the Governor of the Capital, submitted a memorial requesting that temples be constructed and images be cast.
The Emperor then deliberated with Palace Attendant He Shangzhi, Director of the Ministry of Personnel Yang Xuanbao, and others. He said to Shangzhi:

"I have not read many scriptures since my youth, and of late I have had even less leisure. While I have not yet been able to resolve my doubts regarding the causality of the three periods, I do not dare to hold a dissenting view precisely because you gentlemen are the preeminent talents of the age, and I follow what you all revere and believe."

Fan Tai and Xie Lingyun often remarked that the texts of the Six Classics were originally intended to aid the common people and facilitate governance; yet, if one seeks the spiritual essence and ultimate mysteries, how could one not take the Buddhist scriptures as one's guide?

Recently, I read Yan Ying’s “Discourse on the Deduction of Nature” and Zong Bing’s “Refutation of the Discourse on Black and White. These clearly demonstrate the vast profundity of Buddhism; moreover, they are both fully endowed with renowned principles and inspire the human spirit.
If those along the shores of the entire realm were all to cultivate this transformation, then I would sit and achieve Great Peace; what further business would there be?

Recently, Xiao Mozhi submitted a petition for regulations that was not entirely thorough or consistent with the Classics; I have already shown it to you, entrusting you with the task of revising and refining it.

"If there must be something to restrain and prohibit frivolity and excess, provided it does not harm the promotion of the Great [Teaching], then indeed it should be codified in the statutes. Shangzhi replied:

"The masses are for the most part incredulous toward the Dharma; with my own mediocrity and ignorance, I alone maintain a foolish diligence, fearing that through my deficiencies I might bring blemish upon the Great Teaching."
Now, to receive such further praise and encouragement is something I truly do not dare to accept.
As for the eminent figures of former dynasties, they certainly did not fail to live up to their illustrious summons.
However, since those of the central court belong to a distant past, it is difficult to know them all in full detail.

Since crossing the Yangtze River, there have been Wang Dao, Zhou Yi, Yu Liang, Wang Meng, Xie Shang, Xi Chao, Wang Tan, Wang Gong, Wang Mi, Guo Wen, Xie Fu, Dai Kui, Xu Xun, as well as my late ancestors and brothers, the brothers Wang Yuanlin, Fan Wang, Sun Chuo, Zhang Xuan, and Yin Yi. Whether they were the preeminent leaders among ministers and officials, or the paragon models of human relations; whether they directed their sentiments toward the realm between heaven and humanity, or elevated their conduct beyond the mists and clouds—they all received the teachings with resolute devotion, setting their minds upon honoring and trusting them.
Comparing them within this context, Lan, Hu, Kai, Qian, Yuan, Dun, Chong, and Sui were all second only to Huangzhong in their traces, or perhaps they were men of unfathomable depth.

In recent times, both monastics and laypeople have been accustomed to speaking in such a manner; yet, were one to fully enumerate the extraordinary talents and exceptional virtues found among both the "barbarians" and the "Chinese," from the Han and Wei dynasties onwards, how could they possibly be described in full?
Dharma Master Huiyuan once said:
"The transformation brought about by the Śākya [Buddha] is such that there is nothing it cannot encompass.
While it is inherently the source of the Way for those seeking the Path, it is also a vital undertaking for the salvation of the secular world."
"I have privately reflected upon this teaching, and it accords with the profound mysteries of the Dharma. Why is this?
If every household were to observe the precepts, then the entire nation would find respite from punishment."
Thus, when the Buddha’s clarity [Buddhayaśas] reached Zhao, the two Shi rulers diminished their violence;
when the sacred stupa emitted light, Fu Jian curtailed his cruelty.
Therefore, the divine Way provides assistance; this teaching has its origins in antiquity.
Furthermore, what Xiao Mo has petitioned is not entirely without merit.

However, those who truly harm both the monastic and the laity are fundamentally the monks and nuns who lack proper conduct; yet, as their inner disposition and outward appearance are difficult to distinguish, it is not easy to eliminate the former or to accept the latter.
Although gold, copper, earth, and wood involve immense expenditure, they must serve as the locus for meritorious deeds, and it is difficult to cease them abruptly.

Recently, as I contemplated how to strike a balance, I found myself unable to settle on a course of action, whether to proceed or retreat; today, having personally received Your Majesty’s virtuous decree, I am truly relieved and at ease.
Yang Xuanbao stepped forward and said, "This discussion concerns the relationship between Heaven and man; how could it be appropriate for a subject like me to intervene?
I fear that if Qin and Chu were debating the arts of powerful warfare, or Sun Wu and Wu Qi were exhausting their schemes for annexation, they would find nothing of value here."
The Emperor said, "This is not the tool of the Warring States; it is truly as you say. Shangzhi replied:
“If one honors the reclusive and the retired, then warriors will become indolent; if one prizes benevolence and virtue, then martial spirit will decline.

If your ambition lies with Sun Tzu and Wu Qi, and you are merely intent on devouring others, then you have no need for the Way of Yao and Shun—how much less would you require the teachings of Śākyamuni?”
The Emperor was delighted and said, "That the Śākya school has such a person as you is like the Confucian tradition having Ji Lu; it is what is meant by 'evil words do not enter the ear.
From this point on, the Emperor's faith was established, and he began to devote his attention to the Buddhist scriptures.
Whenever he saw Daoyan or observed the various monks, he would immediately discuss the principles of the Way with them.

At that time, Yan Yanzhi had composed the "Discourse on the Contemplation of Separation from Consciousness" (*Lishi guan*) and the "Examination of Discourse" (*Lunjian*). The Emperor ordered Daoyan to debate their similarities and differences;
they argued back and forth for the entire day, whereupon the Emperor smiled and said, "Today, you gentlemen are no less than Zhi Dun and Xu Xun."
Huiyan subsequently composed the *Treatise on Non-arising and Non-ceasing* (*Wushengmie lun*) and the *Brief Commentary on Laozi* (*Laozi lüe zhu*), among other works.
He Chengtian of Donghai, renowned for his vast knowledge of various fields, once asked Huiyan which calendar the Buddha-land would employ.

Yan said: "In India, on the day of the summer solstice, at midday there is no shadow; this is what is called the 'Center of Heaven. Regarding the Five Elements, it corresponds to the virtue of Earth; its color is yellow, and its number is five. Eight *cun* constitute one *chi*, and ten *liang* here correspond to twelve *liang* in this land. The month of *Chen* (the third lunar month) is the beginning of the year."

Furthermore, in calculating the divisions of time and verifying eclipses, he observed the movement of light and shadow with great precision; the positions of the lunar mansions, their degrees, and the years were all established according to systematic rules.
Shengtian had no way to refute him.
Later, when people from the country of Pāri arrived, they indeed confirmed what Yan had said.
The Emperor then commanded Ren Yu to receive [the teachings] from them.

When the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* first arrived in the territory of the Song, its phrasing was exceptionally refined, yet the number of chapters was sparse and brief, making it difficult for beginners to apply their minds to it.
Daoyan, together with Huiquan, Xie Lingyun, and others, added chapter titles based on the *Nirvāṇa* manuscript.
The text was overly plain; he revised it considerably, and several copies began to circulate.
Yan then dreamed of a person of immense stature who addressed him in a stern voice, saying:
"How can you lightly edit and alter the *Nirvāṇa*, the most venerable of sutras!"
Having been thus alerted, Yan Jue was struck with trepidation; he then convened the assembly once more, intending to withdraw the previous edition.
At that time, those who understood the matter all said:
"This was likely intended as a warning for future generations; if it were truly not to be so, why would he have had such a dream at that very moment?"
Yan agreed that this was so.
Shortly thereafter, he again dreamed of a divine being who told him:
"By the power of your propagation of the sutras, you shall surely behold the Buddha."
Huiyan passed away at Dong’an Temple in the twentieth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, at the age of eighty-one.
The Emperor issued an edict stating:
“Master Huiyan possessed profound insight and vast discernment; he was a master craftsman of the Way. That he has suddenly departed this life causes me deep sorrow and grief.”
"You may be granted fifty thousand coins and fifty bolts of cloth.
Yan’s disciple Fazhi possessed divine insight from his youth.
At twenty-four, he went to Jiangling and encountered Master Ya lecturing; he engaged in several rounds of debate, leaving Ya with no ground upon which to establish a rebuttal.
Yajia looked around at the fourfold assembly and said,
"This youth has achieved a brilliant composition.
Zhi smiled and said:
"Thus, the *Feng* and *Ya* [odes] were transformed and composed.
Thereupon, his reputation spread throughout Chu and Ying, and his fame reached the capitals of Jing and Wu.
He was skilled in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* as well as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
4. Shi Huiquan: Shi Huiquan’s secular surname was Cui, and he was a native of Qinghe.

At the age of ten, he already gained renown for his broad learning. He left home to become a monk at a young age and traveled to various regions to receive instruction. Later, he went to Mount Lu, where he further sought guidance from Huìyuǎn.

Hearing that Master Kumārajīva had entered Guanzhong, he traveled from the south to the north to investigate discrepancies and verify points of agreement, providing detailed exegesis on both the new and the old translations.
His demeanor was elegant and refined, and his thought penetrated the profound and subtle mysteries.
The people of that time praised them, saying:
"In the mastery of the spirit, Sengsheng and Daorong were the foremost; in the precision of debate, Sengguan and Sengzhao were the first.
He then composed the "Preface to the Essential Meaning of the Lotus Sutra" to present to Kumārajīva, who said:

"What you have discussed, noble son, is most excellent. You should withdraw for a short while and travel south to the region between the Yangtze and Han rivers, making it your primary task to propagate the Dharma extensively.
After Kumārajīva passed away, he then traveled south to Jingzhou.

The regional governor, Sima Xiuzhi, held him in profound respect and established Gaokui Temple there; as a result, half of the people of Jingchu turned away from heterodoxy and returned to the orthodox path.

When Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty launched his southern campaign against Liu Yu (Hui-zhi), he arrived at Jiangling and encountered Dao-guan. He received him with great sincerity, treating him as if they were old friends from the past.
Consequently, he issued an edict for Dao-guan to serve as an attendant to the Western General of the Middle Command; this was Emperor Wen.
Shortly thereafter, he returned to the capital and stayed at Daochang Temple.

Daogan was already profoundly skilled in Buddhist principles and had investigated the *Laozi* and *Zhuangzi*; furthermore, he was thoroughly versed in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and had extensively studied various Vinaya schools. Consequently, those who sought the Dharma and inquired about the Way filled his lecture hall every day.

In the third month of the first year of the Yuanjia era, on the Shangsi festival, the imperial carriage attended a banquet by the winding stream. Emperor Wen commanded Liu Guan and the court officials to compose poems.
Guan immediately presented his work before the others; its literary style was pure and elegant, and its subject matter was perfectly suited to the occasion.
Wang Sengda of Langya and He Shangzhi of Lujiang both expressed their sincere devotion through refined discourse, finding appreciation beyond the mundane world.
He passed away during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty at the age of seventy-one.

His compositions, including the "Discourse on Distinguishing the Tenet," the "Treatise on the Meaning of Sudden and Gradual Enlightenment," the "Preface to the Ten Similes," and various prefaces in praise of the sutras, have all been transmitted to the world.
At that time, there was also a monk named Sengfu at Daochang Temple; originally a native of Liquan, he specialized in the study of doctrine and wrote a commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
There was also Fayye.
He was originally a native of Chang’an.
He was well-versed in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (both the large and small versions), as well as the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
Because he maintained a vegetarian diet and practiced self-restraint, Princess Jinling built Nanlin Temple for him, whereupon he came to reside there.
5. Shi Huiyi: Shi Huiyi’s secular surname was Liang, and he was a native of Beidi.
He left home to become a monk in his youth; his character was elegant and distinguished, and his aspirations and practices were vigorous and upright.
Initially, he traveled to study between the regions of Peng and Song, where he thoroughly mastered the meanings of the scriptures.
Later, when he arrived in the capital, he related this account:
"In Jizhou there was a practitioner named Facheng, who, at the time of his death, said to his disciple Puyan: '...'"
The numinous deity of Mount Songgao said: "In Jiangdong there is General Liu, who shall receive the Mandate of Heaven; I offer thirty-two jade disks and one catty of gold as tokens of my pledge."
The matter was subsequently reported to the King of Song. The King said to Huiyi,
"An extraordinary omen requires an extraordinary person before it can be brought to fruition."
"If the Master does not go himself, I fear we shall not succeed. Dao-yi then set out.
In the seventh month of the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled to Mount Songgao, but though he searched, he did not find him.

He then burned incense with a sincere heart and practiced the Way until the seventh night, when he dreamed of an old man with a long beard who, leaning on a staff, led him to the place where the jade was located and pointed it out, saying:
"It is beneath this stone."

Yiming then traveled throughout the mountains until he saw a place that was brilliantly radiant, as if seen in a dream. Immediately at the stone altar beneath the shrine, he indeed found thirty-two jade discs of various sizes and one ingot of gold.
The details of this auspicious omen are recorded in the *Song shi* (History of the Song).

After Huiyi returned to the capital, Emperor Wu of the Song received him with exceptional honor; this continued until the Emperor ascended the throne, when his treatment of Huiyi became even more profound.

In the first year of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, Fan Tai, the General of Chariots and Cavalry, established Zhihuan Temple; regarding Fayi as a preeminent leader among the clergy, he earnestly requested him to oversee the initial construction.
Because Fan Tai’s faith was most sincere and pure, Fayi accordingly provided instructions on the ritual protocols.
At that time, people compared Yi to Śāriputra and Tai to Sudatta; thus, the name "Jiyan" (Gṛdhrakūṭa) was established as its designation.
Later, many eminent monks from the Western Regions took up residence in this monastery, either translating the scriptures or instructing others in the methods of dhyāna.
At the beginning of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, Xu Xianzhi, Tan Daoji, and others monopolized the administration of the court.
Sengtai displayed an air of indignation and would often speak out in harsh insults against them.
Xian and the others were deeply distressed.
Those who heard this were all anxious that Sengtai’s safety was in jeopardy; Sengtai himself also feared impending disaster and thus asked Huiyi for a method to preserve his life.
Huiyi said:
"By remaining loyal and obedient in serving one's superiors, the high and the low can maintain mutual affection; what cause for anxiety or worry could there be?
He then urged Tai to donate sixty mu of bamboo grove land to the temple as a means of securing protection from the unseen realm.
Tai followed his advice and ultimately enjoyed its benefits.

When Tai passed away, the third son, Yan, remarked that Yi had previously taken advantage of his father’s precarious situation to solicit land, which he now regretted; consequently, Yan seized the property and refused to give it back.
Yi Bingtai’s final testament was filled with complex and intricate details, widely known to all who saw or heard it.
Yi subsequently moved to Wuyi Temple, where he lived together with Huirui.
He passed away at Wuyi Temple in the twenty-first year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, at the age of seventy-three.
A short time after Yan, he passed away.
Yan’s younger brother, Ye, later became implicated in Kong Xian’s rebellion, and his entire clan was destroyed.
Later, at Qihuan Temple, there was another monk named Shi Sengrui, who was skilled in the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) and held in high esteem by Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty.
6. Shi Daoyuan: Shi Daoyuan’s surname was Kou; his place of origin is unknown. He left the household life and resided at Dong’an Temple in the capital.

In his youth, he maintained strict adherence to the Vinaya, and as he grew older, he practiced the fundamental tenets of the Mahayana teachings. There were no scriptures, numerical treatises, or philosophical discourses with which he was not thoroughly proficient.
Yet he concealed his brilliance and hid his virtues, such that no one in the world knew of them.

Later, while delivering lectures at Dong'an Temple, he analyzed the profound and subtle, penetrating the most obscure depths, causing the long-standing stagnations of antiquity to dissolve like ice melting away.
Thereupon, the students changed their views and unanimously attached themselves to his virtue.
Later, he moved to reside at Pengcheng Temple.
Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, regarding Huiyuan’s conduct as a model for all beings, issued an edict that he should remain in residence at the temple.
He later passed away at his residence at the age of seventy-eight.

His disciple Huilin, whose original surname was Liu and who was a native of Qin Commandery, was well-versed in various sutras as well as the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*. He was adept at witty repartee and enjoyed humor; being skilled in literary composition, he compiled ten volumes of collected works.
He was by nature arrogant and haughty, and he frequently indulged in self-aggrandizement.
Once, when Huiyuan went to visit Fu Liang, Senglin was already seated there; when Huiyuan arrived, Senglin did not rise to pay his respects.
When Yuan’s anger manifested on his face, Hui-liang subsequently punished Seng-lin with twenty strokes of the cane.

Emperor Shizu of the Song dynasty held Seng-lin in high esteem; whenever he summoned him for an audience, he would invariably invite him to share his private couch. Yan Yanzhi frequently mocked this practice, which always displeased the Emperor. Later, [Seng-lin] composed the "Treatise on the White and the Black" (*Baihei lun*), which deviated from the principles of Buddhism.

He Chengtian, the Governor of Hengyang, was on intimate terms with Senglin; they frequently engaged in mutual debate and praise, and he composed the "Treatise on the Nature of Sentient Beings" (*Daxing lun*), both of whom remained mired in a single-sided perspective and reviled the Buddhist teachings.
Yan Yanzhi and Zong Bing examined and refuted these two treatises, each writing more than ten thousand words.
Daolin, having already self-denounced his own dharma, was banished to Jiaozhou.
It is said that the one known in the world as Master Yuan—who saw the "hemp star"—was this very person.
7. Shi Sengbi. Shi Sengbi was originally a native of Wu. By nature his character was open and simple, and his deportment was upright and straightforward.
In his youth, he traveled to Chang’an with Tan Gan of Longguang Temple and studied under Kumārajīva.
Cherishing his time and sparing his strength, he maintained profound and quiet reflection; Kumārajīva held him in particularly high esteem and appointed him to participate in the translation work.
Later, he traveled through famous regions, where he fully observed their customs and transformations.
At that time, there was an invitation for Huibì to serve as the abbot of a monastery. Huibì said:

"The Ultimate Way is not being propagated, and the pure tradition is fading day by day; unless one is fully endowed with both meditative concentration and wisdom, one cannot establish a lasting standard of conduct."
"Furthermore, one should benefit others according to the conditions of the moment; how can one seek only the private excellence of a single temple?
Later, he resided in the regions of Chu and Ying for over ten years.
There, he instructed others in the sutras and precepts, bringing about a great transformation throughout the region south of the Yangtze River.
Jūqú Méngxùn, the King of Hexi, held his reputation in high esteem from afar and dispatched envoys to express his respect, with gifts following one after another.
Later, he resided at Pénghéng Monastery in the capital; Emperor Wén esteemed him highly and frequently invited him to deliver lectures.
He passed away in the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty at the age of seventy-eight. 8.
Shi Huizheng: Shi Huizheng’s secular surname was Wang, and he was a native of Dong'e.
In his youth, he traveled for study between the Yi and Luo rivers; in his later years, he journeyed through Xu and Yan.
His complexion was very dark, yet his insight and awakening were clear and profound.

At that time, there was a śramaṇa in Luoyang named Daojing, who was also a contemporary of exceptional understanding and shared Huijing’s reputation; however, his ears were exceptionally large, so people of the time said:
"In Luoyang, Da Chang has ears as long as his body; in Dong'e, He is black as ink.
When questioned, there is nothing he does not answer; when he answers, there is nothing that does not satisfy.

Jing’s nature is serene and his mind is empty yet penetrating; he is clear-sighted and possesses the power of reflection. Whenever the Wheel of Dharma turns, thousands would immediately carry their book-cases to attend; among the scholars within the realm, there were none who did not assemble there."

He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, annotated the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, and composed the *Lüeji of the Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Zhuigui of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, as well as the *Talming lun* and various eulogies for Dharma masters.
His teachings were widely disseminated in the northern regions but did not spread significantly across the Yangtze River.
He passed away during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty at the age of over sixty. 9.
Shi Sengbao. Shi Sengbao was a native of Jingzhao. In his youth, he studied under Master Kumārajīva in the Guanzhong region.
During the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, he traveled to Beixu and entered the Huangshan Monastery.
There, he visited the masters Jing and Ding to further his studies.
He subsequently established a thirty-seven-day *Samantabhadra* repentance ritual at that location.
On the seventh day, a white crane flew in and alighted before the seat of Samantabhadra; it departed only after the midday incense offering was completed.
On the evening of the twenty-first day, four men dressed in yellow robes circumambulated the stupa several times and suddenly vanished.
Bao possessed ambition and integrity from his youth, and furthermore, he was moved by auspicious signs; consequently, his sense of diligence became even more intense.
He recited over ten thousand words of scripture daily and regularly performed several hundred prostrations before the Buddha.

Later, he traveled eastward down to the capital, arriving just as a lecture was being inaugurated at Qihuan Temple. Disciples gathered like clouds, and the seats were packed shoulder-to-shoulder by officials and commoners alike.
Since Bao had only just arrived, no one yet recognized him; he therefore went to observe the proceedings riding a donkey.
His robes were soiled and tattered, and his appearance bore the traces of wind and dust; as the hall was already cramped, he sat on a donkey saddle outside the door.
Just as the High Seat had finished presenting the topic for discussion, Bao was about to begin speaking when the Dharma Master asked:
"What is the name of this visiting monk?"
He replied, “His name is Bao.
He asked again:
"What is the limit? Bao replied,
"Even those on the high seat may be considered my limits."
He then posed several questions, all of which were beyond the reach of the former master’s intellectual power; the high seat had no way to counter his arguments and thus withdrew in deference.
At that time, when King Hong and Fan Tai heard Bao’s discourses, they marveled at his talent and insight, and invited him to converse with them.
They further requested that he reside at Zhihuan Temple, where he lectured on various sutras, and his propagation of the Dharma continued uninterrupted.
Xie Lingyun of Chenjun heard of his reputation and went to visit him; upon seeing Bao’s spiritual bearing, he was filled with even deeper admiration and submission.
Someone asked him, "What do you think of Master Xie?"
Baobao said, "Lingyun has an abundance of talent but lacks sufficient discernment; he will likely not escape harm himself.
Once, while Baobao was walking along a road, he saw six prisoners being led away for execution. Baobao preached the Dharma for them, exhorting them to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara.
As the bandits approached him at this moment of peril, he prayed with earnest sincerity in every thought.
Suddenly, the escorting officials became heavily intoxicated from drinking wine; the bandits loosened his shackles, and he was thus spared.
He passed away during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.

At that time, there was also one named Shi Fahe at Waguan Temple, who was likewise well-versed in the Abhidharma and enjoyed great renown in his day; he was held in high esteem by Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty and was appointed by imperial decree as the Monastic Head (Sengzhu).
10. Shi Sengquan: Shi Sengquan’s secular surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Haiyang in Liaoxi.
In his youth, he traveled through Yan and Qi, studying the non-Buddhist classics extensively; it was not until he reached the age of twenty that he finally entered the monastic order.
Furthermore, he refined the Tripiṭaka with great precision and became a preeminent master for scholars in the northern lands.
Later, he crossed the Yangtze River and settled in the capital, where he established a grand lecture hall and propagated his teachings throughout Jiangnan.
Zhang Gong of Wu Commandery invited him to return to Wu to lecture; the scholars of Gusu all admired his virtue and turned their hearts toward him.
Initially he stayed at Xianju Temple, and later he rested at Mount Huqiu.

Xuan previously fashioned a sixteen-foot golden image in the state of Huanglong; later, upon entering Wu, he again fashioned a "golden image among men" and enshrined it at the Eastern Temple on Mount Huqiu.

Sengquan was by nature inclined toward giving alms and generously provided for the poor and destitute. He maintained himself with purity and integrity, and his residence was never furnished with more than the bare necessities.
Later, Meng Yi of Pingchang established Fangxian Temple in Yuhang and invited Sengquan to reside there.
He led his followers with such diligent devotion that he never ceased his meditative practices and prostrations; his pursuit of study was so arduous that he eventually lost his sight.
Nevertheless, his self-exertion became even more refined, and he did not abandon his lecturing and teaching.
Zhang Chang and Zhang Fu of the state of Wu, and Dai Yong and Dai Bo of Qiaoguo, all admired his virtue and formed friendships with him, honoring him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
Later, Sengquan traveled briefly to Lin’an County and stayed at the home of the District Magistrate Dong; the Magistrate was a disciple of pure faith.

After Xuan had been staying there for a short time, he fell gravely ill. He constantly saw the image he had fashioned appearing on the western wall, and he also saw various celestial youths all coming to attend to him during his illness.
The disciple Falang dreamed of a platform being carried by several people. When he asked where they were going, they replied, "To welcome Master Quan.
The next morning, [the Master] indeed passed away.
The County Magistrate, Ruan Shangzhi, ordered that [Hui]quan be buried to the right of the tomb of Guo Wenju on Mount Baitu, intending it to be like Liang Hong’s burial beside Yao Li.

Wang Yu, the Special Advancer, and the eminent scholar Dai Yong visited Quan’s grave site, where they carved a stone and erected a stele; Tang Sixian composed the inscription, and Zhang Fu wrote the eulogy.
11. Shi Tanjian. Shi Tanjian’s secular surname was Zhao, and he was a native of Jizhou.

Upon his arrival, he was immediately invited into the palace, where a great assembly of monks versed in doctrine was convened, and Sengyou was instructed to expound upon sudden enlightenment.
At that time, those who vied in debate raised various challenges and objections against him.

Since Sengyou had long cultivated contemplation of the profound mysteries and possessed a fundamental source for his teachings, he was able to seize opportunities to blunt the enemy's edge and advance with inevitable force.
The Emperor then leaned on his desk and expressed his satisfaction.
When Emperor Xiaowu ascended the throne, he especially praised and esteemed them; he subsequently issued an edict for Sengsheng to reside at Xin'an Temple as its presiding abbot.
The Emperor often remarked:

"Master Sengsheng’s solitary spirit shines with absolute clarity, while Master Daoyou gallops straight ahead on his own path alone; they may truly be called masters who have fully realized their teachings, not failing the illustrious legacy of their predecessors."
He passed away during the Yuanhui era of the Song dynasty at the age of seventy-one.
Later, there was the śramaṇa Daoci of Yuzhou, who was skilled in the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
He followed the principles of his predecessors and edited his own commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, reducing it to two fascicles, which is currently circulated in the world.
At that time, Bituobao Huizheng and Changle Jueshi were both renowned for their equal fame and virtue.
He thoroughly mastered the three treatises (*śāstra*), becoming a model for scholars.
He was particularly adept in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and established the doctrine of "non-empty conventional designations" (*amogha-prajñapti*).
32. Shi Huitong. Shi Huitong’s surname was Liu, and he was a native of Pei.
From his youth, his spirit was clear and vibrant, and his noble character was profound and transcendent; he resided at Zhicheng Temple.
Every time he shook his fly-whisk, carriages and canopies would immediately fill the streets.
Xu Zhanzhi of Donghai and Yuan Can of Chenjun treated him with the reverence due to a teacher and a friend.
Emperor Xiaowu highly honored him with noble rank and issued an edict appointing him as a companion to the two princes, Hailing and Xiao Jianping.

Yuan Can composed the "Discourse on Qu Boyu and Yan Hui" and presented it to Liu Tong; Tong engaged in a series of challenging debates and refutations with him, which were subsequently published for the world to see.

Furthermore, he composed commentaries on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, and the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, as well as the "Refutation of the Discourse on Barbarians and Chinese," the "Treatise on Manifesting Proof," the "Treatise on the Dharma-nature," and the "Record of Hexagram Images"; all of these have been transmitted to the world.
He passed away during the Shengming era of the Song dynasty at the age of sixty-three.

Part Five: Biographies of Shi Sengyuan (1) and Shi Tandu (2).

1. Shi Daohui; 2. Shi Sengzhong; 3. Shi Daosheng; 4. Shi Hongchong; 5. Shi Zhilin; 6. Shi Fayuan; 7. Shi Xuanchang; 8. Shi Sengyuan; 9. Shi Senghui; 10. Shi Sengrou; 11. Shi Huiji; 12. Shi Huici; 13. Shi Huilong; 14. Shi Sengzong; 15. Shi Fa’an; 16. Shi Sengyin; 17. Shi Faduo; 18. Shi Zhixiu; 19. Shi Huiqiu; 20. Shi Sengsheng; 21. Shi Zhishun; 22. Shi Baoliang; 23. Shi Fatong; 24. Shi Huiji; 25. Shi Tanfei; 26. Shi Sengyuan. Regarding Shi Sengyuan: His original surname was Zhao, and he was a native of Yingchuan, a descendant of Zhao Yan, the Minister of Works (Sikong) of the Wei dynasty.
In his youth, he was fond of reading books.
After receiving the precepts, he specialized in the study of Buddhist doctrine.
Initially, he traveled to the region of Xu and stayed at Baitasi Temple, where he studied the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma* under the monk Sengsong.
Before three years had passed since he began his studies, his accomplishments exceeded those of ten years; the reputation for his wisdom and insight resounded far and wide.
Daoyuan’s appearance was grand and imposing, his waistband ten spans in circumference, his spirit clear and remote, and his speech elegant and unrestrained.
The hermit Liu Yinzhi donated his mountain residence to serve as a vihāra for them.
Tandu, Huiji, and Daodeng all received their instruction from Huanyuan.

Huiji was also well-versed in the *Śāstra on Numbers*, while Daodeng excelled in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Lotus Sūtra*; both were highly esteemed by the Wei ruler Yuan Hong and enjoyed great renown throughout the state of Wei.
Sengyuan passed away in the fifth year of the Weibo era (429 AD), at the age of sixty-eight, which was the third year of the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty. 2.
Shi Tandu: Shi Tandu’s original surname was Cai, and he was a native of Jiangling.
From his youth, he was reverent and cautious regarding his demeanor, and he had long been renowned for his adherence to the precepts and monastic rules.
His spirit and intellect were sharp and perceptive, surpassing those of others.
Later, he traveled to the capital to study, where he thoroughly mastered the various scriptures.
He studied the *Nirvāṇa*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Vimalakīrti*, and *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* sūtras, exploring their subtle and hidden meanings and contemplating how to express what lies beyond words.
Due to a foot ailment, he traveled westward and arrived at Xuzhou, where he received further instruction on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* from Dharma Master Sengyuan.
He subsequently mastered this treatise thoroughly and became preeminent in his time.
When the Wei ruler Yuan Hong heard of his reputation, he revered him deeply and dispatched envoys to invite him.
Once he arrived at Pingcheng, he opened a grand lecture hall.
Yuan Hong paid his respects by descending from his seat to join the assembly, personally attending to the savoring of the teachings.
Thereupon he settled in the capital of Wei, where his Dharma teachings continued in succession; disciples arrived from afar, numbering more than a thousand.
He passed away in the state of Wei in the thirteenth year of the pseudo-太和 era, which corresponds to the sixth year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty.
He compiled the *Great Commentary on the Essential Meaning of the Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* in eight fascicles, which was widely circulated in the northern regions. 3.
Shi Daohui: Shi Daohui’s surname was Wang; he was a native of Yuyao who resided in Jianye.
At the age of eleven, he left the household life as a disciple of Sengyuan and resided at Lingyao Temple.

When he reached fourteen, he read the *Collected Works of Huiyuan* from Mount Lu and sighed with profound regret, lamenting that his birth had come too late. He then traveled upstream for a thousand li with his friend Zhishun to visit the traces left by Huiyuan; they stayed at the West Temple on Mount Lu for three years before returning to the capital.
At that time, when the King was expounding the meaning of the "Three Characteristics" and had assembled a great multitude of learned monks, Hui was seventeen years old;
he then posed several questions, his speech profound and subtle, and his expositions followed a logical sequence.
The assembly all marveled at this.
Later, he studied under the two Dharma Masters Meng and Bin.
Meng once lectured on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Zhang Rong formulated a series of overlapping challenges.
Daomeng, claiming illness, felt unable to handle so many matters himself, and thus ordered Huì to respond.
Zhang Rong, because Huì was young, harbored a considerable degree of contempt for him.
Hui seized the opportunity to blunt the opponent's sharpness; his words invariably reached the core of principle, and in his responsive exchanges, he possessed ample ease and mastery.
He was proficient in the Mahāyāna and well-versed in the Sāṃkhya school, lecturing on these subjects continuously, and his disciples were exceedingly numerous.
He categorized the various meanings and themes, beginning with the division into chapters and sections.
Chu Cheng and Xie Chaozong were renowned at the time and both held him in high esteem.
Because his mother was elderly and he wished to provide for her needs, Hui moved to reside at Zhuangyan Temple.
Her mother, moved by her resolve, also left the household life to practice the Way; she donated her residence as a meritorious act and constructed a vihāra.
Hui passed away in the third year of the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty at the age of thirty-one.
At the time of his death, he called for his fly-whisk and bestowed it upon his friend Zhishun.
Zhishun lamented, saying:
"A man such as this, whose life did not reach forty years—what a pity!"
Thereupon, he placed his fly-whisk inside the coffin and enshrouded him.
He was buried on the southern slope of Mount Zhong.
Xie Chaozong of Chen Commandery composed the inscription for his stele.
At that time, there were also Xuānqù and Sēngdá at Zhuāngyán Monastery, both of whom were renowned for their scholarly understanding.

Xuānqù was extensively versed in the various scriptures and was proficient in both Buddhist and secular learning; he was particularly adept at presiding over assemblies, and his character and conduct were admirable.
Dacheng was young when his hair turned white; people of the time called him "White-Headed Dacheng. He was also widely learned in various scriptures and was particularly adept at dialectical debate.
However, because of his rigid nature and tendency to offend others, he was exiled to Changsha.
4. Shi Sengzhong. Shi Sengzhong’s secular surname was Sun; he was a native of Lujun.
He left home to become a monk at the age of sixteen and lived in poverty while practicing the Way.
He once traveled to Shouchun, where Master Dao saw him and marveled at his extraordinary character.
Prince Yao of Qiao County esteemed his integrity and character, providing him with the four necessities.
Later, when the Prince requested that he lecture on the *Śata-śāstra*, Sengdao went to listen; upon returning, he remarked to others:
"The saying that 'those born later are to be feared' is truly not empty.
Zhong Miaoshan was proficient in the *Tattvasiddhi*, the three *Śāstra*s, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, and others.
Later, he traveled south to the capital and resided at Zhongxing Temple.
At the beginning of the Yongming era, the Wei envoy Li Daogu arrived on a diplomatic mission and met him within the temple.
The Emperor, recognizing that Zhong possessed a virtuous reputation, issued an imperial decree ordering him to engage in formal discourse with the envoy.
They conversed back and forth for some time, their speech never missing a point. As the sun’s shadow shifted slightly toward evening, Zhong stopped eating.
Gu asked, “Why do you not eat?”
Zhong said, "The dharma of the ancient Buddhas is not to eat after midday. Gu said:
"What constitutes a śrāvaka? Zhong replied,
"Those who are to be delivered by means of the śrāvaka vehicle, for their sake he manifests as a śrāvaka."
At that time, people took this as his formal response.
Thereafter, he remained to lecture and expound the teachings, attracting crowds of disciples who came to listen.
Prince Wenhui of the Qi dynasty and Prince Wenxuan of Jingling repeatedly invited him to occupy the seat of honor as their teacher.
He passed away in the seventh year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty at the age of sixty.

At that time, those whose fame equaled that of Zhong and whose virtue was comparable to his were Tanzhian, Tanqian, Sengbiao, Sengzui, Mindu, and Sengbao; all were proficient in the sutras and śāstras, were held in high esteem by Prince Wenxuan, and took turns presiding over lecture assemblies.
5. Shi Daosheng. Shi Daosheng’s secular surname was Zhu, and he was a native of Pei.

He entered the monastic order in his youth and devoted himself to study; he was proficient in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and was also well-versed in the *Book of Changes*.
He first resided in Xiangzhou; Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty, having heard of his reputation, issued an imperial decree for him to come to the capital, where he stayed at Pengcheng Temple.
Upon meeting him once, Xie Chaozong subsequently revered him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
He then composed the "Discourse on Friendship" (*Shujiao lun*) and the "Discourse on the Fundamental Non-existence of the Source of Birth and Death" (*Shengsi benwu yuan lun*), among other works.
Later, while residing at Tianbao Temple, Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty issued an imperial decree appointing him as the successor to Tan-du as the Head of the Sangha (*Sengzhu*).
Shen Wenji, the Governor of Danyang, had long venerated the teachings of Huang-Lao and harbored deep resentment toward the Buddha.

He consequently established the "Monastic Bureau" under the Ministry of Rites and demanded that monks register their family lineages, intending to purge and cull the ranks of the monastics. However, because Li Sheng was diligent and effective in his leadership, the matter was successfully quelled.
Later, Wenji intentionally hosted a gathering at Tianbao Temple and ordered Lu Xiujing to engage in debate with Daosheng.
Since Daosheng possessed superior reasoning and his speech was eloquent and spirited, they exchanged jests and banter back and forth without a moment’s interruption.
His peaceful intentions could not be fulfilled, and he withdrew with a sense of shame.
He passed away during the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty at the age of over sixty.
6. Shi Hongchong: Shi Hongchong was a native of Liangzhou.
From his youth, he possessed great resolve and diligence; he was proficient in the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*, and had a thorough understanding of the sutras and vinaya.
Toward the end of the Daming era, he crossed the Yangtze River and initially resided at Duobao Temple.
He was exceptionally skilled at posing difficult questions, such that many established masters were defeated by him.
Later, when he himself opened a dharma assembly, sharp debates arose like clashing blades.
Since his thoughts had entered the profound and subtle, and his eloquence was as naturally transcendent as the heavens, he resolved doubts and cleared obstructions without any flaw.
Whenever he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* or the *Ten Stages*, the hall was filled with listeners; Prince Yigong of Jiangxia, the Minister of State under the Song dynasty, held him in high esteem.
When Emperor Ming ascended the throne, he established Xianggong Temple and invited Huichong to serve as its head; thereupon, Huichong moved his residence there.
At that time, there was also the bhikṣu Faxian at Xianggong Temple, who was likewise intelligent and possessed great power of reflection, and was equal in reputation to Huichong.
Tong died during the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty at the age of seventy-two.
He annotated the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchābodhivibhāga-sūtra* and annotated the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.
7. Shi Zhilin. Shi Zhilin was a native of Gaochang. When he first entered the monastic order, he became a disciple of Master Liang.

From his youth, he revered principle and delighted in learning; he carried his book-bag to Chang’an and traveled with his monk’s staff through Jiangzhou and Yuzhou, extensively collecting various scriptures and specializing particularly in the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
When Master Daolang was exiled, twelve of his disciples all followed him beyond the mountain ranges.
Lin then settled in Fanyu, where he purified the coastal regions through his teachings.

At the beginning of the Song dynasty, during the reign of Emperor Ming, an imperial edict provided him with the necessary provisions and dispatched him to the capital, where he resided at Lingji Temple.

His lectures were continuous, and those who received his teachings and submitted to him gathered in great numbers; he clarified that there were three distinct schools regarding the meaning of the Two Truths.

At that time, Zhou Yong of Runan also composed the "Treatise on the Three Schools," which accorded perfectly with Lin’s own views. Deeply delighted by this coincidence, Lin wrote a letter to Yong, saying:

"I have recently heard that you, O Donor, have set forth new insights on the Two Truths and presented the pros and cons of the three schools. Your voice is extraordinary and transcends ordinary standards; although my humble thoughts are not as swift as yours in grasping these matters, I believe that regarding the principles of the world, this alone is the correct path."
Otherwise, it would be unreasonable.
Therefore, I urge you to quickly take up paper and brush.
Recently, I have observed those who travel back and forth; they report that the treatise has already been completed and is being widely circulated with great joy, which is truly most significant.

Furthermore, I have heard from the donor that he fears this undertaking may differ from ordinary times and thus offend the assembly of learners; even though the treatise has been completed, he is certain it must not be brought forth. Hearing this, I was struck with such fear that I could not help but spring up from my bed.

The purport of this teaching does not seem to have been revealed at the outset; it was lost amidst sublime sounds for sixty-seven years. Its principles were loftier than the common tone, and none were able to transmit them.
When I was twenty years old, I was unworthily granted this principle.
I have always believed that by means of this slight awakening, one may attain the Way.
I have privately rejoiced in it at every turn, yet I had no one with whom to share it.
When I was young, I observed that the elders of Chang’an often remarked that the eminent masters of Guanzhong were superior; indeed, this view had long existed there.
During the peak of the Dharma assemblies, those who could truly and deeply grasp this profound meaning were originally not many.
Since this transgresses common human sentiment, those who subsequently hear and receive it are extremely few;
as for its transmission to Jiangdong, there is almost no one at all.

Since I took up the fly-whisk more than forty years ago, I have traveled east and west to lecture, and though I was mistakenly esteemed as preeminent of my time, regarding other systems of doctrine, they appear frequently in the catalogs of patriarchal records; yet as for this particular path, not a single person—whether monastic or lay—has mastered it.

I, this poor monk, have been afflicted by illness for many years; now that my life is at its end and my strength exhausted, I shall soon depart for the West. I reflect that from this day forth, this Way will be forever severed and no longer spoken of.
The donor’s inspiration has arisen without precedent, uniquely pioneering a realm beyond the mundane; I did not expect these words to so unexpectedly reach my ears.
I am both joyful and comforted, truly beyond compare.
To establish and clarify this principle so that the lamp of the Dharma may endure until the end is the foremost merit of practicing the true Way;
even the offering of kingdoms, cities, wives, and children to the Buddha and the Sangha cannot surpass its benefit and merit.
Since I have fortunately been able to provide this exposition, I believe it should be widely proclaimed so that those who appreciate its resonance may see it.

In elucidating the principles of the Dharma, one should not shrink from the duty of benevolence; how could one possibly harbor self-preservation out of regard for the opinions of the multitude, thereby stifling such a rare and extraordinary insight?
If this treatise were completed, I might subsequently fall ill; I fear that when the donor arrives, this illness may become a great obstacle.
My previous words were earnest, for they were no idle discourse.
I intend to transcribe a copy for your gift to this poor monk, so that I may carry it back to the West and cause it to be widely propagated everywhere.
As I am currently somewhat constrained by circumstances, I have entered the mountains to compose this preface; I look forward with deep anticipation to entrusting it to you.
Tanyong consequently produced his treatises;
thus, the tenets of the Three Schools have been transmitted to the present day.
Lin Xing stood eight chi tall; his natural bearing was magnificent and elegant. When he ascended the seat, he roared like a thunderclap, and his speech flowed like a stream.
Later, he took his leave and returned to Gaochang.
He passed away in the fifth year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty at the age of seventy-nine.

He authored the *Treatise on the Two Truths* (*Er-di lun*) and the *Record of the Vibhāṣā and Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (*Bi-tan za-xin ji*), as well as commentaries on the *Twelve Gate Treatise* (*Shi-er men lun*), the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* (*Zhong lun*), and other works.
8. Shi Fayuan: Shi Fayuan’s secular surname was Xin; he was a native of Longxi and a descendant of Xin Pi.
His eldest brother, Yuanming, served as Grand Minister of State under the illegitimate Wei dynasty.
His second elder brother, Fa’ai, was also a śramaṇa.
He was proficient in both the sutras and śāstras as well as in mathematics and divination, serving as the State Preceptor of the Rouran kingdom and receiving a fief of three thousand households.

From his youth, Fayuan was broad-minded and magnanimous, possessing a character that stood out from the crowd; whenever he encountered those who were poor and destitute on the road, he would immediately take off his own clothes to bestow upon them as charity.
When he first entered the monastic life, he served the śramaṇa Zhu Huikai of Liangzhou.
Daokai’s noble virtue was so profound that it communicated with the divine; people of the time said he had attained the first fruit of the path.
Daokai said to Fayuan:

"If your realization is such as this, you will surely be able to provide a framework for the teachings of the later generations. You ought to strive for extensive learning rather than seeking solitary perfection alone."
Thereupon, he took his leave to travel for study, journeying through Yan and Zhao and coming and going between Ye and Luo.
Encountering the time when the Hu invaders were rampant and the regions of Guan and Long were in turmoil, Fayuan braved dangers and traversed perils, never slackening in his pursuit of learning.

In the fifteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he returned to Liangzhou and subsequently proceeded to Chengdu. Later, he traveled east to Jianye, where he relied upon Huiguan of Daochang Monastery as his teacher.
He was devoted to the Mahāyāna and also studied the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika systems alongside it.
He also perused the external classics, including the *Fen* and *Su*.
Later, he entered Mount Lu to maintain stillness and savor meditation; he clarified his thoughts through the five gates and directed his mind toward the three contemplations.
Shortly thereafter, the Provincial Governor Yu Dengzhi invited him to leave the mountains to give lectures.

Later, when Emperor Wen sought out someone who had attained sudden enlightenment in the meaning of the Dharma, he issued an imperial edict for [Seng]shu to descend to the capital, so that the principle of sudden enlightenment might be reaffirmed during the Song dynasty.
When He Shangzhi heard of this, he sighed and said:
"I have often thought that since Master Sengsheng passed away, his subtle words would be forever lost.
Today, hearing again these discourses beyond the mundane, one can truly say that Heaven has not yet allowed its literature to perish."
The Emperor decreed that he serve as the Preceptor of the Five Precepts for Prince Shuo, the Prince of Nanping.
When Emperor Xiaowu ascended the throne, he was further appointed as the Companion to Prince Zishang of Xiyang.
He declined on the grounds of illness, finding it unbearable, and after a long time, he was granted exemption from the duty.
He lived in seclusion at Mount Fang, where he annotated the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Guhyadhātu-sūtra*.
During intervals between his doctrinal discussions, he would occasionally discourse on the *Classic of Filial Piety* and the *Book of Mourning Rites*.
Later, during the Tianbao era, the temple was reconstructed and he was invited to reside there. Consequently, he left the mountains and came out to the city to take charge of the monastic community.

When the Regional Inspector Wang Jingwen went to visit him, he happened upon his lecture on the *Sangfu* (Rituals of Mourning). After engaging in several rounds of discussion, Wang praised him highly before departing.

When Emperor Ming completed the construction of the Xianggong Monastery and opened a grand lecture hall, he carefully selected eminent monks and issued an imperial decree inviting Huì to serve as the presiding Dharma Master.

The Emperor himself descended from his carriage to attend the dharma assembly, with high officials gathered in the seats; such was the splendor of that occasion that all who witnessed it were filled with admiration.
Later, Emperor Wenhui of the Northern Qi again invited him to reside at Linggen Monastery, and he consequently moved there.
The Grand Marshal Wang Jian maintained no casual social ties, yet he treated Fayuan as his teacher, showing the utmost respect in both his correspondence and speech.
He passed away in the seventh year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty at the age of eighty-one.
At that time, there were also Fachang and Zhixing at Linggen Temple, both of whom were extensively versed in the sūtras and śāstras and frequently presided over formal lectures.
Sengchang was particularly adept at engaging in spirited debate and was held in awe by his contemporaries as a master craftsman.
However, his temperament was extremely rigid and stubborn, and he did not conform to worldly customs. 9.
Shi Xuanchang. Shi Xuanchang’s secular surname was Zhao; he was a native of Jincheng in Hexi.
After a short time, his family was destroyed by the Hu barbarians; as disaster was about to reach Chang, the barbarian leader saw him and stopped it, saying:
"This boy’s gaze shoots outward; he is no ordinary child."
He was thus granted exemption and subsequently went to Liangzhou to enter the monastic order.
His original name was Huizhi; later, he encountered Xuangao and served as his disciple.
Xuangao always marveled at him and would deliberate on every matter with him; consequently, he changed his name to Xuanchang to signify the intent of his formal entrustment.
Subsequently, the tyrannical captors annihilated the Buddha-dharma and harmed the śramaṇas; only Fǎchàng managed to escape.

On the seventeenth day of the intercalary fifth month of the twenty-second year of the Yuánjiā era, he set out from Píngchéng, traveling by way of Dàijùn and Shàngyù, crossing the Tàixíng Mountains to the east, passing through Yōu and Jì, and turning south before reaching Mèngjīn.
He held only a bundle of willow twigs and a handful of scallion leaves in his hands.
As the barbarian cavalry pursued him and were about to overtake him, he struck the sand with the willow twigs.
Sand rose up until the sky was darkened, so that neither man nor horse could advance.

After a short while, when the sand subsided, the rider arrived once more; thereupon he threw himself into the river, using only the leaves of scallions inserted into his nostrils to draw breath as he crossed the water, reaching Yangzhou on the first day of the eighth month.
He thoroughly understood the sutras and the vinaya, and delved deeply into the essentials of dhyāna; his prognostications regarding auspicious and inauspicious matters were invariably proven true.
He was extensively versed in the classical texts of the Confucian tradition, including the *Feng* and *Dian*.
As for worldly arts and miscellaneous skills, there were few he did not master.
Initially, the great *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was so vast and profound in its textual meaning that, from time immemorial, no one had ever expounded or explained it.
Fang then exhausted his thoughts in research and investigation, organizing the chapters and comparing the phrases.
His tradition of lecturing continues to this day; he was its originator.
Furthermore, he was proficient in the Three Treatises (*Trisastra*) and served as a preeminent authority for students.
Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty deeply admired and esteemed him, requesting that he serve as a teacher for the Crown Prince; however, he declined the offer three times with firm resolve.
His disciples said to him, "The Dharma Master intends to propagate the Way and save sentient beings, widely proclaiming the sacred teachings."

Now the Emperor, having humbled himself, extends an invitation, and the Crown Prince, with accumulated courtesy, longs to show you respect. If the Way were proclaimed by such a sagely ruler, then the four seas would all turn toward his virtue.
Is it not then the case that your current bold and lofty refusal is merely for the sake of reputation?
Chang said, "This can be discussed with the wise; it is difficult to speak of it with worldly people.
It was only through the events of the Taichu era that [the Emperor] finally realized he had been enlightened beforehand.
From then on, he moved his residence to Jingzhou and stayed at Changsha Temple.

At that time, the śramaṇa Gongdezhí produced the *Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha) and other texts; [Dao’an] edited and corrected their wording, and their phrasing and purport were elegant and incisive.
Furthermore, he extended his hand and produced incense, and water flowed from his palm; none could fathom these wonders.
Toward the end of the Song dynasty, he set sail on a distant journey westward to Chengdu.
Initially residing at Dashi Temple, he personally painted images of the sixteen deities, including Vajrapāṇi and Guhyapada.

In the third year of the Shengming era, he traveled again to the western regions and gazed upon the Min Mountains; there, within the borders of Guangyang County in the northern part of Minshan Commandery, he beheld Mount Qihou and conceived the resolve to spend the remainder of his life there.
He continued to rely on the cliffs and beside the valleys, binding grass together to construct a hermitage.
His disciple Faqi saw a divine being riding a horse, wearing a single-layered blue robe, who circled the mountain once and then pointed out the location for building a stupa.
On the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the first year of the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty,
the foundation stone was laid and a temple established, named Qixing (Qi Prosperity), which coincided precisely with the occasion when the Founder of the Qi dynasty received his imperial mandate.
The movements of Heaven and the affairs of men were in perfect accord across ten thousand *li*.

"There was a man wearing a crimson robe and a *zhe* cap, carrying a wooden chest whose base rested before the bed."
On the twentieth day, he saw two rows of Buddha images approaching; they stood together with palms joined for a long time.
Those attending to his illness merely smelled a rare fragrance, yet could not fathom its significance.
Tong then secretly informed Hui-mi of his agreement.

On the twenty-first day, after he had finished bathing with fragrant water, he performed prostrations and returned to his bed; with his hands joined at his chest, he passed away precisely at midday at the age of seventy.
He was subsequently buried to the south of the monastery.
His disciples Jing, Shen, and others erected a stele beside his tomb; Xie Ju of Chen Commandery and Xiao Ziyun of Lanling both composed inscriptions for it, which were engraved on its two faces.
At that time, there was also the śrāmaṇera Shengjin at Dinglin Shangsi Temple; he had originally been a eunuch.
His pure faith was profound and sincere, so he eventually left the household life and practiced with ascetic discipline.
Once, while practicing dhūta austerities, he went to Mount Dong and stayed overnight beneath a tree.
A tiger came and rubbed its head against him; seeing that Sengjin sat upright and undisturbed, it knelt before him and departed.
Thereafter, whenever he walked or sat alone, he constantly saw a green horse standing guard at his left and right.
26. Shi Huiji: Shi Huiji’s original surname was Qian; he was a native of Yuyang in Wuxing.
At the age of eighteen, he left home to become a monk at Lelin Mountain in Kuaiji, where he followed Dharma Master Huiji to receive his instruction.
By nature he was honest and sincere, his speech devoid of flowery ornamentation; yet he studied diligently from dawn until dusk, never once relaxing or resting.
Later, he left the capital and resided at Zhaoti Temple.
Furthermore, he traveled extensively to visit various masters, synthesizing their divergent doctrines; he thoroughly mastered both the Tripiṭaka and the Vaipulya sūtras.

He widely sought out the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, the *Jñānaprasthāna* (Gāndhārī), and other texts, comparing and verifying them against one another. Consequently, regarding the entire body of the *Abhidharma*, he was preeminent in his time.
Whenever there were difficult or stubborn points, he would unravel and explain them all; among the scholars within the realm, there was no one who did not come to him.
Every time he gave a lecture, thousands would gather with their books upon their backs.
The śramaṇas Sengmin and Fayun were both renowned throughout their generation; they too took up the scrolls to seek his instruction.

The present Emperor held him in high esteem and received him with great favor. In the fourteenth year of the Tianjian era, he returned to Wucheng, where he fell ill and passed away at the age of sixty.
He composed the *Pitan Dayi Shu* (Commentary on the Great Meaning of the Abhidharma) in over one hundred thousand words, which circulated widely throughout the world. 27.
Shi Tanfei: Shi Tanfei’s original surname was Wang; he was a native of Shan County, Kuaiji.
He left home to become a monk at a young age and studied under Dharma Master Huìjī.
By nature he was intelligent and quick-witted, and he had long been renowned for his exceptional grasp of the scriptures.
He thoroughly mastered the profound Mahāyāna sūtras and also extensively read the *Lǎozi*, *Zhuāngzi*, Confucianism, and Mohism.
Later, he traveled east and west to seek instruction, thoroughly exhausting the essential meanings of the sutras and treatises.
Residing at Fahua Tai Temple in his native village, he lectured in continuous succession, and his disciples formed orderly ranks.
Fei’s spirit was vibrant and his aspirations were pure and profound; thus, he attained unparalleled mastery in the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
Furthermore, his discourse was refined and his eloquence was lofty and elegant; his style at the lecture hall was held in high esteem by his contemporaries.
Yuanjian, the Prince of Hengyang of the Liang dynasty, and the recluse He Yin of Lujiang both held his exemplary character in high esteem, inviting him to preach and lecture.
Zhang Rong of Wuguo, Zhou Yong of Runan, and Zhou Yong’s son She, among others, all formed intimate bonds of mutual understanding with him.
He passed away at the monastery in the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era at the age of seventy-six.
His literary compositions were also quite well-known in the world.

Initially, Sengfei had enjoyed great renown in Jiangdong and was appointed by imperial decree as the Monastic Head (Sengzhu) of ten cities; however, just as the official edict was about to be implemented, he passed away before he could take his formal office.
The monks and nuns of that region redoubled their devotion and longing for his virtue.

In Nan Yan Temple of Fei County, there was a śramaṇa named Fazang, who was likewise renowned for his observance of the precepts and vegetarianism; he delighted in releasing living beings to save their lives and promoted the creation of sacred images.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Mingqing in Yuao County who enjoyed a reputation equal to that of Fei.
Qing’s original surname was Zheng; his observance of the precepts was strict and pure, and his scholarly pursuits were refined and elegant.

My original teacher served Master Yan, who was himself a disciple of Hongshi; thus, for three successive generations of master and disciple, they were all held in high esteem in the southeastern region.
The commentary states:
Now, the ultimate truth is beyond words, and its profound essence is deep and tranquil.
Because it is profound and still, the sphere of mental activity is severed; because it is ineffable, the path of language is cut off.
When the path of language is cut off, words would wound its essential meaning;
when the sphere of mental activity is severed, deliberate thought loses its truth.
This is why Vimalakīrti remained silent within his eight-foot square room, and Śākyamuni maintained a profound stillness beneath the twin śāla trees.
One can thus know that because the underlying principle is deep and quiescent, the sages remain without words.
Yet this vast and drifting dream-like realm is fundamentally separated from the ultimate principle;
how could these deluded and ignorant folk be awakened were it not for the teachings?

Therefore, the Sage relies upon his wondrous spiritual essence to respond to things, embodies profound stillness to communicate with the divine, employs subtle words as a ferry across the Way, and entrusts forms and images to transmit the Truth.
Therefore it is said:
"Warfare is an inauspicious instrument; it is employed only when there is no other choice.
Rhetoric is an unreal thing; it is deployed only when there is no other choice."
Thus, beginning at the Deer Park, he took the Four Noble Truths as his initial teaching;
concluding at the Peacock Grove, he took the Three Marks as his ultimate perfection.
The miscellaneous discourses and flowing texts disseminated between these two points number more than eight hundred million.
An elephant carries its burden without exhaustion; the dragon palace overflows without end.
This is intended to enable one to catch the hare by riding upon its tracks, and to know the moon by relying upon the finger.
Once the moon is known, the finger is discarded; once the hare is caught, the tracks are forgotten.
As the Sūtra says:
"Rely on the meaning, not on the words.
This is precisely what that refers to.
Those who stagnate in the teachings claim that the ultimate Way is exhausted within written chapters; those who cling to forms claim that the Dharma-body is fixed at sixteen feet in height.

Therefore, one must exhaustively penetrate the profound intent and skillfully grasp what lies beyond words, adorning oneself with the four types of eloquence to expound widely for others, providing instruction, benefit, and joy—this is the very role of the Dharma Master!

Therefore, the Master traveled to Khotan to seek out the scriptures; through his resolute vow, he extinguished the fires of ignorance and ultimately caused the Prajñāpāramitā to flourish in the eastern lands, transmitting the state of non-conceptualization to the end of time.

Next in rank were Zhu Qian, Zhi Dun, Yu Lan, Fa Kai, and others; they were all of noble and refined character, possessing pure and abundant virtue, and their merit in the beauty of their missionary work was likewise second only to that of the former masters.
Among them was Shi Dao’an, who received his training from the holy master Zhu Fotucheng; Dao’an, in turn, taught his disciple Huiyuan.
Throughout these three generations, there was never a lack of worthy men.
His precepts were strict and his conduct was solemn and clear;

his jewel-like wisdom shone with brilliant intensity. Thus, may the lingering radiance of the sun of wisdom again illuminate the world for a thousand years, and may the fragrant remnants of this land of incense once more perfume the realm of Jambudvīpa.
The spring continues to gush forth; this is truly due to the presence of such a person.
While Master Huiyuan restricted himself to Tiger Creek, Master Dao’an went so far as to share the same carriage.
As for the Way of the noble and refined, there may indeed be those who are perplexed by it.
Nevertheless, whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or staying still, what is appropriate depends solely on the timing.
When the Four Elders went to the Han, they acted when it was time to act;
when the Three Lius resigned from Chu, they withdrew when it was time to withdraw.
The Sūtra states:
"If one wishes to establish the True Dharma, one may listen to [the counsel of] kings and those who bear arms.

Although Hui’an once shared the same carriage with them, he nevertheless offered admonitions on behalf of the common people; thus, he was ultimately able to move the truth and, like parting the clouds, manifest his karmic retribution.
Thereafter, those renowned in Jingzhou and Shanxi took Huiyi and Fahu as their primary teachers;
those in the pure and simple tradition of Mount Lu took Daohchi and Daoyong as their preeminent leaders.
Daorong, Daoheng, Daoying, and Sengzhao possessed virtues of great weight in Guanzhong;
Huisong, Sengrui, Daochang, and Fayuan led the school in Jianye;
while Tan-du and Sengyuan alone held the treasure of Jiangxi.
Chaojin and Huiji further propagated the flourishing tradition of eastern Zhejiang;
although these successive generations rose in prominence, their spiritual practices were all profoundly aligned with the Way.
Thus, the remaining vitality of the Dharma-vehicle has lasted nearly five hundred years, and the excellence of its achievements is truly worthy of praise.
The eulogy says:
The lingering influence has become faint and vast; the waves of the Dharma have circled back upon themselves.
Were it not for the sages of Śākya, who could have sustained that which was about to collapse?
Submerged in tranquility, they are comparable to jade; their distant wisdom is linked like exquisite gems.
Though the axe may strike at their curves and flaws, and dust may fall upon them from the side, once the white silk is dyed, it is ready to receive the transformations that follow.
