3. *Shenyi Shang* (Miracles of the Upper Division) 1.
Zhu Fotucheng 2. Shandao Kai 3. Zhu Fotiao 4. Qiyu **Zhu Fotucheng**: Zhu Fotucheng was a man from the Western Regions; his original surname was Bo.
He left home to become a monk at a young age, being pure and sincere in his commitment to study. He recited several million words of scripture and was adept at explaining their literary meanings.

Although he had not read the Confucian classics or histories of this land, when he debated points of doubt and stagnation with various scholars, his insights matched theirs as perfectly as two halves of a tally; none were able to defeat him.
He himself said:
"I went back to Kaśmīra to receive instruction from renowned masters; throughout the Western Regions, I was universally acclaimed as one who had attained the Way.
This was in the fourth year of the Yongjia era of Emperor Huai of the Jin dynasty.
He came to Luoyang with the ambition of propagating the Great Dharma.

He was skilled at reciting divine mantras and could command spirits and objects; by applying a mixture of sesame oil and vermilion to his palms, he could clearly perceive events beyond a thousand *li* as if they were right before his face, and he could also enable those who had purified themselves through fasting to see the same.
Furthermore, he would listen to the sound of the bell to speak of affairs, and there was nothing that did not prove effective.

He wished to establish a monastery in Luoyang, but encountering the incursions of Liu Yao against the capital, the imperial city fell into turmoil; thus, Fotudeng’s ambition to establish the monastery was ultimately not realized.
He then withdrew into the marshes and wilds to observe the changes of the times.
At that time, Shi Le was stationing his troops at Gepei; he relied solely on slaughter as a means of intimidation, and the number of śramaṇas who met their deaths was exceedingly great.
Fotudeng took pity on the common people and, wishing to transform Shi Le through the Way, traveled to the military headquarters on foot with his staff.
Shi Le’s General Gao Gesheluo had long been a devoted follower of the Dharma; Fotudeng therefore stayed at Gesheluo’s residence.
He briefly received the five precepts and observed the etiquette of a disciple.
Later, when he accompanied Shi Le on military expeditions, he would invariably predict victory or defeat.
Shi Le, becoming suspicious, asked him:
"I have not perceived that you possess extraordinary strategic wisdom, yet you always know the auspiciousness or misfortune of military expeditions;
why is this? Yue replied:
"The General is naturally endowed with divine martial prowess, and your profound spirit is aided by the numinous."
There was a śramaṇa of extraordinary supernatural powers who said, "The General shall soon take possession of the realm; you should already serve as his master.
Everything I have reported to you previously was his word.
Lü was delighted and said,
"This is a gift from Heaven.
He summoned Fotudeng and questioned him, saying:
"What miraculous efficacy does the Buddha-way possess?
Knowing that Shi Le did not comprehend profound principles, Fotucheng realized that he could only be convinced by means of spiritual arts. He therefore said:
"Although the Ultimate Way is distant, it can nonetheless be verified by immediate phenomena.
He then took his alms bowl, filled it with water, burned incense, and recited mantras over it.
In a short while, blue lotus flowers emerged, their radiance dazzling the eyes; Fu Le was thereby moved to faith and conviction.
Fotucheng thereupon remonstrated, saying:
"When the virtue and transformation of a king permeate the entire realm, then the Four Spirits manifest auspicious omens.
When governance fails and the Way declines, [calamities arise]."
Consequently, comets and planetary aberrations appear in the heavens;
their constant forms become manifest,
and signs of fortune and calamity follow in their wake.
"This is indeed a constant sign throughout antiquity and the present, a clear admonition from Heaven and Man.

Shi Le was greatly pleased by this; of those remaining who were destined for execution, eight or nine out of ten benefited from his words. Consequently, among the Hu and Jin peoples of the Central Plains, almost all came to revere the Buddha.
At that time, there were those with chronic illnesses whom no one in the world could cure; Fo Tucheng provided medical treatment for them, and they recovered immediately.
His secret acts of beneficence and silent assistance were beyond counting.
When Shi Le returned from Gebo to the north of the River, he passed through Fangtou.
At night, the people of Fangtou intended to raid the camp.
Fotudeng said to Helü:
"In a short while, the bandits will arrive; you may inform the Duke.
Indeed, it happened exactly as he had said; because they were prepared, they did not suffer defeat.
Fu Jian wished to test Fotudeng, so at night he donned a helmet and armor, sat holding a sword, and sent someone to inform Fotudeng, saying:
"I did not know where the Great General was last night.
Before the messenger had even begun to speak, Fotudeng asked him in turn:
"When there are no enemies in ordinary times, for what reason have you set up a strict watch at night?"
Shi Le treated him with even greater reverence.
Later, driven by anger, Shi Le intended to harm the various Daoist practitioners and also sought to persecute Fotudeng.
Fotudeng then fled to the village of Heilüe, where he told his disciples:
"If General Xin sends a messenger to inquire about my whereabouts, report that you do not know where I have gone.
When Xin’s messenger arrived and searched for Daorong, he could not find him.
The envoy returned and reported this to Shi Le,
who exclaimed in astonishment:
"I harbored evil intentions toward the Sage, and so the Sage has abandoned me and departed.
He did not sleep throughout the entire night, longing to see Tancheng.
Knowing that Shi Le had repented, Tancheng visited him the following morning. Shi Le said:
"What were you doing last night?
Tancheng replied, "You harbored an angry mind; therefore, I temporarily avoided you."
"Your Excellency has now changed your mind; for this reason, I have ventured to come.
Shi Le laughed loudly and said, "The Master of the Way is mistaken."
The source of the moat water for the city of Xiangguo was located five li to the northwest of the city, beneath the Tuanwan Shrine; its waters suddenly ran dry.
Shi Le asked Fotudeng what could cause the water to cease flowing.
Fotucheng said,
"I shall now command the dragon.
Shi Le, whose courtesy name was Shilong, took this to be Fotucheng mocking him and replied:
"It is precisely because the dragon cannot bring forth water that I am asking you this," said Fotudeng.
"These are sincere words, not jests."
"The source of a spring must always have a divine dragon dwelling therein.
If we now go and issue a command, the water will surely be obtainable.
He then went with several disciples, including Fashou, to the headwaters of the spring.
The original source of the spring had long been dry, its cracked earth resembling the ruts of a wagon wheel.
His attendants were filled with doubt, fearing that water would be difficult to find.
Fajing sat upon a rope bed, burned frankincense, and recited several hundred words of incantations and prayers. After three days like this, the water began to flow in a thin, glistening stream.
A small dragon, about five or six inches long, emerged from the water.
When the Daoist masters saw it, they vied with one another to go and look at it, but Fotucheng said, "This dragon is poisonous; do not approach its head."
After a short while, the water rose greatly until the moats and ditches were all filled.
Fo T’eng sat quietly and sighed, saying:
"Two days hence, a small man shall cause a commotion here below."
Shortly thereafter, Xue He of the state of Xiang had two sons; being young and arrogant, they treated a Xianbei slave with contempt and mocked him.
Enraged, the slave drew his blade and stabbed one of the brothers to death, then seized the elder brother in the room and held a knife to his heart.
When a man entered the house, he intended to lay hands upon her.
He said to her:
"Send me back to my own country, and I will spare your son; otherwise, we shall die here together."
Both inside and outside, everyone was struck with alarm and went to see it;
none failed to do so. Shi Le then went there in person to look at it and said to Xue He:
"To send a slave in order to save your son is truly a virtuous deed."
"If this law were once relaxed, it would lead to future harm.
Your Excellency should exercise leniency for now; the state has established laws. He then ordered men to seize the slave, who subsequently killed his son and died.
The Xianbei leader Duanbo attacked Shi Le, and his forces were extremely numerous.
Fearing for his safety, Shi Le questioned Fotudeng, who replied:
"Yesterday, the temple bell rang and said: 'The King of the North will come.'"
"At dawn at mealtime, we shall capture Duanbo.
Shi Le ascended the city wall to observe Bo’s army; seeing neither its front nor its rear, he turned pale with fear and said:
"The army's passage has caused the earth to tilt; how could the waves possibly be captured?
This was merely Gao An’s polite excuse.
He then sent Kui An to question Fotudeng again.
Tong said, "I have already captured Bo. At that moment,
ambush troops emerged from north of the city and encountered Bo, seizing him.
Fotucheng advised Shi Le to pardon Fobo and send him back to his own country.
Le followed this advice and ultimately gained benefit from it.
At that time, Liu Zai had already died; his younger cousin Yao usurped the false throne and styled his reign era as Guangchu.
In the eighth year of the Guangchu era, Shi Yao dispatched his younger cousin, the nominal Prince of Zhongshan, Shi Yue, to lead troops to attack Shi Le.
Shi Le sent Shi Hu to lead infantry and cavalry to resist him.
During the great battle at Luoxi, Yué was defeated and retreated to Shiliangwu, where Tǔ firmly established stockades to defend it.
Tóngchéng and his disciples went from Guansi Temple to Zhongsi Temple.
Upon first entering the temple gate, he sighed and said,

When his disciple Fazuo asked for the reason, Fotudeng replied:
"Yesterday at the hour of Hai, Yue was already captured.
It turned out exactly as he had said.
In the eleventh year of Guangchu, Yao personally led his troops to attack Luoyang.

Le consulted with Fotudeng, who said:

When Xu Guang heard this instruction from Fotudeng, he earnestly urged Shi Le to act upon it.
Shi Le then left his eldest son, Shi Hong, with Fotudeng to garrison Xiangguo, while he himself led the central army’s infantry and cavalry directly toward Luocheng.
As soon as the two armies engaged, Yao’s forces were utterly routed.
Yao’s horse sank into the water, and Shi Kan captured him alive and sent him to Shi Le.

At that time, Fotudeng applied a substance to his palms and observed it; he saw a great multitude, among whom one man was bound with red silk tied around his neck. He then informed Yao Hong of this vision.
At that time, Shi Yao was captured alive.
After Yao was subdued, Shi Le usurped the title of Heavenly King of Zhao, acted as Emperor, and changed the era name to Jianping.
This was the fifth year of the Xianhe era of Emperor Cheng of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
After Shi Le ascended the throne, his devotion to Fotudeng grew ever more profound.
At that time, Shi Cong was about to rebel.
In that year, Fotudeng cautioned Shi Le, saying, "This year there are insects within the onions; eating them will surely harm people. You should order the common people not to eat onions.

In the eighth month, Shi Cong indeed fled.
Fu Le treated him with even greater reverence, consulting him before acting on any matter, and bestowed upon him the title "Great Upādhyāya."
Shi Hu had a son named Bin; later, Shi Le loved him exceedingly, but he suddenly died of a violent illness after two days had already passed.

"The Great Upādhyāya is a divine man of this land; you should go to inform him with all haste, for he will surely be able to bring about blessings.
Fǎtóng then took a willow branch and recited a mantra over it; in a short while, [the monk] was able to rise, and after a brief moment, he had fully recovered.
Consequently, he had his young children mostly raised within Buddhist temples.
Every year on the eighth day of the fourth month, Shi Le would personally visit the temple to perform the ritual ablution for the Buddha and make vows on behalf of his children.

Fo Tucheng said to the assembly, "The sound of the bell says: 'The Dharma King has arrived.'"
“The state will suffer a great calamity; it will not last beyond this year.
In the seventh month of that year, Shi Le died.
His son, Shi Hong, succeeded him to the throne.
After a short time, Shi Hu deposed Shi Hong and established himself as ruler; he moved the capital to Ye and styled his era the Jianyuan.
Hu devoted himself entirely to Daocheng, regarding him with even greater reverence than he had for Shi Le.
He then issued an edict, saying:

"The Upādhyāya is a great treasure of the state; yet honors and titles have not been conferred upon him, nor has he received a high stipend. Since such honor and emolument do not reach him, how can his virtue be distinguished?
From this point forward, it is fitting that he be clothed in brocade and silk, and ride in an ornate carriage."
On the day of the court assembly, He ascended the hall; from the Chief Attendants downward, all assisted in lifting the palanquin.
The Crown Prince and the various dukes supported him from the sides as he ascended.
"The presiding official shall chant 'The Great Preceptor,' at which point the entire assembly must rise from their seats to manifest his dignity.
He further commanded Li Nong, the nominal Minister of Works:
"Inquire after him personally morning and evening; let the Crown Prince and the various dukes pay him a formal visit once every five days to demonstrate my respect."
At that time, Sengcheng was staying at Zhong Temple within the city of Ye. He sent his disciple Fachang north to Xiangguo.

His other disciple Fazuo returned from Xiangguo; they met beneath the walls of Liangji City and stayed there overnight. They conversed by their carriages throughout the night, and as their talk turned to the Upādhyāya, each departed at dawn.
When Fazuo arrived and first entered to have an audience with Fotudeng,
Fotudeng greeted him with a smile and said,
"Last night you were in the same carriage as Fachang; did you two discuss your teacher together?"
The ancients had a saying:
"Is it not called reverence? One does not change even in the darkness.
Is it not called caution? One does not grow negligent even when alone."
"Solitude is the very foundation of reverence and caution; do you not recognize this?
Zuo was struck with astonishment and repented in shame.
Thereupon, the people of the state would often say to one another:
"Do not give rise to evil thoughts; the Upādhyāya knows you.
Whereever Fotucheng was, no one dared to spit, sneeze, or relieve themselves in his direction.
At that time, Crown Prince Shi Sui had two sons in Xiangguo.
Fotudeng said to Sui, "The younger son, Ami, will soon fall ill; you should go to fetch him."
Sui immediately dispatched a messenger to go and see him; indeed, he had already fallen ill.
The great physician Yin Teng and a foreign Daoist claimed they could cure him, but Fotudeng told his disciple Faya:

Shi Sui was addicted to wine and intended to plot a rebellion;
he said to his attendants, "The Venerable possesses supernatural powers; should he discover my scheme, if he comes tomorrow, I shall eliminate him first."
When Chengyue was about to enter the imperial presence to have an audience with the Tiger (Emperor Wu), he said to his disciple Senghui:

As Fotudeng was about to ascend the Southern Terrace, the monk Hui pulled at his robe.
Fotudeng said,
"The matter cannot be stopped."
Before he was even comfortably seated, [Seng]sui rose;
as Sengzhao firmly tried to detain him but could not, his plan was consequently thwarted.
Returning to the monastery, he sighed and said:
"The Crown Prince is inciting a rebellion, and its form is about to take shape.

Fo Tucheng’s expression turned somber, and he said,

He called out,
"The assembly of monks shall offer prayers for blessing," and Fo Tucheng himself also offered prayers.
After a short while, he spoke again, saying:
"If you emerge toward the southeast, you will live; if you go in any other direction, you will perish.
He then once more offered prayers and aspirations.
After a short while, he said, "I have escaped.

More than a month later, Heilüe returned and recounted his own experience: having fallen into the encirclement of the Qiang, while fleeing southeast on horseback, he happened to encounter a man from the imperial entourage who pushed his horse aside to let him pass, saying:
"The nobleman rides this horse, while the commoner rides the nobleman's horse; whether we cross over or not depends on fate.
Having thus managed to obtain the horse, he was able to escape.
Upon calculating the date and time, it was precisely the hour when Fotudeng had offered his incantations and prayers.

Shi Bin, the false Grand Marshal and Duke of Yan, had been appointed by Shi Hu as the Governor of Youzhou to garrison Ji; there, a multitude of wicked men had gathered, and he used them as an excuse to indulge in his tyranny.
Tancheng cautioned Tanhu, saying, "Last night the celestial deity said that you must quickly collect your horses and return them; by autumn, they shall all suffer from festering sores.
Tanhu did not understand these words, yet he immediately issued orders to all locations to collect the horses and send them back.
That autumn, someone slandered Fu Bin to Shi Hu; Hu summoned Bin and whipped him three hundred times.
He then executed Bin’s biological mother, Lady Qi.
Bending his bow and nocking an arrow, Hu personally inspected the punishment he had meted out and, deeming it too light, proceeded to kill five hundred people with his own hands.
Sengcheng remonstrated, saying:

"Those who violate this shall be punished with the same penalty as those who perform illicit sacrifices.

Hu issued a decree stating:
"Du’s deliberation claims that the Buddha is a deity of foreign lands and is not one whom the Son of Heaven or the people of China ought to venerate."

"I have wandered long in Jambudvīpa, beset by these many vexations.

Xuancheng changed his expression and said,
"What kind of words are these?
Tancheng spoke deceptively, saying:
"The Old Barbarian claims to teach the Way, yet he cannot dwell in the mountains in silence.
With his heavy carpets and fine robes—is this not a failure of his discipline?
Shi Tao arrived later.
Fotucheng gazed intently at him for a long time.
Tao was terrified and questioned Fotucheng, who replied,
"I was staring at you because I found your blood smell foul."
In the eighth month, Fotudeng sent ten of his disciples to observe the fast in a separate chamber.
At that time, Fotudeng briefly entered the eastern pavilion.
Emperor Hu and Empress Du asked after his well-being, to which Fotudeng replied:
“There are bandits lurking by your side; within ten days, from west of the Buddhist monastery to east of this hall, there shall be bloodshed.
Be careful not to travel east.”
Empress Du said,
"Is the Venerable One senile? Where is there a thief?"
Tong Cheng then changed his phrasing and said:
"All that is perceived by the six sense-faculties are thieves.
It is natural for the old to become senile; however, as long as the young do not fall into confusion, all will proceed smoothly."
The allegory was no longer manifest.
Two days later, Xuán indeed dispatched men to kill Tão within the Buddhist temple, intending to take advantage of Hǔ’s presence at the funeral to commit a great act of treason.
Because Shi Hu had previously been warned by Fotudeng, he was able to escape harm.
When the matter of his misconduct was exposed and he was about to be arrested, Fotudeng remonstrated with him, saying:
"Since you are the Son of Heaven's own son, why do you inflict such a heavy calamity upon yourself?"
If Your Majesty were to temper your wrath with compassion, I would still have more than sixty years remaining.
If you must execute me, I shall become a comet to sweep down and destroy the palace at Ye.
The tiger did not comply; he pierced Xuan’s jaw with an iron chain, dragged him onto a pile of firewood, and burned him alive.
He arrested more than three hundred of his subordinates and officials, all of whom he had their limbs torn apart by the chariot-wheel execution (huán-liè) and cast into the Zhang River.
Daorong then issued an edict to his disciples to discontinue the fasting retreat in their separate quarters.
More than a month later, a demonic horse appeared; its mane and tail both bore the marks of having been scorched. It entered through the Zhongyang Gate and exited through the Xianyang Gate.
They headed toward the Eastern Palace, but were unable to enter; they fled toward the northeast and soon vanished from sight.
Upon hearing this, Fotudeng sighed and said, "Calamity is about to befall us."
In the eleventh month, Shi Hu held a grand banquet for his ministers in the Great Martial Anterior Hall.
Fotudeng chanted:
"The hall! The hall! Thorns shall form a forest, and they will ruin people's clothes."
The tiger ordered the palace stones to be removed so that they might look beneath; there, thorns were found growing.
Daorong returned to the temple and looked at the Buddha image, saying, "I regret that I was unable to provide it with its proper adornment."
He spoke to himself, saying:
"Could I obtain three years?
He answered himself:
"Neither obtainable nor unobtainable.
He asked again:
"Can it be obtained for two years, one year, a hundred days, or a month?"
He answered himself,
"I cannot," and then remained silent.
Returning to his room, he said to his disciple Fazuo:
"In the year Wushen, the seeds of calamity and rebellion will gradually sprout; in Jiyou, the Shi clan shall perish.
I shall undergo transformation before the chaos breaks out."
He immediately sent someone to take leave of the tiger, saying:
"The nature of things must inevitably change; life and body cannot be preserved.
This poor monk’s body is like a flame or an illusion, and the time for its transformation has arrived."
"Since I have received such exceptionally profound grace, I have ventured to report this in advance.
Huo said with deep sorrow, "I had not heard that Master He was ill; it is only now that he has suddenly passed away."
He immediately left the palace in person, went to the monastery, and offered words of consolation.
Fo Tucheng said to Hu:
"To emerge from life and enter into death is the constant way of the Dao."
The allotment of longevity is fixed; it cannot be extended by human effort.
The Way values the completion of practice, and virtue prizes freedom from indolence.
If one’s conduct remains unimpaired, then even in death, one is as if alive.
To have violated [the law] yet obtained a reprieve was not what he desired.
As for why his intent remains unfulfilled: it is because the state’s mind dwells upon the principles of the Buddha, and in its upholding of the Dharma, it is without stinginess.
Temples have been established and made magnificent and grand; in accordance with such virtue, it is fitting that they enjoy auspicious blessings.

Yet their administration is violent and fierce, employing excessive and cruel punishments that flagrantly violate the sacred scriptures and secretly contravene the dharma precepts; failing to reform themselves, they shall ultimately receive no blessings or protection.

If one subdues the mind and transforms its concerns, bestowing kindness upon the common people below, then the state’s mandate will be prolonged, and both the clergy and the laity will rejoice and rely [upon it]; when life comes to its end, one will pass away without any lingering regrets.
The tiger, wailing with grief and sobbing, knew that he was certain to pass away; it immediately dug a grave and prepared a burial mound.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month, he passed away at the Ye Palace Temple.
This was the fourth year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu of the Jin dynasty.
Gentry and commoners alike wailed and rushed to the funeral, filling the land with grief.
He was one hundred and seventeen years of age.
He was subsequently buried at Chaimo in western Linzhang, in the very tomb that Shi Hu had constructed for himself.
Shortly thereafter, Liangdu and Xiuzhuo rose in rebellion; the following year, Shi Hu died, and Ran Min usurped the throne and massacred the clan, until the entire Shi lineage was extinguished.
Min’s childhood name was Jiknu; he was the very person of whom Fo Tucheng had previously said, "Ji Zi has formed a forest.
On the left side of Tucheng’s breast there was originally a hole, four or five inches in circumference, which penetrated all the way through to his internal organs.
At times his intestines would protrude from within, and he would sometimes plug the opening with cotton wool.
When he wished to read at night, he would pull out the cotton wool, and the entire room would become brilliantly illuminated.
Furthermore, on days of fasting, he would go to the water’s edge, draw out his intestines to wash them, and then return them to their place inside.
Fotucheng stood eight chi tall, with a dignified and elegant bearing.

On the days he delivered lectures, he would focus solely on the essential principles, ensuring that the entire text—from beginning to end—was clear and intelligible.
Furthermore, his compassion permeated all living beings as he rescued those in peril and suffering.
When the two Shi rulers were tyrannical and powerful, inflicting cruelty and injustice, had it not been for Fotudeng sharing the same day [of death] with them, who could have spoken of such things?
It is simply that the common people have received these benefits, using them daily without being aware of it.
The dozens of monks, including Fotiao and Subhūti, all originated from India and Kangju.
Traveling tens of thousands of *li* from afar, they crossed the shifting sands on foot to visit Fotucheng and receive his instruction.

All were profoundly adept at the subtle principles and investigated the most profound mysteries.
Fotucheng himself stated that his birthplace was over ninety thousand *li* from Ye, and that he had abandoned his home to enter the Way one hundred and nine years prior.
He did not drink wine beyond his teeth's capacity, nor did he eat after midday; he did not tread upon what was contrary to the precepts, being without desire and without seeking.

He then recruited a search party for the tiger’s carcass and unearthed it at Dongming Pavilion; the corpse was stiff and undecayed.
Li Jun stepped upon it and cursed, saying, “You dead barbarian, how dare you frighten the living Son of Heaven!”
"You have completed the construction of this palace, yet it has been plotted against by your own son; how much more so by a stranger?

this is what Ma Ru referred to as the "Single-Pillar Palace.

He served Fotudeng as his teacher and resided at Changshan Temple for many years.
His conduct was simple and unadorned, and he did not employ flowery speech; at that time, everyone held him in high esteem.
In Changshan, there were two brothers who followed the Dharma, living a hundred li away from the monastery.
His elder brother’s wife fell gravely ill; he transported her to the side of the monastery so she would be close to medical treatment.
Since his brother had received the imperial decree to serve as a master, he was constantly at the monastery during the day to consult him on the practice of the Way.
On another day, Zhu Fashu went to his brother’s house.
His younger brother questioned his sister-in-law in detail about her ailment and inquired after his elder brother’s well-being. Fashu said:
"The patient is somewhat better; your elder brother is as usual.
After Zhaodiao had departed, the younger brother also spurred his horse and followed after him.
When it was mentioned that Zhaodiao had just arrived, the elder brother said in surprise:
"The Upādhyāya has not yet left the monastery this morning; how could you have seen him?
The brothers disputed over this and questioned Tanyue about it.
Tanyue laughed and did not answer, leaving them all equally astonished.
Tao once entered the mountains alone for a year or half a year, carrying several *sheng* of dried rice; upon his return, there was always some left over.

Someone once followed Tao on a mountain journey for several dozen *li*; when evening fell and it began to snow heavily, Tao entered a stone cave that served as a tiger’s den to stay the night. When the tiger returned, it lay down together with him before the entrance of the cave.
Tiao said to the tiger, "I have taken away your dwelling; how can I feel but shame?
The tiger then lowered its ears and went down the mountain.
His attendants were struck with terror and alarm.
Later, Daotiao himself determined the date of his death; when people from near and far all arrived, he spoke to them all, saying:
"Heaven and earth endure for a long time, yet they still undergo collapse and destruction; how much more so for human beings—how could one expect to exist forever?"
"If one can sweep away the three impurities and focus the mind in true purity, then although our physical forms may differ, we shall surely share the same realization.
The assembly all shed tears and earnestly entreated him.
Tiao said, "Birth and death are matters of destiny; how can they be requested?
Tiao then returned to his room and sat upright, covering his head with his robe, and passed away suddenly.

Several years later, while eight lay disciples were felling timber in the Western Mountains under Huiyuan’s direction, they suddenly saw him atop a high crag. His robes were bright and clean, and his countenance was serene and joyful. All were filled with wonder and joy, and prostrating themselves, they asked:
"Is the Upādhyāya still alive?"
Tiao replied, "I am always here.
He then inquired whether his old acquaintances were available, and after a long while, he departed.
The eight men then abandoned their work and returned home, telling their fellow practitioners what had happened.
Having no means to verify it, the group together opened a tomb and lifted the coffin; they no longer saw the corpse, but only the clothes and shoes remained there.
A record states:
"This Zhu Fotiao translated the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra* (Fa jing jing), the *Daśajñāna* (Shi hui), and other works.
According to Shi Dao’an’s *Catalogue of Scriptures* (*Jing lu*), it says:

During the Guanghe era of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, there was the śramaṇa Yan Fotiao, who, together with An Xuan, the Commandant of the Capital, translated the *Dharmadarśana-sūtra* (Fa jing jing) and the *Daśajñāna* (Shi hui), among other works.
The account [of Buddhabhadra] is found in the "Biographies of Translators.
However, the Buddha-tiao mentioned here was a person from the middle period of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
To see that their names are identical and immediately assume they are one and the same person is erroneous.
4. Jīvaka. As for Jīvaka, he was a man from India. He traveled throughout the lands of China and the Rong peoples without a fixed abode;

he was unconventional and possessed of miraculous qualities, acting according to his own nature and disregarding worldly conventions. His conduct was inconsistent, and people of the time were unable to fathom him.
Setting out from India and traveling as far as Funan, he passed through various coastal regions and reached Jiaozhi and Guangzhou, where there were many miraculous occurrences.
Upon arriving at Xiangyang, he wished to find transport to cross the river.
The boatman, seeing that the śramaṇa Fa was clad in tattered and shabby robes, treated him with contempt and did not take him aboard.
When the boat reached the northern bank, Fayu had already crossed over.

As they proceeded further, they encountered two tigers; the tigers lowered their ears and wagged their tails, and Fayu stroked their heads with his hand, whereupon the tigers moved aside from the path and departed.
Those who saw him on both banks followed him in great crowds.
Reaching Luoyang at the end of the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, all the monastics there prostrated themselves before him;
yet Fotudeng knelt in the Hu fashion, remaining serene and unmoving in countenance.
At times he would inform others of the experiences of his previous lives, claiming that Zhi Fayuan had come from among oxen and Zhu Faxing had come from among humans.
He also mocked the various monks, saying their robes were too ornate and did not accord with the simplicity of the Dharma.
Upon seeing the palace city of Luoyang, he remarked,
"It resembles the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, differing only in that natural phenomena and human affairs are distinct.
Daoyi then said to the śramaṇa Jīśāmī:
“The artisans who built this palace came from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; once it was completed, they returned to the heavens.
Beneath the tiles on the ridge of the roof, there should be fifteen hundred tools.”
At that time, everyone said, "In the past, we heard that this craftsman actually placed his tools beneath the tiles.
Furthermore, it was said that after the palace was completed, he was subsequently killed."

At that time, Teng Yongwen of Nanyang, the Governor of Hengyang, was residing at Manshui Temple in Luoyang. He had been ill for years without recovery; both his legs were cramped and bent, rendering him unable to stand or walk.
Yu went to see him and asked,
"Do you wish for your illness to be cured?
He then took a cup of pure water and a branch of willow, brushed the water with the willow, and raised his hand toward Yongwen while reciting a mantra.
This was repeated three times.
Then, he grasped Yongwen’s two knees with his hands and made him stand up; immediately, Yongwen rose and walked as before.
In this temple, there were several dozen withered *sīmā* trees that had died.
Daoyu asked Yongwen, "How long has it been since this tree died?
Yongwen replied,
"It has been many years."
Fayou then recited incantations toward the tree, following the ritual methods used for the Yongwen tree.
Immediately, the tree sprouted new shoots and flourished with lush, spreading foliage.
It was already in the midst of the summer heat.
There was a man suffering from a chronic tumor who was on the verge of death.

Jiyi placed his alms bowl upon the patient's abdomen, covered it entirely with a white cloth, and recited thousands of words of incantation and aspiration; immediately, a foul odor permeated the entire room.
The patient said, "I am alive.
Jiyu ordered someone to lift the cloth, and there were several liters of something like dregs or mud in the vessel, so foul-smelling it could not be approached; the patient subsequently recovered.
Due to the military chaos in Luoyang, he took his leave and returned to India.
The śramaṇa Zhu Faxing of Luoyang was a monk of eminent standing;
people of the time compared him to Master Yue.
Thereupon, Yin Qiu requested of Fayu, saying:
"Since you, Venerable Sir, are a monk who has attained the Way, I pray that you will leave behind a single word as a perpetual admonition. Fayu replied:
"Very well; let all the assembled people gather.
Once the assembly had gathered, Fayou ascended the high seat and said:
"Guard your speech, restrain your body and mind, and be careful not to commit any evil deeds."
"By practicing all that is wholesome, one thus attains deliverance from the world.
Having spoken these words, he remained silent in meditation.
Daowang again entreated him, saying:
"I pray that the Venerable One will grant me what I have not yet heard.
As for the meaning of such verses as these, even an eight-year-old child can already recite them from memory; this is not what one expects from a man who has attained the Way."
Yu smiled and said,
"Though one may recite [the scriptures] at the age of eight, if one does not practice them at the age of a hundred, what benefit is there in such recitation?
Everyone knows to revere those who have attained the Way, yet they do not realize that it is through practice that one attains the Way for oneself."
"How tragic! Though my words are few, those who practice them will be many.
Thereupon, he took his leave and departed.
Several hundred people each invited Daoyi to dine at their homes, and Daoyi consented to go to them all.
At dawn the next day, there was a Daoyi in each of the five hundred houses; those who had first invited him thought he had come to their home alone.
Later, when they questioned one another, they finally realized that it was an emanation body that had descended.
Once he set out, the various practitioners escorted him as far as Henan City;
Yu walked slowly, and those who pursued him could not catch up.
Sengyu then drew a line on the ground with his staff and said, "At this point,
we part. On that very day, someone arriving from Chang'an saw Sengyu in that temple.
Furthermore, the merchant Hu Shideng encountered Faxian at Liusha on that very day as evening fell; he had already traveled over nine thousand li.
After returning to the Western Regions, his final whereabouts remained unknown.
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Nine: Miraculous Manifestations, Part One;
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Ten: Miraculous Manifestations, Part Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huijiao of Jiaxiang Temple in Kuaiji during the Liang Dynasty.
3. Miraculous Manifestations, Part II 1. **Gandhara**: Originally a person from the Western Regions, he came to Luoyang and resided there for many years.

2. **Hualuojie** (Huiguo) 3. **Zhu Fahui** 4. **An Huize** 5. **Shengong** 6. **Shi Tanhuo** 7. **Shi Zong** 8. **Beidu** 9. **Shi Tanshi** 10. **Shi Falang** 11. **Shao Shuo** 12. **Shi Hui'an** 13. **Shi Faqi** 14. **Shi Senghui** 15. **Shi Huitong** 16. **Shi Baozhi** 1. **Gandhara**: Gandhara was originally a man from the Western Regions who arrived in Luoyang and remained for many years.
Although the assembly respected his character and conduct, none were ultimately able to fathom him.
Later, he said to the monks, "To the southeast of Luoyang lies Mount Panchi; on that mountain there is the site of an ancient temple whose foundations still remain. We should rebuild it together."
The assembly did not yet believe him, so they followed him to investigate.
Upon entering the mountain and reaching a certain spot where the terrain on all four sides was level, he pointed and declared:
"This is the site for the monastery."
He immediately dug there and indeed found a stone foundation beneath the site of the temple.
Later, when he pointed out the locations for the lecture hall and the monks' quarters, everything was verified exactly as he had said.
The assembly was filled with wonder and admiration, and they collectively renovated and established the temple, appointing Le as its abbot.

The monastery was more than one hundred *li* from the capital city of Luoyang; every morning he would go to the various monasteries in Luoyang for the midday meal, and every evening he would invariably beg for a bowl of oil to return to his monastery and light lamps.
Taking this as his constant practice, he never faltered or failed.
There was a man of great physical prowess who wished to follow Bāṣpa to observe his pace; though he ran until he was drenched in sweat, he always suffered from being unable to keep up.
He was compelled to grasp the corner of his *kāṣāya*, and hearing only the sound of a fierce wind, he no longer felt fatigue; in a short while, they arrived at the monastery.
It was later unknown where Shi Le ended his life.
2. Hālaka. Hālaka was originally a native of Fanyang.
He left home to become a monk in his youth and recited two million words of scripture.
By nature he was profound and mysterious; he observed the precepts with strict discipline, was skilled in deportment, and possessed a handsome appearance.
He practiced the dhūta austerities extensively and stayed alone in the mountains and wilds.
In the ninth year of the Taikang era of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, he visited Luoyang briefly; at that time, a pestilence was spreading widely, and deaths occurred in succession.
He treated them with incantations until eight or nine out of ten were cured.
In the first year of the Yuankang era of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, he traveled west and stayed in a stone grotto on Mount Louzhi, where he sat in meditation.
Since this room was far from water, people at the time wished to dig a channel for it.
Daoye said, "There is no need to trouble yourselves."
He then rose and pressed his left foot against the stone wall to the west of the chamber; the wall caved in up to his toes.
Once he withdrew his foot, water gushed forth from within—fragrant, pure, soft, and delicious, flowing without ceasing throughout the four seasons.
All who came to drink were relieved of hunger and thirst, and their illnesses were cured.
In the eighth year of the Yuankang era, he sat upright and passed away; his disciples cremated him according to the rites of the Western Regions.
The body was cremated for several days, yet it remained sitting amidst the flames; it did not turn to ash or charcoal, so it was moved back into the stone chamber.

Later, during the Xianhe era of the Jin dynasty, the Western Regioner Zhu Ding, whose courtesy name was Anshi, traveled to that country and personally observed it; the corpse sat upright and solemn, having already been there for over thirty years.
After his meditation, he traveled to the capital and transmitted [the teachings] to both monastics and laypeople.
3. Zhu Fahui: Zhu Fahui was originally a native of Guanzhong.
He was upright and possessed strict observance of the precepts; he entered Mount Songgao and served Fotudeng as his teacher.
In the first year of the Jianyuan era of Emperor Kang of Jin, he went to Xiangyang and stayed at Yang Shuzi Temple.
He did not accept separate invitations; whenever he went out to beg for food, he would always carry a rope bed with him, which he would set up and sit upon along open and spacious paths.
At times, when it rained, he would cover himself with an oil-silk cloak.
When the rain ceased, only the rope bed was visible, and no one knew where Hui was.
Even before inquiries had subsided, Hui was already back upon the bed.
Every time he spoke, he said to his disciple Fazhao:
"In a past life, you broke the leg of a chicken; its retribution will soon arrive.
Shortly thereafter, Fazhao was thrown by someone, and his leg became permanently crippled.
Later, he said to his disciples, "There is an old man in Xinye who is about to pass away; I wish to deliver him.
He then proceeded along the ridges between the fields and indeed saw an old man plowing a field with an ox.
Huì begged the Duke for an ox, but the Duke would not give it to him. Huì went forward and grasped the ox’s nose himself; the Duke, fearing his extraordinary nature, finally bestowed it upon him.
Huì led the ox away, offered prayers of blessing, and after walking seven paces, he turned back and returned the ox to the Duke.
Duke Gong died a few days later.

Later, when Yu Zhigong, the General Who Conquers the West, was stationed at Xiangyang, he had long been one who did not uphold the Dharma; upon hearing that Huì possessed extraordinary spiritual traces, he became deeply envious of him.
Huìyù told his disciples, "The retribution for my past deeds is approaching; I exhort you, my kinsmen, to diligently cultivate merit and goodness.
Two days later, he was indeed arrested and executed at the age of fifty-eight.
On the verge of death, he said to the people:
"Three days after my passing, there shall be torrential rain.
When the appointed time arrived, it indeed poured down in torrents; the water at the city gates reached a depth of one zhang, submerging the residents, and many died.
At that time, there was a man named Fan Cai, a native of Langzhong in Basi.

He had originally been a śramaṇa who practiced divination in the market of Hedong; he walked barefoot and wore tattered clothes, changing his garments only once between winter and summer, and his predictions were frequently proven accurate.
Later, he eventually withdrew from the Way and became defiled by secular life, practicing the teachings of Zhang Ling.
4. Anhui: As for Anhui, his clan and lineage are not detailed.
From youth, he lacked constancy in character, yet he was outstanding and extraordinary compared to others; he was skilled in formal calligraphy and proficient in eloquent discourse.

During the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty, there was a widespread epidemic throughout the land. Zhe prayed with utmost sincerity day and night, vowing that the heavenly deities would descend with medicine to heal the myriad people.
One day, as he stepped out of the temple gate, he saw two stones shaped like jars and suspected they were extraordinary objects.
Upon opening it to examine it, he found that there was indeed divine water within.
Those who drank and took it all recovered from their illnesses.
Later, while residing at Dashi Temple in Luoyang, he personally transcribed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin jing) in minute characters on yellow silk, binding it into a single scroll.
The characters were as small as mung beans yet clearly legible; there were more than ten copies in total.
He gave one copy to Hu Mu, the wife of Zhou Zhongzhi of Runan, for her veneration.

Hu Mu crossed the river carrying the scriptures with him. Later, when his residence was overtaken by a spreading fire, he was in such a state of haste that he had no time to retrieve the scriptures; he wept in grief and was filled with remorse.
After the fire was extinguished, he recovered them from the ashes.
The color of the scroll's head-axle is entirely without flaw.
At that time, among those who witnessed it together, there were none who did not turn away from heterodoxy and reform their faith.
This scripture is currently at the residence of the Head Nun of Jianjing Temple in the capital.
At that time, there was also one named Kang Huichi in Luoyang, who was likewise said to possess spiritual wonders and supernatural powers. 5.
Master She: Master She was a man from the Western Regions.
He was serene and tranquil, practicing the cultivation of vital breath (*qi*) and abstaining from the five grains; he could travel five hundred li in a single day.
His predictions of future events were as clear as looking at one's own palm.
He arrived in Chang’an in the twelfth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era.

He was able to subdue divine dragons with secret mantras; whenever there was a drought, Sengjian would regularly request him to perform the dragon-subduing rite. In a short while, the dragon would descend into his alms bowl, and it would then rain heavily from heaven.
Yao Chang and his ministers personally examined the bowl and all marveled at its wonders.
Yao Chang enshrined it as the national deity; both officials and commoners prostrated themselves before it. From that time on, there was no longer any fear of scorching droughts.
In the twelfth month of the sixteenth year, he passed away without illness; Yao Jian wept for him with profound grief.

Seven days after his death, because of his divine and extraordinary nature, Jian attempted to open the coffin to look inside; he could not find the remains of the body anywhere, and only the burial shrouds remained.
In the seventeenth year, from the first month until the sixth month, there was no rain.
Fu Jian reduced his meals and removed the musical instruments from the court to welcome the harmonious qi; consequently, rain fell in the seventh month.
Jian said to Zhu Yong of the Secretariat,
"If Master She were still alive, would I be so distressed by the drought as this?
Is this man not a great sage!"
Tong said: "This art is profound and far-reaching; it is truly a marvel from the distant past. 6.
Shi Tanhuo: It is not clearly known where Shi Tanhuo was from.
He maintained a vegetarian diet and practiced asceticism, constantly dwelling among burial mounds or beneath trees, specializing in converting sentient beings through his supernatural powers.
At that time, the Xianbei ruler Tou Fa-lu-gu of Hexi had usurped control of Xiping, styling himself King and naming his era Jianhe.
In the eleventh month of the second year of the Jianhe era, Huo came from Xiping in Henan carrying a single *khakkhara* (monk’s staff), which he had others kneel before.
He said, "This is the Eye of Prajñā; by honoring it, one may attain the Way."
When people gave him clothing or other items, he would immediately cast them upon the ground or set them adrift in the river.
After a short while, the garments would return of their own accord to their original owners, not soiled by anything at all.
He traveled as swiftly as the wind; even those with great strength who pursued him were constantly exhausted and could not catch up.
When speaking of people’s births and deaths or their nobility and meanness, there was not the slightest error.

If someone hid his staff (khakkhara), he would suddenly close his eyes for a short while and immediately know its location. People marveled at these miraculous wonders, yet in the end, none could fathom them.
However, those who followed the Buddha because of him were very numerous.
Luguo had a younger brother named Noutan, who was appointed as General of Chariots; his influence eclipsed that of the puppet state.
He was by nature suspicious and jealous, committing many acts of treachery and harm.
Huo often said to Tan,
"We should cultivate goodness and practice the Way to serve as a bridge for future generations. Tan replied:
"Since my ancestors' time, I have reverently served Heaven, Earth, and the famous mountains and great rivers.
Now that I suddenly embrace Buddhism, I fear I may contravene the intentions of my forebears.
If you, sir, can go without food for seven days and yet remain as usual in countenance, then you shall be a divine being of the Buddha-way, and I shall surely revere you."
He then had someone guard Huo in secret for seven days, yet Huo showed no sign of hunger or thirst.
Tán sent the śramaṇa Zhìxíng to secretly bring cakes as a gift to Huo, who said:
"Whom have I ever deceived? Would I deceive the King?"
Tan Shen was deeply amazed by this and showed him profound reverence; consequently, he changed his faith, curbing his killing and promoting compassion.
As the people of the country received his protection, they all hailed him as "The Great Master."
As he entered and exited the streets and alleys, the common people all came out to welcome him and pay him their respects.
Tan had a daughter who was critically ill; she requested Huo to save her life. Huo said:
"Life and death are matters of destiny; even the sages cannot alter them, so how could I possibly prolong my life?
I can only know when it will come.
Tan continued to entreat him.
At that time, the rear gate of the palace was closed;
Huo said, "Open the rear gate immediately!
If it is opened in time, you will live; if not, you will die."
Tandun ordered it opened, but before he could do so, he passed away.
In the third year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, when Tanshihuo was defeated by the Xianbei ruler Bobo and the Liang region fell into military chaos, no one knew where he had gone.
7. Shizong. As for Shizong, it is unknown where he was from.
He constantly wore hempen garments, sometimes doubling them as a quilted robe; therefore, he was known in the world as the "Hemp-Cloth Daoist."
His body was covered with many sores and scabs, and his temperament was inconsistent.

He frequently stayed at the Baizu (White Earth) monastery in Guangling, where he rented out his room as a singer; he would pull on his rope to express joy and contentment, and whatever money he received, he would immediately give away to others.
He had no fixed place of residence, appearing sometimes in seclusion and sometimes in public.
At that time, Tanqi, the Magistrate of Jiangdu from Gaoping, heard of him and summoned him.
His responses were swift and nimble, free from any hesitation; he was profoundly learned in antiquity and eloquent in expounding both the profound mysteries and Confucian classics.
He then composed a poem, saying:
"Those with desire suffer from insufficiency; those without desire likewise have no sorrow.
Yet none compare to the pure and empty one, who wears a rope belt and a dark fur robe."
"Wandering through this world, I am like a drifting boat unmoored from its moorings.
Just as I am about to bring an end to my worldly entanglements, I shall settle my aspirations upon the mountain slopes.
Tandi, realizing he was no ordinary man, sent him back to his own place.
He left behind thirty bolts of cloth, all of which he gave away to beggars.
Later, there was a practitioner whose name was unknown, who always carried a staff and a box with him.
Once, approaching dusk, he went to visit the Magistrate of Haiyan and said, "I wish to travel for several days and would like to borrow a person for a short time; could you provide one?
The Magistrate replied:
"Take whichever you please," he said.
Thereupon, he selected the boy who tended the geese and ducks, whose appearance and clothing were the most unsightly, and took him away.

In an instant, they arrived at a mountain; on the mountain was a house, and within the house were three men of the Way (śramaṇas). They greeted each other with joy and conversed together, though the boy did not understand them.

When he reached midday and was exhausted, the practitioner, appearing as a young boy, went to the host to beg for food. He received a small bowl of food that looked like dried mugwort; upon eating it, his hunger ceased.
As dusk approached, the Daoist was about to take his leave when he heard someone inside the house ask,
"Do you know where Shi Zong is?"
"What will become of his banishment?
The practitioner said, "He will be at Bai-tu on the northern bank of the Jiang River in Guangling, Xuzhou; by that time, his period of banishment will have come to an end."
The people inside the house then wrote a letter saying,
"Give this to him because of you.
The practitioner handed the letter to the boy.
At dawn, he arrived at the county seat and met with the magistrate, saying,
"I wish to stay here for a few days.
The magistrate replied:
"Very well. He asked what was inside the box, and the reply was:
"It is merely some written correspondence."
The practitioner was often sleeping in the hall, with his box and staff placed at the head of his bed.
He ordered a servant to take them away during the night, wishing to examine them.
The practitioner already knew this, so every evening he would hang his staff and box high up; when [the thief] came down to lie there, he could never find them.
Later, he took his leave of the magistrate, saying:
"I intended to stay for a short while, but since you constantly wish to steal from others, I shall depart at once."
He ordered his youngest son to be summoned and asked him about his recent experiences.
The boy said, "The practitioner had me hold a staff and we drifted away; at times I could hear only the sound of waves beneath my feet."
He further mentioned that a letter from a person in the mountains had been left with him, still tied within the waistband of a child's garment.
He ordered it opened and examined, but no one could understand its contents.
Thereupon, he transcribed it and sealed the original letter.
He had someone escort this young boy to the White Earth Mound (Baitu Ling) to deliver him to Shi Zong.
When Zong opened the letter, he was greatly astonished and said,
"How did you obtain a letter from the Immortal of Penglai?"

Later, when Daozong traveled south to the regions of Wu and Kuaiji, he once passed by a fishing weir. Seeing fishermen engaged in a large-scale catch, Daozong stepped into the upper reaches of the stream to bathe; immediately, the shoals of fish all dispersed.
His secret salvation of sentient beings was thus.
Later, he stayed at the Great Temple on Mount Long in Shangyu.

He was skilled in discussing the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*, and had thoroughly mastered the *Zhonglun* and the classics on filial piety; yet he concealed his brilliance and remained hidden from view, such that no one in the world knew of him.
Xie Shao, Wei Mazhi, and Fangzhi of Kuaiji were all men of profound scholarship and extensive learning, and they all received instruction from him.

Later, while a śramaṇa staying with them heard Zong conversing with someone at night, the visitor spoke quite extensively about matters concerning Mount Penglai; by dawn, however, no one knew where Zong had gone.
Tao Yuanming’s "Record of Encountering the Dharma Master San-yi at Bai-tu" is one such instance.
It is also said that a merchant traveling by sea saw a śramaṇa on a solitary island, who requested that he deliver a letter to Shi Zong.
He placed the book inside the boat; when his companions wished to look at it, the book adhered to the boat and would not come loose.
Upon reaching the White Earth Island (Pāṇḍubhūmi), the book flew up and approached Huizong; Huizong caught it and took it away.
8. Beidu. As for Beidu, his name and surname were unknown.
He frequently crossed over water by riding on a wooden cup, and thus he was named after this practice.
He was first seen in Jizhou.
He did not cultivate minor practices, yet his supernatural powers were preeminent; no one in the world could fathom their origin.
Once, while staying as a guest in a household in the north, he noticed a golden image in the house, which he secretly stole and took away.
The head of the household woke and pursued him; seeing him crossing at a leisurely pace, he galloped his horse after him but could not catch up.
Upon reaching the Mengjin River, he placed wooden cups upon the water and relied on them to cross the river; without the need for wind or oars, he moved as swiftly as if flying.
Before long, he crossed the river and reached the capital.
There he saw Shi Ke, who was about forty years old; he wore a belt made of twisted rope and tattered rags that barely covered his body.
His speech was erratic, appearing and disappearing unpredictably, and his moods shifted between joy and anger without consistency.
Sometimes he would bathe in freezing ice and frost; sometimes he would wear wooden clogs while climbing onto his bed; or he would walk barefoot into the marketplace.
He carried nothing but a single reed basket, possessing no other belongings whatsoever.
He first went to the abode of the practitioner Fayi at Yanxian Temple, where Fayi received him in a separate room.
Later, wishing to go to Yanbu River, he boarded a boat by the riverbank.
Someone called out for him to cross over, but he was unwilling to carry him.
The man then balanced his feet upon the edge of the cup, looking around and chanting verses; the cup then flowed naturally of its own accord, taking him straight to the northern bank.
While traveling toward Guangling, he encountered a village house where the Li family was observing the Eight Precepts (Bāguānzhāi).
Having no prior acquaintance with them, he entered the hall directly to sit down and placed a reed basket in the middle of the courtyard.
Because his appearance was so haggard, the crowd had no sense of reverence for him.
When Li saw a reed basket blocking the road and wished to move it to the side of the wall, several men tried to lift it but could not budge it.
When he had finished eating, he took them away and said with a smile, "The Four Heavenly Kings' Li family.

At that time, a young boy peered into the basket and saw four small children, each several inches tall, with handsome features and bright, clean clothing; he then pursued them in search, but could not find where they had gone.
Three days later, he was seen sitting beneath a dense tree on the western boundary.
Li knelt and prostrated, requesting him to return home so that he might provide offerings for a month.
However, Dao did not strictly observe the fast; he drank wine, ate meat, and even consumed pungent raw fish, no different from a layperson.
The common people presented offerings to him, some of which he accepted and others he did not.
Liu Xingbo of Pei served as the Regional Inspector of Yanzhou and sent an envoy to invite him;
carrying his grain sacks on his back, he traveled there.
Xingbo sent someone to lift and examine it, but more than ten people could not move it.
When he looked at it himself, he saw only a single worn-out hemp cloth and a wooden cup.
Later, when he returned to Li’s house, he remained there for another thirty-odd days.
At dawn, he suddenly said, "I wish to have a cassock; have it ready by noon.
Li immediately set about preparing it, but by noon it was not yet finished.
Fadu went out for a short while, but did not return by nightfall.
Throughout the entire district, people smelled an extraordinary fragrance and suspected it was some kind of omen.
Searching everywhere for Fadu, they finally found him beneath the northern cliff, lying dead upon a tattered *kāṣāya* robe spread upon the ground.
From head to toe and from front to back, lotus flowers sprouted from his body;
the flowers were exceedingly fresh and fragrant, yet they withered in a single night.
The people of the town jointly provided for his enshrinement and burial.
A few days later, someone arrived from the north and reported that he had seen Du carrying a reed basket on his back traveling toward Pengcheng.
They then opened the coffin together and found nothing but a pair of shoes.
Having arrived at Pengcheng, he encountered a layman named Huang Xin, who had deep faith in the Buddha-dharma. Upon seeing Sengdu, Huang Xin prostrated before him and invited him to his home.
His family was extremely poor, possessing nothing but barley porridge.
Du Gan remained in a state of serene joy for only half a year when he suddenly said to Xin,
"You should find thirty-six bundles of reeds; I must use them."
He replied, "I happen to have exactly ten coins here; being poor, I have no means to buy more, and I fear I shall not be able to complete the task. Daodu said:
"You need only search; there must be some within the house.
Xìn immediately conducted a thorough search and indeed found thirty-six pieces, which he arranged in the courtyard.
Although the number was correct, many were broken and damaged.
Zhibin looked at them one by one in succession and found that they were all brand new and intact.
He sealed them back up and told Zhibin to open them; upon doing so, he saw that they were filled with coins and silk, amounting to approximately one million.

Those who understood the matter said that this was Beidu manifesting his body in another land; whatever offerings he received, he redirected them to give to Xin, and Xin accepted them all as meritorious deeds.
After about a year, Beidu took his leave and departed.
He joyfully set about preparing provisions.
When he saw the provisions still intact the following morning, he did not know where the boat had gone.
After about a month had passed, he returned once more to the capital.
At that time, there was one Zhu Wenshu from Chaogou who had been a devotee of the Dharma since his youth.
Sengdu frequently visited his home.
Wenshu said to Sengdu:
"The disciple has cast off his body and fallen into suffering; I pray that you will rescue him.
If he should be reborn in a good realm, I pray that you will become his dharma-fellow.
But Dūḍabha gave no answer.
Mañjuśrī said with joy, "The Buddha-dharma is silent; by its silence, it has already granted its consent.
Later, he traveled eastward and entered Wu Commandery.
On the road he saw a fisherman, so he approached him to beg for a fish.
The fisherman gave him one that had been caught as bait.
He took it in his hands, played with it by turning it over and over, and then threw it back into the water, where it swam away.
He also saw a fisherman and asked him for some fish.
The fisherman scolded him in anger and would not give any.
Fadu then picked up two pebbles and threw them into the water; immediately, two water buffaloes began fighting within his net.
The net having been shattered and ruined, the ox was no longer to be seen, and Du had already vanished.
When they reached Songjiang, he then held the canopy aloft above the water and rode across to the other bank.
He traveled through Kuaiji and Shan County, ascended Mount Tiantai, and returned to the capital after several months.
At that time, there was a foreign monk named Saṃghaṭa who was staying at Changgan Temple in the capital.
There was a visiting monk named Sengwu who shared a room with Zha; through a crack in the window, he saw Zha take the temple’s spire, lift it up into the clouds, and then lower it back down.
Wu did not dare speak,
but only felt a profound sense of reverence and admiration.
At that time, there was a man surnamed Zhang and named Nu, whose origins were unknown.
He rarely appeared to eat, yet he was always plump and cheerful; throughout both winter and summer, he constantly wore only single-layered cotton garments.
As he walked along the road, he saw Zhang Nu and smiled with joy.
Khaṭa said, "I saw Cai Tun in the east, questioned Ma Sheng in the south, and met Wang Nian in the north. Now, as I am about to go to see Bei Du, I have come to meet you."
Zhang Nu then inscribed a poem upon a locust tree and sang:
"Within the vast expanse of the Great Mystery, the illumination shines forth with clarity.
Why do you, deluded and ignorant one, allow yourself to be so confused as to invite calamity?"
In the realm of pleasure, few people venture; the path of suffering is like overturning a sack. Without the steadfast integrity of the pine and cypress, how could one withstand the wind and frost?
Dwelling idly beyond the purple mists, I sing long songs that emerge from the vast heavens.
When the translucent spirit transcends the realm of formlessness, one should perceive the lands where conditions arise.
The planet Jupiter shone for the Han sovereign, and the morning star graced the King of Yin.
Yet I am not one of those two immortals; I have obscured my traces within the nine directions.
"I also see the commoners of the age, whose very sight causes my eyes to ache with sorrow.
To briefly observe their worldly thoughts through song—how could one ever exhaustively record them all in written verses? Khaṭa said:
"Previously, I saw the Master contemplating in a secluded ravine, sitting for a hundred years.
Great compassion perfumed his heart, as he serenely contemplated a skeleton.
He also composed a verse, which says:
"Vast and far-reaching are the affairs of the world, which may either increase or diminish one's welfare.
They cause the desires to defile the spirit, giving rise to perverse joy and satisfaction.
Only this wise man possesses profound awakening and foresight."
Contemplate the form as floating foam; gaze upon the shadow as a fleeting flash of lightning.
The accumulation of fame and glory leads to stumbling and failure; treat ornate robes and caps with contempt.
Seeing physical beauty as empty, contemplate objects and grieve their transformation.
Abandoning turmoil and severing worldly existence, they cut off habitual tendencies and eliminate attachment.
Verdant branches provide curved shade; white *máohú* grass serves as a thatched roof.
They sip hemp-water by the garden ridges and drink from the cascading stream beside the cliff.
"Wisdom and concentration are the means of illumination; the wondrous truth is called the retinue.
May compassion increase, and may deep contemplation never weary.
Having finished speaking, they each departed.
After some time, these two men were no longer seen.
According to tradition, they had departed for Mount Nanyue together with Sengwu, but did not reach their destination.
Zhang Nu met with Beidu, and they conversed at great length on matters that others could not understand.
Fadu remained in the capital for a short time before wandering about without a fixed residence; when invited, he would sometimes go and sometimes not.
At that time, there was a Chen family in Nanzhou who possessed considerable wealth and provisions; Fadu went to their home and was treated with great hospitality.

It was heard that there was another Bei-du in the capital; the five sons of the Chen family all lacked faith, so they went down to the capital to see him, and indeed he was just like their own Bei-du in appearance and character.
Chen prepared for him a lidded box containing honeyed ginger, along with a knife, frankincense, hand towels, and other items.
Daodu immediately ate all the honeyed ginger until it was gone, yet the remaining objects remained exactly as they were before his knees.
The five members of the family, suspecting that this was indeed their own Beidu, left two younger brothers behind in the capital to guard him, while the other three returned home.
At home, Beidu remained as he had been before; there were even incense and a knife by his knees, though it was unusual in that he no longer ate honey or ginger.
He then said to Chen, "The knife is dull; you may sharpen it for me.
When the two younger brothers both returned, they reported that he had already moved to Lingjiu Monastery.
His family suddenly requested two sheets of yellow paper to compose a document; however, no characters were formed on the writing, and the two sides matched perfectly as one.
Chen asked, "What kind of contract or document are you, Venerable Sir, making?"
Fadu did not answer, and in the end, no one could fathom why.
At that time, Zhu Lingqi, a commoner from Wu Commandery, was returning from Gao-li when his ship encountered a gale and was driven off course; after nine days, it reached the shore of an island.
On the continent there was a mountain, which was exceedingly high and vast. Lingqi entered the mountain to gather firewood and saw a path leading to human habitation.
He then took several people with him and followed the path, begging for alms.
After traveling more than ten li, they heard the sound of a *ghaṇṭā* and the fragrance of incense smoke; thereupon, they together invoked the Buddha's name and prostrated themselves.
In a short while, they saw a monastery that was exceedingly magnificent and radiant, mostly adorned with the seven treasures.

He saw more than ten monks, all of whom were stone figures, neither moving nor shaking; he then prostrated himself before them and, after walking back a short distance, heard the sound of a chanting leader, so he went back to look again, only to find they were still stone figures.
Lingqi and the others said to one another, "This is a holy monk; we, being sinful people, have been unable to behold him.
Thereupon, they all exhausted their sincerity in repentance.
They went further and saw a true person (a *satpuruṣa*) preparing food for Qi and the others.
The flavor of the food was that of vegetables, yet its fragrance and excellence were unlike anything in the world.
When they had finished eating, they all prostrated themselves in worship and requested that he return quickly to their home village. A monk there said:
"This place is more than two hundred thousand *li* from the capital.
However, provided you maintain a sincere heart, there is no need to worry about the journey not being swift.
He then asked for the date of departure, saying:
"Do you know the Daoist Master Beidu?
He replied, "I know him very well."
He then pointed to the north wall, where there was a bag hanging from which a mendicant’s staff and alms bowl were suspended, saying:
"This is the property of Beidu; I now give this bowl to you so that you may present it to him."
He also wrote a letter and placed it inside a casket.

He further had a blue bamboo staff and said, "Simply cast this staff into the water ahead of the boat and sit quietly within the vessel; without needing to exert any effort, you will surely arrive quickly."
Thereupon, they took their leave, and he had a śrāmaṇera escort him to the gate, saying to him:
"Go by this path; after traveling seven *li*, you will reach the boat. You need not follow the previous road."
As instructed, we turned westward and traveled about seven *li* until we reached a boat, which was exactly as described.
We heard only the sound of the boat passing over the trees on the mountain summit; no water was visible at all.
After three days, they arrived at the Shitou (Stone Head) reach of the Huai River and stayed there; the bamboo staff was no longer to be seen.
When the boat entered the Huai and reached Zhuque Gate, they saw Beidu riding upon the railing of a large ship, striking it with his staff and saying, "Horse, horse, why do you not go?"
The onlookers were very numerous.
Lingqi and the others paid their respects from afar while aboard their boat.
Sengdu then descended from his own boat to take the letter and the bowl.
He opened the letter and looked at it; no one recognized the characters.
Du laughed loudly and said, "Does this mean you want me to return there?"
He took the bowl and threw it into the clouds, then caught it again, saying, "I have not seen this bowl for four thousand years.
Daodu stayed mostly with Fayi at Yanxian Temple; at that time, people regarded this bowl as a miraculous object and vied with one another to go and see it.
One account states:
"The *lingqi* boat drifted to a remote mountain, where it encountered a monk who said, 'I am a disciple of Master Du.

In the past, I died at Zhicheng Temple while carrying my master’s bowl. Now, because of you, I shall return the bowl to my master; simply have one person hold the bowl at the prow of the boat and another pull straight behind, and we shall arrive in safety.'"
"As instructed, I have indeed attained complete salvation.
At that time, on the day when Beidu of Nanzhou was riding the railing, he went out early in the morning and did not return until evening.
The next morning, Chen saw six characters written in blue on the door leaf that read:
"Gate of Merit and Virtue; A Spirit Descends.
The characters were barely legible, and from then on, Beidu’s visits to the family ceased entirely.
In the capital, Beidu still traveled between the mountains and the towns, frequently performing divine incantations.
At that time, a maidservant of Yu Chang stole property and fled; although she was pursued in four directions, she was not captured, so Yu Chang questioned Beidu.
Du said, "He has already died in an empty tomb by the banks of the Jincheng River.
When they went to look, it was indeed as he had said.

At that time, Kong Ningzi was serving as a Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate. While staying at his official residence, he suffered from dysentery and sent a messenger to request the services of Fadu.
After Fadu finished his incantations, he said, "It will be difficult to recover."
He saw four ghosts, all of whom were mangled and mutilated.
Ningzi wept and said, "In the past, when Sun En incited a rebellion, our home was plundered by soldiers; both my parents and my uncle were subjected to cruel and agonizing suffering."
Ningzi subsequently died.
Furthermore, Hu Mu, the wife of Qi Xie, fell ill; though many treated her, she did not recover.
Later, he invited monks to hold a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*). Among those seated for the feast was the monk Cong Dao, who urged him to welcome Beidu.
Once Du arrived, the patient was healed immediately after a single incantation.
Qi Xie served him as his master and subsequently composed a biography for him, recording his origins and spiritual wonders; its general outline is the same as that described above.

In the ninth month of the third year of the Yuanjia era, Sengzhao took his leave of Sengxie and entered the capital, leaving ten thousand coins and goods with him, entrusting him to organize a vegetarian feast on his behalf; thus they parted.
When he reached Chishan Lake, he fell ill with dysentery and died.
Daohar immediately organized a vegetarian feast for his benefit and escorted the corpse back to Jianye to be buried on Mount Fuzhou.

In the fourth year, there was a man named Shao Xin from Wuxing who was a devout follower of the Dharma; when he contracted a severe case of smallpox, no one dared to attend to him, so he wept bitterly while reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara.
Suddenly he saw a monk arrive, who said he was a disciple of Beidu.
The monk said, "Do not worry; my master will soon come to see you."
He replied, "The Preceptor has already passed away; how could he possibly come here?
The practitioner said:
"What difficulty is there in coming back?
[The Master] then took a handful of powder about the size of a small box from his belt and gave it to him to consume; the illness was immediately cured.
Furthermore, there was one named Du Seng'ai who lived at the foot of South Hill; he had previously served Beidu.
The child’s illness was extremely grave, so [the father] thought longingly that he could not obtain the Du Lian Shen Zhou (the "Du-Lian Spirit-Mantra").
The next day, he suddenly saw Du arrive; his speech was as usual, and Du immediately recited the mantra for him, whereupon the patient was cured.
On the eighth day of the third month in the fifth year, Sengdu returned once more to the home of Qi Xie.
Lü Daohui heard that Ren Da, Du Tianqi, Shuiqiu Xi, and others had all seen him together; they were all greatly astonished and immediately rose to prostrate themselves before him.
He addressed the multitude, saying:
"The coming year shall be one of great misfortune; you should diligently cultivate meritorious deeds.
The Dharma Master Fayi possesses profound virtue; you should go to him to restore this ancient temple, thereby averting calamities and disasters."
After a short while, he heard a monk above calling for Du.
Du then took his leave, saying, "I, this poor monk, shall head toward the regions of Jiao and Guang; I shall not return."
Qi Xie and the others saw him off with great courtesy, after which he vanished without a trace.
In recent generations, it has also been said that there have occasionally been those who saw him; however, as the details of these accounts are not certain, nothing can be reliably transmitted.
9. Shi Tanshi. Shi Tanshi was a native of Guanzhong.
Since his entry into the monastic order, he had performed many miraculous deeds.
Toward the end of the Dàyuán era of Emperor Xiào Wǔ of the Jìn dynasty, he took several dozen volumes of sūtras and vinayas and traveled to Liaodong to propagate the teachings.
He manifested the bestowal of the Three Vehicles and established them in the precepts of refuge; this was the beginning of how Goguryeo heard the Way.
At the start of the Yixi era, he returned once more to Guanzhong to guide and instruct those in the Three Fu regions.

From the beginning, his feet were white, surpassing his face in color; even when he walked barefoot through mud and water, they never became stained. Consequently, everyone in the world called him the "White-Footed Venerable.

At that time, there was a man from Chang’an named Wang Hu, whose uncle had been dead for several years. Suddenly, the uncle’s form appeared to him and returned, leading Hu on a tour of the hells to show him the various retributions.
When Hu Ci returned, Shu said to him, "Since you already understand cause and effect, you should simply serve the 'white-footed' āraṇyaka.
