Hu went to visit the various monks everywhere; seeing only that Shi’s feet were white like his face, he consequently served him.
At the end of the Jin dynasty, Helian Bobo, a Xiongnu chieftain from Shuofang, ravaged Guanzhong, slaughtering countless people.
At that time, Shi also encountered his execution, yet the blade could not harm him; Helian Bobo marveled at this and granted a general amnesty to all śramaṇas, sparing them all from death.
He then went into seclusion in the mountains and marshes to practice the dhūta austerities.
Later, when Tuoba Tao reconquered Chang’an and monopolized power over Guanzhong and Luoyang,
there was a man named Cui Hao of Boling who, having studied heterodox ways since his youth, harbored suspicion and jealousy toward the Buddhist teachings.

Having already occupied the position of a false counselor and being the one upon whom Tuoba Tao relied for trust, he then joined with the Celestial Master, the Kou family, to persuade Tao that Buddhism was of no benefit and harmed the interests of the people, urging him to abolish it.
Having been deluded by these words, Tuoba Tao, in the seventh year of the spurious Taiping era, proceeded to destroy the Buddha-dharma.
He dispatched military troops to burn and plunder monasteries, and ordered all monks and nuns within his domain to disrobe and return to secular life.
Those who fled or went into hiding were all pursued by dispatched messengers, and upon their capture, they were invariably executed by decapitation.
Within the borders of the realm, there were no longer any śramaṇas.
At first, [the heretics] merely remained secluded in deep, remote places where military forces could not reach.

Toward the end of the Taiping era, it first became known that the time for Daohua’s transformation was approaching; on the day of the Yuanhui festival, he suddenly arrived at the palace gate leaning on his monk’s staff.
An official reported:
"There is a man of the Way whose feet are as white as his face, entering through the gate."
Tao ordered him to be executed according to military law, yet he was repeatedly decapitated without being harmed.

When this was hastily reported to Tao, Tao became greatly enraged and struck him with the sword he himself wore; his body remained otherwise unaltered, except for a mark where the blade had touched, appearing like a line of thread.
At that time, tigers were being raised in cages in the northern garden; Da ordered that Shi be used to feed them.
The tigers all remained hidden and dared not approach him at all.
When he tested this by having the Heavenly Master approach the cages, the tigers would immediately roar and growl.

Daohui then realized that the Buddha’s transformation was sublime and honored, surpassing what could be achieved by Huang-Lao; he immediately invited Daoshi up to the hall, prostrated at his feet, and repented for his previous errors.
He began by preaching the Dharma, clearly elucidating the principles of cause and effect.
Daokao was filled with shame and dread, and subsequently contracted a malignant disease.

The two families of Cui and Kou were next stricken with severe illnesses; believing their transgressions lay with those two families, Daokao then executed and exterminated both households, leaving not a single member of either clan remaining.
He issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom to restore and propagate the orthodox teachings.
Shortly thereafter, Tuoba Tao passed away, and his grandson Tuoba Xian succeeded him; the latter began to widely propagate the Buddha-dharma, a tradition that has flourished down to the present day.
At first he was known, but later his end was unknown.
10. Shi Falang: Shi Falang was a native of Gaochang.

From childhood, he practiced with such rigorous austerity that many miraculous signs appeared. He concealed his brilliance and accumulated virtue, such that no one could fathom the stage of his spiritual attainment.
Master Lang’s disciple, Shi Fajin, was also a śramaṇa of lofty conduct.
Once, while Jin was sitting alone with his door closed, he suddenly saw Lang standing before him and asked, "Where have you come from?"
He replied,
"I entered through the keyhole. He asked:
"Accompanied by monks from afar, we have arrived just as midday approaches; we pray that you will provide us with a meal.
Jin immediately prepared the food, yet he heard only the sound of the ladles and bowls, for no people were to be seen at all.
Formerly, Huiyuan of Mount Lu once sent a *kāṣāya* robe to Daojin, who immediately accepted it as a religious offering (*dakṣiṇā*).
Daolang said, "The assembly of monks has already departed; you should take it on another day."
Later, he saw a cook approach and take the robe, and as the cook stepped forward, [the Master] immediately gave it to him.
When he inquired of the regular cooks, they all said they had not taken it; only then did he realize that this was a provisional manifestation by the Great Sage to take it.
When the Wei invaders destroyed the Buddha-dharma, Lang traveled west to Kucha.
The King of Kucha made an agreement with the Great Dhyāna Master of that country:
"If anyone who has attained the Way arrives, you must inform me, and I shall provide him with offerings."
When Faliang arrived, he informed the king of this, and the king received him with the rites due to a sage.
Later, he passed away in Kucha.
On the day his body was cremated, two springs gushed forth from between his eyebrows, shooting straight up into the sky.
The multitude marveled at this rarity and collected his bones to erect a stupa.
Later, when people from the Western Regions came to the northern lands, they recounted these events in full detail.
At that time, there was also a śramaṇa named Zhizheng in Liangzhou; he too was austere and possessed extraordinary conduct, serving as a spiritual advisor to the ruler Yang Nandang.
Later, he entered a stone cave in the Shanxia Mountains and did not return. 11.
Shao Shuo: Shao Shuo’s original surname was Shao and his given name was Shuo; he was a native of Shikang.
He had no fixed dwelling and wandered about in a daze as if insane; he was a man with a large mouth and coarse, unattractive features.
Children liked to pursue and play with him.
At times, he would enter taverns to drink to intoxication along with others.
By nature, she was fond of the Buddha-dharma; whenever she saw a Buddhist image, there was none she would not bow before and praise, her feelings of sorrow and devotion moving her to shed tears.
She originally had three sons and two daughters; the eldest son, Huisheng, also left the household life to become a monk.
Shuo also left the household life to enter the Way at the beginning of the Song dynasty, styling himself Master Shuo.
Whether coming or going, whether entering or departing, he did not distinguish between day and night.
He traveled through the various counties of Yizhou and even into the lands of the Man people; in all these instances, he used humorous speech and jesting to exhort others toward goodness.
If he sleeps on the floor at a person's house, there will surely be a death in that household.
If he begs for a fine mat from someone, a young child will certainly perish; at that time, people all regarded this as an omen.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, during the procession of the sacred image in Chengdu, Huishuo crawled among the crowd and assumed the form of a lion.
On that day, the local commanderies and counties also reported seeing Huishuo in the shape of a lion; thus, they realized he was a manifested body.
The Provincial Inspector Xiao Huikai, along with Liu Mengming and others, all treated him with great respect.
Mengming dressed two of his concubines in men’s clothing and tested Shi by saying,
"Would it be acceptable to provide these two people to you as attendants?"
Shi was a man who delighted in rhythmic verse;
he then said to Ming, "I would rather beg for wine to soak and swallow myself than spend the remainder of my years with this fellow."
Later, one morning, [Fang] suddenly donned a cloth cap and went to visit Meng Ming.
Shortly thereafter, Meng Ming passed away.
Prior to this, Meng Ming’s Chief Secretary, Shen Zhongyu, had revised the regulations for flogging and caning, making them more severe than the standard code.
Shi said to Yu: "The clamor of heaven and earth arises from this; if you remove the flogging and the barriers, you will obtain the status of a Prefectural Governor.
Yu believed him and removed them.
When Mengming passed away, Zhongyu indeed took charge of the affairs of the state.
He died on the first day of the ninth month in the first year of the Yuanhui era of the Song dynasty at Tongyun Temple on Mount Min.
As he was dying, he spoke to the practitioner Fajin, saying:
"Expose my remains and quickly tie your sandals on your feet.
They did as instructed and carried the corpse out to place it behind the temple.
After two days had passed, the body was nowhere to be seen.
Shortly thereafter, someone came from Pí County and reported to Sengjin:
"Yesterday I saw Master Shu in the marketplace; he was wearing a shoe on only one foot and spoke indistinctly, saying:
'This youth has no propriety; he has lost one of my shoes.'"
Startled, Jin questioned the śrāmaṇera, who replied:
"Recently, when we were carrying a corpse out, I was so terrified that I could not properly tie the strap of my right shoe, and consequently lost it."
His traces were strange and extraordinary, beyond all measure.
In the end, his final destination remained unknown.
12. Shi Huian: It is not known where Shi Huian was from.
In his youth, he was captured by barbarians and became a slave to people of Jingzhou; he served his master with such diligence and industry that the master held him in great affection.
At the age of eighteen, he was permitted to leave the household life and resided at Pipa Temple in Jiangling.
His appearance was plain and unrefined, so people generally looked down upon him.
At that time, while he was still a śrāmaṇera, whenever the assembly of monks sat in rows for a meal, they would invariably have him serve the water.
An often carried an empty pitcher from the top of the row to the bottom, yet the water never ran out.
At that time, everyone regarded him as extraordinary.
Upon receiving full ordination, he gradually manifested miraculous traces.

Once, on the evening of the last day of the month, while attending the *poṣadha* ceremony with his fellow student Huiji in the lecture hall, the doors had not yet been opened; Dao’an then took Huiji’s finger and entered through a crack in the wall, exiting in the same manner.
Sengji was deeply startled and terrified, not daring to speak.
Later, as they sat together beneath the stupa, [the monk] spoke to Ji, saying:
"I am about to travel far; I now take my leave of you."
Shortly thereafter, celestial music and fragrant flowers were seen filling the air.
Sengji was struck with such terror that he could not utter a word.
Dao’an spoke to him again, saying:
“Be careful not to speak recklessly of my past and future deeds; to do so will surely bring retribution.
Only to a layperson in white robes from the southwest—one who is a bodhisattva newly resolved in the Way—may you explain them in full.”
Thereupon he took his leave and joined a merchant caravan to travel up the Xiang and Chu rivers.
Midway, he suffered from severe dysentery and became critically ill;
he said to the boatman, "My life must surely come to an end. Simply set me ashore; there is no need for a coffin or wood."
"After his breath has ceased, you shall immediately offer him to the insects and birds.
Following these words, the merchant went out and lay down by the riverbank.
At night, he saw flames issuing from the man's body; filled with wonder and fear, the merchant went to observe him, only to find that he had already passed away.
The merchant traveled as far as Xiangdong, where he saw Dao’an had already arrived there before him; shortly thereafter, the merchant lost sight of him again.
Later, when Sengji arrived at Zhiqui Temple, he visited the hermit Liu Qiu of Nanyang and recounted the matter in detail.
Liu Qiu immediately rose and prostrated toward him from afar, saying to Sengji:
"This is a man who has attained the Way; he has entered the Fire-Light Samādhi.
At that time, there were also the monks Senglan and Fawei in Shu, both of whom possessed extraordinary traces, leading people of the age to suspect they too had attained the fruits of sainthood.
13. Shi Fakui: Shi Fakui’s original surname was Wan; he was a native of Yuqian in Wuxing.
He left home to become a monk in his youth and became a disciple of Fakai of Zhiguan Temple in the capital.
Kai had long possessed the merit of learning and was particularly proficient in the classics and histories; Wang Huan and Wang Su of Langya both took him as their teacher.
Kui was by nature reverent and silent, seldom speaking; he maintained his integrity with simple sincerity, remaining aloof from worldly affairs.
He recited one volume of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
In the monastery, there was an elder, Dharma Master Chen-sheng, who was elderly and ill; [the master] relied upon him for support, and he protected and cared for him most devotedly.
When Sheng passed away, his funeral rites were conducted according to the Dharma.
Whenever he received offerings during vegetarian assemblies, he accumulated them to fashion a sandalwood image of the Buddha.
Once the image was completed, he personally organized a great assembly in its honor.
His family resided in the Great Market of the capital. On this morning, he returned home, then went to Dinglin Monastery, and finally returned to Zhiguan Monastery.
When the three locations were subsequently investigated, they all saw him arrive for the midday meal; indeed, he had attended all three places at one and the same time.
That evening, he returned to his room and lay down to rest, whereupon he passed away suddenly.
His corpse was remarkably fragrant and supple, and two fingers of his hand remained bent.
The assembly all realized that he had attained the second fruit of the path.
At that time, while he was still a śrāmaṇera, his spiritual traces were so extraordinary that they eventually reached the ears of Emperor Wu.
The Emperor personally visited him, holding a convocation of monks and providing offerings.
Both Emperors Wenhui and Wenxuan came to his room to pay their respects and arranged for his funeral rites.
The common people flocked there like clouds, offering repeated and abundant donations.
With the gains thus obtained, he constructed a stupa for the Jīvana Monastery.
This was the seventh year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty.
14. Shi Senghui: Shi Senghui’s secular surname was Liu; it is unknown where he was from.
He resided in Jingzhou for several decades.
Liu Qiu of Nanyang established Zhiqui Temple and invited him to dwell there.
People of the time saw him for fifty or sixty years, yet he never grew old.
His movements were casual and lacked any great display of dignified decorum.
When he went to the homes of the sick, those who were met with anger would surely die, while those who were met with joy would surely recover; at that time, everyone took this as an omen.
Regarding all those he had not previously known, Hui would inquire in full detail about their relatives and whether they were living or deceased.
Once, Hui went to the riverbank and informed the ferry official that he wished to cross;
the official refused him passage on the grounds that the boat was too small.
In a short while, Hui was seen there; the people on both banks all marveled at his spiritual wonder.
On the same day, Zhen Tian of Zhongshan and Che Tan of Nanping both invited him.
Hui went to both of them.
Later, when the two families conducted an investigation, they finally realized he had manifested multiple bodies.
During the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, Emperor Wenhui invited him down to the capital; on his way, he passed by Baozhi.
Zhi patted his back and said,
"Son of the Red Dragon.
He said nothing more.
Later, when Hui returned to Jingzhou, he encountered Liu Jingfu, the Regional Inspector of the West’s Chief Secretary. Suddenly overcome with grief, Hui threw himself upon him;
a few days later, Jingfu was indeed killed by the Provincial Governor.
Later, when he arrived at the south of the city of Xiangzhou, he suddenly said that there were stone tablets beneath the ground.
When the people tested this by digging, they indeed found two of them.
As for Huì, his final whereabouts remained unknown.
Some say he passed away in Jiangling during the Yongyuan era.
At that time, there was also a monk named Shi Huiyuan at Changsha Temple in Jiangling; he had originally been a servant of the śramaṇa Huiyin.
Yin saw that he possessed faith and consequently ordained him as a monk.
He continued to practice the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (Banzhou sanmei).
After several years of diligent effort, he manifested supernatural powers, such as being able to divide his body to attend invitations and to prophesy the rise and fall of dynasties.
15. Shi Huitong: Shi Huitong was a man of unknown origins. During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he was seen in Shouchun.
His attire was unconventional, and his sleeping quarters were never fixed. He traveled through villages and towns, drinking, feasting, and eating no differently than ordinary people.
He constantly referred to himself as "Zheng Sanqi" (Zheng the Cavalier Attendant) and spoke of future events, which were occasionally proven correct.
In Jiangling, there was a man named Bian Senggui who traveled to Shouchun for trade.
As he was about to return to his hometown, he encountered Huitong on the road, who said he wished to entrust some goods to him.
Although the monk insisted on carrying the heavy burden himself, Huitong pressed him to place it upon his shoulder; yet the monk did not perceive its weight at all.
After traveling several *li*, he took his leave and said to Senggui:
"I have an elder sister who is a nun in Jiangling;
her name is Huixu, and she resides at San-ceng Temple. You may convey my regards to her, telling her that I intend to go there soon."
Having finished speaking, he suddenly vanished.
Looking back at his pack, the items he had entrusted were also missing.
When the monk returned home, he found Huixu and related the matter in detail.
Since Huixu had no such younger brother, he did not know how this could be so.
He therefore traveled back and forth to Shouchun to search for him, but in the end, they did not meet.
Later, Daotong went to Jiangling himself, only to find that Huixu had already passed away.
He entered their rooms and questioned them in full detail, remaining in Jiangling for a short time.
Whenever he passed by people's graves along the way, there were none whose clan names, family lineages, and the dates of their deaths he did not know thoroughly.
When he was questioned by others, his responses were always exactly as they had described.
At times, he would even point out thieves from afar and describe their crimes; consequently, when the bandits saw him approaching from a distance, they would invariably take secret paths to flee.
Furthermore, on the river ferry road, he encountered a man whom he suddenly struck with his staff, saying:
"Hurry back home and see what has become of your family!"
When this man returned home, he was indeed struck by a spreading fire, and his house and possessions were completely consumed.
At the beginning of the Yongyuan era of the Qi dynasty, he suddenly went to an acquaintance, Ren Yang, and requested wine with great urgency, saying:
"I must now travel far away; we shall not meet again."
"To express my gratitude to all my spiritual friends, it is most fitting that I prioritize the diligent cultivation of wholesome deeds.
Having finished drinking the wine, he went to the side of the wall and lay down on the ground.
Upon checking him, he was already dead.
Ten days later, another person saw him in the marketplace.
They pursued him and conversed for a long while before he vanished. 16.
Shi Baozhi: Shi Baozhi’s original surname was Zhu, and he was a native of Jincheng.
He left home to become a monk at a young age and resided at Daolin Monastery in the capital, where he served the śramaṇa Sengjian as his upādhyāya and devoted himself to the practice of dhyāna.

At the beginning of the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he suddenly became eccentric; his dwelling was unsettled and his meals were taken at no fixed time. His hair grew several inches long, and he often walked barefoot through the streets and alleys carrying a single *khakkhara* staff, upon which he hung a pair of scissors and a mirror, or sometimes one or two bolts of silk.
During the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty, he gradually manifested extraordinary signs.
He would go several days without eating, yet show no sign of hunger.
When he conversed with people, his words were initially difficult to understand, but later all proved to be efficacious and verified.
At times he would compose poems whose words resembled prophetic records.
The gentry and commoners of the capital all served him together.
Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty, deeming him a deluder of the masses, had him arrested and detained in Jiankang.
At dawn the next morning, people saw him entering the marketplace.
Upon returning to inspect the prison, Zhì was still there.
Zhì said to the prison official:
"Two carriages carrying food are coming outside the gate; rice is served in golden bowls. You should take it.
Shortly thereafter, Prince Wenhui of Qi and Prince Ziliang of Jingling both sent food as offerings for Zhì.
It turned out exactly as he had said.
Lü Wenhuan, the Magistrate of Jiankang, reported the matter to Emperor Wu.
The Emperor immediately welcomed him in and had him reside in the rear hall.
At one time, the inner banquets were screened off, and Zhì also went out with the assembly.
Shortly thereafter, on Mount Jingyang, there was still one Zhì remaining together with seven monks.
The Emperor grew angry and dispatched officials to investigate his whereabouts. The interrogating officers reported:
"Faxiang has been absent from the palace for a long time; he is currently using ink to smear his body.

At that time, the Sangha Chief Faxian wished to present a robe to Faxiang, so he sent a messenger to the two monasteries of Longguang and Jibin to seek him out, but both replied: [that Faxiang was not there].
"She departed yesterday morning after staying overnight.
He then went to the house of Li Houbo, where she usually stayed, to search for her;
Houbo said, "Zhi was here practicing the Way yesterday; she fell asleep at dawn and has not yet awakened."
The messenger returned and reported this to Xian, who only then learned that [Hui]zhi had divided his body and stayed overnight in three places.
Zhi often walked about bare-chested even in the height of winter.
The śramaṇa Baoliang wished to give him a patched robe, but before he could speak, Zhi suddenly approached, took the robe, and departed.
On another occasion, he went to someone's house to request raw fish for his meal. The person prepared and sought it out for him, and having eaten his fill, he departed.
Upon returning and looking into the basin, he saw that the fish were swimming about as lively as before.

After recording this, Zhi, by means of Emperor Wu’s supernatural power, beheld Emperor Gao beneath the earth, who was constantly suffering the pain of being pricked by awls and knives; from that time on, the Emperor permanently abolished the use of awls and knives.
Hu Xie, the Commandant of the Palace Guard of Qi, was ill and requested [the services of] Zhi.
Zhi went to him and recorded:
"I am humbled by your clear summons."
The next day, he did not go at all.
That very day, Xi passed away; his corpse was carried back to his home.
Zhi recorded:
"Regarding 'brightly bending,' it means the corpse will emerge the following day.
Sima Yin Qizhi, the Grand Commandant of Qi, accompanied Chen Xian-da while he was stationed at Jiangzhou; this is his farewell inscription.
He drew a tree on paper with a crow perched upon it, saying,
"In times of urgency, you may climb this. Later,
when Xinda rebelled, [Dao'an] remained in Zhenzhou under Qi's command.
Upon his defeat, Qi zhi fled into Mount Lu.

As the pursuing cavalry were about to overtake him, Qi zhi saw a tree in the forest; atop the tree was a crow exactly as depicted in the portrait. Realizing its significance, he climbed it, yet the crow did not fly away at all.
The pursuers saw the crows and, believing there was no one there, returned;
thus, [Sengzhi] was ultimately spared.
Sang Yan, a cavalry officer of the Qi state, intended to plot a rebellion and went to visit [Seng]zhi.
Zhi saw them from afar and fled, shouting loudly:
"They are surrounding the Tai City, intending to commit rebellion; they will hack off heads and rip open bellies!
Less than ten days later, the matter broke out.
Xie Yan rebelled and fled to Zhufang, where he was captured by others; as predicted, they indeed decapitated him and cut open his belly.
Prince Zhonglie of Poyang of the Liang dynasty once invited Baozhi to his residence for a gathering.
Suddenly, he ordered that thorn branches be sought with great urgency; once they were obtained, he placed them upon his gate, the reason for which remained unfathomable.
A short while later, the King departed to serve as the Governor of Jingzhou.
His clarity in prescient discernment was of this sort on many occasions.
Zhi frequently traveled between the two monasteries of Xinghuang and Jingming.
When the present Emperor ascended the throne, he received great honor and respect.
Previously, during the Qi dynasty, there were many prohibitions regarding the movement of the Venerable Zhì. Now, upon the accession of the present Emperor, an edict was issued stating:

"The traces of Master Zhì are constrained by the dust and grime of the world, yet his spirit wanders in profound stillness. Neither water nor fire can scorch or soak him; neither snakes nor tigers can harm or frighten him."
Regarding his understanding of Buddhist principles, he surpasses those of the Śrāvakas and above;
in discussing his hidden conduct, he is more eminent than the recluses and immortals.
How can one constrain him with the empty prejudices of ordinary worldly people? Why is such narrow-mindedness carried to this extreme?
"From now on, as you travel along the road, you may enter and exit at will; do not be forbidden again.
From that time forward, Hui-zhi frequently entered and exited the restricted area.
In the winter of the fifth year of the Tianjian era, there was a drought; although the ritual sacrifices for rain (*yujì*) were performed in full, no rain fell.
Zhì suddenly submitted a memorial, saying:
"My illness has not improved, and I request that the authorities provide medical treatment for me.
If I do not submit this petition, the authorities ought to subject me to flogging."
"I pray that you will preach the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* in the Huaguang Hall to request rain.
The Emperor then ordered the śramaṇa Fayun to preach the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*. When the preaching was finished, it snowed heavily throughout the night.
The record further states:
"He prepared a basin of water and placed a blade upon it.
Shortly thereafter, rain fell heavily, providing sufficient moisture to both high and low lands.
The Emperor once asked Daoyi, saying:
"Your disciple’s afflictions and delusions have not yet been eliminated;
how may they be treated? He replied:
"Twelve. Those who understand consider this to be the medicine for curing delusions through the twelve links of dependent origination.
He was asked again about the meaning of the "twelve," and he replied:
"The meaning lies within the timing of writing characters and the measurement of the hours.
Those who understood this took it to mean that writing occurs throughout the twelve periods of the day.
He asked again,
"When shall the disciple attain a tranquil mind for cultivation? He replied:
"Peaceful Restraint.
Those who understand it believe that "restraint" means to cease; one ceases only when the state of ultimate peace and bliss is attained.
Later, when Fayun was lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra* at Hualin Temple, he reached the passage: "Suppose there were a black wind..."
Zhi suddenly asked whether wind exists or not.
He replied, “In terms of conventional truth it exists; in terms of the ultimate truth, it does not.”
After exchanging words three or four times, Zhi laughed and said, "If the essence is a provisional existence, this too cannot be understood; it is difficult to understand.
His expressions were often obscure and recondite, being generally like this.
There was a man named Chen Yulu, whose entire family served Sengzhi with profound devotion.
Sengzhi once manifested his true form to him, and its radiant features were like those of a Bodhisattva image.
For over forty years, Sengzhi’s fame and miraculous manifestations were renowned, and the number of men and women who venerated him cannot be counted.
In the winter of the thirteenth year of the Tianjian era, he said to those in the rear hall of the palace:
"The Bodhisattva is about to depart.
Less than ten days later, he passed away without any illness.
The corpse was fragrant and supple, its features serene and joyful.
As he was about to die, he lit a single candle and entrusted it to Wu Qing, an attendant of the rear palace.
Qing immediately reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor sighed and said,
"The Great Master will not remain with us any longer.
By lighting this candle, was he perhaps entrusting his final affairs to me?"
Consequently, he was provided with a lavish funeral and interred on the peak of Dulong on Mount Zhongshan.
A Kaishan Vihāra was subsequently established at the site of the tomb;
Emperor Wu commanded Lu Chui to compose an inscription for the interior of the burial mound, and Wang Yun to carve the epigraph for the temple gate.
Accounts of his surviving portraits exist in various places.
When he first manifested his spiritual traces, he was approximately fifty or sixty years old, yet he did not grow old even at the end of his life; no one could fathom his age.
There was a man named Xu Jiedao who resided at Jiurui North Street in the capital.
He claimed to be the younger brother of Master Zhi’s maternal uncle, being four years younger than him; by calculation, Master Zhi should have been ninety-seven years old at the time of his death.
At the beginning of the Liang dynasty, there were also Daoxiang and Senglang in Shu, who likewise possessed supernatural powers, it is said.
The Discourse states:

"The transformation wrought by the divine Way serves primarily to suppress the arrogant and powerful, to humble the disrespectful and conceited, to blunt the ferocity of the violent, and to unravel the entanglements of worldly dust."
As for the flying wheel that controlled the precious treasures, the faithful and virtuous submitted to it;
as for the towering rock that pierced the mists, the powerful warriors lay hidden within.

One should know that supreme governance is without artifice, and whether things are hard or soft depends on the transformative power of the Way. Since Emperor Huai of Jin lost control of the government and the emperors Hui and Min were driven into exile, the Central Plains were ravaged by invaders and the various Qie tribes rose in chaotic rebellion. First, Shi Yuan and Shi Yao committed usurpation and tyranny; later, Shi Le and Shi Hu followed with their audacious atrocities.
As the commanderies and kingdoms fell into fragmentation and the people suffered the slaughter of the burning cauldron,
Master Tancheng took pity on the onset of war’s blades and lamented that the infliction of punishments and harm had no end.
He thus manifested divine transformations at Gepo and displayed his prophetic records throughout Xiang and Ye.
Relying on secret mantras, he rescued those whose lives were nearly spent; employing fragrant incense, he extracted those facing imminent peril.
Gazing at the bells reflected in his palms, he settled matters of good and ill fortune, ultimately causing the two Śiṣyas to prostrate themselves in submission.
When the son from the remote frontiers arrived, his transformative grace moistened all living things;

indeed, there was nothing by which it could be compared. Subsequently, figures such as Fotiao, Qiyu, Shi Gong, and Beidu either concealed their brilliance and obscured their shadows, stooping to conform with the deluded world, or manifested supernatural wonders, foretelling future portents from afar;
some returned to life after death, while others left their graves empty after burial.
The spiritual traces and strange marvels are unfathomable in their origins.
However, as the established canons differ, so too do the methods of exclusion and inclusion.

For instance, regarding Liu An and Li Tie, the historical records regard them as plotting usurpation and practicing licentious sorcery, whereas the registers of the immortals regard them as having attained transcendence and soaring upon the clouds.
Now, what is esteemed in principle is its conformity with the Dao;
what is esteemed in action is its benefit to all things.
Therefore, expedient means (quan) involve departing from the ordinary to conform with the Dao, utilizing them to accomplish affairs.
However, regarding the accounts recorded in previous biographies, their details cannot be fully investigated.
It may be that he was a manifestation of the Dharmakāya responding to conditions, or perhaps one who had transcended as a lofty and reclusive immortal.
Yet, simply to have a single individual who possesses both [qualities] is sufficient.
For instance, when Huize touched the fragrant jar, he was able to cause a chronic illness to be cured;
when Shi Zong passed by the fishing weir, he caused the submerged fish to regain their lives;
and when Bazu faced the blade, he remained unhurt, thereby allowing the legacy of the Dharma to begin anew.
Baoshi manifested multiple bodies through the circular door, whereby the emperors increased their faith in him.
Though he was harmonious with the light, it did not defile his essence; though he shared in the dust of the world, it did not alter his true nature.
Therefore, the literary records of former dynasties all include them in their catalogs.

As for those who boast of their pseudo-arts and heterodox ways that disturb the times—claiming to soar aloft by means of divine elixirs or to achieve longevity through fragrant fungi; or like those who say their roosters crow from amidst the clouds or their dogs bark from the heavens; [these are merely empty fancies].
The serpent and the crane do not die; the tortoise is numinous for a thousand years—is this not what makes them extraordinary?
The encomium says:
Earth derives its essence from water and moisture; metal is produced by the refining of fire.
The strong and defiant were transformed, as they feigned submission to his majesty and authority.
His clarity illuminated the land of Xiang, opening and guiding the accumulated rivers.
He bestowed grace upon these two regions and brought peace to those four borders.
If one does not rely [upon them], how can the lives of the people be preserved?
*Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume Ten;
*Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume Eleven.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huijiao of Jiaxiang Monastery in Kuaiji during the Liang Dynasty.
4. Practitioners of Dhyāna: Twenty-one persons. Practitioners of Vinaya: Thirteen persons. 1.

Zhu Sengxian (1) Zhu Sengxian, whose original surname was Fu, was a native of Beidi. [The remaining entries for the practitioners of Dhyāna and Vinaya follow in the same format. ...21. Shi Huiming (21). 1. Zhu Sengxian (1): Zhu Sengxian, whose original surname was Fu, was a native of Beidi.

He was steadfast in his endurance of hardship and virtuous in his observance of precepts and moderation. He subsisted on vegetarian food and recited the sutras, making the practice of dhyāna his primary pursuit.
He frequently dwelt alone in mountain forests, practicing the dhūta ascetic practices beyond the reach of ordinary people.
At times he would enter meditative absorption for several days, yet he never showed any signs of hunger.
At that time, Liu Yao invaded and ravaged the Western Capital, leaving both the court and the common people in chaos.
At the end of the Taixing era of the Jin dynasty, Daoxian retreated south to the region east of the Yangtze River.
There, he again visited famous mountains to cultivate his constant practice.

Later, when he was afflicted by a severe and protracted illness, he focused his thoughts on the Western Pure Land with such profound and sincere devotion that he beheld the true countenance of Amitābha Buddha descending before him.

A light shone upon his body, and his ailment was completely cured. That very evening, he rose to bathe and recounted what he had seen to his fellow residents and those attending him during his illness, further expounding upon the laws of cause and effect with words of exceptional clarity and precision.
At dawn on the following day, he sat upright and passed away.
A extraordinary fragrance filled the room, which did not dissipate for over ten days.
2. Bo Sengguang (or Tan Guang): Bo Sengguang—also known as Tan Guang—is of unknown origin.
In his youth, he practiced the arts of meditation.
At the beginning of the Yonghe era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled to Jiangdong and took refuge at Mount Shicheng in Shan County.

The local mountain folk all said that this place had long suffered from the calamity of fierce beasts and that the traces of human presence had been severed for a long time due to the violent depredations of a mountain deity.
Guan Guang showed no sign of fear; he hired men to clear the path and went forward, leaning on his staff.
After traveling several li, a great wind and rain suddenly arose, and a pack of tigers let out a fierce roar.
At Mount Nan, Guang saw a stone chamber and took up residence within it; there he practiced dhyāna with palms joined, making it his dwelling place for settling the spirit.
When the rain ceased at dawn the following day, he entered the village to beg for food, returning to the chamber again in the evening.
After three days, he dreamed of mountain deities, some appearing in the form of tigers and others with the bodies of snakes, who vied with one another to frighten Guang.
Yet Guang remained entirely unafraid.
After three days, he again dreamed of a mountain deity who said that he was moving to reside on Hanshi Mountain in Zhang’an County and offered to cede his dwelling to him.
Thereafter, firewood and foraged goods flowed in from all directions, and both monastics and laypeople venerated him.
Those who came to study under Yuele built thatched huts beside his dwelling, which gradually developed into a monastery; thus it was named Yinyue (Hidden Peak).
Whenever Guang entered meditative absorption, he would not emerge for seven days.
He dwelt in the mountains for fifty-three years and reached the age of one hundred and ten.
At the end of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, he covered his head with his robe and passed away while sitting peacefully.
The assembly of monks all assumed he had entered meditative absorption as usual.

After seven days had passed, they marveled that he did not arise; they went together to look at him and found his complexion to be normal, with the sole exception that there was no breath in his nostrils.
Although many years had passed since the deity’s departure, his physical remains had not decayed.

In the second year of the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty, Guo Hong was serving as the magistrate of Shan; he entered the mountains to pay his respects and attempted to touch the chest [of the statue] with a *ruyi* scepter, whereupon a sudden gust of wind arose.
The clothing was scattered and lost, leaving only the white bones behind.

Hong was filled with great shame and fear; he collected them and placed them in his room, stacking bricks around the outside and plastering it over. He painted an image of the figure, which still exists to this day.
3. Zhu Tanyou (also known as Fanyou), a native of Dunhuang. From his youth, he practiced asceticism and cultivated meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Later, he traveled to the region east of the Yangtze River and stayed at Mount Shicheng in Shan County, where he lived on alms and practiced seated meditation. Once,
while traveling to the home of a practitioner of the "single-row" *gū* (poisonous insects) for alms,
after Huiyou had finished his incantations and prayers, a centipede suddenly leaped out from among the food.
Tanyou ate with great relish and experienced no ill effects.
Later, he moved to a stone grotto on Mount Chicheng in Shifeng to practice seated meditation.
Dozens of fierce tigers crouched before him, yet Tanyou continued to recite the sutras as usual.
A tiger was sleeping alone; Sengyou struck its head with his *ruyi* (magic wand) and asked why it would not listen to the sutra. Shortly thereafter, the pack of tigers all departed.
After a while, powerful snakes emerged in competition, each more than ten spans in girth, circling back and forth and raising their heads toward Sengyou; after half a day, they too departed.
One day later, a deity manifested his form and approached Sengyou, saying:
"Since the Dharma Master’s majestic virtue is so profound, you have come to reside on this mountain; I, your disciple, shall readily offer my chamber to you."
Daoyou said, "I have been searching for these mountains in hopes of meeting you; why not dwell together?
The spirit replied:
"Your disciple is not at fault; it is simply that my followers have not yet been fully harmonized by the transformative power of the Dharma, and their speech is consequently difficult to restrain.
When people from afar come and go, they may inadvertently cause offense or provoke one another."
"The paths of humans and spirits differ; that is why I have departed.
You said, "What deity was it originally?"
"How long have you lived here? Where do you wish to move?
The spirit replied, "I am the son of the Emperor of Summer; I have dwelt on this mountain for over two thousand years."
"Hanshi Mountain is where my maternal uncle resides; you should go there to dwell.
He then returned to the temple on the northern side of the mountain.

As they were about to part, [the uncle] took Huiyou by the hand and presented him with three caskets of incense. Thereupon, with drums beating and horns blowing, he ascended into the clouds and departed.
On Mount Acheng there was a solitary rock standing alone, rising elegantly above the clouds.
Huiyou hewed stones to create a ladder and ascended the rock to sit in meditation; he joined bamboo tubes to transport water for his daily use.
There were more than ten practitioners of Chan who had achieved realization there.
When Wang Xizhi heard of this, he went specifically to visit; gazing up at the lofty peaks and drawing them near with his mind, he paid his respects and returned.
[These sites include] the cliffs of Chicheng, the waterfalls of Tiantai, Lingxi, and Siming.
They are all interconnected;
yet Mount Tiantai rises as a precipitous cliff, its peaks and ridges brushing against the heavens.
According to ancient tradition:
Above is a magnificent vihāra where those who have attained the Way reside.
Although there is a stone bridge spanning the ravine, jagged rocks block the path, and the moss is green and slippery; since time immemorial, no one has been able to reach it.
When Tanyou reached the bridge, he heard a voice from the air saying:
"I know of your sincerity and devotion; you shall not cross now.
Ten years hence, you shall come of your own accord."
Tanyou felt despondent at heart; he stayed overnight in the central hall that evening and heard the sound of the chanting of the *saṃghāṭa-sūtra* during the practice of the Way.
At dawn, wishing to proceed further, he saw a man with white hair and eyebrows who asked him where he was going.
Tanyou answered him fully on his intentions.
The Duke said, "You are a person of birth and death; how could you possibly go?"
"I am a mountain deity, and thus I have informed you.
Daoyou then withdrew and returned.
On his way back, he passed by a stone chamber and stopped there for a midday rest.
Suddenly, clouds and mist gathered in gloom, and everything within the room began to cry out.
Sengyou’s expression remained undisturbed.
The next morning, he saw a person wearing a single-layered robe approach him and say:
"This is my dwelling; I was away from home yesterday and consequently caused this disturbance, for which I feel profound remorse.
Daoyou said, "If this is your residence, please return it to you."
The deity said, "My household has already moved; please remain here.
Daoyou stayed for a short while.
Sengyou always regretted that he had not been able to cross the Stone Bridge.
Later, after purifying himself through ritual fasting for several days, he wished to go there once more.
He saw the horizontal rock suddenly open, and having crossed a short distance over the bridge, he beheld the shrine and the divine monk, exactly as previously described.
They burned incense together for the midday meal.
When the meal was finished, the divine monk said to Huiyou:
"Ten years from now, I shall naturally come here; for now, I cannot stay."
Thereupon he returned. Looking back at the crosswise stone, it had closed back together as it was before.
During the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, there appeared a portentous star, and the Emperor issued a general edict to all the states:
There was a virtuous śramaṇa who instructed him to perform a fast and repentance to avert calamity.
Sengyou then prayed with utmost sincerity, and there was a mysterious response.
At dawn on the sixth day, he saw a small boy dressed in blue clothes come to him and say: "I repent my transgressions."
"The Dharma Master Heng-lao exhausted himself in his labors, and that evening the stars withdrew.
Another account states:
"It was the monk Bo Sengguang who warded off the stars."
The details are unknown.
At the end of the Taiyuan era, Huiyou passed away in his mountain chamber;
his corpse remained seated upright, and his entire body was green in color.
At the end of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, the recluse Shen Shibiao entered the mountains and climbed a rocky peak, where he saw that Sengyou’s corpse remained incorruptible.
Subsequently, whenever anyone wished to go and observe it, they were invariably obscured by clouds and mist, such that no one could glimpse it.
At that time, there were also Huikai and Huizhen, who were likewise skilled in the practice of dhyāna.
They entered Mount Lingmi in Yu’ao and each constructed a meditation cell for a *fangzhang*; these still exist to this day.
4. Shi Huiwei. Regarding Shi Huiwei: it is unknown where he was from.
He resided at the Great Monastery in Chang’an.
His observance of the precepts was pure and clear; he frequently dwelt in mountain valleys, cultivating the practice of dhyāna-concentration.
A headless ghost appeared, yet Wei’s expression remained unchanged;
he then said to the ghost, "Since you have no head, you are free from the affliction of headaches—how fortunate you are!"
The ghost then vanished its form and returned as a belly-less ghost, possessing only hands and feet.
Sui again said:
"Since you have no belly, you are free from the anxieties of the five viscera; how joyful this must be!"
After a short while, she again assumed a different form; Daowei dismissed her in accordance with his words.
Later, at another time when the weather was bitterly cold and snowy, a woman came seeking lodging for the night.
Her appearance was upright and elegant, her garments bright and fresh, and her demeanor charming and refined; she declared herself a celestial maiden, saying:
"Because this superior person possesses virtue, Heaven has sent me here to offer you consolation."
As she spoke thus, attempting to sway his resolve, Wei remained firm and resolute, his mind undisturbed.
He then said to the woman, "My heart is like extinguished ashes; do not test me with this leather bag."
The woman then ascended into the clouds and departed;
looking back, she sighed and said, "The waters of the sea may be exhausted, and Mount Sumeru may be overturned, yet that superior person maintains a firm and steadfast resolve."
Later, in the third year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled to the Western Regions together with Faxian;
his final destination remains unknown. 5. Śikṣānanda: Śikṣānanda’s surname was Sūn, and he was a native of Liangzhou.

He came to reside at Yanxing Monastery in Guanghan, where he constantly practiced meditative concentration as his primary vocation. He was also skilled in the observance of the Vinaya, remaining untainted by even the slightest transgression.
He passed away in the fifth year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty; as he approached death, five-colored light issued from his mouth, filling the interior of the monastery with its radiance.

His final testament instructed that his body be cremated; his disciples carried this out, and when his limbs and joints were entirely consumed, only a single finger did not burn, which they subsequently buried beneath a stupa.
6. Zhitanlan. Zhitanlan was a native of Qingzhou. He maintained a vegetarian diet, delighted in meditation, and recited three hundred thousand words of scripture.

During the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled to Shan County; later, he stayed at Mount Chicheng in Shifeng, where he saw a location with clear and expansive woods and springs, and took up residence there.
After several days had passed, he suddenly saw a man many times his own height who scolded Hulan and ordered him to leave.
He also saw various strange birds and beasts that repeatedly terrified Hulan.
Seeing Lan looking serene and self-contented, he knelt down and paid his respects, saying:
"Zhūqīwáng is my maternal uncle; I am now going to Mount Wéiqīng to join him, and I offer this place to you for your acceptance."
Three years later, he suddenly heard the muffled sound of chariots and cavalry, with attendants filling the mountain peaks.

Shortly thereafter, a man wearing a *zhé* cap appeared, identifying himself as King Zhūqī. After Tong had advanced to meet him, twenty-three people followed—his wife, children, and others—all of whom were of exceptionally handsome and upright appearance, surpassing anything seen in the world.
Having arrived at Lan’s location, after the customary greetings were concluded, Lan asked where he resided.
He replied,
“Mount Weiqing in Le’an County.”
"Having long admired your reputation for wisdom, I now come with my family to seek refuge under you; I beg you to accept me as a lay disciple and grant me the precepts.
Senglan immediately conferred them upon him.
Once the dharma had been received, [the patron] offered ten thousand coins and two jars of honey, then took his leave and departed.
Suddenly, the sound of whistling flutes and vibrating pipes was heard, their resonance shaking the mountains and valleys.
More than ten members of the monastic community, including Lán, both heard and witnessed this.
He passed away on the mountain during the Yuánxī era of the Jìn dynasty at the age of eighty-three.
7. Shi Faxu. Shi Faxu’s surname was Hún; he was a native of Gaochang.
His virtuous conduct was pure and prudent, and he maintained a vegetarian diet while practicing dhyāna meditation.
Later, he entered Shu and practiced as a dhūta ascetic among the tombs of Master Liu; tigers and rhinoceroses in the mountains and valleys did not harm him.
He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
He constantly dwelt within a stone chamber, practicing both meditation and recitation.
During the height of summer, he passed away inside the chamber; for seven days, his body did not emit any odor.
To the left of the corpse was a fragrance that only ceased after ten days. Every evening it emitted light that illuminated the surrounding area for several li.
The villagers immediately erected a stupa over the corpse. 8.
Shi Xuangao: Shi Xuangao’s surname was Wei; his original name was Lingyu, and he was a native of Wannian in Fengyi.
His mother was surnamed Kou; she originally believed in non-Buddhist teachings.
When she first married into the Wei family, she conceived her first child, a daughter who would later become Gao’s eldest sister.
From birth, she had faith in Buddhism and prayed on behalf of her mother, vowing that no divergent views should enter their household and that they might serve the Great Dharma.

In the third year of the Hongshi era of the pseudo-Qin dynasty, the mother dreamed that a foreign monk scattered flowers throughout her room; upon waking, she conceived, and on the eighth day of the second month of the fourth year, she gave birth to a son.
Suddenly, a rare fragrance filled the house, and a brilliant light shone upon the walls, which only subsided at dawn.
Because these were auspicious omens accompanying her son's birth, his mother named him Lingyu (Divine Nurturing).
The people of the time held him in high esteem and further called him Shigao.
At the age of twelve, he took leave of his parents to enter the mountains, but for a long time they did not grant him permission.
One day, a scholar stayed overnight at Gao’s house and said that he intended to go into seclusion on Mount Zhongchang.
The parents immediately placed him upon a high seat.
That evening, everyone saw the villagers gathering together to see him off; the next morning, the villagers all came to pay their respects to Gao.
The parents said:
"Yesterday you already escorted him away; why do you seek him again today?
The villager replied, "I have no idea where he went; how could I have allowed him to be taken away?"
Only then did his parents realize that those who had welcomed and escorted them the previous day were divine beings.
When Tanyao first arrived at the mountain, he wished to leave the household life immediately;
however, the mountain monk would not permit it, saying:
"If my parents do not grant their permission, I shall not be able to receive the Dharma.
Thereupon, Sengao returned home for a short time to petition for entry into the Way.
After twenty days had passed, he finally fulfilled his original aspiration.
Having turned his back on secular life and departed from worldly ways, he changed his name to Xuangao.
He was naturally intelligent and possessed innate knowledge; his learning required no further reflection.
By the age of fifteen, he was already expounding the Dharma for mountain monks.
After receiving the precepts, he applied himself with single-minded devotion to dhyāna and the Vinaya.
Hearing that the Dhyāna Master Buddhabhadra was propagating the Dharma at Shiyang Temple in Guanzhong, Hui Gao went there to become his disciple.
Within ten days, he had attained a profound mastery of the methods of dhyāna.
Guṇabhadra sighed in admiration, saying:
"Excellent, O Son of the Buddha! You have been able to realize such depths."
Thereupon, he lowered his countenance and humbly declined, refusing to accept the status of a teacher.
Daogao then took up his staff and traveled west to Qin, where he lived in seclusion on Mount Maiji.
Over a hundred students gathered at the mountain to revere his righteous teachings and receive his instructions in the way of meditation.

At that time, there was a śramaṇa from Chang’an named Shi Tanhong, a eminent monk of the Qin region who lived in seclusion on this mountain; he met with Gao and became his close friend due to their shared vocation.
At that time, Qi-fu Chiban possessed Longxi, which bordered the territory of Liang to the west.
There was a foreign dhyāna master named Dharmapriya who came to his kingdom,
led disciples, established a community, and instructed them in the way of dhyāna.
However, as the samādhi of right reception is both profound and subtle, those among the monks of Longyou who have inherited its transmission are few.
Daogao therefore wished to lead the assembly by personally receiving the dharma from Vimalākṣa.
Within ten days, Pi instead revealed his true intentions.
At that time, there were two monks in Henan who, though appearing as śramaṇas in form, possessed power equal to that of the false ministers.
Acting according to their own whims and violating the monastic rules, these two monks harbored a deep resentment toward the learned monks.

Once Dharmapriya had returned west to Śrāvastī, the two monks then slandered and instigated Xuan Gao against Prince Man, the heir apparent of the King of Henan, claiming that he was amassing a multitude of disciples and would become a calamity for the state.
Manxin, believing the slander, intended to inflict harm upon him; however, his father would not permit it, so he banished Gao to Linyang Tang Mountain in Hebei.
According to local tradition, this mountain was said to be the dwelling place of a multitude of immortals.
Accompanied by three hundred disciples, he went to reside in a mountain hermitage.

His demeanor remained composed and natural; his practice of meditation and wisdom grew ever more refined. Through his profound sincerity, he moved the unseen realm, and many miraculous manifestations occurred.
The stone chimes resonated without being struck, and the incense naturally emitted its fragrance.
Arhats and immortal adepts frequently came to visit.
Ferocious beasts became docile and submissive, and locusts and poisons were eliminated as pests.
Among his eminent disciples, there were over one hundred who wielded their mastery with ease across the six gates of meditation.
Among them was one named Xuanshao, a native of Longxi in Qinzhou.
He had thoroughly investigated all the various dhyānas, and his supernormal powers were sovereign and unimpeded.
Water issued from his fingers to provide for the high-ranking [monks'] washing and rinsing; this water was fragrant and pure, twice as extraordinary as usual.
He frequently obtained supramundane flowers and incense to offer to the Triple Gem.
There were eleven others whose spiritual anomalies were like those of Shao.
Later, Shao entered Tangshu Mountain and departed by shedding his mortal coil like a cicada.
Formerly, Dharma Master Tanhong of Chang’an migrated to the regions of Min and Shu, where his Way flourished throughout Chengdu.
King Jie of Henan, impressed by his high reputation, dispatched an envoy to welcome him.
Upon hearing that Sengao had been banished, Daohong vowed to vindicate his integrity; thus, disregarding the hardships of the mountain paths and braving the dangers, he obeyed the command.
Having arrived in Henan and completed the formalities between host and guest, he said to the King:
"Since you possess such profound discernment and far-reaching insight, why do you believe slanderous words and cast out the worthy?
It was precisely for the sake of presenting this one petition that I have traveled from over three thousand li."

The king and the crown prince were filled with shame and remorse; they immediately dispatched a messenger to visit Hui-gao, using humble words and prostrations to apologize and request that he return to their city.
Since Hui-gao’s heart was set on providing universal salvation, he forgot his resentment and went to answer the summons.
Just as he was about to leave the mountains, the grasses and trees within them were broken and crushed, and fallen rocks blocked the path.
Daogao made this prayer:
"I have vowed to propagate the Way; how could I allow myself to be detained in one place?"
Thereupon the wind subsided and the road opened, and he gradually returned to his kingdom.
The king, along with his ministers and citizens, waited by the roadside to welcome him.
Both the court and the commoners paid him reverent homage, honoring him as the National Preceptor.
Having completed his proselytization in Henan, he proceeded to travel through the Liang territories.
Juqu Mengxun treated him with profound respect and service, convening assemblies of eminent guests to hear his sublime and superior expositions.
At that time, there was Fan Sengyin in Xihai, who also received instruction from Daogao.

His aspirations were narrow and his capacity limited; having obtained but little, he considered himself satisfied, claiming he had already attained the rank of Arhat and had fully exhausted the gates of dhyāna.

Baogao then secretly employed his supernatural powers to cause Huiming to see, within the state of meditative concentration, the infinite worlds of the ten directions and the various different Dharma-gates taught by the Buddhas therein.

During a single summer, Faxian searched for what he had seen and was unable to exhaustively record it; only then did he realize that the waters of meditative concentration are bottomless, and he felt great shame and trepidation.
At that time, Tuoba Tao of the Wei barbarians had usurped the throne and occupied Pingcheng, and his army was invading the borders of Liang.
Tao’s maternal uncle, Yangping Wang She, requested that Baogao return with him to the puppet capital.
Once they reached Pingcheng, Baogao widely propagated his teachings.
The puppet crown prince, Tuoba Huang, served Baogao as his teacher.
Once, when Huáng was slandered and came to be suspected by his father, he said to Gāo, "I am being falsely accused and subjected to suffering;
by what means can I escape it? Gāo instructed him to perform the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* fasting ritual (*jīnguāngmíng zhāi*).

After seven days of earnest repentance, Baozhao then dreamed that his grandfather and father both appeared, wielding swords with fierce majesty, and asked him: "For what reason did you believe slanderous words and unjustly suspect the Crown Prince?"
Daohuao was startled awake and assembled his ministers in great numbers, informing them of his dream.
The ministers all said, "The Crown Prince is without fault; it is truly as the Imperial Spirit has proclaimed in its decree."
Tao had no further doubts regarding the Crown Prince;
this was indeed due to the power of Gao’s sincere devotion.
Tao consequently issued an edict, saying:
"I have inherited the glorious legacy of my ancestors and intend to propagate this great foundation, expanding its prosperity for ten thousand generations.
Although my military achievements are manifest, the civilizing influence of culture has not yet flourished; this is not the way to honor the governance of Great Peace."

Now that the realm within the borders enjoys peace and security, and the common people are prosperous and flourishing, it is appropriate to establish institutions as a law for ten thousand generations.
Indeed, Yin and Yang undergo cycles of alternation, and the four seasons follow a sequence of succession.
To entrust one’s son with the office and hand over the state to a worthy man is the means by which weariness is relieved and stability is secured for a long duration;
it is an immutable, excellent ordinance from antiquity to the present day.

My various meritorious ministers have labored diligently for a long time; they should now retire from office to return to their residences, enjoying their noble ranks with ease and grace, nourishing their spirits and prolonging their lives, while merely discussing the Way and presenting counsel.
There is no need for him to further occupy the arduous and distressing offices of the officials.

Let it be ordered that the Crown Prince assist in managing the myriad affairs of state and preside over the hundred ministries; furthermore, let worthy and virtuous men be promoted to fill the various posts, and having selected individuals for their appointments, let them be subject to promotion or dismissal based on their performance.
Therefore Confucius said, "The younger generation is to be feared;
who knows that those yet to come will not surpass those of the present?
Thereupon, the court officials and the common people all addressed the Crown Prince as their sovereign.
The petition was submitted as per the formal protocol, with each section separated by white paper.

At that time, Cui Hao and the Celestial Master Kou had previously gained favor with Emperor Tao; fearing that once Huang succeeded to the throne, they would be stripped of their power and authority, they slandered him, saying:
"Regarding the Prince's previous actions, he truly harbors treacherous intentions."
However, because he has mastered the arts of the High Road, he caused the late Emperor to appear in his dreams.
As such rumors and accounts of his deeds gradually spread, if he is not executed and eliminated, he will surely become a source of great harm.
Tao Chao subsequently accepted [the proposal], whereupon he became violently enraged and immediately issued an edict to arrest Hui-gao.
Previously, Hui-gao had privately told his disciples:
"The Buddha-dharma is destined to decline; must Master Chong and I be the first to suffer its calamity?"
At that time, among those who heard this, there was none who did not feel profound regret.
There was then a śramaṇa from Liangzhou named Shi Huichong, who was the preceptor to Han Wande, the Minister of the Interior under the puppet Wei dynasty.
Since his virtue was second only to that of Gao, he too was subjected to suspicion and obstruction.
In the ninth month of the fifth year of the spurious Tai-ping era, Gao and Master Chong were both imprisoned.
On the fifteenth day of that month, he met his end at the eastern corner of Pingcheng; he was forty-three years of age.
This was the twenty-first year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
On that evening, none of his disciples were aware of it.
At the third watch of the night, they suddenly saw light encircle the stupa at Gaoxian’s dwelling three times before re-entering the meditation cave.
Upon hearing a voice from within the light saying,
"I have already passed away," the disciples finally realized he had entered parinirvāṇa; they wailed in grief, their lamentation reaching the point of utter desolation.
Subsequently, they went to the desolate wilderness south of the city to receive the remains, where they bathed the body and prepared it for enshrinement.
They also attended to the remains of Master Chong, placing them in a separate location.
Among the monastics and laypeople throughout the capital, there was none who did not express profound lamentation and astonishment.

At that time, the disciple Xuanchang was in Yunzhong, six hundred li from the capital of Wei. One morning, he suddenly saw a man who informed him of the transformation and provided him with a horse capable of traveling six hundred li.
Thereupon, he lashed his whip and returned; arriving at the capital in the evening, he found that the Master had already passed away.
Overwhelmed by grief and inconsolable, he joined his fellow students in weeping and said:
"The Dharma has now perished; will it ever flourish again?"
"If he recovers from his illness, please ask the Upādhyāya to rise from his seat.
The Upādhyāya’s virtue is not that of an ordinary man; he will surely take pity upon him.
Having finished speaking, Hui-gao opened both eyes slightly, and their radiance returned to a state of serenity.
His body broke into a profuse sweat, and the sweat was exceedingly fragrant.
After a short while, he sat up and said to his disciples:
"The transformation of the Great Dharma follows conditions in its flourishing and decline."
"Prosperity and decline reside in outward manifestations, while the underlying principle remains eternally serene.
I only think that before long you all shall likewise be like me; only Xuanchang shall attain the crossing to the South."
"After you have passed away, the Dharma shall surely flourish again.
Cultivate your minds well and do not allow yourselves to feel regret midway.
Having spoken thus, he lay down and passed away.
The next day, when the coffin was to be moved for cremation, the national regulations would not permit it; consequently, a tomb was prepared and he was interred there.
Both monastics and laypeople were filled with grief, wailing and sobbing until their voices failed.

There was a śramaṇa named Fada, who served as the Monastic Rectifier (Sengzheng) of the pseudo-state; having long admired his lofty character, he had not yet had the opportunity to receive instruction from him.
Suddenly hearing of his passing away, he wept and said:
"The Sage has departed from this world; upon whom shall we rely?"
For several days he did not eat, constantly calling out:
"O Supreme Sage, you possess sovereign power; why can you not manifest yourself once?
In response to his voice, [the Sage] was seen flying high through the air and arriving.
Da prostrated himself in worship and entreated him with piteous cries, wishing to be saved and protected.
Gaoge said, "Your karma is heavy and difficult to rescue; what can be done?"
"From this day forward, by repenting according to the Vaipulya sutras, I shall receive a light retribution.
Da said, "If I am to escape a painful retribution, I pray that you will show me compassion and save me."
Gao said, "If one does not forget all things, how could it be limited to you alone? Da spoke again:
"Where were the Dharma Master and Master Chong born together?
Gao replied, "I vowed to be born in an evil age to rescue and protect sentient beings; thus, I have returned to be born in Jambudvīpa."
"Master Chong constantly prayed for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), and he has already fulfilled his heart's desire.
Da then asked, "I venture to ask,
Master, at what stage of realization have you now arrived?"
Gao said, "Among my disciples, there are those who already know this.
Having finished speaking, he suddenly vanished.
Da Mi visited several of Baogao’s disciples and they all said that he was a Bodhisattva who had attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
In the seventh year of the Taiping era of the Later Yan, Tuoba Tao indeed destroyed the Buddha-dharma, exactly as Baogao had foretold.

At that time, during the reign of Juqu Mogaon of the Hexi state, there was a śramaṇa named Tanyao, who was also renowned for his mastery of meditation; Zhang Tan, the Grand Tutor of the puppet regime, held him in the highest esteem and treated him with the reverence due to a teacher.
9. Shi Sengzhou. Shi Sengzhou’s origins are unknown. By nature he was lofty and fierce, possessing extraordinary resolve and integrity.
He concealed his brilliance and obscured his traces, such that no one could know him.
He constantly practiced *dhūta* and sat in meditation atop Mount Songgao.
When the Wei barbarians were about to destroy the Buddha-dharma, Zhou said to his disciples,
"A great calamity is imminent."
He then entered Hanshan with several dozen of his followers.
The mountain lies four hundred li southwest of Chang’an; its valleys and gorges were perilous and inaccessible to military forces, so he chose it as his place of residence.
Before long, the Wei invaders unleashed their violence, and all those who remained were slaughtered.
Subsequently, they repented and exterminated the Cui clan, subsequently reviving the Buddha-dharma.
When the illegitimate Prince Yongchang was stationed in Chang’an, he received imperial orders to reconstruct [the monastery] and sought out śramaṇas.
At that time, it was said that there was a monk on Mount Hanshan whose virtuous deeds were extraordinary; the King immediately dispatched an envoy to invite him.
He declined repeatedly on the grounds of old age and illness, ordering his disciple Sengliang to go forth from the mountain in his stead.
Shortly before his passing, Zhou told his disciples, "I am about to depart.
That evening, he saw fire emerge from behind his corded couch and consume his body; it was only after three days that it was completely extinguished.
Smoke and flames billowed to the heavens, yet the chamber was not consumed by fire.
His disciples collected the remaining ashes and constructed a brick stupa over them.
The disciple Sengliang, whose secular surname was Li, was a native of Chang’an; he received his training under the monk Sengzhou.
At first, when King Yongchang invited monks, none dared to respond; they all feared that since the Buddha-dharma had only recently begun to flourish, there might be unforeseen dangers.
Daoliang said, "The transmission of the Dharma depends on individuals, and it is precisely for this day."
"If we are executed, it shall be our own fate;
if we manage to remain whole, then there will be hope for the Way to flourish once more.
Furthermore, Sengzhou added his encouragement, whereupon he accompanied the messenger to Chang'an.
Before he had arrived, the king and the people swept and sprinkled the streets and alleys, waiting and welcoming him from every house.
The king went out in person along the road, touched his feet, and paid him homage.
Sengliang expounded upon the warnings of calamity and blessing, instructing them in the principles of cause and effect.
His words were concise yet profound in their reasoning, harmonious yet earnest.
Those who listened were moved both by sorrow and joy, each unable to contain themselves.
Thereupon, he restored the old temple and invited śramaṇas.
The Great Dharma flourished once more in Guanzhong;
this was due to the efforts of Huiliang. 10. Shi Huitong: Shi Huitong was a native of Guanzhong.
In his youth, he resided at Taishou Temple in Chang’an, where he maintained a vegetarian diet, recited mantras, and chanted the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

Initially, he studied the practice of dhyāna under the Chan Master Huizhao of Liangzhou, receiving instruction in the contemplative practices of the Dharma-gates; he became highly proficient in these disciplines.
He constantly prayed for peace in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, desiring to lodge his spirit in that realm.
While suffering from a slight illness, he saw a person appear within his meditation; the figure was most dignified and noble, and spoke to him in a familiar voice, saying:
"The auspicious time has arrived."
In a brief moment, he beheld the Buddha of Infinite Life, his radiant light and marks shining brilliantly.
Tong consequently awakened to dhyāna and related in detail to his fellow students what he had seen; having finished speaking, he passed away.
A wondrous fragrance remained in the room, only subsiding after three days. He was fifty-nine years of age.
11. Shi Jingdu. Shi Jingdu was a native of Yuhang in Wuxing. In his youth, he was fond of hunting;
on one occasion, he shot a pregnant deer, causing it to miscarry.
The mother deer, though suffering in pain, still lay on the ground licking her fawn.
Dao Du was then awakened in his heart; he consequently broke his bow and snapped his arrows, left the household life, and subsisted on vegetarian food.
He recited more than three hundred thousand words of the sutras.
He constantly dwelt alone in the mountains and marshes, practicing seated meditation and reciting the scriptures.
Whenever there was a vegetarian assembly in a town, he would invariably light nine lamps himself and sit upright until dawn as an act of offering; he continued in this manner for many years.
Later, he suddenly told his disciples:
"Prepare fragrant water for a bath. He then preached the Dharma for several thousand verses, exhorting them on the causes and effects of birth and death.
Having finished speaking, he passed away peacefully and suddenly.
Pipes and drums, along with fragrant smoke, arrived from the sky.
At that same time, dozens of his attendants all heard and saw this.
12. Shi Sengcong (釋僧從): Shi Sengcong; it is not detailed who this person was.
By nature he was serene and tranquil; he lived in seclusion at Pùbù Mountain in Shǐfēng.

His learning encompassed both the inner and outer teachings, and he diligently cultivated the five gates of meditation. He did not consume the five grains, subsisting instead solely on dates and chestnuts.
He was nearly a hundred years old, yet his physical strength remained robust and his ritual recitations never ceased.
He shared a bond of friendship with the hermit Chu Boyu, meeting as companions beneath the trees.
Whenever they discussed the Way or expounded upon its principles, they would invariably remain together for two or three nights.
Later, he passed away in the mountains.
13. Shi Facheng: Shi Facheng was a native of Liangzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of sixteen and became thoroughly versed in the Sutras and Vinaya.
He did not eat the five grains but subsisted solely on pine resin, dwelling in seclusion within mountain caves and making the practice of dhyāna his primary pursuit.
During the Yuanjia era, Prince Huaisu of Donghai was appointed as the governor of Basi; having heard of his reputation, he sent an escort to welcome him, and they met at Fucheng.
During the summer retreat, he lectured on the Vinaya; when the session concluded, he took his leave to return home.
He subsequently stayed at Guanghan, where he again propagated the methods of dhyāna.
Later, while suffering from a slight illness, he addressed the assembly, saying:

Cheng constantly recited the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*. He then attempted to recite it by his own strength, but having only managed half a fascicle, his breath failed him and he could not endure it. He then had someone read it aloud; as soon as one full recitation was completed, he joined his palms and passed away.
More than ten attendants were present during his illness, all of whom saw a dark-blue horse in the sky carrying a golden coffin on its back, ascending into the air and vanishing.
14. Shi Huilan: Shi Huilan, surnamed Cheng, was a native of Jiuquan.
In his youth, he and Xuangao were both renowned for their practice of silent contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
Senglan once traveled to the Western Regions, where he carried the Buddha’s alms bowl upon his head; subsequently, in Jibin, he received the essentials of dhyāna from the bhikṣu Dharmatrāta.
Dharmakṣema once entered meditative absorption and traveled to Tuṣita Heaven, where he received the Bodhisattva precepts from Maitreya.
Later, he conferred these precepts upon Fali.
Fali returned to Jibin and, in turn, conferred the precepts upon the various monks of that region.
Later, he returned home by way of Henan.

There, Muye, the son of the Prince of Tuyuhun, and his younger brother Qiong, having heard of Senglan’s virtue, dispatched an envoy along with provisions and wealth, instructing him to establish the Zuojun Temple in Shu, where Senglan subsequently resided.
Later, he moved to Latian Palace Temple.
Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty invited him to the capital, where he resided at Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhong.
When Emperor Xiaowu established Zhongxing Temple, he again issued an imperial decree ordering him to move and reside there.
The Zen monks of the capital all followed him to receive his instruction.
Shen Yan of Wuxing and Meng Yi of Pingchang both admired his virtue and established meditation halls for him within the monastery.
He passed away during the Daming era of the Eastern Jin dynasty at the age of over sixty.
15. Shi Faqi: Shi Faqi’s secular surname was Xiang; he was a native of Pi in Shudu.
Having lost both parents at an early age, he served his elder brother as if he were a father.
At fourteen, he left the household life and studied the practice of dhyāna under Zhimeng, practicing contemplation together with Falin of Lingqi Temple.
