All that Meng was familiar with and understood, he had already realized through direct realization.
Later, meeting Xuanchang, he again followed him to advance in his studies.
When Xuanchang went down to Jiangling, Daoqi also followed him there.
Of the ten stages of the contemplation gates (*daśavihāra-dvāra*), nine have already been attained.
There remains only the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the lion’s-awakening samādhi) that has not yet been perfected.
He sighed deeply and said:

"From the Western Regions to the shifting sands, from the northern wastes of the dark desert to the eastern exploration of Yu’s Cave, and reaching as far south as Mount Heng and Mount Luo, I have seen only this one disciple who possesses a unique share of the Dhyāna lineage."
Later, he passed away at Changsha Temple at the age of sixty-two.
A divine light shone upon his remains, and his body became even more fragrant and pure.
At that time, there was also one named Shi Daoguo at Longhua Temple, who likewise became renowned for his practice of dhyāna.
16. Shi Daofa. Shi Daofa, surnamed Cao, was a native of Dunhuang.
He entered the monastic life from his youth and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of dhyāna, while occasionally performing divine incantations.
Later, while traveling to Chengdu,
he arrived at the residences of Wang Xiuzhi and Fei Kengzhi, who requested that he serve as the abbots of Xingle and Xiangji Monasteries.
He disciplined the assembly according to the Dharma, constantly practiced alms-gathering (piṇḍapāta), and did not accept private invitations or communal monastic meals.
Of whatever he obtained through begging for alms, he would always set aside a portion to give to insects and birds.
Every evening, he would strip off his clothes and sit exposed to the elements to feed the mosquitoes and gadflies; he continued in this manner for many years.
Later, while in meditative concentration, he saw Maitreya emit a light from between his eyebrows that illuminated the retributions of the three evil realms.
Thereupon, he redoubled his diligent efforts and remained constantly seated without reclining.
In the second year of the Yuanhui era, he passed away while in a state of meditative concentration.
He sat upright upon his meditation bench, his countenance as serene as ever.
17. Shi Puheng. Shi Puheng, whose secular surname was Guo, was a native of Chengdu in Shu Commandery. His family name was Guo, and he was a man from Chengdu in Shu Commandery.
When he was a child, he often saw holy monks preaching the Dharma in the air amidst the sunlight; when he described this to his family members, they did not believe him.
Later, he earnestly sought ordination and resided at Anle Temple in Zhizhi.
He lived alone in a single room, did not establish a circle of followers, and practiced the meditation of stillness, becoming skilled in the entry, exit, and maintenance of meditative absorption.
He was of one mind with the Vinaya Master Shu Tao.

He claimed that he had entered the Fire-Light Samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), in which light descended straight from his brow down to the *vajra* limit; within this light, he clearly perceived various forms and images, as well as the karmic retributions of his past lives, for the most part with great clarity.
He passed away in the third year of the Shengming era of the Song dynasty at the age of seventy-eight.
A month before his death, he suddenly took leave of his relatives and acquaintances; yet he showed no sign of sorrow on his face, which people of the time regarded as mere joking.
On the day he was about to pass away, he showed slight signs of illness; only a single slave from his lay family attended him. At dawn the next morning, he sat upright and died.
The slave, not understanding, forcibly made him lie down, yet the corpse ultimately remained unbent.
When the assembly of monks came and saw him, they invited him to sit.
He bent three fingers of his hand while extending the rest.
The monks tried to pull them, but they extended as soon as he let go of them; once extended, they would bend again.
While alive his body was black, but after death it became even more pure white.
Thereupon, he was cremated according to the rites for attaining the Way.
As the stacked firewood first began to burn, smoke of five colors arose, and an extraordinary fragrance wafted forth.
The provincial governor Wang Xuanzai then composed a eulogy for it, saying:
"The Great Awakened One is infinitely formless; his suspended response prizes the forgetting of tranquility.
In a single thought one meets the site of enlightenment; thus, ten thousand kalpas pass in emptiness."
Faithful mind is like a phantom in the east; encountering the Sage is like a reflection in the west.
The wondrous intent clarifies the three realms; the divine spirit is transmitted within the state of the four dhyānas.
Worldly things are thus disparate, yet the principle of true nature is eternally radiant.
"He concealed his brilliance while dwelling in this floating world;
his enduring virtue now transforms the far reaches. 18. Shi Fawu. Shi Fawu (no. 18) was a native of Qi.
The family made their living through agriculture and sericulture; they had six sons, all of whom had reached adulthood.

When Wu was fifty years old, he lost his wife, and the entire household became deeply despondent and yearned for the Way. The seven members of the family, father and sons alike, all left the household life together to become monastics.

Traveling south as far as Wuchang, he toured the mountains and waters and saw that the southern slope of Mount Fan was a suitable place for secluded retirement; it had previously been the dwelling of the hermit Guo Changxiang, whereupon he resolved to spend the remainder of his life there.
At that time, Ren Hui of Chenliu, the Governor of Wuchang, heard of this and marveled at him; he accordingly cleared a path through the mountains and constructed dwellings for him.
Sengwu did not eat polished rice, but usually subsisted on wheat porridge, eating only once a day.
He recited the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
He constantly practiced the *caṅkrama* (walking meditation) during the six periods of the day, practicing *dhūta* austerities in mountains and marshes, not avoiding tigers or rhinoceroses.
At times he sat in meditation beneath trees, sometimes remaining there for days without rising.
He passed away in the mountains in the seventh year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty at the age of seventy-nine.
Later, the śramaṇa Daoji followed in his noble footsteps.
Now, in Wuchang, the place where he resided is called Toudousi (Head-Dhūta Monastery).
19. Śramaṇa Sengshen: Śramaṇa Sengshen, surnamed Wang, was a native of Qi in Taiyuan.
Shen of Jin was a descendant of the Biaoqi General; his ancestors had resided in Qiaojun for generations.
Shen renounced the world in his youth and stayed at Shijian Temple in Shouchun, where he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.
He had always maintained that without dhyāna there is no wisdom; thus, he devoted himself single-mindedly to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Hearing that Dharmamitra’s path was flourishing in the capital, he brushed off his robes and crossed the river, settling at Lingyao Temple.
He diligently received their instructions, thoroughly exhausting all their profound mysteries.
At that time, a band of robbers entered the mountain; he sat upright and remained motionless.
The thieves then stripped off their clothes and offered them to him, and he further preached the Dharma to instruct and exhort them.
The bandits were filled with shame and, sweating profusely, paid their respects and departed.
Hui-gao of Lingjiu Monastery followed him to receive instruction in the practice of dhyāna; he then requested Dao-shen to return to the monastery and separately established a meditation hall for him.
Later, Zhang Zhenhou of Qinghe again invited him to reside at Xixuan Temple.
Both Wenhui and Wenxuan treated him with great reverence, while Fu Yan and Xiao Chifux both sought his counsel regarding the precepts and instructions.

When King Jingze entered the room to look for Shen, he saw him just as he was entering into dhyāna. He then snapped his fingers and stepped out, saying, "A holy man! He immediately offered a thousand hu of rice and requested to receive the Three Refuges.
He passed away in the eighth year of the Yongming era at the age of seventy-five.
At that time, there were Sengqian, Chaozhi, Fadai, and Huisheng, all of whom practiced Chan and likewise possessed their own extraordinary traces of spiritual achievement.
20. Shi Tanchao: Shi Tanchao’s surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Qinghe.
He stood eight chi tall, and his deportment was dignified and worthy of admiration.
He lived on vegetarian food and wore simple cloth robes, finding contentment in these alone.
Initially, he resided at Longhua Temple in the capital.

Toward the end of the Yuanjia era, he traveled south to Shixing, where he toured the mountains and rivers extensively; he would often sleep alone beneath trees, yet neither tigers nor rhinoceroses harmed him.
During the Daming era, he returned to the capital.
Upon the accession of Emperor Taizu of the Qi dynasty, he received an imperial edict to travel to Liaodong to propagate and extol the Way of Chan.
He remained there for two years, extensively disseminating the teachings of the Dharma.
At the end of the Jianyuan era, he returned to the capital; shortly thereafter, he traveled once more to Lingyuan Mountain in Qiantang.
Whenever he entered meditative absorption, he would not rise for many days.
Later, suddenly hearing the sound of wind and thunder, he saw a man enter carrying a ceremonial tablet, identifying himself as Yan Zhendong Tong.

After a short while, a man arrived; his appearance was most upright and handsome, and he was accompanied by a retinue of attendants moving in graceful succession. He descended from his seat to pay his respects and introduced himself, saying:
"I am a disciple living seven *li* away, and I am the local magistrate of this area."
When the Dharma Master arrived, I came specifically to pay my respects:
A man from Fuyang County had previously excavated a hillside at Luzi Mountain to make bricks, thereby encroaching upon and destroying a dragon’s dwelling.
The dragons were all enraged and caused three hundred days of drought.
"It has now been over a hundred days since the wells and ponds have run dry and the sowing of fields has come to an end forever.

Since your virtue and wisdom, Master, penetrate the divine, we wish to respectfully request that you proceed ahead; you will surely be able to move the spirits and bring moisture to the common people, so that the merit may be attributed to you."
Chao said, "The rising of clouds and the falling of rain are fundamentally due to the power of the donor; what could a poor monk like me possibly do?
The spirit said:
"Your disciples and followers can only raise clouds, but cannot bring down rain; that is why I have come to request your help.
He granted the request, and the deity vanished in an instant.
Chao then traveled south; after five days, he reached Mount Chiting and offered prayers and preached the Dharma for the dragons from a distance.
When night fell, the dragons all transformed into human form and came to pay their respects to Chao.
Xiao Chao further preached the Dharma for him, whereupon he requested the Three Refuges and confessed himself to be a dragon.
Chao then asked him to send down rain, but the dragon merely looked at him and remained silent.
That night, it appeared again in Chao's dream and said:
"Originally, I made this vow out of anger; now that the Dharma Master has guided me toward the good, I dare not disobey his command. At the hour of *bhu* tomorrow, rain shall surely fall.
The next morning, Sengchao went immediately to Linquan Temple and sent someone to inform the magistrate to prepare boats on the river and recite the *Sūtra of the Dragon King* by the sea.
The county magistrate immediately invited the monk to board a boat at Shishou and recite the sutras;
as soon as the recitation was finished, a great rain fell.
High and low lands were all sufficiently watered, and the harvests of the year were bountiful.
Hui-chao passed away in the tenth year of the Yongming era at the age of seventy-four.
21. Shi Huiming: Shi Huiming’s secular surname was Kang; he was a native of Kangju.
The ancestors of Ming had fled to Eastern Wu to escape political turmoil.
In his youth, Ming left the household life and resided at Dongsi on Zhang’an.

During the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty, he ascended Mount Chicheng with other śramaṇas and beheld the incorruptible remains of Master Huiyou in a stone chamber; yet the meditation hall was overgrown with weeds, and no one followed in his lofty footsteps.
He then hired laborers to excavate and trim the site, further establishing halls and chambers, and fashioned a reclining Buddha as well as an image of Master Huiyou.
Thereupon, he settled his mind in meditation and recitation, dedicating the remainder of his life to austere practice.
Later, while in meditative concentration, she saw a goddess who called herself Lü Lǎo, saying that she would constantly provide protection and guardianship.
At times, white monkeys, white deer, white snakes, and white tigers would play before her steps; they were so tame and docile that they moved about without causing anyone fear.

Prince Wenxuan of Jingling of the Qi dynasty, having heard of his reputation, paid him profound respect and repeatedly dispatched three envoys with earnest and insistent invitations; he then temporarily departed for the capital.
Upon arriving at the Prince’s residence, Wenxuan honored him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
After a short time, he took his leave to return to the mountains; though they earnestly entreated him to stay, he would not remain, and they thus provided him with the means for his departure.
At the end of the Jianwu era, he passed away in the mountains at the age of seventy.
The Treatise says:
As for dhyāna (meditative concentration), it is spoken of as that which wondrously transforms all things; thus, there is no phenomenon it does not take as an object and no realm it does not discern.
Yet, in taking phenomena as objects and discerning realms, it is only through stillness that clarity arises.
It is like a deep pool where, when the waves have subsided, one can see clearly through to the fish and stones;
once the water of the mind has become clear, its concentrated illumination leaves nothing hidden. As the *Laozi* says:
"Heaviness is the root of lightness; stillness is the sovereign of agitation.
Therefore, lightness must take heaviness as its foundation, and agitation must take stillness as its basis.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"It is like taking medicine: one temporarily sets aside household affairs for the sake of the body.
Once one's strength has been restored and health regained, one returns to attend to domestic duties.
In the same way, by using the power of meditative concentration to take the medicine of wisdom, once its strength is attained, one returns to transform sentient beings."
Thus, the four immeasurables and the six supernormal powers arise from dhyāna;
the eight liberations and the ten totalities are accomplished only by relying on meditative concentration.
Therefore, one knows that dhyāna-samādhi is of great utility indeed!
Since the Bequeathed Teachings were transmitted to the East, the path of Chan meditation was also bestowed.

Previously, An Shigao and Dharmarakṣa had translated various *dhyāna* sūtras; subsequently, monks such as Sengguang and Tanyou followed these teachings to cultivate their minds, ultimately accomplishing sublime deeds.
Thus, he was able to transcend worldly pleasures within and subdue demonic portents without.
He banished ghosts and spirits to the deep crags and beheld divine monks upon the precipitous rocks.
Subsequently, when the śramaṇa Zhìyán personally traveled to the Western Regions, he invited the Kasmirian meditation master Buddhabhadra to further transmit this dharma to the Eastern Land.
Xuángāo, Xuánshào, and others also personally received these ritual protocols.
Their movements were entirely governed by numerical sequences, and their transitions reached the ultimate limits of returning to purity.
Subsequently, Sēngzhōu, Jìngdù, Fǎqī, Huìmíng, and others followed in succession like a flight of geese.
However, the application of dhyāna is manifested through the supernormal powers (abhijñā).
Thus, it causes the three thousandfold world system to reside within a single pore, and the four seas to coalesce into solid butter;
one passes through stone walls without obstruction, and supports the great assembly without omission.

As for the mundane ways of the world and the commonplace arts of the immortals, they are still able to arrest waves and stop rain, or incant fire to burn down a nation; even if one departs with profound loftiness only to rise again, or follows transformation while remaining seated in the Way and its Law—how is this anything extraordinary?
If one is like Udraka Rāmaputra, one will ultimately be harassed by birds and beasts;
if one is like the Unicorn Sage (Ekaśṛṅga-ṛṣi), one will finally be disturbed by Śaṇḍa.
In both cases, although the path of the mind was restrained, it remained associated with craving and views.
Compared to the sun and moon, how could the light of a firefly or a torch ever be their equal?
[The author] praises:
"Dhyāna is profound and silent; samādhi is deep and vast."
If one were to suspend worldly concerns, one would then prepare for a profound quest:
abandoning evil at the five gates, gathering in the groves of the nine stages;
withering and incinerating the mountains and seas, amidst the convergence and dispersion, the ascent and descent.
Now that virtue is so abundant, how could one not exert the mind?

5. *Minglü* (Clarifying the Vinaya), Chapter Fifty-three: Biographies of Monks. 1. Shi Huiyou; 2. Shi Sengye; 3. Shi Huixun; 4. Shi Sengqu; 5. Shi Daoyan; 6. Shi Sengyin; 7. Shi Daofang; 8. Shi Daoying; 9. Shi Zhidao; 10. Shi Faying; 11. Shi Falin; 12. Shi Zhicheng; 13. Shi Sengyou. 1. Shi Huiyou: Shi Huiyou was a native of Jiangzuo (the region south of the Yangtze).
He left home to become a monk at an early age and resided at Xin Temple in Jiangling.
From his youth, he maintained a vegetarian diet and observed strict moral conduct; his innate nature was upright and honest.
After receiving full ordination, he devoted himself exclusively to the precepts of the Vinaya.
At that time, the Vinaya Master Vimalākṣa from the Western Regions came to Jiangling and extensively propagated the Vinaya Piṭaka; Sengyou followed him to receive instruction.

After reflecting deeply for a long period, he attained a profound mastery of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü); his lectures continued without interruption, and among the Vinaya masters of Shensi, there were none who did not revere him as their authority.
Later, he passed away in Jiangling.
He authored the *Shisong yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Ten Recitations Vinaya) in eight fascicles.
2. Shi Sengye: Shi Sengye’s second [entry]. Shi Sengye, surnamed Wang, was a native of Henei.
From childhood, he was intelligent and quick-witted, and he extensively studied a wide range of scriptures.
Later, he traveled to Chang’an to study under Master Kumārajīva.
Upon seeing the newly translated *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, he devoted himself exclusively to the mastery of this text.
Tongjun’s natural talent was such that he thoroughly mastered all profound mysteries.
Kumārajīva sighed in admiration, saying:
"He is the Upāli of future generations."
Encountering many hardships in Guanzhong, he sought refuge in the capital.
Zhang Shao of Wu, admiring his integrity and simplicity, invited him back to Gusu and built Xianju Temple for him; its location was serene and open, surrounded by a long river.

As the head of the school, he upheld the transformation of others through teaching without ceasing; scholars from the Three Wu regions flocked to him like spokes converging on a hub, shoulder to shoulder.
Furthermore, during the intervals between his lectures and guidance, he directed his mind toward the gates of Chan meditation.
Every time he sat in formal meditation, a rare fragrance would immediately fill the room.
Those nearby who sat with him all heard it together; there was no one who did not marvel at this divine wonder.
In the past, when Master Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong, he had not yet translated the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*; instead, he first translated the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
It was only when Saṃghadeva entered the Qin territory that the full text was transmitted.
Therefore, the *Śīlaparivarta* and the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* are identical in their essential meaning, though they differ slightly in their phrasing.
As for the *Karmavācanā*, it has been corrected to conform entirely to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda*.
At present, both versions are transmitted and recited together.
Sengye passed away in Wuchong in the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era at the age of seventy-five.
His disciple Huiguang followed in his footsteps regarding conduct and principles, and he too frequently presided over public lectures.
3. Shi Huiyun. Shi Huiyun’s family name was Zhao, and he was a native of Zhaojun.
From his youth, he maintained a vegetarian diet and practiced asceticism.
He traveled to Chang’an, where he received instruction from Master Kumārajīva.
He studied the sutras and śāstras with great refinement, excelling particularly in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
He subsequently composed new regulations whose principles permeated all time.
During the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, he returned to reside in Guangling and extensively opened a lecture seat for the Vinaya.
During the Yuanjia era, he arrived at the capital and stayed at Daochang Temple.
The temple monk Huiguan was also proficient in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*; regarding Xun as a model for all beings, Huiguan then requested that he go to propagate the teachings at another temple.
Thereupon, he moved to reside at Changle Temple.
He passed away at his residence in the second year of the Daming era, at the age of eighty-four.
4. Shi Sengqu. Shi Sengqu’s secular surname was Lai, and he was a native of Wu.
He left the household life to become a disciple of the monastic community.

He thoroughly mastered the various sutras and commentaries, with a particular expertise in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya). Furthermore, he was proficient in historical records and composed works of literary elegance.

He first resided at Mount Huqiu in Wu; Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, having heard of his reputation and admired his character, issued an imperial decree for him to come to the capital to serve as the *Sengzheng* (Chief Administrator) and *Yuezhong* (Chant Leader), where he stayed at Zhongxing Temple.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Sengding who claimed to have attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
Yu assembled the saṃgha to investigate and adjudicate the matter, ordering him to manifest his supernormal powers (ṛddhi).
Sengding said:
"I do not manifest [my powers] for fear of violating the precepts.
Qu examined the Vinaya texts and found that there are four causes and conditions by which one may manifest the supernormal power of *ṛddhi*:
first, to sever the net of doubt; second, to destroy false views; third, to eliminate arrogance; and fourth, to accomplish meritorious virtues.
Since Ding’s conduct was so flagrantly deceptive, he was expelled on that very day.
Xu then composed the "Treatise on Admonishing the Assembly" to demonstrate his future karmic legacy.

As Xu’s learning encompassed both the inner and outer teachings and his observance of the Vinaya was flawless, both monastics and laypeople took refuge in him, with their carriages following one after another like the tracks of wheels.

The Young Emperor received the five precepts from him, while Prince Yuzhang Zishang revered him as a dharma friend; Yuan Can and Zhang Fu both met him once and were so moved that they removed their canopies to show respect.
Later, he moved to reside at Zhuangyan Monastery, where he passed away at his dwelling at the age of fifty-eight.

He composed the *Shengman Wenzhi* (The Essential Meaning of the Śrīmālā-sūtra) and authored the two-fascicle *Sengni Yaoshi* (Essential Matters for Monks and Nuns), both of which circulate in the world today.
At that time, there was also the Vinaya Master Daobiao, who was sincere and possessed noble conduct.
Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty issued an edict requesting that Jinxi Wang Shuang receive the precepts from him.
5. Shi Daoyan: Shi Daoyan was a native of Xiaohuang in Yongqiu.
He possessed a few virtuous precepts and was well-versed in the Vinaya. He meticulously studied the four schools of Vinaya, synthesizing their various traditions.

Furthermore, as the Vinaya-piṭaka had been transmitted to the East, the Sanskrit and Chinese pronunciations differed, causing the texts to become somewhat disordered. Fearing that future generations would have no place to seek clarification, he synthesized their essential tenets and titled his work *The Treatise on Resolving and Correcting the Four Schools of Vinaya*.
Later, he traveled to Pengcheng, where he propagated the Vinaya-piṭaka; he eventually passed away there at the age of seventy-five.
At that time, there was also a monk named Shi Huiyao residing at Xixuan Temple.
He was also well-versed in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
6. Shi Sengyin: Shi Sengyin, surnamed Li, was a native of Longxi in Qinzhou. His family had been practitioners of the true faith for generations.
At the age of eight, Yìn left the household life and was able to observe the perpetual fast.
By twelve, he subsisted on vegetarian food.
Upon receiving full ordination, his adherence to his principles became even more steadfast.
He constantly roamed through the gardens of the mind, achieving profound mastery of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, and recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
Hearing that in Xiliangzhou there was the Dharma Master Xuangao, who excelled both in meditation and wisdom, he took up his book-box and followed him as a disciple.
Thereupon, he mastered the gates of dhyāna and gained a profound understanding of the essentials of the Vinaya.
After Master Gao passed away, he traveled west again to Ba and Shu, where he devoted himself exclusively to propagating the teachings.
Shortly thereafter, he descended eastward and stayed at Pipa Temple in Jiangling, where he sought further instruction from Huiche.
Tche-ming was renowned in his time, and his Way spread beyond the mundane world.
Having studied under Yin Yen for some years, he thoroughly mastered the sutras and the Vinaya; thus, the influence of Chan and wisdom permeated the regions of Jing and Chu.
The provincial governor, Prince Liu Xiuyou of Shanyang, and the Chief Secretary Zhang Dai both consulted him regarding the precepts and the Dharma.
Later, the Regional Inspector, Prince Huiruo of Baling, and Prince Jingsu of Jianping both halted their carriage at the meditation hall, bowing their knees in respectful homage.
Later, while lying ill for a short time, he asked his attendant,
"Is it noon yet? The attendant replied:
“I have attained the middle [state].
He then sought water to rinse his mouth, his countenance remaining serene.
Suddenly he passed away; he was eighty years of age.

At that time, there was also the Vinaya Master Chengju of Shangming Temple in Jiangling, who was likewise well-versed in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, as well as the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Abhidharma* treatises.
7. Shi Daofang. Shi Daofang’s surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Wucheng in Guanghan.
His spiritual practice was pure and upright.
From his youth, he excelled in the study of the Vinaya and resided at Changle Temple in Guanghan.
Whenever he prostrated before the Buddha and burned incense, the smoke would rise straight up into the crown of the Buddha’s head.
He also diligently instructed his disciples to reform their evils and practice goodness; as for those who did not reform, he would weep for them until his tears flowed.
Later, he passed away at his residence at the age of one hundred and twenty.
8. Shi Daoying: Shi Daoying is unknown; it is not clear who he was.
At first, he resided at Lingyao Temple to practice meditation; later, he relied upon the two Vinaya masters Guanzhi and Daoxun to receive instruction in the *Vinaya*.

He was particularly proficient in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, maintaining his integrity through a vegetarian diet and ascetic discipline.
Zhuangyan Daohui and Zhichixiu of Zhicheng both took him as their model for monastic discipline.
Zhang Yong invited him to return to Wu Commandery, while Cai Xingzong further requested that he reside in Shangyu.
Later, in the capital, he established Xianxin Temple in Louhu Garden and was invited to reside there once again.
His lecture sessions were frequent and his disciples were very numerous.
He passed away in the second year of the Shengming era at the age of eighty-three.
At that time, there was a man named Shi Huiyou, originally from Dantu, who entered the monastic order at the age of thirty.
He disciplined his body with rigorous austerity and diligently studied the Vinaya teachings.
At the beginning of the Qi dynasty, he went to Mount Dong to lecture on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

By nature he was gentle and prudent.
At the age of seventeen, he left home and resided at Lingyao Temple.
He maintained a vegetarian diet and had few desires; apart from his six monastic requisites, he possessed almost nothing else in addition.
His learning was comprehensive across the Tripitaka, and he was particularly proficient in the Vinaya-piṭaka.
He Shangzhi, admiring his virtue, paid him formal respects and invited him to reside at the Falun Temple he had constructed.
Previously, when the Wei barbarians had suppressed the Buddha-dharma, the subsequent restoration of the faith resulted in many deficiencies in the transmission of the precepts.
Having already vowed to propagate the Way, he did not shrink from hardships; thus, accompanied by more than ten fellow practitioners, he traveled to Hulao.
He gathered Daoist masters from the five provinces of Luo, Qin, Yong, Huai, and Yu, and they assembled at Yinshui Temple.
He lectured on the Vinaya and elucidated the precepts, further expounding upon the methods of receiving the Dharma.
Thus, the prohibitions against monks in the puppet state were fully preserved; this was the power of the Way.
Later, when he returned to the capital, Wang Huan, who had been appointed as the regional governor of Xiangzhou, took him along with him on his journey.
He passed away in the second year of the Yongming era at the age of seventy-three in the region of Xiang.

At that time, there was also one Chaudu at Waguan Monastery in the capital, who was likewise proficient in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, and is said to have authored the seven-fascicle *Vinaya-li*.
10. Shi Faying. Shi Faying’s secular surname was Suo, and he was a native of Dunhuang.

He left home at the age of thirteen to become a disciple of Faxiang. He resided at Gongfu Temple in Liangzhou and, together with his fellow student Fali, became renowned for their mastery of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
After Huiying had humbly accepted [the teachings], he required no further instruction in his studies, for he retained everything upon hearing it once.
He investigated the Vinaya-piṭaka with great precision and extensively perused the sūtras and śāstras.
Toward the end of the Yuanjia era, he went down to the capital and resided at Xinting Temple.

When Emperor Xiaowu moved his capital southward, he renovated this temple; because Sengying’s scholarly learning was exceptionally clear and comprehensive, the Emperor issued an edict appointing him as the *Sengzheng* (Monastic Rectifier) for the metropolitan area.
Later, he resigned from his post and returned to Duobao Temple.
He constantly practiced meditative concentration in a secluded chamber and also occasionally opened a lecture hall for the Vinaya.

When Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty ascended the throne, he again issued an edict appointing him as the Sangha Chief; the provisions and support granted to him were twice those of the standard regulations.
Using his accumulated offerings from the faithful, Sengying commissioned the production of scriptures, images, and a medicinal repository (yaocang), which were enshrined at Changgan Temple.
He passed away in the fourth year of the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty at the age of sixty-seven.
He compiled the *Jiśu jieben* (Sūtra of the Ten Recitations) along with the *Jie-mo* (Karmavācanā), among other works.
At that time, there was also Vinaya Master Huíwén of Tiānbǎo Monastery, who was likewise well-versed in the various sections of the Vinaya and was served by Wáng Huàn of Lángyá.
11. Shi Falin. Shi Falin’s secular surname was Yue; he was a native of Linqiong in Jinyuan.
He left home to become a monk in his youth and resided at Pei Temple in Shu Commandery.
Devoted exclusively to the study of the *Vinaya*, he applied his mind to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong lü), constantly lamenting that there were no excellent masters or lineages in Shu.
Shortly thereafter, Master Yin arrived in Shu; Falin then disciplined himself, gripping his stylus with such intensity that he practiced day and night without ceasing.
When Huīyin returned to Shaanxi, [Huìyuǎn] again followed him for several years.
He thoroughly mastered the intricacies of all the Vinaya texts.
Later, he returned to Shu and resided at Lingjian Temple.
Among the monks and nuns of the Yi region, there were none who did not revere him.
He constantly prayed for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).
Whenever he recited the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* or the *Contemplation Sūtra*, he would invariably see a śramaṇa of exceptionally handsome and imposing stature standing before him.

In the second year of the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty, his illness worsened and did not subside; he focused his thoughts on the Western Pure Land and practiced ritual repentance without ceasing, until he saw various worthies and sages all assembled before him.
He then recounted what he had seen to his disciples and instructed them to cremate his body after his death.
Having finished speaking, he joined his palms and passed away.
They immediately piled wood at the crossroads of Xinfan to burn the corpse; the smoke and flames soared toward heaven, and it was only after three days that they were extinguished.
The remains were collected and a stupa was erected at that very spot.
12. Shi Zhicheng: Shi Zhicheng (12), surnamed Pei, was originally a native of Wenxi in Hedong.
He was a descendant of Wei Hui, the former Regional Inspector of Jizhou.
His ancestors had fled from political turmoil and settled in Jingkou.
It is said that from childhood he was resolute and spirited, taking great pleasure in archery and horsemanship.
At the age of seventeen, he followed Wang Xuanmu and Shen Tan on a northern expedition against the Xianyun.
Whenever they encountered combat and the clash of blades, he was never without a heart of compassion, feeling the pain as deeply as if it were his own.
He then sighed and said,
"To harm others for one's own benefit is not the will of a benevolent person.
Once the matter was settled, he laid down his armor.
Upon reading the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses*, he was deeply moved to realization.

Understanding that a hundred-year lifespan is not guaranteed and that kingdoms and cities are not of ultimate importance, he entered the meditation hall of Master Zong at Nanjian and requested the five precepts.

During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, the Master Yan of Yizhou was invited to the capital to receive offerings; [Daoxuan] expressed his intention to come and take refuge in him, and Yan received him with great kindness.
When Yan returned to Wenjiang, Daoxuan followed him on the journey upward and entered the monastic life at Pei Temple in Shu, taking Yan as his preceptor; he was then thirty-six years of age.
He then devoted himself exclusively to the Vinaya section, gaining profound mastery of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, and also recited the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (Small Version).
Later, he traveled east to Jiangling, where he received further instruction in Chan and Vinaya from the two masters Yin and Ju.
Encountering the chaos of the Jiagou rebellion, he moved his residence to the capital, where he met Master Ying at Xinghuang Monastery while the latter was lecturing on the Vinaya.
His inquiries resolved profound and obscure points, and his speech reached the very core of the matter; those present at that assembly could not help but marvel and praise him.
Dinglin Faxian encountered him at a lecture hall; hearing that his discourse was pure and profound, he brought him to stay at the mountain monastery.
Thereupon, they recited the *Prajñāpāramitā Hṛdaya Sūtra* (Small Chapter) together and studied the Vinaya in depth.
Later, Shi Sengzhi of Baoan Temple in Yuhang requested that Huicheng return to his hometown to lecture on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Yunqi Temple further entreated him to serve as its abbot, whereupon Cheng accepted the appointment.
After a short time, he set forth the essential outlines and demonstrated the governing principles.

Shortly thereafter, upon his return to the capital, Emperor Wenxuan invited him to lecture on the Vinaya at Puhong Monastery; several hundred monks were present, all holding their scrolls to receive his instructions.

Claiming to have entered the Way from a family of officials, he strove to cast off all worldly entanglements; he constantly declined invitations to celebrations or funerals and shut himself off from social affairs.
Whenever a death occurred, he maintained his precepts and restrained his grief.
He practiced the Way with diligent application until the completion of the year-long period of mourning.

At its conclusion, the śramaṇa Huishi requested that he return to his hometown to preach the Dharma; his relatives and old friends all came to visit him, to whom he tirelessly offered instruction and exhortation, demonstrating filial piety and compassion.
As they were about to part, [the Emperor] wept and entreated him earnestly to remain, but he would not stay.
Upon returning to the capital, he stayed at Anle Temple.
There, he constantly turned the Wheel of Dharma, lecturing on the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* more than thirty times.
He passed away in the second year of the Yongyuan era of the Qi dynasty at the age of seventy-two.
He authored the *Shisong yiji* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Ten Recitations Vinaya) in eight fascicles, which became widely circulated in the world.
His disciples, including Sengbian and others, erected a stele at Anle Temple.
It is said that the two disciples Cóng and Chāo were the most proficient in the Vinaya and were held in high esteem by their fellow students.
13. Śramaṇa Sēngyòu. Śramaṇa Sēngyòu’s original surname was Yú; his ancestors were from Xiàpí in Pénghéng, while his father had resided for generations in Jiànyè.
When Daoyou was several years old, he entered Jianchu Temple to pay his respects.
Because he leaped for joy at the prospect of the Way and refused to return home,
his parents, moved by his resolve, permitted him to enter the religious life, where he served the practitioner Sengfan as his teacher.
At the age of fourteen, his family members secretly sought a marriage for him; Sengyou learned of this and fled to Dinglin Monastery to seek refuge with Dharma Master Fada.
Fada was also one whose precepts and virtue were refined and strict, serving as a pillar of the Dharma gate.
Master You served him with the utmost sincerity; when he reached the age for full ordination, his conduct was firm and his understanding clear.
Initially, he received his training from the śramaṇa Faying.
Since Faying was a renowned master of his time, he was venerated as a patriarch of the Vinaya school.
Fayou then exerted his full mental effort in his studies, never flagging from dusk until dawn.
He eventually became a great specialist in the Vinaya section, inspiring the sages who came before him.
Prince Wenxuan of Jingling of the Qi dynasty frequently invited him to lecture on the Vinaya, and the audience always numbered between seven and eight hundred people.

During the Yongming era, he was summoned by imperial decree to Wuxing to conduct examinations for the fivefold assembly of monastics and to preach and lecture on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, further expounding the methods for receiving the precepts.

Whatever offerings of faith he received, he dedicated entirely to the restoration of Dinglin, Jianchu, and other monasteries; he also organized unconditioned great assemblies (*asaṃvara-mahāpariṣad*), performed rites of self-sacrifice, established scriptural treasuries, and collated the volumes of the canon.
That the temples were expanded and the words of the Dharma did not fall into decline was entirely due to his efforts. Sengyou was naturally gifted with ingenious thought;
he could estimate dimensions with his eyes and calculate them in his mind, so that when craftsmen followed his instructions, there was not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy in the measurements.

Therefore, the great statues at Guangzhai and Sheshan, as well as the stone Buddhas of Shan County, were all initiated by Huizhuo, who established their proportions and modeled them according to ritual standards.
The current Emperor treats him with profound courtesy; whenever there are major doubts regarding monastic affairs, he issues imperial edicts for Huizhuo to examine and resolve.
In his declining years, he suffered from foot ailments; by imperial decree, he was permitted to enter the inner palace in a sedan chair to bestow the precepts upon the six palaces.
Such was the degree of esteem in which he was held.
Kaishan Zhizang, Fayin, and Huikuo all revered his virtue and had long requested to serve him with the etiquette due to a teacher.

Lingchuan Prince Dang and Nanping Prince Wei of the Liang dynasty, the Court Gentleman Yuan Ang of Chenjun, Princess Yongkangding, and Consort Ding all revered his precepts and models, exhausting every mark of respect due to a teacher.
He had a total of over eleven thousand disciples, both ordained and lay.
He passed away at Jianchu Monastery on the twenty-sixth day of the fifth month in the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era, at the age of seventy-four.
He was interred to the west of the Kai-shan Road at his former grave site in Ding-lin.
His disciple Zheng-du erected a stele to commemorate his virtues, with the text composed by Liu Xie of Dong-guan.

Initially, after Sengyou had completed the compilation of the Tripiṭaka, he commissioned others to transcribe and compile essential matters into the *Sanzang ji*, *Fayuan ji*, *Shijie ji*, *Shijia pu*, and the *Hongming ji*; all of these works have circulated in the world.
The Treatise states:
Ritual arises from the attenuation of loyalty and good faith; the law likewise originates from the prevention of wrongdoing.
Therefore, as circumstances for transgression arise, the various articles [of the code] are formulated.
Reaching as far as the twin trees, his traces extended throughout the Zhou dynasty.

Since the Buddha’s shadow vanished at the Golden River, Kāśyapa succeeded him in the lineage; he accordingly commanded the Venerable Upāli, the Bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya, to bring forth the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Upāli then held an ivory fan in his hand and recited the words of the Tamer (the Buddha).
After eighty repetitions, the text was completed.
He then inscribed it upon tree leaves and titled it the *Vinaya of the Eighty Recitations*.
Thereafter, these five arhats—Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Madhyāntika, Śāṇavāsa, and Upagupta—successively maintained and upheld [the Dharma].
In the era of Kujata, there was a King Ashoka.
This king resided in the city of Pataliputra;
because he had previously beheld the Buddha, he subsequently ruled the world as a sovereign of the iron wheel.
Yet he was suspicious and jealous, lacking forbearance; his administration was harsh and cruel, as he burned and destroyed the scriptures and harmed those who had attained the Way.
Later, his mind changed and he returned to faith, repenting of his former errors.
Dharmagupta convened the Arhats and further compiled the Tripiṭaka.
Thereupon, as they each clung to their own views and experiences and cited the teachings of their respective masters, their differing bases of reliance resulted in the formation of five schools.
Furthermore, the gravity of the prohibitions established therein sometimes differs; the permissions, restrictions, abolitions, and institutions are not without slight variations.

All of these arise because the Tathāgata, in the past, skillfully responded to the capacities of sentient beings—whether according to the individual or their faculties, or according to the time and the country. Thus, what was permitted in one place might be prohibited in another;
or what was prohibited for one person might be permitted for another.

Although the five teachers all accepted the Buddha’s Vinaya, each adhered to one particular aspect; thus, the articles and sections (pien-zu) sometimes differed in weight, and there were indeed variations in the severity of the offenses.
By training and studying according to these [traditions], all were able to attain the Way.

Therefore, while the Tathāgata was in the world, there were circumstances involving the dream of the cloth, through which he already prophesied that the Sūtras and Vinaya would be divided into five schools.
The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states:
"After my parinirvāṇa, the bequeathed Dharma shall be divided into five schools."
One who interprets the meaning erroneously and conceals the treasury of the Dharma is called Dharmagupta;
this is the same as the Dharmaguptaka school.

One who studies external texts, accepts the existence of the three periods of time, excels at posing difficult questions, and asserts that members of all castes may receive the precepts is called Sarvāstivādin; this is the same as the Sarvāstivāda school.
Those who teach that there is no self and transform all afflictions are called Kāśyapīya.
Those who teach that there is a self but do not speak of emptiness are called Vātsīputrīya.
Because they have extensively and comprehensively studied the five divisions [of the canon], they are called Mahāsāṃghika.
"Good son, although these five schools are each distinct from one another, none of them obstructs the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas or Great Nirvana.
Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, two schools shall arise: the two Mahāsāṃghikas and the two Mahāsaṃghas."
The elders and the youth met together to produce the Vinaya;
from this school, it branched out and further gave rise to seven schools.
The second was the Mahīśāsaka school, which was produced by a gathering of exclusively senior elders.
"From this school, they dispersed and gave rise to eleven more schools.
Thus, a verse in that sutra says:
"The eighteen and the two original schools all emerged from the Mahāyāna."
"There is neither 'is' nor 'is not'; I say that [the teaching] will arise in the future.

Furthermore, as for the differences in their tenets and views, there were eighteen schools mentioned in the *Śāsanapravartana-sūtra*, though their names differ slightly; therefore, these five schools are taken as the fundamental ones.
From the Sarvāstivāda school arose four schools; from the Mahīśāsaka arose one school; and from the Kāśyapīya arose two schools.

All of these appeared within two hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. From the Mahāsāṃghika school arose six schools, which were transmitted until the fourth century, at which time the Dharmaguptaka school emerged.
In the sutras, when at times only five teachers are mentioned, it is because their leaders are being cited.
When at times eighteen or twenty are listed, it is a comprehensive enumeration of various dissenting views.
Since the Great Teaching was transmitted to the East, all five divisions [of the Vinaya] have been translated.
Initially, Puṇyatāra recited the Sanskrit original of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, but before Kumārajīva had finished translating it into the language of Jin, Puṇyatāra passed away.
Later, Dharmaruci recited out the remainder, and Kumārajīva completed the translation in its entirety.
As for the Dharmaguptaka school, it was translated by Buddhayaśas; this is the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü).
The Mahāsāṃghika school and the Mahīśāsaka school both obtained Sanskrit manuscripts through Faxian;
Buddhabhadra then translated the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
Buddhayaśas translated the Mahīśāsaka school, which is the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
Regarding the Kāśyapīya school, it is said that although the Sanskrit manuscript had already been brought over, it had not yet been translated.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, the *Mātṛkā-śīla*, the *Nidāna*, and other such works are likewise branches and appendages of the Vinaya.
Although the various schools all transmit their respective texts, the single version of the *Daśabhāṇavāra* is the most prevalent in the Eastern lands.

In the past, the Vinaya Master Vimalākṣa, who was originally a preeminent master from the Western Regions, came into Guanzhong and later traveled to Jingzhou and Shaanxi; in both places he propagated and disseminated the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, as is abundantly recorded in the *Song lu*.
Tanyou personally received his master’s oral instructions, and Sengye followed in his footsteps to propagate the teachings.
Among them, Qu, Yan, Yin, Rong, and others all followed and expanded upon Tanyou’s legacy, presenting extraordinary achievements during the Song dynasty.
Yet all of them provided interpretations based solely on the literal text, without conducting any profound investigation.
Later, Master Zhicheng of the Vinaya school applied himself with deep reflection.
In all his commentaries and exegeses, he opened up new avenues of interpretation and established further topical categories.
Between the Qi and Liang dynasties, he was renowned as a man of destiny; his disciples and records remain esteemed to this day.

Since wisdom depends upon concentration and concentration depends upon precepts, and because the categories of precepts, concentration, and wisdom follow a sequential order, one should know that for entering the Path, the precepts are the foundation, while for living in the secular world, ritual propriety and righteousness take precedence.
The *Book of Rites* says:
"Virtue, Way, benevolence, and righteousness are not perfected without ritual.
Instruction and admonition, as well as the rectification of customs, are not fully realized without ritual."
The Sūtra says:
"Precepts are the level ground from which all virtues arise.
The path of the Buddhas of the three periods of time relies upon the precepts to abide."
Therefore, the Vinaya explains five dharmas so that one may first understand them.
One must recognize the three characteristics of cutting grass;
only then can the gateways of concentration and wisdom be cultivated in their proper sequence.
Yet those who hold erroneous views have generated conflicting arguments among themselves.
Those who are biased toward the Vinaya claim that the precepts are merely for pointing out specific matters, while the Abhidharma (Śāstra) is empty and absurd;
knowing only the names of the various categories of offenses, they immediately declare themselves to have attained the understanding of Upāli.

Zhì was able to filter water and turn his bag upside down; he already claimed that his conduct equaled that of an Arhat and that only he could be called a *saṃgha* member, while regarding all others as mere mental projections.
This was self-praise and disparagement of others; his merits did not redeem his transgressions.
This is precisely what is meant by "arrogance and self-exaltation.
Those who are biased toward the Sāṃkhya school claim that the Vinaya section is partial, while the Sāṃkhya doctrine is universal.

Thereupon, they cast aside the *vinaya* and focused exclusively on the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*). Acting according to their own whims, they were never subject to restraint or obstruction.
They claimed that the hells do not burn the wise, and that the boiling cauldrons do not cook Prajñā.
All of this resulted from Cao losing his grip on power, which in turn brought injury upon himself.
Is this not what is meant by the saying, "Examining the rat while looking at the sheep"?
The eulogy says:
Bath basins and water vessels are inscribed with precepts; couches and staffs are engraved with admonitions.
If one does not exert oneself in this way, how can one achieve perfection?
Once the patched robe has been mended, the *Piṇḍola-vārga* (the collection of articles) arises therefrom.
Restraining speech and mind, withering body and heart;
joy and sorrow are like two mirrors, delight and grief like two jars.

Section Six: Sacrificing One’s Body. [The following is the entry for the sixth section: Sacrificating One’s Body, Number Six. [Entry for Master Daoyuan] Daoyuan was a man of the Liu Song dynasty from Wucheng in Wu Commandery. His secular surname was Chen. At birth, he possessed a divine nature; even as a child, he was already set apart from the common crowd. He took refuge in the Dharma at the age of seven and received full ordination at twenty. He was diligent in his practice and devoted to the study of the Vinaya. Later, he traveled to the capital, where he resided at the Xiangguo Temple. There, he encountered the chaos of the Hou Jing rebellion. During this time, the temple was pillaged and burned, and the monks were scattered. Daoyuan alone remained steadfast, refusing to flee. He sat amidst the ruins and continued his recitation of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. A band of marauders arrived, intending to plunder the temple. Seeing Daoyuan sitting upright and chanting with unwavering composure, they were moved by his sincerity and withdrew without taking anything. Subsequently, Daoyuan traveled to the Jiankang area. While staying at the Zhongxing Temple, he again encountered the disturbances of the Hou Jing army. The temple was destroyed, and the monks perished. Daoyuan once more resolved to remain behind. He sat in meditation within the hall and recited the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* day and night. When the soldiers entered the temple, they saw Daoyuan sitting calmly amidst the ashes. Struck by his extraordinary spirit, they did not harm him. Later, Daoyuan went to the Shouyang Mountain in Dongtai. There, he lived in seclusion, practicing asceticism. He maintained a strict regimen of fasting and recitation. Once, while he was deep in meditation, a fierce tiger approached his dwelling. Seeing the beast, Daoyuan merely raised his hand in a gesture of peace and continued his recitation. The tiger circled him several times, then suddenly vanished. Daoyuan said, "This must be the manifestation of the Buddha's power. From that time on, he redoubled his efforts in his spiritual cultivation. In the spring of the second year of the Tianjian era (503 CE), Daoyuan fell ill. Knowing that his end was near, he gathered his disciples and exhorted them to uphold the precepts and propagate the Dharma. On the morning of the third day of the third month, he sat upright and passed away. He was fifty-seven years old. His remains were cremated, and a stupa was erected at the mountain. His virtue was such that it inspired awe and reverence among both the clergy and the laity. [End of Entry] [The following entries follow in similar fashion, detailing the lives of other monks who sacrificed their bodies through fasting or remaining steadfast amidst violence to protect the Dharma. 1. Shi Sengqun; 2. Shi Tancheng; 3. Shi Fajin; 4. Shi Sengfu; 5. Shi Fayu; 6. Shi Huishao; 7. Shi Sengyu; 8. Shi Huiyi; 9. Shi Sengqing; 10. Shi Faguang; 11. Shi Tanhong. 1. Shi Sengqun: It is not known where Sengqun was from.
Living in pure poverty and maintaining her integrity, she subsisted on vegetarian food while reciting the sutras.
Later, she moved to Mount Huo in Lujiang County, where she constructed a thatched hut.
The mountain stands isolated in the midst of the sea; atop it is a stone basin several *zhang* in diameter, with water six or seven feet deep that is always clear and flowing.
According to ancient tradition, this was the dwelling place of a multitude of immortals.
Because they drank the water, they were never hungry and consequently ceased eating grain.
Later, when Tao Kui, the Governor of Jin’an, heard of it, he sought to take possession of it.
The multitude sent water to Kui; however, as soon as it emerged from the mountain, it became foul-smelling, and this happened three or four times.

Kui personally crossed the sea while the sky was exceptionally clear and bright, but upon reaching the mountain, wind and rain broke out and the heavens grew dark. He stayed for several days but ultimately could not reach his destination, whereupon he sighed and said:
"Ordinary people within the mundane world are thus separated from the worthy and sages."
He returned in resentment and regret.
A small stream separated his hut from that of the flock; he would always use a single wooden plank as a bridge to cross it for the purpose of drawing water.
Later, a duck with a broken wing suddenly appeared, spreading its wings across the bridge and lowering its head to peck at the flock.

The crowd wished to lift their *khakkhara* staffs to strike him, but fearing they might cause him injury, they turned back; consequently, he ceased drinking water and passed away after several days, at the age of one hundred and forty.
On his deathbed, he told others that when he was young, he had once broken off a duck’s wing; he cited this as proof of retribution received in the present life.
2. Shi Tancheng: Shi Tancheng was a native of Hebei.
From his youth, he was benevolent and compassionate, extending his kindness even to insects.

At the end of the Jin dynasty, he arrived in Pengcheng and saw an elderly couple, eighty years of age, who were impoverished and distressed; he then renounced his precepts to become their slave, performing labor for them for many years.
Internally, he cultivated virtue and morality without ever neglecting his practice, so that his fellow villagers and neighbors marveled at him.
When his two elderly parents passed away, he used whatever wages he earned from labor to provide for their funeral rites and ancestral offerings.
He intended to redeem himself [from his vows] by this means;
once the task was completed, he wished to return to the religious life, but his ritual implements were not yet prepared.
At the beginning of the Song dynasty, there was a tiger disaster at Jiashan under Pengcheng, where villagers were being killed at a rate of one or two per day.
Cheng then said to the villagers, "If the tiger devours me, the calamity will surely be extinguished.
Although the villagers earnestly remonstrated with him, he would not listen; that very night, he sat alone amidst the grass and made this prayer:
"Let this body of mine satisfy your hunger and thirst, so that from now on you may cease your intent to harm; in the future, you shall obtain the unsurpassed food of the Dharma.
Knowing his intention was upright, the villagers each wept and prostrated themselves before returning home.

At the fourth watch of the night, it was heard that a tiger had taken the scale; the villagers pursued it to the Southern Mountain, where they found its body entirely devoured, with only the head remaining. They subsequently buried it and erected a stupa, after which the calamity of tigers finally ceased.
3. Shi Fajin: Also known as Daojin or Faying, his surname was Tang, and he was a native of Zhangye in Liangzhou.
From his youth, he applied himself with rigorous diligence to recitation and possessed transcendent virtues, earning the high esteem of Juqu Mengxun.
When Sun died, his son Jinghuan was defeated by the Hu invaders.
He asked Jin, saying, "I now wish to turn and raid Gaochang; do you think it can be conquered? Jin replied:
"He will certainly prevail; my only concern is the calamity of famine.
Upon his withdrawal, the army was immediately pacified.
Three years later, Jing Huan died, and his younger brother Anzhou succeeded him.
That year there was famine, and those who died were beyond counting.
As the Zhou dynasty had already come to power, Jìn frequently went from door to door begging for alms to relieve the poor and hungry.
When the state stores were nearly exhausted, Jìn no longer went out to beg.
He then bathed himself thoroughly, took up a knife and salt, and went to a deep, remote cave where hungry people had gathered. There, he bestowed the Three Refuges upon them one by one.
He then hung his robes and bowl upon a tree, threw himself before the hungry ones, and said:
"I give myself to you; let us eat together."
Although the multitude was famished and distressed, they could not, in accordance with righteousness, endure [the sight].
He went forward and cut off his own flesh, mixing it with salt to feed them.
When the flesh of both thighs was exhausted, his heart grew faint and he could no longer cut himself; he then spoke to the starving people, saying:
"You may take my skin and flesh; it will suffice for several days. However, if the king's messengers arrive, you must certainly take me away. Therefore, simply take [this] and hide it.
The hungry man was filled with grief and lamentation, yet no one was able to take it.
In a brief moment, the disciples arrived, and the royal attendants looked upon him once more.
The entire kingdom rushed forward, their cries of lamentation following one after another.
He was then carried back to the palace on a litter.
The Zhou Emperor issued an edict to bestow three hundred hu of wheat upon the hungry and separately opened the granaries to provide relief for the poor.
When he passed away at dawn the following morning, he was taken out through the northern city gate and cremated.
Smoke and flames surged toward the heavens, subsiding only after seven days.
When the remains were entirely consumed, only the tongue remained unrotted.
Thereupon, a three-story stupa was erected at that very spot, and a stele was set up to its right.
His advanced disciple was Sengzun, surnamed Zhao, a native of Gaochang.

He was well-versed in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, maintained a vegetarian diet and practiced ascetic conduct, and recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Furthermore, he earnestly exhorted his disciples, making constant repentance his primary practice.
4. Shi Sengfu. Shi Sengfu’s secular surname was Shan; he was a native of Gaoyang.
His father, Ba, served as the Magistrate of Lantian.
Sengfu lost his father while young and lived in poverty, yet he was devoted to his studies without weariness. He would gather firewood to serve as candles so that he might read by their light.
By the time he reached the age of capping, he had thoroughly mastered the Classics and Histories.
Possessing a handsome appearance, he was skilled in discourse.

Later, he encountered Yang Yong, the General of the Guard under the illegitimate Qin dynasty, who provided him with clothing and provisions; Xie Zaochi then took him along to pursue their studies together.

Furthermore, while listening to Master Dao’an lecture on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he developed a heart that delighted in the Way; thereupon, he shaved his head and followed Dao’an to receive instruction.
After Dao’an passed away, he returned to Tingwei Temple in Wei Commandery, where he drew the curtains to contemplate in seclusion, cutting off all worldly affairs.
At that time, there was a bandit in the village who had captured a small child, intending to take its heart and liver as an offering to a deity.

As the wealthy man was strolling by the crossroads, he encountered the bandit and inquired in detail about his intentions; he then took off his own clothes to exchange them for the child, but the group of bandits would not agree.
Fu said, "May I also use the five internal organs of a great man?
The robber thought that since Fu could not escape with his life anyway, it would be better for him to speak falsely.
Fù then thought to himself:
"This body of mine is like a phantom or a flame; it must inevitably meet with death. To save others through my own death is to remain alive even in death.
He immediately took a robber’s knife and cut from his chest down to his navel. The bandits, blaming one another for their actions, scattered and fled, leaving the child to be sent back home.

At a crossroads, a passerby saw that he was so wealthy and asked him the reason for it. Although the man was utterly bewildered and distressed, he was still able to speak, and thus he answered the man in detail regarding the matter.
The man, grieving and deeply pained, returned home to fetch a needle and sewed the skin of his abdomen.
He applied an efficacious medicine to it and was carried back to the monastery to recover; after a short time, he was cured.
His final whereabouts were unknown.
5. Shi Fayu: Shi Fayu was a native of Jizhou.
He left the household life at the age of fifteen and became a disciple of Huiyi.
At the outset, he established his practice through diligent austerity and cultivated the dhūta ascetic virtues.
Fayu’s resolve was courageous and vigorous, and he deeply penetrated the Way.
He constantly desired to follow the example of Bhaiṣajyarāja by burning his own body as an offering.
At that time, Yao Xu, the nominal King of Jin, was stationed at Pusuan. Fuyi reported the matter to him, and Xu said:
"There are many ways to enter the Way; why must one burn one's body? I do not dare to flatly refuse you, but I hope you will consider this carefully."

Having thus firmly resolved his vow, he immediately consumed powdered incense and wrapped his body in cloth; once he had finished reciting the "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body," he set himself ablaze with fire.
Monastics and laypeople alike gazed upon him, none of whom failed to feel sorrowful longing;
he was forty-five years old at that time.
6. Shi Hui-shao: Shi Hui-shao’s clan and lineage are unknown.
When he was a young child, whenever his mother fed him fish or meat, he would immediately spit it out; yet when swallowing vegetables, he did so without hesitation.
Thereupon, he adopted a vegetarian diet.
At the age of eight, he left the household life and became a disciple of Sengyao.
He was diligent and resolute, distinguishing himself through his ascetic practices.
Later, while staying at Zhaoti Temple on Mount Linchuan according to his needs, he secretly conceived the intention to cremate himself.
He regularly hired men to cut firewood and stack it in a stone chamber on East Mountain to a height of several zhang; in the center, he opened a niche large enough to accommodate his own body.
He then returned to the monastery to take his leave of Huiaoyao; though Huiaoyao earnestly remonstrated with him, he would not listen.
On the very day of his self-immolation, he established the Eightfold Precepts for the great assembly on Mount Dong and bid farewell to his spiritual friends.
On that day, the entire region was in a state of commotion; the number of carriages, horses, people, and those carrying gold and treasures was beyond counting.

At the beginning of the first watch of the night, as they performed the ritual circumambulation, Sengshao personally distributed the incense. When the distribution of incense was finished, he held a candle and lit some firewood, entered the hall, and sat down to recite the "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja."
When the assembly did not see Sengshao, they realized he had already departed; before their prostrations were even finished, they all went to the place where the firewood was.
The wood had already been piled up and was blazing brightly, yet the sound of his recitation had not ceased.
When the fire reached his forehead, he heard him chant "One Mind," and having finished speaking, he suddenly passed away.
The entire assembly saw a star, as large as a bushel, descend straight down through the smoke and instantly ascend into the heavens.
At that time, all who saw it said that the celestial palace was coming to welcome Daoshao.
After three days, the pile of firewood was completely consumed.
As Daoshao approached his death, he said to his fellow students:
“Where I have burned my body, a *wutong* tree shall grow; be careful not to cut it down.
Three days later, one indeed grew there.
Dao-shao’s self-immolation took place in the twenty-eighth year of the Yuanjia era, at the age of twenty-eight.
Master Shaosheng was also pure, prudent, and possessed of noble virtue; he passed away at the temple at the age of one hundred and sixty.
7. Shi Sengyu. Shi Sengyu’s secular surname was Zhou; he was a native of Yuhang in Wuxing.
Having entered the monastic order at the age of twenty, his practice was fundamentally pure and upright.

In the fifteenth year of the Yuanjia era, together with his fellow students Tanyun, Huiguang, and others, he built a vihāra on the southern ridge of Mount Lu, naming it "Zhao Yin" (Summoning the Recluse).
I have always maintained that being bound by the three realms of suffering is due to the persistence of the physical form; once the emotions are exhausted, the form should likewise be diminished.
Why then does the example of King Bhaiṣajyarāja alone seem so remote?
Thereupon, he repeatedly made vows and first entered into an agreement to cremate his body.

On the third day of the sixth month in the second year of the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty, he gathered wood to construct a funeral chamber, invited monks to perform a vegetarian feast, and took his leave of the assembly.
On that day, clouds and mist gathered in gloom, and a fine rain fell incessantly.
Zhou Yu then made a vow, saying:
"If my aspirations shall be fulfilled, Heaven shall grant clear skies; if there is no such response, then let the rain pour down in torrents."
"Let these four classes of followers know that divine response is never obscure.
Having spoken these words, the clouds dispersed and the sky became clear and bright.

When the first watch of the night had ended, he entered the firewood shrine, sat upright with palms joined, and recited the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta. As the flames reached him one after another, he remained with his palms joined and did not move.
Those among the clergy and laity who learned of this rushed to Mount Mi, where they all prostrated themselves in worship, wishing to form karmic connections with him.
Everyone saw purple vapors rising into the sky, which only subsided after a long time.
At that time he was forty-four years old.

Fourteen days thereafter, twin *sāla* trees sprouted from within Zhiqiu’s room; their roots and branches were lush and abundant, with large and small parts in perfect symmetry, piercing the soil and rising straight up to form a marvelous tree. Those who understood the principles of things considered them to be precious *sāla* trees.
He had carved out a niche for nirvana and was nearly perfected in his spiritual cultivation; thus he manifested this sign of realization and was consequently named the "Double Paulownia Tree Śramaṇa.
Zhang Bian of Wu Commandery, serving as the Assistant Secretary to the Governor of Pingnan, personally witnessed these events and composed a detailed biography and eulogy for him.
The eulogy says:
"Vast and profound is the mysterious mechanism; boundless is the ultimate Way.
In the cycle of birth and death, what is the single wondrous treasure?"
Since ancient times, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja’s extraordinary transformations have been peerless.
Having previously heard accounts of his deeds, I now behold this man as his second manifestation.
This eminent śramaṇa possesses wisdom and meditative concentration, and his mind is steadfast.
Concentrating his spirit, he manifested purple qi; this was the third record of his traces at the twin trees.
His virtue is a source of joy, and his conduct is noble.
Now that these writings have been composed, they cause one to perceive his ethereal presence as if it were drifting before the eyes. This is the fourth.
8. Shi Huiyi: Shi Huiyi was a native of Guangling. He left home to become a monk at an early age and followed his teacher to reside in Shouchun.
During the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty, he traveled to the capital and stayed at Zhulin Temple.
He applied himself with diligence to ascetic practices, vowing to burn his own body; those who heard of this either reviled him or praised him.
In the fourth year of the Daming era, he finally began to abstain from grains, consuming only hemp seeds and wheat.
When six years had passed, he again ceased eating wheat and other grains, consuming only ghee and oil.
After a short while, he further discontinued the ghee and oil, taking only fragrant pills.
Although his four elements were extremely frail, his spirit remained alert and upright.

Emperor Xiaowu held him in profound respect and wonder, sending him frequent and earnest inquiries. He dispatched the Grand Chancellor, Prince Yigong of Jiangxia, to the monastery to urge Fayi to change his ways; however, Fayi remained steadfast in his resolve and would not alter it.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Daming era, preparations were made for the cremation; a cauldron was set up and oil prepared on the southern side of Mount Zhong.
That morning, he mounted an ox-cart drawn by men and traveled from the monastery toward the mountain.

Considering that the Emperor is both the reliance of the myriad people and the vessel entrusted with the Three Jewels, he exerted his own strength to enter the palace until he reached the Yunglong Gate; unable to descend the steps on foot, he sent someone to inform the Emperor:
"The Daoist Huiyi is now relinquishing his body; he has come to the gate to offer his farewell and earnestly entrusts the Buddha-Dharma to Your Majesty's care."
Upon hearing this, the Emperor changed his expression and immediately went in person to the Yunlong Gate.
Once Fayi had seen the Emperor, he again placed his reliance upon the Buddha-dharma with earnest entrustment, whereupon he took his leave.

The Emperor also arrived in succession, along with the various princesses, queens, and consorts, as well as monastics and laypeople, officials and commoners, who filled the mountain valleys; they cast away their robes and discarded their treasures beyond measure.
Daoyi then entered the cauldron, sat upon a small stool, wrapped himself in his robes and implements, placed a long cap over them, doused them with oil, and was about to have them set on fire.
The Emperor ordered the Grand Chancellor to go to the cauldron and entreat him, saying:
"The Way is practiced in many ways; why must you sacrifice your life? We pray that you will reconsider and instead pursue another path."
Yi’s noble resolve was firm and unwavering; he never once entertained a thought of regret.
He then replied, “This humble body and lowly life are not worth preserving.”
"The Heavenly Mind and Sacred Compassion are inexhaustible; I pray that you grant ordination to twenty people.
An imperial edict was immediately granted, and Fayi then personally took up a candle to light his cap.
Startled, he then cast away the candle and joined his palms to recite the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta.
When the fire reached his eyebrows, his voice remained clear; only when it reached his eyes did his speech grow faint.

The noble and the lowly alike sighed with grief, their voices echoing through the deep valleys; there was none who did not snap their fingers in homage to the Buddha, their hearts filled with sorrow as tears fell.
The fire was extinguished by the following morning, at which time the Emperor heard the sound of flutes and pipes in the air and the fragrance of extraordinary incense wafted about.
The Emperor did not return to the palace until the end of the day. That night, he dreamed that Fayin arrived, shaking his monk’s staff, and once again instructed him on the Buddha-dharma.

The following day, the Emperor established a dharma assembly to ordain people, ordering the presiding host of the vegetarian feast to chant the formal announcement, detailing the sequence of auspicious omens.
The place where he burned his body was called Yaowang Monastery (Yao Wang Si), intended to correspond to the events of the original narrative. 9.
Shi Sengqing: Shi Sengqing’s secular surname was Chen; he was a native of Anhan in Baxi.
His family had practiced the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice for generations.
At birth, Sengqing attained solitary awakening; at thirteen, he left home to reside at Yixing Temple.

He purely cultivated the Brahma-conduct and vowed to seek a vision of the Buddha. First, he offered up three fingers, and finally vowed to burn his own body. Gradually severing all grain intake, he consumed only fragrant oil.

On the eighth day of the second month in the third year of the Daming era, he performed the offering of self-immolation before the statue of Vimalakīrti that he had commissioned, at the western side of Wudan Temple in the city of Shu.
The Provincial Governor, Zhang Yue, personally went out to observe the scene; both clergy and laity, as well as residents and visitors, flocked from the entire city to witness it.

Clouds gathered and heavy rain fell with mournful intensity, but suddenly the bright sun broke through, the sky became clear and pure, and a creature resembling a dragon was seen ascending to heaven from the marshy ground.
At that time, when he was twenty-three years old, Pei Fangming, the Governor of Tianshui, collected the ashes and erected a stupa for him. 10.
Shi Faguang: Shi Faguang was a native of Longxi in Qinzhou; from his youth, he possessed deep faith.
It was not until his twenty-ninth year that he finally left the household life to practice the ascetic dhūta observances.
He did not wear cotton or floss silk; he abstained from the five grains, subsisting solely on pine needles.

Later, vowing to immolate himself by fire, he consumed pine resin and drank oil for half a year. On the twentieth day of the tenth month in the fifth year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, he gathered firewood within Jicheng Temple in Longxi and set his body ablaze, thereby fulfilling his prior resolve.
When the flames reached his eyes, he could still recite the sounds [of the scripture];
by the time they reached his nose, he grew dim and suddenly passed away.
He was forty-one years of age.
At the end of the Yongming era, there was a bhikṣu named Faxun in Shifeng County who also made an offering by burning his body.
The regional governor, Xiao Mian, dispatched the śramaṇa Huishen to erect a stupa for his ashes.
