11. Shi Tanhong. Shi Tanhong was a native of Huanglong.
From his youth, he cultivated the practice of the precepts and specialized in the Vinaya-piṭaka.
During the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, he traveled south to Panyu and resided at Tai Temple.
In the evening, he went again to Xianshan Temple in Jiaozhi.
There he recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, vowing to take rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
In the second year of the Xiaojian era, he gathered firewood on the mountain, secretly entered among the piles, and immolated himself with fire.
The disciples pursued and caught up with him, embracing him to bring him back; half his body was already rotting away, but after a month he recovered slightly.
Later, when a religious assembly was held in a nearby village, the entire monastery went there.
On this day, Hong again entered the valley to burn his body; the villagers pursued him, but his life had already come to an end.
Thereupon they added more fuel and advanced the fire, which was only completely consumed the following day.
On that day, the villagers all saw Daohong’s body, golden in color, riding a golden deer and traveling westward with great haste, without pausing for greetings.
Only then did the monastics and laypeople realize his divine extraordinariness; together they collected his ashes and bones to erect a stupa over them.
The Treatise says:
That which is most highly esteemed by those possessing form is the body;
that which is most cherished by those with conscious emotions is life.
Therefore, those who consume fat and drink blood, riding in fine carriages and wearing light garments, do so because they desire joy and contentment.
Those who ingest *shu* and hold *dan* in their mouths, guarding against the physical while cultivating their nature, do so because they desire longevity.
As for such matters as plucking a single hair to benefit the world, they are stingy and do not do it;
when it comes to giving up a single meal to sustain another's remaining life, they cherish it and will not give it away.
This is an excessive fault.
Since there have been those of vast knowledge and far-reaching vision who have set aside their own interests to enrich others;
who have realized that the three realms are but a dwelling in the long night, and awakened to the four modes of birth as being like a dream or an illusion.
The spirit soars beyond the flight of feathers, while the physical frame remains stagnant within the vessel of the body.
Therefore, from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, not a single thought is entertained;
kingdom, city, wife, and children are abandoned as if they were mere weeds and chaff.
The person discussed here now is likely one such as these:
Sengqun treated his mind as a single duck and drowned himself by cutting off the water;
Sengfu stopped to save a single child and cut open his own abdomen to preserve his life.

Fajin cut his own flesh to feed others, and Tancheng offered himself as fodder for a starving tiger; these were all those who esteemed the way of universal salvation and forgot themselves to benefit all beings.
In the past, when the Prince cast himself down, his merit surpassed that of nine kalpas;
when he cut his own flesh to ransom a bird, the three thousandfold world system was struck with awe and trembled.
Truly, such a person as this was by nature transcendent and loftily sublime.
Subsequently, from Fayu down to Tanhong, all of them reduced their physical bodies to ashes and cast aside their cherished attachments;
some prayed for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) out of emotion, while others aspired to be born in the Land of Contentment (Zhi-zu) through their vows.
Thus, twin paulownia trees manifest within the chamber, and a single pavilion appears from mid-air.
Auspicious omens shine brilliantly, emerging in succession with the passing of time.
Nevertheless, as the holy teachings differ, their prescriptions regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited likewise vary.

If one possesses great authority for the sake of sentient beings and acts in accordance with the timing, benefiting them in myriad ways, this is not something that can be regulated by formal teachings.
Thus, a sutra says:
"To burn even a single finger or toe is superior to the giving of a kingdom or a city."
If one is an ordinary monk who has left the household life, it is fundamentally through dignified deportment that he should gather and influence others.
Yet now, by mutilating his physical form and destroying the appearance of a field of merit, when examined in discourse, there are both gains and losses.
Success lies in forgetting the self; failure lies in violating the precepts.
Thus Nāgārjuna said:
"A bodhisattva who has newly begun their practice cannot simultaneously fulfill all the perfections."
Some may fulfill generosity (*dāna*) while failing in filial piety, such as the prince who threw himself to the tiger;
others may fulfill wisdom (*prajñā*) while failing in compassion (*maitrī*), such as inspecting others to cut off their food.
These all arise because their practice has not yet reached perfect completeness, and thus there are inevitably excesses and deficiencies.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that there are eighty thousand families of worms within the body that share the same vital energy as the person.
When human life comes to an end, these worms perish along with it.
For this reason, after an Arhat has passed away, the Buddha permitted the cremation of the body.
Some say that he was cremated even while still alive, perhaps because his life-force had been lost to insects;
others say that since even Arhats enter the fire, what is there to be surprised about?
As for those who say one enters the fire-light, they have already relinquished their life;
it is by means of the power of spiritual wisdom that they subsequently set themselves ablaze.
Nevertheless, even a Bodhisattva of the Ground-nature cannot avoid the physical body of retribution.
At times they cast their bodies into masses of fire; at times they tear apart their skeletons to divide among men.
One should know that the discourse on killing insects is thus thoroughly detailed in its ultimate implications.
Indeed, the three poisons and the four inversions are the very roots of birth and death.
The seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path are truly the essential routes to Nirvana.
Why must one first burn and roast the physical body before escaping suffering?

If one’s spiritual rank is close to attaining the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) yet one’s outward traces remain identical to those of an ordinary person, there may be times when one sacrifices the body for the sake of sentient beings; such matters are beyond the reach of mere verbal discourse.

As for those among the ranks of ordinary beings, their discernment is not broad; they ultimately do not realize that practicing the Way for the remainder of one's lifespan is superior to merely casting off one's body and life.
Some seek to win renown for a single moment, while others desire to leave a name for ten thousand generations.
When one stands on the verge of fire and approaches the fuel, remorse and fear intersect with piercing intensity.
Once one's words have been widely proclaimed, shame robs one of their integrity.
Thus, to labor at such tasks with forced compliance and undergo myriad sufferings in vain—if this is the case, it is not what is meant by the Way.
The eulogy says:
If a person exerts their will, even metal and stone are not the ultimate excellence.
They refine that which they hold most precious, praying for that jeweled city.
The fragrant wutong trees are lush and verdant; the purple halls float with lightness.
As smoke rises and radiates its brilliance, auspicious signs are exhaled and blessings are contained.
Its beauty shall endure for a thousand autumns, and its fragrance shall be transmitted for ten thousand generations.

7. Reciting the Sūtras, Section Seven. Twenty-one individuals: 1. Shi Tansui; 2. Shi Faxiang; 3. Zhu Fachun; 4. Shi Sengsheng; 5. Shi Fazong; 6. Shi Daojiong; 7. Shi Huiqing; 8. Shi Puming; 9. Shi Fazhuang; 10. Shi Huiguo; 11. Shi Fagong; 12. Shi Sengfu; 13. Shi Huijin; 14. Shi Hongming; 15. Shi Huiyu; 16. Shi Daosong; 17. Shi Chaobian; 18. Shi Fahui; 19. Shi Senghou; 20. Shi Huimi; 21. Shi Daolin. 1. Shi Tansui: It is not known where he was from.
He left home to become a monk at a young age and resided at Baima Monastery in Heyin.
Wearing simple cloth garments and subsisting on vegetarian food, he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, regularly completing it once every day.
Furthermore, he was profoundly adept at the essential meanings of the sutras and would also provide expositions for others.
Once, in the middle of the night, he suddenly heard a knock at his door, which said, "I wish to invite the Dharma Master to preach the Dharma for a ninety-day period."

Sui did not permit it; yet, as he pressed his request insistently, he eventually went there. However, he was still in a state of sleep, and upon awakening, he found himself already within the shrine of the White Horse Mound deity, together with a disciple.
From then on, he went there in secret every day, with no one else aware of it.
Later, as a monk from the temple passed before the shrine, he saw two high seats: Sui was seated to the north and his disciples were to the south, and there was the sound of someone lecturing.
Furthermore, the scent of a wondrous incense was perceived, whereupon both monastics and laypeople spread the word, all declaring it a divine marvel.
At the end of the summer retreat, the deity bestowed one white horse, five white sheep, and ninety rolls of silk.
When the incantations and prayers were finished, they each departed.
Thereafter, Sui’s final destination was unknown. 2.
Shi Faxiang: Shi Faxiang’s surname was Liang; it is uncertain who he was.
Xiang lived constantly in the mountains practicing asceticism and recited over one hundred thousand words of scripture. Birds and beasts gathered at his side, all as tame as domestic poultry.

At the shrine of Mount Tai, there was a large stone chest containing wealth and treasures. While traveling through the mountains and staying overnight beside the temple, Xiang suddenly saw a man dressed in black robes and a martial crown, who ordered him to open the chest; as soon as the man finished speaking, he vanished.

The stone lid of the casket weighed more than a thousand *jun*, yet when they tested it by attempting to lift it, it rose up with effortless ease; thereupon, they took the wealth within and distributed it to the poor.
Later, he crossed the Yangtze River and stayed at Yuecheng Temple.
Suddenly, he began to roam about recklessly and live in dissipation; he acted as a buffoon and jester, and at times even went about naked, offending the high officials of the court.
Sima Tian, the General Who Guards the North of the Jin dynasty, detested his lack of moderation and invited him to drink poisoned wine.
He drained three cups one after another; his spirit remained clear and serene, tranquil and undisturbed. Sima Tian was greatly amazed by this.
He passed away at the end of the Yuanxing era of the Jin dynasty at the age of eighty.
At that time, there were Zhu Tanguai and Zhu Sengfa, both of whom practiced asceticism and were moved by spiritual resonance.
He was able to invoke rain through divine incantations and was thus revered by Sima Yuanxian, the Regional Inspector of Yangzhou.
Fahu also excelled in divine incantations and was honored by Sima Daozi, the Prince of Kuaiji and Chancellor of the Jin Dynasty.
He founded Zhicheng Temple there. 3.
Zhu Fachun: It is not known where Zhu Fachun was from.
He left home to become a monk in his youth and resided at Xianyi Temple in Shan-yin.
Tao Kuxing was virtuous and well-versed in reciting the *Old Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
During the Yuanxing era of the Jin dynasty, he purchased an old house for the temple on Lan-zhu.
As he was returning at dusk, his small boat encountered a storm upon the lake.
With single-minded devotion, he relied solely upon Avalokiteśvara, reciting the name without ceasing. Suddenly, he saw a large drifting boat; boarding it, he was saved.
Upon reaching the shore, he searched for the boat’s owner but found none, and in an instant, it vanished. Both monastics and laypeople marveled at this divine response.
His final whereabouts were unknown. 4.
Shi Sengsheng: Shi Sengsheng’s secular surname was Yuan, and he was a native of Pi in Shu Commandery.
He left home to become a monk in his youth and gained renown for his ascetic practices.
Song Feng and others from Chengdu requested him to serve as the abbot of Sanxian Temple.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
He often recited the sūtras in the mountains; a tiger would come and crouch before him, departing only after he had finished his recitation.
Later, whenever he chanted and recited the scriptures, he would invariably see four attendants standing by his side as a guard.
Although he was advanced in years, his diligence and devotion grew even more intense.
Subsequently, when he fell slightly ill, he spoke to his attendant, saying:
"I shall depart; after my death, you may perform the cremation of my body.
His disciples followed his final instructions. 5.
Shi Fazong: Shi Fazong was a native of Linhai.

In his youth, he was fond of hunting; once, while in Shan County, he encountered a pregnant doe that had miscarried from being shot. The mother deer, still clutching the arrow, continued to lick her young on the ground.
Thereupon, Zong was moved to repentance and realization, understanding that the desire for life and the love for offspring are common to all sentient beings.
Thereupon, he broke his bow and snapped his arrows, renouncing the world to pursue the path of practice.

He constantly sustained himself by begging for alms, observing the discipline of eating only once a day, and undergoing ascetic hardships throughout the six periods of the day to repent for his past transgressions.
He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
He would often ascend the platform to chant them aloud, the sound of which reached far and wide.
More than three thousand men and women received his precepts and took refuge in him; he subsequently expanded his residence and established it as a vihāra.
Because he recited [the sutra] as his guiding focus, it was titled the "Dharma-Flower Terrace" (Fahua Tai).
As for Zong, his final destination remains unknown. 6.
Shi Daojiong. Shi Daojiong’s secular surname was Ma; he was a native of Fufeng.
When he first left the household life, he was a disciple of Dao Yi.
When Dao Yi fell ill, he once dispatched Sengjiong and three others—four men in total—to Henan to gather stalactites from Mount Huo.

After traveling several li into the cave, they had to cross a stream by stepping across wooden beams; three of them drowned, and their torches were also extinguished. Sengjiong judged that there was no way to escape.
Jiong had long been a reciter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, relying solely on the sincerity of this practice and maintaining mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara.
After a short while, he saw a light like a firefly; though he pursued it, he could not catch it, and thus he was able to emerge from his burrow.
Thereupon, she advanced in her cultivation of dhyāna, and her disciplined conduct became ever more refined.
She frequently performed several *Puxian* (Samantabhadra) fasts, each of which was accompanied by auspicious responses.
Sometimes she saw a foreign monk enter and take a seat; at other times, she saw a man on horseback arrive. In neither case had they yet exchanged greetings before they suddenly vanished.
Later, he traveled south to the capital with four fellow students to observe the local customs and culture.
At night, they crossed a river by means of ice; midway through, the ice broke, and three of them drowned.
Jiong again returned his sincerity to Avalokiteśvara; he then felt as if something were lifting him up from beneath his feet, and seeing a red light before him, he rode upon the light to the shore.
Tadu resided at Nanjian Temple, where he constantly took the *Pratyutpanna Sūtra* as his primary practice.
Once, entering into meditation during the middle of the night, he suddenly saw four men driving a carriage arrive at his room and call out for him to board it.
In a sudden flash, he was unaware of himself until he found his body at Shen Bridge behind the commandery.
He saw a man sitting on a *huchuang* chair by the road with several hundred attendants; upon seeing Jiong, the man started in surprise and said, "You are but a practitioner of meditation."
That man then said to his attendants, "I had previously intended merely to inform him of the location; why have you suddenly troubled the Dharma Master with such an honor?
Thereupon, he prostrated himself and took his leave, ordering someone to escort Sengjiong back to the monastery.
He knocked on the door for a long time before it finally opened; upon entering the monastery, he found his room still locked, and the assembly could not fathom why this was so.
In the twentieth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, Prince Yiqing, the Prince of Kang of Linchuan, took him to Guangling, where he passed away.
7. Shi Huiqing. Shi Huiqing was a native of Guangling.
He entered the monastic order and resided at Mount Lu Monastery.
His studies encompassed both the Sutras and the Vinaya; he was pure and possessed strict observance of the precepts.

He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Daśabhūmika*, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*; every night he chanted these aloud, and he constantly heard the sound of finger-snapting and voices of praise from within the darkness.

Once, while traveling at Xiaolei, he encountered wind and waves, and his boat was on the verge of capsizing; Sengqing continued to recite the sutras without ceasing, and he perceived that as the boat drifted upon the waves, it was as if someone were pulling it, until suddenly they reached the shore.
Thereupon, he redoubled his earnestness and became even more diligent.
He passed away at the end of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty at the age of sixty-two.
8. Shi Puming. Shi Puming’s secular surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Linzi.
He left home to become a monk at a young age; by nature he was pure and simple, wearing coarse cloth and eating vegetarian food, making the practice of repentance and recitation his primary vocation.
He recited the two sutras, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*.
While reciting [the sutra], he used separate clothing and a separate seat, never allowing them to become defiled or mixed with others.
Every time he reached the "Chapter on Encouraging Resolve," he would invariably see Samantabhadra riding upon an elephant, standing before him.
While reciting the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, he also heard voices chanting music from the air.
Furthermore, he was skilled in incantations, and all whom he healed were cured.
A fellow villager, Wang Daozhen, had a wife who was ill; he invited Sengming to come and perform the incantation for her.
When she entered the room, the wife immediately fainted.
Shortly thereafter, she saw something resembling a wild cat, about several feet long, emerge from the dog-hole; because of this, she recovered.
Once, when Ming was walking by a shrine along the water, the shamans and mediums said of their own accord:
"The deity saw him and all fled in haste.
He passed away during the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty at the age of eighty-five.
9. Shi Fazhuang: Shi Fazhuang’s secular surname was Shen, and he was a native of Huainan.
He left home to become a monk at the age of ten and became a disciple of Huiyuan of Mount Lu.
In his youth, he established his reputation for his austere discipline.
In his later years, he traveled to Guanzhong to receive instruction from Master Dao Rui.
At the beginning of the Yuanjia era, he went to the capital and resided at Daochang Temple.
By nature, he was simple and unadorned, maintaining only a single meal a day.
He recited the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

Every night after midnight, as he chanted, those in neighboring rooms would constantly hear sounds like the clashing of weapons and the presence of a ceremonial guard before Zhuang’s dwelling; this was truly because celestial deities had come to listen.
He passed away at the monastery at the beginning of the Daming era of the Song dynasty, at the age of seventy-six.
10. Shi Huiguo: Shi Huiguo was a native of Yuzhou. From his youth, he devoted himself to a life of asceticism and austerity.
At the beginning of the Song dynasty, he traveled to the capital and stayed at Waguan Temple.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.
Once, while in the latrine, he saw a ghost who paid his respects to Guo, saying:

"In the past, when I served as the *karmadāna* for the community of monks, I was slightly deficient in accordance with the Dharma; consequently, I fell among the *purīṣabhakṣaka* (feces-eating) spirits.
As the Master’s virtue has long been lofty and eminent, and your mind is set upon compassion, I pray that you will assist me with a means to deliver me."
He further stated, "In the past, there were three thousand coins buried beneath a persimmon tree; I wish to retrieve them to cultivate merit.

Accordingly, he informed the assembly and had the ground excavated. Indeed, they obtained the three thousand coins, with which he commissioned a copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and established a religious assembly.
Later, he saw this ghost in a dream, who said:
"I have already attained rebirth, which is far superior to my former state.
Indeed, he passed away in the sixth year of the Taishi era of the Song dynasty at the age of seventy-six.
11. Shi Fagong. Shi Fagong’s surname was Guan, and he was a native of Yongzhou.
When he first left home to become a monk, he resided at Anyang Temple in Jiangling.
Later, he traveled to the capital and stayed at Dong’an Temple.
From his youth, his ascetic practices were extraordinary; he wore cloth garments, subsisted on beans and wheat, and recited more than three hundred thousand words of scripture.
Every night as he chanted, a sublime fragrance and a wondrous aroma would emanate, which all those who entered Sengqiong’s room could perceive together.
Furthermore, he used worn-out hempen robes as a nest for fleas and lice, constantly wearing them to nourish them.
Emperor Wu, Emperor Wen, and Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty, as well as Prince Yixiu of Hengyang, all revered his pure virtue.
Whatever offerings he received through his faith, he constantly distributed to the poor and the sick, never keeping anything for private hoarding.
During the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he returned to the West and passed away there at the age of eighty.
At that time, there was also one named Senggong among those in black robes; his virtue and practice were lofty and brilliant, and he oversaw the affairs of the monastery.
He too did not eat polished rice, consuming only beans and wheat.
12. Shi Sengfu. Shi Sengfu’s origins are unknown.
Orphaned at a young age, he was raised by a servant.
At seven years old, he entered the monastic order as a disciple of Tanliang.
His learning was comprehensive across the various sutras; he maintained a vegetarian diet and recited dharanis.
He chanted the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty held him in high esteem and appointed him by imperial decree as the abbot of Pengcheng Temple, where he led the assembly with great merit.
He passed away at the end of the Taishi era of the Song dynasty at the age of sixty-six.
13. Shi Huijin: Shi Huijin’s secular surname was Yao; he was a native of Wuxing.
In his youth, he was bold and courageous by nature, possessing the character of a *yòuxiá* (wandering knight-errant).

At the age of forty, he suddenly attained awakening as his mind opened of its own accord; he subsequently left secular life and resided at Gaozuo Temple in the capital. There, he ate vegetarian food, wore plain clothing, and vowed to recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
He applied himself with such diligent effort that he would fall ill whenever he took up a scroll.
He then made a vow, wishing to produce one hundred copies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to repent for his past obstructions.
He had initially gathered one thousand six hundred coins when a robber arrived and asked whether he possessed anything to advance. He replied:
"There is only the money for the scriptures remaining with the Buddha.
Upon hearing this, the bandits felt ashamed and departed.
Thereupon, they gathered offerings from the faithful and were able to complete the scriptures, fulfilling the quota of one hundred volumes.
After the scripture was completed, his illness also slightly abated.
Having successfully finished reciting one volume of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, his aspirations were fulfilled, and his rigorous discipline became even more steadfast.
She constantly dedicated her various meritorious deeds, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nourishment (An-yang).
Not long before her death, she suddenly heard a voice from the air saying:
"Your vow has already been fulfilled; you will certainly attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land."
In the third year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, he passed away without illness at the age of eighty-five.

At that time, there was also the monk Shi Sengnian at Longhua Temple in the capital, who recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, maintained a vegetarian diet, and withdrew from the world.
14. Shi Hongming. Shi Hongming’s original surname was Ying; he was a native of Shanyin, Kuaiji.
He left home to become a monk in his youth, being austere and diligent with strict observance of the precepts, residing at Yunmen Temple in Shanyin.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, practiced meditative concentration, and diligently performed rites of repentance, never ceasing throughout the six periods of the day.
Every morning, his water jar would fill itself; it was truly as if celestial youths were serving him as attendants.

Once, while Ming was practicing seated meditation at Yunmen, a tiger entered his room and crouched before his bed; seeing that Ming remained upright and unmoving, it eventually departed after a long time.
On another occasion, he saw a young boy coming to listen to Ming reciting the sutras.
Ming asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, "In the past, I was a śrāmaṇera at this monastery who stole food from beneath the curtains; I have now fallen into the latrine.
Having heard of the spiritual accomplishments of the Honored One, I have come to listen to his recitation of the sutras. I pray that you will employ skillful means to help me escape this misfortune."
The next day, Ming immediately preached the Dharma to exhort and transform them;
only after they had attained understanding did he withdraw. Later, while entering meditative absorption at Shemuo Rock in Yongxing, a mountain spirit again came to disturb him.
He clearly caught him and bound him with a waist-cord; the ghost apologized and begged for release, saying, "I shall not dare to come again.
He was then released.
Thereupon, he vanished from sight.
During the Yuanjia era, Meng Yi of Pingchang, the Prefectural Governor, admiring his genuine simplicity, invited him to reside at the Dao-shu Vihāra.
Later, Ji Yang Jiang established Zhaoxuan Monastery in Yongxing County and again invited Ming to reside there.

Toward the end of the Daming era, Dong of the Tao family also established Bolin Monastery in the village for Ming, requesting him to return and dwell there; he instructed them in meditation and the precepts until his disciples were gathered in great numbers.
He passed away at Bolin Temple in the fourth year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, at the age of eighty-four.
15. Shi Huiyu: Shi Huiyu was a native of Huanglong.
He came to travel to the capital and stayed at Linggen Temple.
From his youth, he was devoted to learning and visited various masters extensively.

He was skilled in debate and possessed a refined character; whenever he heard people being praised or disparaged, he would immediately plug his ears and refuse to listen, or sometimes interrupt with contrary remarks.
His water jar and robes were plain and simple; he completed his daily sustenance with a single midday meal.
He was diligent and maintained strict discipline, prioritizing the salvation of suffering beings.
He recited the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Furthermore, he practiced the discipline of meditation with particular proficiency in the five gates.
Once, while sleeping, he saw three men come to knock at his door; they were all dressed in fresh and clean robes and caps, and each held a flowered parasol.
He asked in advance,
"Whom are you looking for?
and the answer was given:
"The Dharma Master ought to die; therefore, we have come to welcome him.
Yu replied, "I have some minor affairs yet unfinished; may I request a year's extension?"
He replied, "So be it.
When the following year had completed its full cycle, he passed away.
This was the seventh year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty; he was fifty-seven years of age.
At Yusi Temple, there was also a śramaṇa named Fapu, who likewise habitually practiced and recited the sutras.
16. Shi Daosong. Shi Daosong’s secular surname was Xia; he was a native of Gaomi.
He entered the monastic order at the age of ten. From his youth, he was profound and reserved, possessing a resolute will for spiritual application.
After receiving full ordination, he devoted himself exclusively to the study of the Vinaya.
He recited three hundred thousand words of scripture.
In his interactions with those above and below him, he never displayed an expression of joy or anger.
By nature he delighted in giving and renunciation; whatever offerings and sustenance he received, he gave them all away to others.
Aside from his water jar and robes, he possessed almost nothing else.
During the Yuanhui era of the Song dynasty, he came to the capital and resided at Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhong.
He maintained tranquility in his secluded chamber, never ceasing his practice of repentance and recitation.
Whenever anyone came to visit him, he would invariably preach the Dharma and offer exhortations to them in lieu of a meal.
Those who followed him to request the precepts were exceedingly numerous.
Later, he passed away in the mountains at the age of forty-nine. 17.
Shi Chaobian: Shi Chaobian’s secular surname was Zhang; he was a native of Dunhuang.
From his youth, he possessed a divine insight that emerged in solitude, and his conduct was profoundly deep and steady.
He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vajracchedikā*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.
Hearing that the Buddha-dharma flourished in the capital, he traveled from Xihe, passing through Ba and Chu, until he reached Jianye.
Shortly thereafter, he traveled east to Wu and Yue to admire the mountains and waters, staying for a short time at a temple near the city of Shanyin.
Later, he returned to the capital and resided at Dinglin Shangsi Temple.
Living in seclusion to nurture his fundamental nature, he dedicated the remainder of his life to the mountain monastery.
He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* with a daily limit of one complete recitation; his mind was so agile that his speech followed effortlessly, and he always possessed surplus energy.
He paid obeisance to the thousand Buddhas more than one million five hundred thousand times in total, never venturing outside his door for over thirty years.
He passed away at the mountain monastery in the tenth year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, at the age of seventy-three.
He was buried to the south of the monastery; the śramaṇa Sengyou erected a stele at the site of the tomb, and Liu Xie of Dongxian composed the inscription.

At that time, there were the śramaṇas Faming of Linggen, Sengzhi of Qihuan, and Fading of Yizhou, all of whom had recited over one hundred thousand words of scripture and possessed the highest virtue through their ascetic discipline.

18. Shi Fahui: Shi Fahui’s original surname was Xiahou. From his youth, he maintained a resolute will characterized by diligent austerity, and his observance of the Vinaya was as strictly pure as ice.
Toward the end of the Daming era of the Song dynasty, he traveled east to the Cave of Yu (Yuxue) and lived in seclusion at Tianzhu Mountain Monastery.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* in its entirety.
Clad in coarse cloth and subsisting on vegetarian fare, he devoted himself to life beyond the mundane world, remaining in his tower for more than thirty years without descending.
When princes and nobles halted their carriages there, they would merely pay their respects at the door of his room before returning.
Only Zhou Yong of Nanyang, whose faith and understanding were both profound, was treated with special attention by him.
At that time, those who admired his virtue and hoped for an audience would sometimes rely on Yong to intercede on their behalf.
At that time, Yijian passed away at the mountain monastery in the second year of the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty, at the age of eighty-five.
At that same time, there was a monk named Shi Tanyou on Mount Xuanliu in Yueye; he too subsisted on vegetarian food and recited the sutras, making rigorous asceticism his primary practice.
19. Shi Senghou. Shi Senghou’s secular surname was Gong; he was a native of Xiliangzhou.
At the age of eighteen, he adopted a vegetarian diet and engaged in ritual repentance.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled to various regions to observe and transform [the people through his teachings].
At the beginning of the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty, he came to the capital.
He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* sūtras.
He would complete one full recitation of them every two days, continuing in this manner for over sixty years.
When Xiao Huikai entered Shu, he invited [Hou] to travel with him.
Later, when Huikai and Yi Jia were implicated in a crime and returned to the capital, Hou also returned to the capital.
He subsequently established a stone chamber on Hougang to serve as a place for peaceful meditation.
From the time he first entered the gate of tranquility until the end of his life, he never once brought fish, meat, or pungent vegetables near his teeth.
Should his foot’s shadow even slightly deviate from its path, he would immediately pass the day in fasting.

In the second year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, he began to feel slightly unwell; by midday he was unable to eat. He then sought water to rinse his mouth, joined his palms in reverence, and passed away at the age of eighty-nine.
At that time, there was Shi Huiwen of Puhong, who also recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.
He maintained a vegetarian diet and possessed high moral integrity.
20. Shi Huimi: Shi Huimi’s secular surname was Yang; he was a native of Huayin in Hongnong.
He was a descendant of Han Taishou Zhen.
At the age of sixteen, he left the household life.
After receiving full ordination, his resolve was to practice seclusion; he thus entered Mount Zhongnan in Chang’an.

The rocky valleys were steep and precipitous, such that no tracks could reach them; yet he carried his staff upon his back and went forth alone, undisturbed by fierce tigers or formidable rhinoceroses.

Having recited the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* since his youth and having mastered the cultivation of samādhi, he then cut through the thatch to build a hut, making it a dwelling for his spirit.

When the time arrived, he would take his alms bowl and enter the village; having finished his meal, he would return to his quarters to practice meditation and recitation. He continued in this manner for eight years.

Later, hearing that the Dharma was flourishing in Jiangdong, he traveled to the capital to observe and transform others, staying at Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhong, where he pursued his studies as before.

He was warm and respectful in his conduct, humble and yielding; his countenance showed no sign of joy or anger. His moral precepts were refined and lucid, and he encouraged transformation through teaching without weariness. He consulted the wise and sought out what was good, always as if he had not yet received enough.
Whenever anyone, whether lay or ordained, came to the mountain to prostrate, he would always preach the Dharma to guide them, using this as a substitute for fine delicacies.
From the time of his renunciation until his old age, he permanently abandoned all pungent vegetables, fermented liquors, and fresh meats; for over thirty years, he did not step outside his door.

He practiced meditative concentration day and night, constantly recited the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and performed rites of repentance during the six periods of the day, always taking the lead among the assembly.
He passed away in his mountain retreat on the fifteenth day of the intercalary eighth month in the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, at the age of seventy-nine.
He was buried to the south of the monastery, and a stele was erected to commemorate his virtues.
At that time, there was also a śramaṇa named Faxian at Dinglin Temple, who likewise recited the scriptures and possessed long-standing virtuous conduct.
Later, he returned to Wu to serve as the Sangha Administrator (Sengzheng) and passed away there.
21. Shi Daolin: Shi Daolin was originally a native of Shanyin, Kuaiji.
He left home to become a monk in his youth and maintained strict observance of the precepts.
He was proficient in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Lotus Sūtra*, and he recited the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*; Zhang Xu of the Wu state paid him ritual homage.
Later, he resided at Quanlin Temple in Fuyang County.
The temple was frequently haunted by ghosts and monsters, but these vanished once Lin took up residence there.
Lin’s disciple Huishao was pinned down by a collapsing building, causing his head to sink into his shoulders; Lin offered prayers on his behalf.
During the night, Yao saw two Brahmā practitioners pull out his head; when he rose in the morning, it had returned to its original state.

Thereupon, Lin prepared a vegetarian feast for the Holy Sangha, spreading new silk upon the bed. When the feast concluded, he saw human footprints upon the silk, each more than three feet long. Everyone marveled at this miraculous manifestation.
Originally, people in Fuyang established seats for the "Holy Monk" (Śāstṛ) in every household to offer him food.
By the beginning of the Liang dynasty, Senglin moved to reside at Qixi Temple.
He passed away in the eighteenth year of the Tianjian era at the age of seventy-three.
The treatise states:
The benefits of reciting and chanting are great, yet those who achieve their full merit are rare.
This is truly because *dhāraṇī* is difficult to attain, while forgetfulness arises easily.
As stated in the sutras, even a single phrase or a single verse of *śamatha* is praised by the sages.

For this reason, Tan-sui attained spiritual communion with a stone gully; Seng-sheng was moved by divine protection in mid-air; Dao-jiong was rescued from peril; and Hui-qing was granted deliverance when he was on the verge of death.
All of these arise because genuine virtue fills the interior, thereby causing responsive manifestations to be revealed externally.
As the Sūtra says:
"The six-tusked elephant descended into the chamber, and the Four Heavenly Kings guarded the seat."
Is this not indeed far from being a mere fiction?

When the cold is intense and the night is still, under the bright moon of a long night, dwelling alone in a quiet chamber, one chants and recites the scriptures; the voice is robust and resonant, and the characters are distinct and clear.
This is sufficient to cause the spirits to leap for joy and the consciousness to be filled with delight.
This is what is meant by singing and reciting the words of the Dharma, taking this as music.
The eulogy says:
The Dharma-body being remote, that which it entrusts to is but words.
Reflecting deeply and turning back over these words, their benefit and utility are inconceivable.
Let there be no indolence in the three karmas; let there be striving throughout the six periods of the day.
Manifested beings then provided protection, and transformed multitudes came to join him.
As for such genuine virtue, who could possibly compare with it?
*Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume XII.
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Thirteen: Masters of the Propagation of the Dharma and Guides.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huijiao of Jiaxiang Temple in Kuaiji during the Liang Dynasty.
Section Eight: Propagation of Merit (Xingfu), the Eighty-fourth Category.

1. Shi Huida; 2. Shi Huiyuan; 3. Shi Huili; 4. Shi Huishou; 5. Shi Senghui; 6. Shi Tanyi; 7. Shi Senghong; 8. Shi Sengliang; 9. Shi Fayi; 10. Shi Huijing; 11. Shi Faxian; 12. Shi Faxian; 13. Shi Senghu; 14. Shi Fayue. 1. Shi Huida: His secular surname was Liu, and his original name was Sahe. He was a native of Lishi in Xihexi, Bingzhou.

In his youth, he was fond of hunting. At the age of thirty-one, he suddenly experienced a brief death; after a day had passed, he revived and witnessed in full detail the retributive sufferings of the hells. There he encountered a Daoist practitioner who claimed to be his teacher from a previous life. This man preached the Dharma to him and instructed him, urging him to leave the household life and travel to Danyang, Kuaiji, and Wujun to seek out the stupas and images of King Aśoka. He was to pay homage and repent for his transgressions, thereby expiating his past sins.
Upon waking, he immediately left the household life to study the Way, changing his name to Huida.
He applied himself with diligence to meritorious deeds, making ritual repentance his primary practice.
During the Ningkang era of the Jin dynasty, he arrived at the capital.
Previously, Emperor Jianwen had constructed a three-story pagoda at Changgan Temple. After its completion, it emitted light every evening.

When Sengda ascended Yuecheng and looked out, he saw that the pinnacle of this pagoda alone displayed an extraordinary color; he immediately went there to pay his respects, praying with utmost sincerity day and night.
At night, he saw light emanating from beneath the stupa. He then informed others to dig it up together; after digging about one zhang deep, they discovered three stone tablets.
Beneath the central tablet was a covered iron casket; inside the iron casket was a silver casket, inside the silver casket was a gold casket, and within the gold casket were three śarīras.
There was also a fingernail and a single hair; the hair, when extended, measured several feet in length, and when coiled, it formed a spiral, its luster dazzlingly radiant.
This was one of the eighty-four thousand stupas erected by King Aśoka during the reign of King Jing of the Zhou dynasty.
As both the clergy and the laity marveled at this marvel, they erected another stupa to the west of the original one to enshrine the śarīra.
In the sixteenth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, Emperor Xiaowu further expanded it to three stories.

Furthermore, in the past, during the Xianhe era of the Jin dynasty, Gao Kui, the Governor of Danyang, excavated a golden image from within the waters of Zhanghou Bridge. It lacked a halo or pedestal, yet its craftsmanship was exceedingly exquisite.
On the front [of the image] was a Brahmi inscription stating that it had been fashioned by the fourth daughter of King Aśoka.

When Huikai loaded the image onto a cart and reached the mouth of Changgan Lane, the ox refused to move further; no human effort could control it, so they let the ox follow its own course, which led them directly to Changgan Temple.

About a year later, a coastal fisherman named Zhang Xishi found a copper lotus pedestal floating on the water at the mouth of the estuary; he immediately took it and delivered it to the county office.
He submitted a memorial to the Imperial Court, by imperial decree the image was placed beneath the feet [of the statue], whereupon it fit perfectly.

Later, five monks from the Western Regions came to see Huikai and said, "In the past, we obtained an image of King Aśoka in India; arriving at Ye, we encountered the chaos of war and hid it by the riverbank."
Now that the royal roads have been opened, I have searched for it in vain.
Recently, I received a dream which said that the image had already reached Jiangdong and was in the possession of Gao Kui.
Therefore, I have traveled far across mountains and seas, desiring only to behold and pay homage to it.
Hui-li then led them to Changgan. When the five men saw the image, they sighed deeply and wept; the image immediately emitted light that illuminated the interior of the hall.
The five men said, "The halo was originally present, but it is now at a distance; it shall also arrive here in due course."
In the first year of the Xian’an era of the Jin dynasty, Dong Zongzhi, a pearl diver from Hepu County in Jiaozhou, found a Buddha’s halo at the bottom of the sea.
The Regional Inspector submitted a memorial regarding this discovery, and Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty issued an edict to bestow it upon this image.
The hollows were exactly identical, and the color and luster were of one kind.
After more than forty years, auspicious responses occurred in both the east and west, and the halo and pedestal finally became complete.
Because the shrine and image were so miraculous, Faxian redoubled his efforts in devotion.
Later, he traveled east to Wu County to pay homage to the stone image.

This image had floated to the mouth of the Hudu Estuary on the Wusong River during the final years of the Western Jin dynasty, specifically in the first year of the Jianxing era, the year of Guiyou (313 CE).
The fishermen suspected it was a sea deity and invited shamans and priests to welcome it; however, the wind and waves grew even more violent, and they returned in terror.

At that time, there were followers of the Yellow Old Man (Laozi) who claimed it was the spirit of the Celestial Master; they went together again to receive it, but the tossing waves remained as before.
Later, there was a lay follower of the Buddha named Zhu Ying, a resident of Wu County, who heard of this and sighed in admiration, saying,
"Could this not be the manifest response of the Great Awakened One?
He then purified himself through fasting and, together with the nun Bo of Dongyun Temple and several other believers, traveled to the mouth of the Hudu River.
With utmost devotion, they prostrated themselves and chanted praises to his supreme virtue; immediately, the wind and waves became calm.
From afar, two figures were seen floating down the river, which turned out to be stone statues. On their backs were inscriptions: one was named "Vipaśyin" and the other "Kāśyapa."
He was immediately escorted back and installed at Tongxuan Temple.
The local gentry and commoners of Wu marveled at his spiritual wonders, and many turned their hearts toward him in devotion.
Da resided at Tongxuan Temple for a total of three years, prostrating himself with piety day and night without ever ceasing for even a moment.
Shortly thereafter, Jin traveled to Kuaiji to pay homage at the Zhifu Stupa.
This stupa was also built by King Aśoka; having fallen into ruin over the years, only its foundations remained visible.

Daqiao focused his mind and concentrated his thoughts, whereupon he beheld a divine light erupting in flames. Consequently, he constructed a niche and a stone platform; from then on, no birds dared to alight or gather there.

Furthermore, those who engaged in hunting or fishing near the temple were invariably unsuccessful in their pursuits. As this spiritual resonance was transmitted among both the clergy and the laity, none failed to be moved to faith.
Later, the Prefect Meng Yi further expanded [the temple].

He traveled east and west to pay his respects at the imperial court, repeatedly presenting memorials that attested to miraculous signs; he remained diligent and earnest throughout his life without ever wavering.
Later, his whereabouts became unknown. 2.
Shi Huiyuan: Shi Huiyuan was a native of Hebei. By nature he was good, and his countenance showed no sign of either joy or anger.
He constantly practiced meditation and recited the sutras, and he took it as his regular vocation to exhort others toward meritorious deeds.

At the beginning of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, he established a monastery on Mount Ping in Wuling. There were more than twenty monks who lived on vegetarian fare in seclusion, forever cutting off all contact with the outside world.
He passed away in the fourteenth year of the Taiyuan era.

After his death, someone entered the mountains below Wudang and saw him; his countenance was exceptionally serene, and he left a message for the monks of the monastery, telling them not to let the monastic affairs fall into ruin.

From then on, the sound of a *ghaṇṭā* (bell/chime) would frequently be heard from the air within the monastery at appropriate times; the assembly gathered according to this signal without ever missing the proper occasion.
The śramaṇa Zhu Huizhi resided there.

Huizhi was diligent and austere, maintaining strict observance of the precepts; later, he ceased eating grain and subsisted solely on pine and cypress, eventually ascending a mountain to cast off his mortal coil like a cicada shedding its shell.
3. Shi Huili. As for Shi Huili, it is unknown who he was.
During the Yonghe era of the Jin dynasty, he came to travel in the capital.
He constantly begged for food, practiced the austere dhūta observances, and cultivated merit.
During the Xingning era of the Jin dynasty, [Dao'an] submitted a petition requesting that the site where Tao Kan had lived be established as Waguan Temple.
When the foundation for the stupa was first marked, it was to the west of the current location.

Every evening the marker would shift eastward by more than ten paces; though it was retrieved in the morning, it had already moved again. Dao'an and his associates secretly observed this and saw a man wearing a vermilion robe and a military cap who pulled the marker and placed it to the east. They subsequently erected the stupa at that spot, which is the location of the present-day stupa.
A reporter said:
"Thirty years after the temple is established, it shall be consumed by a celestial fire.
On the night of the seventh month in the twenty-first year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty, a fire spontaneously broke out.
There were several dozen monks at the temple, yet none of them knew anything [of the omen]. When they saw the stupa had become a heap of ashes the following morning,
the Emperor said,
"This is an inauspicious sign for this country."
He immediately issued an edict to Yang Fashang, Li Xu, and others, ordering them to restore [the temple] with all haste.
By the ninth month, the Emperor passed away.
There were five images crafted by Dai Andao, as well as a sixteen-foot golden image repaired by Dai Yong.
Formerly, when a cast image was first completed, its face and head were exceptionally thin; the various artisans were at their wits' end, so they invited Sengyong to examine it.
Sengyong said, "It is not that the face is thin, but rather that the arms and shoulders are too thick."
Once the arms and shoulders had been filed down, the facial features naturally became full; there was no craftsman who did not sigh in admiration.
Furthermore, a jade image from Siṃhala measuring four chi and two cun was also present among them.
Formerly, the King of Siṃhala heard that Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty was devoted to the Dharma; therefore, he dispatched the śramaṇa Dharmagupta to present this Buddha image as a tribute.
It traveled for more than ten years on the road before finally reaching the Jin territory during the Yixi era.

Once, when Wang Mi, the Minister of Education, entered the palace, he saw an eunuch at the entrance of the eastern掖门 (ye-men) tossing a game of *chū* (a type of board game). Wherever the pieces landed during the play, light would invariably emanate from those spots. Finding this strange, he ordered them to dig there, and they discovered a golden image; including its halo and pedestal, it was seven chi and two cun tall.

Mì immediately reported this to the throne; Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty welcomed him into the palace to provide offerings. Toward the end of the Jingping era of the Song, he was sent out to Waguan Temple, where he now resides at Longguang Temple.
4. Shi Hui-shou. Shi Hui-shou brought peace and happiness to people.
During the Xingning era of the Jin dynasty, he came to travel in the capital.
He maintained a vegetarian diet and practiced asceticism, constantly cultivating meritorious deeds.
Once, while traveling, he passed by the garden of Wang Tanzhi. Every night, he would dream of establishing a temple within that garden; this happened several times.
When Huiyuan wished to ask Wang for a place to build even a single room, he did not yet dare speak of it, but first told his story to Song Qi, the gardener who tended the grounds.
Qi said, "The garden of the Wang family is likely not what you have in mind. Shou replied:
"If my sincerity can move [the divine], why should I worry about not obtaining it?
He then went to the king and presented his request.
The king was greatly pleased and granted his permission immediately.
He first established a small hut, and every evening he again dreamed that a blue dragon came from the south and transformed into a pillar for a Buddhist stupa (*kṣetra*).
He sent a novice monk to search along the Xinting River; there, the monk saw a long piece of timber coming down with the current.
Shou said, "This must certainly be what I saw. Thereupon,
he hired men to pull it up, erected it as a *stūpa* pillar (*khaṣṭra*), and constructed a single story upon it.
Monastics and laypeople gathered in competition, all marveling at his divine wonders.
Dao-tan immediately donated his garden to establish a monastery, naming it after his native place and calling it "Anle Monastery" (Anle Temple).

To the east was the residence of Wang Ya, the Governor of Danyang; to the west, the residence of Liu Dou, the Governor of Dongyan; and to the south, the residence of Fan Ning, the Governor of Yuzhang—all of which were donated to form the monastery.
Later, the śramaṇas Daojing, Daojing, and others further renovated and adorned it, so that it remains magnificent and splendid to this day.
5. Shi Senghui: It is unknown who Shi Senghui was.
From his youth, he had been fond of cultivating meritorious deeds.
During the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, together with Chang'an people, he traveled to Changsheng and established a monastery within the village of Po’u in the capital.
He first demarcated the site and erected several thatched huts, whereupon he assembled the monks to offer a vegetarian feast.
At midnight, two lamps inside the hall suddenly moved of their own accord, advancing forward several dozen paces; yet the oil wicks remained as they were, without spilling or overturning.
The great assembly was struck with wonder and consulted the elders, all of whom said that the place where the lamp had moved was the foundation of a stūpa built in ancient times by a foreign monk.
Thereupon, they went together to restore and establish it.
Because a lamp moved to manifest an auspicious omen, the temple was consequently named Chongming Temple. 6.
Shi Sengyi. Shi Sengyi was originally a native of Yuhang in Wuxing.
From his youth, he possessed faith and insight, and early on he established a character that transcended the mundane world.
When he first left home, he resided at Mount Lu Monastery, where he relied upon Huiyuan to study.
He maintained a vegetarian diet and observed rigorous ascetic discipline, earning the high esteem of his fellow disciples.
Later, he traveled to Guanzhong and again took Kumārajīva as his teacher; he extensively studied the Sūtras, Vinaya, Abhidharma, and Nyāya, and also recited the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
In the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled to Kuaiji together with his fellow practitioner, the śramaṇa Tanxue, to explore the mountains and waters.

Upon reaching the northwest of Qinwang Peak, he beheld five peaks standing side by side, resembling Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; thereupon, he constructed a thatched hut and named it the "Fahua Jingsha" (Lotus Hermitage).
The Prefect Meng Yi and the wealthy man Chen Zai both inclined their hearts toward him and drew near to his virtue, supporting his endeavors until they were successfully accomplished.
Daoyi maintained a vegetarian diet and drank from mountain streams for over thirty years; he passed away in the twenty-seventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty at the age of seventy.
A stele was erected at the mountain temple to commemorate his enduring virtue;
the text was composed by Kong Huan of Kuaiji.
His companion, the śramaṇa Tanxue, later moved and selected a site north of Qinwang Mountain, naming it the "Leling Vihāra."
There were also Yaoxiang and Guanqian, both renowned monks from Mount Dong, who all took up residence there together.
At that time, there was a monk named Shi Daojing, originally of the noble Wang clan of Langya; he was the great-grandson of Wang Xizhi, the Right General of the Jin dynasty.
Seeking seclusion from the world, he left the household life, his heart still attached to the mountain valleys.
He dwelt on Mount Ruoye and established the Xuānlìu Vihāra.
Later, out of reverence for the Sangha, he relinquished his full ordination and devoted himself exclusively to the ten precepts.
7. Shi Senghong. Shi Senghong was a native of Yuzhou who resided at Waguan Temple in the capital.
From his youth, he cultivated his person with meticulous integrity.
Later, leading those with whom he shared a karmic affinity, he commissioned a sixteen-foot golden image. Once the casting was completed, the mold had not yet been opened.
At that time, at the end of the Jin dynasty, the prohibition against using copper was extremely strict; those who violated it were invariably executed.

At that moment, Emperor Wu of the Song, serving as Chancellor, had Hóng imprisoned in the Chancellor’s residence for his offense. There, Hóng did nothing but recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, single-mindedly taking refuge in the Buddha image.
At night, the image he had cast appeared in a dream; it stroked Hong’s head with its hand and asked, "Are you afraid? Hong replied.
He thought to himself that he would surely die.
The image said,
"Do not grieve."
He saw that the chest of the statue was about a foot square and its copper color was scorched and bubbling.
When it came time for the execution, the governor’s assistant supervised the killing, but the ox bolted and the carriage was wrecked; consequently, the date was rescheduled.
Subsequently, an edict arrived from Pengcheng stating:
"The monk Senghong has not yet been executed; he may be pardoned.
Thereupon, he was granted his life.
Upon reopening the mold, it was indeed found that there were scorch marks on the chest of the image.
Later, Senghong died as a result of his ascetic practices.
8. Shi Sengliang: It is unknown who Shi Sengliang was.
From his youth, he was renowned for his ascetic discipline.
Desiring to cast a sixteen-foot golden image, he required a considerable amount of copper;

as this could not be obtained through ordinary begging, he heard that the temple of Wu Zixu at Tongxi in the jurisdiction of Xiangzhou contained many bronze vessels. However, the temple was extremely awe-inspiring and no one dared to approach it. Upon hearing this, Sengliang went there to obtain them.
He informed the Regional Inspector Zhang Shao, requesting one hundred strong men and ten large ships. Shao said,
"Since the temple is so efficacious, those who offend it will surely perish."
"Furthermore, since there are barbarians guarding it, how could it possibly be obtained? Liang replied,
"If it is indeed a matter of merit, it shall be shared with you, O donor."
"If there be any fault, I shall personally bear its consequences.
Shao immediately provided him with men and a boat; after traveling for three days and three nights, they arrived at the temple site.

Liang and his laborers advanced together, but when they were about twenty paces from the temple building, there appeared two bronze cauldrons with a capacity of over a hundred *hu* each, within which was a giant serpent over ten *zhang* long that emerged to block the path.
Fazhao then adjusted his deportment and held his staff, offering several dozen words of incantatory prayer; the snake suddenly vanished.
Shortly thereafter, a man appeared holding a bamboo tablet and stepped forth, saying:
"I have heard that the Dharma Master’s spiritual practice is extraordinary and that your undertaking for the merit of others is weighty; I have now come specifically to join you in your joy."
Thereupon, he ordered men to carry it away by palanquin.
Since the bronze of the temple was so abundant, they did not take even one-tenth of it, yet the boat was already full.
Only at the head of the deity’s bed was there a spittoon, inside of which was a lizard about two feet long, darting in and out.
The advisors all said that the deity most cherished this object, so Zhongliang refused to take it and departed;
he encountered favorable winds and currents, and by the time the various tribes reported the matter and gave chase, they could no longer catch up with him.
Upon returning to the capital, the casting of the image was completed, though the flaming halo remained unfinished.
Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty commissioned a circular halo of gold leaf for it, which was then installed at Pengcheng Temple.
During the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, Emperor Ming moved the statue to Xianggong Temple, where it remains to this day.
9. Shi Fayi: Shi Fayi was a native of Jiangzuo.
He was fond of cultivating meritorious deeds and established fifty-three temples.
During the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, Zhu Yingzi, the Libationer of Mount Zhong, was his disciple.
Previously, Sun En’s followers from the Jianyi rebellion had fled to this mountain; [Hui]yi took a small portion of its outer lands and established a temple with them, naming it "Yanxian Temple."
Later, Beidu came and went to this temple, saying:
"There will soon be various transformations here, but it shall become excellent in the future.
Its location faces the heavenly realm, making it easy to perform meritorious deeds."
Soon after, it was consumed by a wild fire.
Later, Qi Xie, Zhang Yin, and others followed the instructions of Beidu; the details of their discourse are recorded in the "Biography of Du.
Subsequently, they traveled together with Fayi through mountainous terrain, intending to establish another site, but finding no water, they were unable to remain there.
Reflecting upon the words of Beidu, he exhausted his sincerity in performing rites of repentance and prayed for the waters of the Western Pond.
After three days, his earnest and compassionate devotion reached its peak.
Suddenly, he heard a voice in the air, and something fell with a thud to the ground.
Fearing it might be gold or silk, he had people dig about two chi deep; instead, a clear stream gushed forth and eventually formed an unceasing brook, whereupon he established a temple.
It is unknown where his life ended.
10. Shi Huijing: Shi Huijing was a native of Nanhai.

In his youth, he traveled to study in the regions of Jing and Chu; he was also broadly proficient in the sutras and śāstras. However, because he constantly devoted himself to meritorious works, he did not achieve full success in scholastic learning.
In all his travels and undertakings, he erected stupas and images, assisting in the completion of various meritorious works.
Later, upon returning to his hometown, he further renovated the Yunfeng and Yongan monasteries.
Since Jing was refined in his observance of the precepts and his moral resolve was stern and clear, the monks and nuns beyond the passes all sought him out for instruction and guidance.
Later, he was appointed by imperial decree as the Chief Administrator of Monks (*Sengzhu*), where he proved highly effective in training and leading them.
Zhang Jing had a young slave and a śrāmaṇera who were suddenly struck by a ghost. Later, a mountain spirit appeared before Jing and apologized for his transgression, saying:
"My subordinates did not understand and needlessly harassed the Dharma Master’s attendants."
After a short while, they all recovered completely.
Whenever he performed meritorious deeds, he dedicated them all toward the Western Land.
On the day of his death, a wondrous fragrance filled the room, which only dissipated after a long time.
11. Shi Faxian: Shi Faxian was a native of Guangzhou.

Originally residing at Beisi (North Temple), the temple had fallen into decay over many years. Faxian led his circle of devoted followers to renovate and repair it, subsequently renaming it "Yanxiang" (Extended Auspiciousness).
Later, he entered Mount Zangwei and founded a temple. After the temple was completed, two youths came hand-in-hand singing:
"Zangwei possesses the Way and virtue; its joy and bliss are far from ended."
As soon as he finished speaking, he suddenly vanished.
The entire monastery was struck with wonder and sighed in admiration of his divine marvels.
Later, after Xian had entered into meditation, he suddenly saw a person come and say:
"The cords of the *qing* stone are about to snap; why do you not repair them?
Xian started up in alarm and went to look; the stone was on the verge of falling to the ground, but by his own hand he caught it, preventing it from breaking.
Since his ordination, Shi Faxian constantly exhorted others toward meritorious deeds while dwelling his mind in dhyāna and the precepts, never failing in his conduct.
His final destination is unknown. 12.
Shi Faxian: Shi Faxian’s secular surname was Xu; he was a native of Yanshui in Xihai.
Previously, he followed his maternal uncle to Liangzhou and there entered the monastic order.
In the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he finally descended to the capital and resided at Dinglin Shangsi Temple.
He was extensively versed in the sutras and the vinaya, and his resolve and practice were steadfast and vigorous.
He was well able to provide relief and assistance.

As the community planned to repair the temple buildings, they first heard that Master Meng had traveled westward and had personally witnessed numerous miraculous phenomena; thereupon, he vowed to sacrifice his own life in order to go and behold the sacred traces.
In the third year of the Yuanhui era of the Song dynasty, he set out from Jinling and traveled west to Ba and Shu. His route passed through Henan and traversed the territory of the Rouran.
Upon reaching Khotan, he intended to cross the Pamir Mountains, but encountering the suspension bridges cut off, he returned from Khotan.

He obtained one tooth of the Buddha, fifteen śarīra relics, as well as the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, the *Pāpadeśanā-mantra*, and the "Devadatta Chapter"; he also acquired a gilded image from the Kingdom of Kucha, and thus returned home.
The route was perilous and obstructed, as can be seen from its separate record.

The Buddha’s tooth relic was originally in the kingdom of Udyāna; it came from Udyāna to Rouran, and from Rouran to the territory of Liang. It has been fifty-five years since the tooth was presented and brought back to the capital.

He privately venerated and served [the deity] in secret, with no one else aware of it; it was not until Emperor Wenxuan had a visionary dream that the practice was transmitted to both the clergy and the laity.
His observance of the Vinaya was pure and refined, and his virtue served as a model for all beings.

Wang Su and Wang Rong of Langya; Zhang Rong and Zhang Quan of Wuguo; and the śramaṇas Huiling and Zhizang, among others, all prostrated themselves at his feet and revered his admonitions and instructions.

During the Yongming era, he was appointed by imperial decree as a monastic head (*saṃgharāja*) together with Xuanchang of Changgan Temple, each assigned to oversee the southern and northern banks respectively.
Xuanchang was originally from Qinzhou; he too maintained a pure and strict adherence to the Vinaya, and Crown Prince Wenhui honored him as his preceptor in the precepts.

After Daoxian was summoned by imperial decree to the Three Wu regions, he was instructed to carefully select members for both the monastic and lay assemblies; Daoyang also traveled east, once again expounding upon the methods of receiving the precepts.

At that time, both monks Daoxian and Daoyang had studied the Vinaya regulations since their youth and did not seek worldly fame; when conversing with Emperor Wu, they always addressed him by name and did not sit.

Later, when the monk Zhong of the Zhongxing Monastery was received by the Emperor at the Qianhe Hall, the Emperor asked him how things were going. Zhong replied, "I, a poor man of the Way, have recently been plagued by illness.
The Emperor took offense at this and questioned the Minister Wang Jian:
"When former-generation śramaṇas converse with emperors, what titles do they use?"
"Did he sit in the main hall?
Jian replied, "During the Han and Wei dynasties, the Buddha-dharma had not yet flourished; thus, I have seen no records or biographies concerning it."
Since the Wei dynasty gradually flourished, those who called themselves "poor monks" (pindao) were also permitted to take their seats [at court].
This was likewise the case at the beginning of the Jin dynasty.

During the middle period, figures such as Yu Bing and Huan Xuan both sought to compel śramaṇas to pay full homage [to the sovereign], but amidst the conflicting deliberations of the court, these matters were all eventually shelved.
During the Zhongchao period of the Song dynasty, the imperial court also frequently ordered him to perform formal salutations, yet in the end these were never carried out.
From that time until the present, he has mostly taken part in seated assemblies while referring to himself as "the poor practitioner" (pindao).
The Emperor said:

"If even the two monks Chang and Xian, whose spiritual accomplishments are such as these, still address me by name, how much more so for others? To bow down before them would be excessive; there is no objection to their addressing me by name."
From that time on, śramaṇas all began to address emperors by their personal names; this custom originated with Chang and Xian.
Chang passed away at the beginning of the Jianwu era, at the age of seventy-five.
Sengxian passed away at the end of the Jianwu era and was buried together with Sengchang on the southern slope of Mount Zhong.
His disciple Sengyou erected a stele by his tomb, and Shen Yue of Wuxing, the Governor of Danyang, composed the inscription.
The Buddha’s tooth relic and the image obtained in the Western Regions were both kept at Upper Dinglin Temple.

On the first day of the first month of the third year of the Putong era, several men carrying weapons suddenly knocked on the door at nightfall, claiming that a servant of Prince Linchuan had rebelled. Someone reported that the man was up in the Buddha-tooth pavilion; they requested that the pavilion be opened for inspection. The temple authorities immediately opened the pavilion in accordance with their words.

The Master arrived before the seat of the Buddha’s tooth relic, opened the casket, and took out the tooth. He prostrated three times in homage, placed the tooth in a silk handkerchief, and departed toward the east of the mountain.
To this day, his whereabouts remain unknown. 13.
Shi Senghu. Shi Senghu was originally from Shan in Kuaiji.
He entered the monastic order in his youth and devoted himself to constant ascetic discipline; his observance of the precepts was rigorous and pure.
Later, he resided at Yinyue Temple on Mount Shicheng.
To the north of the temple was a green cliff rising straight up for over several dozen zhang; in its center, there was a shape resembling the *jvālāmukha* (flame-light) halo of a Buddha.
Above was a grove of trees with curved trunks casting deep shade.
Whenever Senghu passed by the location of the wall, he would invariably see a brilliant radiance and hear the sounds of stringed instruments, pipes, and songs of praise.

Thereupon, holding aloft an incense burner, he made a vow to carve a ten-zhang stone Buddha into the face of Mount Bo, respectfully emulating the thousand-fathom countenance of Maitreya, so that all who possess the karmic affinity might together behold the three assemblies.
During the Jianwu era of the Northern Qi dynasty, he recruited both monastics and laypeople to begin the carving and shaping.
Though several years passed in excavation, only the basic outlines were completed.
Shortly thereafter, the guardian fell ill and passed away.
At the time of his death, he made this vow:
"That which I have undertaken was not originally intended to be accomplished within a single lifetime.
In my second existence, this aspiration shall bear fruit."
Later, there was the śramaṇa Sengshu, who inherited his predecessor’s unfinished work; however, lacking the necessary resources, he was unable to bring it to completion.

In the sixth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, Lu Xian of Wu Commandery, who was serving as the Magistrate of Shifeng, returned to his home country after leaving office. While staying overnight at Shan Creek, he encountered a storm with blinding rain and darkness. Terrified, Xian fell into a light sleep and suddenly dreamed that three practitioners of the Way came to him and said:
"Your faith and conviction are firm and upright; you shall naturally find peace and security."

His Highness the Prince of Jian’an has been afflicted by illness that has not yet healed; if you can complete the stone image being fashioned by the monk Hu at Shan County, he will surely recover and find peace.
"The profound principle is not empty; it is fitting that we should mutually illuminate it.

After Xian had returned to the capital for a year, he gradually forgot his previous dream. Later, as he was leaving the gate, he saw a monk who said he wished to stay overnight while listening to a lecture. Thereupon, [the monk] spoke:
"Do you still remember the matter concerning Prince Jian'an which you were entrusted with last year at Shanxi?"
They were all simultaneously seized with fear and replied,
"We do not remember.
The practitioner smiled and said:
"You should reflect upon this further," he said, and immediately took his leave.
All present realized that he was no ordinary man; they hurriedly ran out in their sandals to inquire after him, but having pursued him for a hundred paces, he suddenly vanished.
Xian’s mind was suddenly opened and he understood; he clearly remembered his previous dream, which had been of the third monk seen at Shan Creek.
Xian immediately galloped to inform Prince Jian’an, who then reported it to the Emperor. An imperial edict was issued appointing Vinaya Master Sengyou to take sole charge of the image-making project.
The King’s faith deepened even further, and he was filled with such boundless joy that he drew out gold and silver to vow to complete the work.

One day before Sengyou arrived, the monk Huicheng of the monastery dreamed of a great deity in black robes, accompanied by a formidable retinue, standing at the site of the niche and deliberating upon the proportions. When morning came, Vinaya Master Sengyou arrived; such was the divine response.

Originally established by Saṃgharakṣita, the niche he had excavated was too shallow; thus, he deepened it by five *zhang* and further fashioned the usnīṣa and bodily features. As the carving was nearing completion and the polishing was about to finish, suddenly in the middle of the night, the area where the *vajra* (thunderbolt) symbol was located turned crimson and protruded upward.
At present, the area on the chest of the image where the *svastika* (myriad-character) mark should be remains without a gold inlay, and its original red color still remains there.
The construction of the image began in the spring of the twelfth year of the Tianjian era and was completed in the spring of the fifteenth year.

The seated statue was five zhang in height, and its standing form was ten zhang tall; a three-tiered platform was constructed before the niche, and furthermore, gate pavilions, halls, and various foundations were established to provide for offerings.
Scholars and commoners from the four distant quarters all brought incense and flowers, gathering there from ten thousand *li* away.
As they traveled back and forth making offerings, the tracks left by their footsteps were so dense as to be impassable.
Since the statue was completed, the illness of Prince Jian’an had gradually abated, and his original ailment was fully restored.
The king later changed his fief, and he is the present Prince of Nanping. 14.
Shi Fayue: Shi Fayue was a śramaṇa who observed the precepts and maintained a vegetarian diet.
At the end of the Qi dynasty, he was appointed by imperial decree as the head of the monastic community (*saṃghapati*) and resided at Zhengjue Temple in the capital.
He diligently cultivated meritorious deeds, becoming a refuge for the fourfold assembly.

Huiyue once heard that at Songwang Temple in Pengcheng there was a golden image eighteen feet tall, commissioned by Wang Zhongde, the General of Chariots and Cavalry and Governor of Xuzhou; its craftsmanship in depicting the radiance of the Buddha’s features was considered the finest in the region south of the Yangtze.
If there should be calamities or malevolent spirits within the borders of the province, or if monks and nuns should incur sudden misfortune or provoke conflict, the image will sweat.
The greater or lesser amount of this sweat corresponds to the intensity or mildness of the impending disaster.
At the beginning of the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, Pengcheng fell under northern control, and the various barbarian tribes collectively sought to relocate the statue;
they mobilized ten thousand men, yet in the end were unable to move it.

At the beginning of the Qi dynasty, several commanderies in Yanzhou intended to rise in rebellion to align with the south, and they likewise coerced the monks into assisting in the defense of camps and moats.
At that time, the barbarian leader, the Duke of Lanling, attacked and captured this camp, seizing the various śramaṇas.
Thereupon, he took all the monks of the two provinces into custody and confined them within the siege lines.
The envoys of the spurious court slandered him, accusing him of aiding the rebellion; at that moment, the statue broke into a sweat, and the entire hall became damp.
