At the time, Liang Wang Liang was stationed at Pengcheng and also possessed a degree of faith; he went in person to the location of the statue and sent men to wipe it, but as soon as they did so, the sweat would reappear, and in the end, none could stop it.
The King then burned incense and prostrated himself, making a vow with a sincere heart:
"The assembly of monks is without fault; I, your disciple, shall personally provide protection and ensure they do not suffer calamity."
"If my sincere devotion moves you, I pray that the sweat will cease as soon as it is wiped away.
Thereupon, he wiped it with his own hand; as he wiped it, it became dry immediately.
The King reported this matter in detail, and all the monks were granted pardon.
Having joyfully beheld these spiritual wonders, Yue vowed to pay his respects;
however, as the frontier barriers stood in the way, he was unable to fulfill his wish.

Furthermore, in the past, Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty attempted to cast a golden statue eighteen feet tall, but it failed to complete four times; consequently, he reduced its height to fourteen feet.
Yue then, together with the śramaṇa Zhijing of Baima Monastery, led those of like affinity in their desire to remodel the eighteen-foot image of Amitāyus, thereby fulfilling their aspiration.
The initial gathering of gold and copper occurred toward the end of the Qi dynasty; however, as the world’s fortunes declined, the project was again subjected to rejection.

It was not until the Liang dynasty that the matter was first reported to the throne, whereupon an imperial edict was issued granting permission and providing assistance for the creation of the pedestal and base.
Materials and skilled artisans were provided according to the requirements.
On the third day of the fifth month in the eighth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, the casting was undertaken at Xiaozhuangyan Temple.

The master craftsmen originally calculated that forty thousand *jin* of copper would suffice for the Buddha’s body; however, once the molten metal had been poured and exhausted, it had not yet reached the chest.
The common people brought copper beyond measure, casting it into the furnaces as it was poured; yet the mold remained unfilled, just as it had been before.

He again dispatched a report to inform the Emperor, who issued an edict granting three thousand *jin* of "merit-copper. When the palace officials first began measuring and delivering it, they saw a sheep-cart carrying the imperial decree arrive at the site of the statue, with the copper already positioned by the furnace. Thereupon, the bellows were blown and the metal melted, and with a single casting, the mold was filled.
In that brief interval, both the man and the carriage vanished.
When the bronze emerged from within the platform, it was only then realized that what had been sent forth previously was truly a manifestation of spiritual response.
The craftsmen leaped for joy, and both monastics and laypeople offered their praise.
When the mold was opened and measured, it had miraculously increased to nineteen *zhang* in height, yet its radiant features remained unchanged.
Furthermore, two large coins were still visible within the folds of the robe, having not melted away at all; no one could fathom how this came to be.
In the past, forty thousand *liang* of copper were measured out; according to the calculations, there was a surplus.
Later, three thousand more were added, yet the total remained short and incomplete.
Nevertheless, auspicious signs emerged mysteriously and subtly, arising from within the mind’s design.
Thus we know that the profound resonance of the divine principle is likely beyond the reach of human affairs.
When the painted image was first completed, the bhikṣu Dàozhāo would often perform prostrations and repentance rites during the night.
Suddenly, he saw the place where the image stood become brilliantly and transparently illuminated.
After observing it closely for a long time, he realized the extraordinary nature of the divine radiance.
Three days after the casting, before the mold had even been opened,
there was a Chan master named Daodu, a monk of lofty integrity, who offered his seven-strip *kāṣāya* robe to contribute toward the expenses of opening the top of the head.
Shortly thereafter, he saw two monks from afar kneeling to untie the hair-knot of the image; as they drew near to observe it, the figures suddenly vanished.
At that time, the two monks Yue and Jing passed away one after the other.
By imperial decree, the matter of the image was entrusted to Sengyou of Dinglin Temple.
On the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month of that year, the image was moved to Guangzhai Temple; during this month there had been no rain, and consequently there was considerable dust.
When it was about to become clear that the image was to be moved, light clouds spread across the sky at night, and a fine rain moistened the earth.

Sengyou was walking near the location of the image, contemplating the weather, when he saw from afar a flame-like radiance rising and falling beside the image, appearing like lamps or candles, and he also heard the sounds of striking the ritual gong, chanting, and prostrating.
Upon entering the room and looking closely, everything was suddenly extinguished; Jiang Xiaosun of Fangsi witnessed this as well.
That night, merchants on the Huai River all heard the sound of a large merchant vessel approaching below, urging the construction of the bridge with voices sounding like several hundred people.
One can thus know that the importance of this sacred vessel is such that how could it have been brought here by human means?
Later, its pedestal and halo were recast, both accompanied by auspicious signs of fragrant winds.
From the region west of the Pamir Mountains to the east, this alone is the foremost of all golden images.
The Treatise says:

In the past, King Udayana first carved sandalwood, and the Parthian King first cast a golden image; both were faithful reproductions of the true countenance, with exquisite craftsmanship depicting the wondrous features.
Consequently, they were able to radiate light and manifest auspicious omens, causing people to rise from their seats in reverence and offer devotion.
As for the two stupas of hair and nails and the two platforms of the robe and shadow, these were all established as precedents during the Tathāgata’s lifetime.
From the time he withdrew his traces by the river until his cremation outside the forest, the eight kings requested a share of the relics and returned to their respective kingdoms to erect stupas.
Together with the two sites of the vase and the ashes, these constitute the ten sacred sites established therein.

As for the places where [the Buddha] attained the Way, preached the Dharma, entered Nirvana, as well as the uṣṇīṣa, the cranial bone, the four teeth, the pair of footprints, the alms bowl, the staff, the spittoon, the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, and so forth.
Stupas were erected at all these sites and inscriptions were set up to commemorate their divine wonders.
More than a hundred years later, King Aśoka dispatched envoys across the sea to dismantle these stupas and distribute the relics.
Later, encountering wind and waves, many were lost or left behind.
Consequently, they are occasionally encountered even today among the sea creatures.
Thereafter, eighty-four thousand [beings] arose because of this.
The daughters of King Aśoka also successively gave rise to pure faith; they together carved stone and melted gold to depict the divine forms.
These images were so efficacious that they floated upon rivers and seas, manifesting their transformations throughout the eastern provinces.
Although spiritual traces had already communicated themselves in secret, they had not yet been manifested to sight or hearing.
It was only when Cai Yin and Qin Jing returned from the Western Regions that the image of Śākyamuni on a cotton cloth (śāṭaka) was first transmitted.
Thereupon, at the Liangtai and Shouling [monasteries], their likenesses were depicted side by side.
From that time forward, images and pagodas were established in competition with one another as the times progressed.
Reaching the Great Liang dynasty, the remaining radiance flourished even more extensively.
The Dharma-body is formless; it manifests form only because of responsive resonance. Since there are disparities in the resonance that perceives it, its manifested forms necessarily differ.
If the path of the mind is vast and desolate, the true countenance will be separated from transformation; if one’s aspirations are earnest and sincere, even wood and stone will open their hearts.
Thus, Liu Yin’s ultimate filial piety and sincerity moved Heaven, such that inscriptions appeared spontaneously upon his cauldrons and granaries;
Ding Lan exhausted himself in the rituals of warmth and purity, and because of his devotion, the wooden mother changed her expression.
Lu Yang turned back his spear and the sun reversed its course; the wife of Qi wept so bitterly that the city wall collapsed.
All of these cases stem from their profound compassion penetrating the very nature of their being, which caused auspicious omens to manifest before their eyes and ears.

For instance, Huida summoned light at the site of his monastery; Huili invoked a miracle at the foundation of a stupa; Huishou expressed his sincerity through a floating log; Senghui manifested proof by shifting a lamp; both Hong and Liang forgot their physical forms while casting statues; and both Yi and Xian gave their lives for the sake of the monastery.

Dharmadatta focused his resolve upon the tooth and bone relics, and Jingling thereby achieved spiritual resonance; Senghu harbored his aspirations at Shicheng, and Nanping consequently attained a response.

Recently, there was a nine-cubit image at Guangzhai Temple that illuminated the capital region; though the Song Emperor attempted to cast it four times, he failed, whereas the Liang Emperor completed its form with a single casting.
The wondrous features emerged without flaw, and the auspicious bronze, though scarce, became more than sufficient.
Thus we know that the Way relies on people for its propagation and the spirit responds through things; how could this be called empty?
Therefore, when one sacrifices to a spirit as if the spirit were present, the way of spirits is communicated;
when one venerates a Buddha image as if it were the Buddha’s own body, the Dharma-body responds.
Therefore, entering the Way must take wisdom as its foundation, and wisdom must take merit as its basis.
It is like a bird equipped with two wings, which can suddenly soar to a height of a thousand fathoms;
or like a carriage with two wheels, which can gallop a thousand li in a single run.
How diligent they were! How exhorting they were!
The eulogy says:
The true countenance eclipses the radiance [of the sun], yet its brilliance is transmitted through metal and stone.
Therein lie stupas and images upon which those who harbor longing and devotion rely.
They manifest wonders to signify the ultimate, and display auspicious omens of majestic power.
Hidden within crags or emerging from the earth, they float upon the waters or fly through the air.
Sincere indeed is the path of the mind; it must surely accord with the truth without deviation.

Chapter Nine: Masters of the Sūtras (Jing-shi). 1. Bo Faqiao 2. Yi Zhitanyue 3. Shi Faping 4. Shi Sengrao 5. Shi Daohui 6. Shi Zhizong 7. Shi Tanchuan 8. Shi Tanzhi 9. Shi Sengbian 10. Shi Tanping 11. Shi Huiren 1. Bo Faqiao: A native of Zhongshan.
In his youth, he took pleasure in reciting scriptures, yet lacked a resonant voice; he often lamented this lack of fluency.
Thereupon, he abstained from grain for seven days and seven nights, prostrating himself before Avalokiteśvara to pray for an immediate response.
His fellow students earnestly admonished him, but he vowed not to change his mind.
On the seventh day, he felt a sudden opening within his throat; he immediately sought water to rinse his mouth and said, "I have received a response."
Thereupon he made three musical strikes; the sound of the bells reached for nearly a *li*, and those far and near were struck with wonder and came all to observe and listen.
Thereafter, he recited several hundred thousand words of scripture, chanting day and night with such pathos and elegance that it moved the divine spirits.
When he reached the age of ninety, his voice remained unchanged.
He passed away in Hebei during the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu of the Jin dynasty;
this was toward the end of Shi Hu’s reign.
He had a disciple named Sengfu, whose monastic conduct was likewise pure and lofty. 2.
Zhi Tanyue: Zhi Tanyue was originally a person from the Yuezhi; he resided in Jianye.
He left home to become a monk at a young age, living in austere purity and subsisting on vegetarian food while resting at Mount Huqiu in Wu.
At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty, he was invited by imperial decree to the capital, where he resided at Jianchu Monastery.
Emperor Xiaowu received the five precepts from him and revered him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
Yao was uniquely gifted with a marvelous voice and excelled at chanting the scriptures.
He once dreamed that a celestial deity bestowed upon him the methods of vocal intonation; upon waking, he accordingly composed new melodies.
The Brahma-sounds were pure and elegant, soaring in four directions and turning back upon themselves.

They reversed and folded at the throat, resonating in layered cadences; though Dong'e was the first to innovate and Kang Hui followed later, even their mastery of cyclical progression could not match the exquisite subtlety of this flute-like resonance.
Later generations who transcribed his works followed none other than his methods.
The six-character Buddhist hymns he composed have resounded in fame to this day.
He passed away at his residence at the age of eighty-one.
3. Shi Faping. Shi Faping’s family name was Kang; he was a native of Kangju.
He resided in Jianye.
Together with his younger brother Fadeng, he left the household life and stayed at Baima Temple.
He became a disciple of Tan Yue, and together they transmitted their master’s legacy.
His resonance was pure and elegant, and his delivery was versatile and boundless.
Later, the brothers both moved to the Jetavana Monastery; although the younger brother’s appearance was somewhat unattractive, his voice surpassed that of his elder brother.
The Great General of the Song dynasty was hosting a vegetarian feast at the Eastern Palace; at first, he looked down upon [the monk] based on his appearance.
However, upon hearing him recite the *Tri-samaya* (Threefold Pledge), he immediately pressed his hands together in admiration and was moved to spiritual reverence, exclaiming:
"It is truly said that 'to judge a person by their appearance leads to the loss of Zi Yu.'"
Later, when Master Yan of Dong’an began his lecture and they had finished reciting three sections of the sutra together, Yan slowly moved his fly-whisk and said,
"Reciting the sutra in this manner does not diminish the merit of giving a formal lecture."
Thereupon, the assembly dispersed.
The following day, the topic was reopened; those who deliberated considered it a path of mutual fulfillment.
Both brothers passed away at the end of the Yuanjia era.
4. Shi Sengrao. Shi Sengrao was a native of Jiankang.
He entered the monastic order and resided at Baima Monastery.

He was skilled in epistolary composition and various arts, but he was particularly renowned for his mastery of vocal music, attaining fame during the reigns of Emperors Wu and Wen of the Song dynasty.
His resonant chanting was leisurely and elegant, harmonious, refined, and plaintively brilliant, rivaling that of Daorong.
Daorong was skilled in the three *Prātimokṣa* recitations and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Every time he raised his voice in pure *brahman*-chanting, both monastics and laypeople would be moved to the core of their hearts.
The monastery has a Prajñā Terrace where many constantly circumambulate it while chanting the *Brahma-wheel* (the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*) as an act of offering.
Those traveling along the road who hear this sound invariably halt their carriages, linger in reflection, snap their fingers, and invoke the name of the Buddha.
He passed away in the second year of the Daming era of the Song dynasty at the age of eighty-six.

At that time, there were also Chaoming and Minghui in the same monastery; having practiced *fanbai* (Buddhist chanting) together since their youth, they later engaged in recitation during long periods of fasting, both of whom were renowned in their day.
5. Shi Daohui. Shi Daohui’s secular surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Chaisang in Xunyang.
He entered the monastic order at the age of twenty-four and resided at Mount Lu Monastery.
His conduct was pure and upright from the start, and he had extensively studied the classics.
Having been uniquely endowed with a natural talent for vocal intonation, he was particularly fond of chanting and recitation.
His delivery of sounds possessed a marvelous quality, being fashioned without fixed constraints; his phrasing of lines and parsing of sentences were elegant and distinct.
Later, he left the capital and stayed at Anle Temple, where his reputation for reciting scriptures became so great that it flourished throughout the imperial city.
In his later years, he moved to Zhulin Temple in Zhufang, where he recited tens of thousands of words of the sutras.
Every evening he would recite and chant, and he would frequently hear the sound of finger-snapping and the chanting of *sādhukāra* from within the darkness.
He passed away in the second year of the Daming era of the Song dynasty at the age of fifty-one.
6. Shi Zhizong. Shi Zhizong’s secular surname was Zhou, and he was a native of Jiankang.
He left the household life and resided at Xie Temple.
He was widely learned and possessed great erudition, being particularly skilled in the melodic recitation of scriptures.
The sound was exceptionally clear and refreshing; it was as if during a long night of the Eight Precepts,
when after midnight, the fourfold assembly began to nod and the "sleep-serpents" came upon them one after another,
Master Zong would ascend the seat and deliver a single turn of the Dharma, his Brahma-voice resonating and piercing the clouds.
There was none whose spirit was not opened and whose body was not refreshed, who did not attain a sudden and clear awakening.
He passed away in the third year of the Daming era at the age of thirty-one.
At that time, there were Huibao and Daoquan; although they did not live concurrently, their methods of practice were similar.
His voice was exceptionally rich and his intonation lofty; yet, as for the compositions he produced, there was nothing of merit to be found.
During the Song dynasty, Minghu suddenly came to admire Daoquan, and critics remarked that this was because he had encountered his time.
7. Shi Tanyuan. Shi Tanyuan’s secular surname was Zhi, and his ancestors were originally from the Yuezhi.
He resided in Jiankang.

He was deeply devoted to both the profound mysteries of Daoism and Confucianism, and his mind wandered freely through the meanings of Buddhist doctrine. He was skilled at discussing the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi, and he also annotated the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Furthermore, he was adept at the formal script (zhengshu) and frequently donated his calligraphy for inscriptions on sutras.
He was skilled at chanting and recitation, possessing an inexhaustible range of melodic tones; his Sanskrit compositions were novel and extraordinary, standing out as preeminent throughout antiquity.
Prince Yikang of Pengcheng, Fan Ye, and Wang Tanshou all associated with him in close friendship.
At first, Huiqian resided at Jihuan Temple; later, he moved to Wuyi Temple.
When Fan Ye was executed, there were twelve funeral processions at his gate, yet no one dared to approach.
Xian collected his belongings and clothing, arranging everything for his funeral rites.
When Emperor Xiaowu heard of this, he sighed in admiration and said to Xu Yuan,
"When you compose the *Song Shu*, do not omit this man."
Wang Sengqian served as governor of Xiangzhou and the Three Wu regions, and [Senglang] accompanied him on official tours in both places.
He passed away in the fourth year of the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty at the age of ninety-nine.
At that time, there were Shi Fachang of Daochang Temple and Shi Daoyan of Waguan Temple, both of whom were renowned for their rich and plaintive chanting.
Although he did not compete with those who attained high rank through rapid promotion, he was nevertheless ranked next in order. 8.
Shi Tanzhi: Shi Tanzhi’s secular surname was Wang; he was a native of Jiankang.
He left the household life and resided at Dong’an Temple.
By nature he was elegant and refined, skilled in deportment.
He was able to discourse on Zhuangzi and Laozi, as well as the sutras, śāstras, books, and histories, having extensively studied and mastered them.
Possessing a lofty and resonant voice, he was particularly fond of chanting and recitation.
Although he relied upon the preceding schools, he stood out with unique and novel insights.
His lofty style was pure and penetrating, conveying his meaning with more than ample grace.
Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, Xiao Si-hua, Wang Sengqian, and others all held him in profound esteem.
When Sengqian was appointed to the governorship of Xiangzhou, [Huiyuan] accompanied him on his journey.
When Xiao [Yuanzong] governed Wu, he again invited him to enter [the capital].
He passed away in the state of Wu in the fifth year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, at the age of seventy-nine.
At that time, there were Daolang, Farin, Zhixin, and Huiguang, none of whom possessed profound understanding; they were merely capable of reciting the texts with some skill.
Daolang held the tones too loosely, Farin favored excessive emphasis on the strikes, Zhixin was adept at slanting the modulations, and Huiguang delighted in letting his voice soar.
9. Shi Sengbian. Shi Sengbian’s secular surname was Wu, and he was a native of Jiankang.
He entered the monastic order and resided at Anle Temple.
From his youth, he delighted in reading the scriptures and received instruction from the two masters Qian and Chang.
In the beginning, he followed the style of his predecessors, but in his later years, he applied himself with greater deliberation.
His compositions were elegiac and balanced, standing peerless at the start of the Qi dynasty.
Once, while observing a fast at Liu Shao’s residence in Xinting, he debated the meaning of a scripture read during the first watch of the night and finally attained a profound realization.
Suddenly, a flock of cranes descended and gathered before the steps; as soon as Hui Bian finished rolling up his scroll, they all flew away at once.
From this, his reputation resounded throughout the world, and he became renowned both far and near.
Later scholars all took him as their master.

On the nineteenth day of the second month in the seventh year of the Yongming era, Prince Wenxuan of Jingling, the Minister of Education, dreamed that he was chanting a passage from the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* before the Buddha.

Upon hearing the same sound, he awoke and immediately rose to go into the Buddha hall; following the method from his dream, he further chanted one section of the *Old Vimalakīrti*, finding that the melody and voice flowed beautifully, and he applied himself to it with diligence every day.

At dawn the following morning, he immediately assembled the śramaṇas from the capital renowned for their vocal mastery: Longguang Puzhi, Xin’an Daoxing, Duobao Huiren, Tianbao Chaosheng, as well as Sengbian and others.
The collection concludes with the composition of sounds.
Bian’s transmission of one section of the *Ancient Vimalakīrti* and one section of the seven-syllable verses of the *Ruiying* are truly masterpieces that define his school.
Among later generations, there were occasional transmitters of his teachings, yet they all distorted and omitted its essential substance.
Daoben passed away in the eleventh year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty.
During the Zhongxing period, there was the monk Senggong, who at that time was equal in fame to Daoben, though he later withdrew from the monastic path.
10. Shi Tanping. Shi Tanping’s secular surname was Yang; he was a native of Nan’an in Jianwei.
In his youth, he traveled to the capital to study the art of chanting and recitation, eventually settling at Baima Temple.
His vocal intonation was highly refined, yet he remained self-assured even before dawn; at that time, his contemporaries had not yet recognized his excellence.

Thereupon, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the rules of performance and practiced them with even greater diligence. In his later years, he finally emerged from the crowd, and everyone unanimously changed their perception of him.
He recited the three *Benqi jing* (Sūtras on Past Deeds) with exceptional mastery of their tones.
Later, he returned to Shu and resided at Longyuan Temple.
Those in Ba and Han who were moved by his voice all revered him as a model of vocal excellence.
Every time he uttered a single sound in the Brahma-voice, birds and horses would cry out in grief, and those traveling on the road would halt their steps.
Consequently, he had a bronze bell cast, vowing that in the future he might always possess the eight qualities of the Brahma-voice and the four types of analytical eloquence.
The bronze bell at Yongshu originated from this;
later, it was finally kept where he resided.
At that time, there was a monk in Shu named Lingdaoguang, who was also somewhat skilled in chanting and recitation.
11. Shi Huirin: Shi Huirin’s secular surname was Kuai, and he was a native of Jiankang.
He left home to become a monk in his youth and resided at Beiduobao Temple.
He possessed no other practice or understanding; he simply took delight in musical sounds.
He first studied under Master Bian of Anle and fully mastered his methods;
yet, with a style that was both plaintive and exquisitely subtle, he specifically sought to surpass him.

After Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty experienced a dream, he assembled various masters of the scriptures, and together with Huiren, they refined the traditional melodies and categorized the new variations.
He compiled forty-two sections of the *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra* (The Response of Auspiciousness), which were the most extensive and sublime among those he mastered through patience.

Thereupon, he instructed more than forty people—including Huiman, Sengye, Sengshang, Chaolang, Sengqi, Chaoyou, Huixu, Falü, Tanhui, Sengyin, Huitan, and Faci—to study under him as his disciples of endurance; thus, the Dharma has been transmitted down to the present day.
Ren died in the first year of the Longchang era at the age of over forty.
Shi Falin’s rhythmic modulation of phrases was exceptionally refined, possessing a distinct melodic quality.
Shi Tandi appeared unremarkable at first glance, yet the longer one observed him, the more outstanding he became.
Shi Huinian possessed a delicate and refined air from his youth, yet he was exceptionally meticulous and elegant.
Shi Tanguan was brisk and incisive; his calligraphy followed established methods.
Shi Tanjin was also a master of the eight skills, excelling in the composition of the *Huanguo pin* (Chapter on Returning to the Country).
Shi Huichao was skilled in the three *kṣaṇas*, yet later he could not maintain his excellence.
Shi Daoshou was timid in his initial approach; Changdao’s work is worthy of admiration.
Shi Tan-diao transcribed with refined elegance, yet one regrets that his craftsmanship was not yet sufficient.
All these individuals were renowned during the Qi dynasty.
In the regions of the left bank of the Zhe River, Jiangxi, Jingxia, and Yongsu, there were also quite a few who engaged in recitation;
however, their efforts were merely for contemporary verse and chant, lacking any high reputation, and thus they are not worth recording in this transmission.
The treatise states:
Now, the composition of chapters and sections is intended to fully express one’s inner thoughts and to extol one’s sentiments and aspirations.
The composition of songs and chants is intended to allow the flavor of the words to flow gracefully and for the phrasing and rhythms to harmonize with one another.
Therefore, the "Preface to the Book of Poetry" says:
"When emotion is stirred within, it takes form in speech.
When speech is insufficient, one therefore chants and sings."
However, as for the songs of the Eastern lands, they form verses by binding together rhymes;
whereas the hymns of the Western regions compose gāthās to harmonize with the sound.
Although songs and hymns differ from one another, both accord with the pitch-pipes and harmonize with the musical notes of Gong and Shang; only then do they become profound and wondrous.
Therefore, when songs are performed upon metal and stone instruments, they are called "music" (yue);
when praises are set to pipes and strings, they are termed "chanting" (bai).
Now, the sages established music, and its virtues are fourfold:
It moves Heaven and Earth, communicates with the spiritual intelligences, brings peace to the myriad people, and perfects the natures of all classes.
Like listening to a chant, it likewise possesses five benefits:
the body does not grow weary, what has been memorized is not forgotten, the mind does not become exhausted, the voice is not impaired, and the devas rejoice.

Thus, Pañcaśikha sang and played the lute in the stone chamber, entreating the opening of the first gate to the nectar of immortality; the Śuddhāvāsa devas performed dances and hymns at the twin śāla trees, offering their gratitude for the grace of a single transformation.
In the intervals between these, they were extolled according to the occasion, and their melodies were perfected wherever they resounded—
such as the subtle voice of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa at nightfall, or the resonant chanting of Devadatta within the Brahma palace.
Sometimes the principle of signlessness is rendered upon the pipes and flutes;
sometimes the sounds of fundamental practice are proclaimed beneath the zithers and lutes.
In each case, the music rises and falls in resonance with the spirit, as praised by the Buddha.
Thus, the *Xianchi* and *Shaowu* have nothing with which to match its skill; the *Jichu* and *Liangchen* have nothing with which to compare its subtlety.
Since the Great Teaching flowed eastward, those who have translated its texts have been numerous, yet those who have transmitted its oral chanting have been few.

This is truly because the Sanskrit sounds are repetitive while the Chinese language is monosyllabic and unique; if one uses Sanskrit phonetics to chant Chinese words, the sounds will be too numerous and the verses too cramped;
if one uses Chinese melodies to chant Sanskrit texts, the rhymes will be too short for the length of the phrasing.
Therefore, while the golden words [of the Buddha] have been translated, the resonance of the Sanskrit sounds has remained untransmitted.
It was first the Prince of Chen-si of the Wei dynasty, Cao Zhi, who deeply loved the principles of prosody and devoted his mind to the phonology of the scriptures.
Having mastered the auspicious resonance of the Pañcavimśati-sāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā and being moved by the divine composition at Mount Yú,

he then edited and refined the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Pratyutpanna-saṃvidhāna*) and the *Sūtra of Past Occurrences* (*Pūrva-yoga*) to establish them as the fundamental authorities for scholars.
In oral transmission, there were more than three thousand pieces; in written notation, there were forty-two.

Later, Bo Qiao and Zhi Yue also claimed to follow the tradition of Chen Si (Cao Zhi), yet they favored supernatural communication and produced works through distinct divine inspiration; they modified and altered ancient melodies, leaving behind only ten pieces.
During the Jianping era of Shi Le, a celestial deity descended into the hall of An-yi and chanted the sounds of the scriptures for seven days before ceasing.
Those who transmitted these accounts at the time all became corrupted and lost.

By the time of the Song and Qi dynasties, there were figures such as Tanqian, Sengbian, the Grand Tutor (Taifu), and Wenxuan, all of whom diligently praised and chanted [the texts], applied themselves with meticulous care to their musical prosody, compiled various differing versions, and deliberated upon their structural categories and precedents.
Preserving and following the ancient methods, there were originally only some three hundred sounds.
From that time forward, many of these sounds were lost.
Everyone took it upon themselves to pay attention, yet their efforts at restoration and supplementation differed.
Thus, teachers have differed in their methods and families have each devised their own systems.
This is entirely due to a lack of understanding regarding the principles of sound and a failure to apply proper correction.
Indeed, that music moves the heart has been so since ancient times.
Thus, when the Master of Mystery sang his hymns, the crimson geese were so captivated they would not move;
when the Bhikṣu’s voice flowed forth, the azure birds were so delighted they forgot to fly.
Even when Tanping moved his melodies, he caused birds and horses alike to crouch and hesitate.
When Sengbian modulated his tones, he could even cause the great cranes to halt their flight.
Although people’s capacities vary in depth, the art of evoking resonance is likewise secondary only to that.
Thus, when Kui struck the stones and tapped them, all the beasts followed in dance.
When the *Xiao* and *Shao* music were performed nine times, the phoenixes came and displayed their graceful forms.
If even birds and beasts can be moved by such resonance, how much more so must humans and spirits be?
However, the excellence of chanting the scriptures lies simply in this: the value resides in achieving harmony between both the sound and the text.
If there were only sound without text, then the mind for the Way would have no means by which to arise;
if there were only text without sound, then worldly sentiments would have no means by which to enter.
Thus, it is as the Sūtra says: "To praise the Buddha’s virtues by singing with a subtle and wondrous voice"—this is precisely what that refers to.

Yet, scholars of recent times, having merely grasped a fragmentary portion of the melody from beginning to end, claim to have achieved renown in their own day; they never once give a thought to the beginning and conclusion of the entire scriptural text.
Some break the sentences to fit the melody, while others divide the prose to complete the rhyme.
Not only is the sound insufficient, but the text itself fails to convey its meaning.
Those who listen only feel increasingly dazed, and upon hearing it, they find nothing but an increase in their drowsiness.

Alas! It is to be pitied that the eight true bright pearls have their radiance obscured before they are even displayed, and the hundred-flavored pure milk has become thin of its own accord without being diluted. Alas!
If one can masterfully penetrate the essential meaning of the scriptures and thoroughly comprehend the principles of musical tones—
arranging the three registers and seven notes in their proper sequence without confusion,
and aligning the five-syllable lines and four-character phrases with perfect precision— then one is truly proficient.

Within this, there are the movements of rising, tossing, sweeping, and lifting; of leveling, bending, releasing, and striking; of gliding, flying, retreating, and turning; and of reversing, layering, and playful coquetry.
When the rhythmic cadence moves, it flows and meanders without end; when the throat is opened, its transformations are inexhaustible.
Thus, it can brilliantly manifest the eight musical tones and gloriously propagate the seven virtues.
It is majestic yet not fierce, concentrated yet not stagnant;
it is gentle yet not vulgar, firm yet not sharp.
Clear yet undisturbed; turbid yet unobscured.
Truly sufficient to give rise to and elucidate subtle words, and to gladden and nourish the divine nature.
Thus, by listening to sounds, one may delight the ears.
Listening to these words can open one’s heart.
If this is so, it may be said that the Sanskrit sounds are profound and subtle, such that they bring joy to those who hear them.
Furthermore, according to the customs of India, all songs and chants concerning the Dharma are termed *bhāṣya* (or *bhai*).
In this land, chanting the sutras is termed *zhuan-du* (recitation), while singing praises is called *fan-bei* (Brahma-singing).
In the past, when the devas offered hymns of praise, they invariably set them to musical rhythms and accompanied them with stringed and wind instruments.
Since the fivefold assembly differs from worldly conventions, it is appropriate that they take melodic chanting as their excellence.
Tracing the origin of *brahmaghoṣa* (Buddhist hymns), its inception was signaled by Emperor Chen Si (Wenxuan).
He first composed the "Hymn to the Prince" (*Taizi song*) and the "Hymn to Śyāma" (*Shan song*), for which he subsequently created the musical melodies.
The techniques of exhaling and inhaling, as well as the modulation of voice, were all transmitted through divine instruction.
The earnest contemplation practiced by the present [monks] is surely due to the influence of that tradition.
Later, the lay practitioner Zhi Qian also transmitted the three-part Buddhist chants (fanbai), but these too have been lost and no longer exist.
There is a chapter titled "Discourse on Common Deliberation" (*Gongyi*) in circulation; I fear it may be a remnant of excessive humility.
Only the *Nirvāṇa* Sanskrit chants composed by Kang Senghui are still transmitted to this day.
This refers to a single musical measure performed with reverence; the text originates from the two-fascicle *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and is thus called the *Nirvāṇa-bhaiṣajya* (Nirvāṇa chant).
By the Jin dynasty, Dharma Master Gaozuo was the first to transmit the *Mili* [chant].
The mudrā-text for the current practice of the Grounds (bhūmi) is precisely this ritual method.
The six-word verse composed by Master Ye is the single melodic chant of "Great Compassionate Pity," which continues to be performed by practitioners today.
Recently there has been a chant from Xiliangzhou, originating in the region west of the Passes and flowing into Jinyang; this is what is known today as the "Face Like the Full Moon.
All of these various melodies were composed by renowned masters.
Subsequent generations continued these works, yet they were rife with errors and omissions.
At times, novice śrāmaṇeras and children transmitted them to one another;
of the established rules of former times, hardly a single one remains—how lamentable!
Since this is likewise an example of the category of "Sound" (śabda), it is included at the end of the treatise.

10. Chàngdǎo (Chanting and Exhortation) 1. Shi Dàozhào 2. Shi Tányǐng 3. Shi Huìqú 4. Shi Tánzōng 5. Shi Tánguāng 6. Shi Huìfēn 7. Shi Dàorú 8. Shi Huìchóng 9. Shi Fǎyuàn 10. Shi Fǎjìng 1. Shi Dàozhào Shi Dàozhào’s surname was Qū; he was a native of Píngxī.

In his youth, he was skilled in correspondence and possessed broad knowledge of the classics and histories. At the age of eighteen, he left home to become a monk and resided at Qiyuan Temple in the capital.
He perused the various canonical texts and made the practice of public recitation his primary vocation.

His voice was clear and resonant, washing away and awakening the dusty minds of others; his discourse was timely and grounded in concrete reality, never issuing forth in isolation. He walked alone at the dawn of the Song dynasty.

Once, while Emperor Wu of Song was observing a fast in the inner palace, he spoke briefly during the first watch of the night regarding the rapidity of a hundred-year lifespan and how death and extinction occur in an instant.
"Suffering and joy vary according to the causes that summon them.
The Tathāgata responds with compassion to the six realms, and Your Majesty extends pity and care to all beings. The Emperor spoke these words of praise for a long time.
When the fast was concluded, he separately bestowed thirty thousand coins as a donation.
Wang Gui, Prince of Linchuan, received the five precepts from him and honored him as his family preceptor.
He passed away in the thirtieth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty at the age of sixty-six.
The disciple Zhao Hui-ming, surnamed Jiao, was a native of Wei Commandery.
His spirit and character were exceptionally refined; having inherited the master’s tradition from his ancestors, he too was renowned in his time.
2. Shi Tan-ying. Shi Tan-ying was a native of Kuaiji.
He left home to become a monk at a young age and was scrupulously observant of the precepts. He recited over one hundred thousand words of scripture and resided at Changgan Temple.
By nature humble and frugal, he prioritized the gentle guidance of others through virtue.
Therefore, he devoted himself to chanting with a natural and peerless excellence.
Whenever he was invited, he attended regardless of whether the host was noble or lowly, treating the poor and the wealthy with equal impartiality.
When Zhang Chang heard of this, he sighed in admiration, saying:
"His speech was fluent and eloquent, fully capable of expounding profound principles.

Sengying once suffered from ringworm sores that persisted despite prolonged treatment. He constantly maintained an image of Avalokiteśvara within his room, prostrating before it morning and evening, seeking relief from this ailment.

At another time, he suddenly saw a snake crawl from behind the image up the wall onto the roof; shortly thereafter, a young rat fell from the roof to the ground, its body drenched in saliva and mucus, appearing as if dead.
He waited to observe the situation; it appeared that the child might still be saved, so he took a bamboo scraper to remove the saliva and mucus.
He had also heard that the saliva from a snake that has swallowed a rat can cure skin ailments, so he scraped off the saliva and applied it to the scabies.
Once the ointment had been applied everywhere, the rat was restored to life.
Within two nights, its sores and wounds were completely healed.
Only then did he realize that both the snake and the rat were the result of his prayers and entreaties.
Thereupon, he applied himself with diligence to transforming and guiding others, his resolve becoming even more steadfast.
He was held in the highest esteem by Liu Yigong, the Prince of Jiangxia and Grand Chancellor of the Song dynasty.
Later, he passed away at his residence at the age of eighty-one.
3. Shi Huiqu. Shi Huiqu was a native of Danyang.
He entered the monastic order and resided at Waguan Temple.
He read and perused the sutras and treatises, and had a broad acquaintance with secular literature and history.
He was proficient in many arts, yet he was especially skilled in chanting and exhortation.
His spoken words formed elegant compositions, and his extemporaneous writings were produced with such breadth of learning that there was nothing in them that was not exquisite.
He visited Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty and General of Chariots and Cavalry Zang Zhi; both treated him with kindness and friendship, holding him in high esteem and affection.
When the Prince of Qiao was stationed in Jingzhou, he invited him to accompany him there.
Later, after his rebellious schemes were thwarted, he returned to the capital and held an assembly at Liangshan.
Shortly thereafter, the Prince of Qiao was defeated, and Xu returned to the capital.
Subsequently, when Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty held a vegetarian feast, Xu served as the *changdao* (chant leader). The Emperor asked Xu:
"What is this gathering today like compared to that at Mount Liang?
Qu replied, "Heaven's Way assists those who act in accordance with righteousness; how much more so when one acts in rebellion?"
The Emperor was pleased with this.
The following morning, he presented him with a separate gift of ten thousand coins.
Later, by imperial decree, he was appointed as the *upadhivāra* (chief administrative officer) of the capital city.
At the end of the Daming era, he passed away at the monastery at the age of seventy-two.
4. Shi Tanzong: Shi Tanzong’s secular surname was Guo, and he was a native of Moling.
He left the household life and resided at Lingwei Monastery.
From his youth, he was fond of learning and attained a broad mastery of the various classics.
His skill in expounding the teachings was peerless in his time;
his eloquence suited the occasion, and his adaptability was inexhaustible.
Once, while presiding over the *chàngdǎo* (invocation) for Emperor Xiaowu, after the ritual of the Five Dharmas of a Bodhisattva had been completed, the Emperor laughed and said to Zong:
"What transgressions do I have that you should perform this repentance for me?"
Zong said: "In the past, even the most sagely Yu Shun spoke of 'my transgressions, which you, my assistants, must correct.
Tang and Wu likewise declared, 'If the myriad people have committed offenses, it rests with me alone.'"
When sage-kings took blame upon themselves, it was surely to provide a model for the world.
Your Majesty’s virtue surpasses that of past ages, and your sageliness rivals that of the Yu and Yin dynasties; as you tread the Way with humble reflection, how could you alone be exceptional?
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
Later, when Empress Shuyi of the Yin clan passed away, a memorial assembly was held on the twenty-first day; he invited Sengzong in its entirety.
At that time, Sengzong began to lament that the ways of the world are floating and false, and that all affection must inevitably end in separation.
"Alas! The virtuous character of the Yin family had not yet fully flourished with glory when they perished in their prime; yet today we gather their fragrance. These words are profoundly moving.
The Emperor remained drenched in sorrow for a long while, his appreciation for their extraordinary merit becoming even deeper.
Later, he passed away at his place of residence, having authored the *Record of Stupas and Temples in the Capital* in two fascicles.
At that time, there was also a monk named Shi Sengyi at Lingwei Monastery, who was likewise skilled in chanting and preaching.
He produced new melodies for the *Śyāma-sūtra*, which were plaintive, resonant, and well-ordered. 5.
Shi Tanguang: Shi Tanguang was a native of Kuaiji.
He followed his teacher and resided at Changsha Monastery in Jiangling.
By nature, his mind delighted in the Five Classics, poetry, and prose, as well as mathematics and divination; there was nothing he did not thoroughly understand.
When he was nearly thirty years old, he sighed deeply and said:
"All that I have studied until now has been merely worldly matters."
"The profound principles of the Buddha-dharma have not yet stained me by even a single hair; how could shaving my head be appropriate for me?
Thereupon, he set aside his former pursuits and listened to various sutras and treatises.
His insight and awakening surpassed those of others; upon hearing them once, he immediately attained full understanding.

Wenwang Yiji, Prince of Hengyang of the Song dynasty, while stationed in Jingzhou, sought out śramaṇas of profound insight and principle with whom to discuss the Buddha-dharma; his reputation was highly esteemed throughout the region, and he was deemed fit for such a grand responsibility.
Guang firmly declined, but the King went to his quarters in person to earnestly entreat him; he finally complied with the command.
The King provided him with carriages, robes, and laborers, and granted him a monthly stipend of ten thousand coins.
Whenever a vegetarian assembly was held, there was no one to serve as the presiding master.
The King said to Guang, "To guide and lead all living beings is the very foundation of virtue. How can you, O Venerable One, decline this? I pray that you will certainly exert yourself.
Guang then changed his mind and practiced chanting, composing texts for repentance.
Whenever he presided over the assembly while holding the incense burner, both monastics and laypeople would look up to him with deep reverence.
Later, when he returned to the capital and resided at Lingwei Monastery, Prince Xi of Yiyang went out to govern Beixu and took Fayuan with him.

When Emperor Jinghe lost his virtue and Yiyang rose in rebellion, [the authorities] took advantage of Hui-guang’s prior foresight; they presented him with the *Qiyao* (The Seven Luminaries) to test his insight. Hui-guang kept his mouth shut and remained silent, so that the matter was settled and he escaped punishment.

Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty held a religious assembly at the Xianggong Temple; hearing Guang’s chanting and exhortations, the Emperor praised him as excellent and immediately issued an edict bestowing upon him the three robes, a water flask, and an alms bowl.
Later, he passed away in the temple at the age of sixty-five.
6. Shi Huifen. Shi Huifen’s secular surname was Li, and she was a native of Yuzhou.
From childhood she possessed extraordinary character; at the age of twelve, she left the household life and resided at Changshan Temple in Gushu County.
His learning was profound and extensive, and his ascetic practices were rigorous and austere.
Whenever he attended a vegetarian feast or assembly, he would invariably preach the Dharma for the great multitude.
Throughout the regions of Liang and Chu, all submitted to his transformation.
When the Wei barbarians destroyed the Buddha-dharma, she returned south to the capital.

Upon reaching Wujiang, the pursuing cavalry were about to overtake her, but there was no boat at the riverbank. Sengfen single-mindedly recited the name of the Buddha; suddenly, a drifting boat appeared, and by boarding it, she escaped capture.
Upon arriving at the capital, he stayed at the Baima Monastery.

At that time, Yuan Min-sun, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief, often remarked that monks were biased and narrow-minded, and thus not worth engaging in discussion. He therefore ordered his attendants to keep watch for a śramaṇa, intending to test him by speaking with him.
When Daofen arrived, Yuan first questioned him on the principles of the Three Vehicles and the Four Noble Truths, and then debated the essentials of Laozi, Zhuangzi, Confucius, and Mozi.
Since Daofen was already well-versed in the classics and scriptures, and his speech was fluent and eloquent, [Yuan was impressed].
From dawn until evening, Yuan was unable to exhaust her [in debate].
Thereupon, he revered her as his teacher and ordered all his disciples to receive the precepts from her.
Daofen was also skilled in divine incantations, and whatever she treated invariably proved effective.
Later, when his illness became critical and he was taking medicinal pills, someone urged him to take them with wine.
Daofen said, "I have observed the precepts for a long time; how could I violate my integrity by taking them with wine just as I am about to die?"
He then said to his disciples,
"I am now departing.
He passed away at Xingfu Temple in the third year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty at the age of seventy-nine.
At the time of his death, he left behind instructions and writings, which state as follows.
7. Shi Daoru: Shi Daoru, surnamed Shi, was a native of Bohai.
He resided in Guangling.
From his youth, he harbored pure faith and aspired to the life of a renunciant.
When Liu Yiqing, the Prince of Linchuan of the Song dynasty, was stationed in Nan-Yuanzhou, Rui reported the matter to him.
The Prince supported his resolve and submitted a memorial for his ordination.

After leaving the household life, he subsisted on vegetarian food and devoted himself to recitation and study; in all his activities, he exhorted others to reform their evils and cultivate goodness. Revered by those both near and far, he eventually became a spiritual guide.
It is said that he did not engage in prior composition, but rather his teachings were spontaneously formed as they were uttered.
At the end of the Yuanjia era, he went to the capital and stayed at Jianchu Temple.

The Prince of Changsha requested him to serve as his preceptor for the precepts; the Chancellor Lu (Liu Yiqing) and his brothers, including Liu Zhongsun, jointly purchased the former temple of Zhang Jing'er to establish a monastery for Huiru, which is the present-day Qifu Temple.
Xu Ru died in the eighth year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty at the age of eighty-one.
At that time, there was also the monk Shi Sengxi of Xianxin Temple, who was likewise skilled in chanting and exposition, and whose reputation flourished during the late Song and early Qi periods.
8. Shi Huizhong: Shi Huizhong’s surname was Min, and he was a native of Lu State.
He lived as a sojourner in Jinling.

From an early age, he harbored faith and awakening, and possessed the aspiration to follow the Way; though his vow had not yet been fulfilled, he already maintained a long-term fast and a vegetarian diet.
Whenever he led the assembly for vegetarian feasts and assemblies, he would always personally serve as the chant leader (*cangdao*).
After doing so for many years, his reputation reached the ears of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty.

In the sixth year of the Daming era, an imperial edict was issued for him to leave the household life at Xin'an Temple; thereupon, he specialized in performing the duties of the chant leader and preacher.
By nature he was clear and quick-witted, with a profound and deep understanding.
His speech required no deliberation; it flowed forth like water when the moment was right.
All who had the fortune to hear him remained for two or three nights, their devotion and sincerity further increased.
Later, he moved to reside in the meditation hall of Waguan Monastery.
He passed away in the fifth year of the Yongming era at the age of seventy-three.
At that time, there was also the monk Shi Fa-jue at Waguan, who likewise emphasized the practice of profound wisdom and was also renowned during the Qi dynasty.
9. Shi Fayuan. Shi Fayuan’s original surname was Zhong and his given name was Wuli; he was originally from Changshe in Yingchuan.
His ancestors had moved to Changcheng in Wuxing to escape the disturbances.
Wan wished to remain permanently as the supervisor of Meigen Ironworks, while Shen Min was appointed to succeed him.
Previously, the official documents had not been audited; consequently, Shen Min alone bore the full burden of the liability. Wan then appealed for the charges to be divided between them.

His family had long served the deities, and he himself was practiced in drumming and dancing, as well as various worldly arts; furthermore, he fully mastered the subtleties of divination by stalks and hexagrams, as well as physiognomy.

At that time, the śramaṇa Sengdao was the preeminent figure in Jiangxi; he considered Huiyuan’s unauthorized attempts to rectify the local clergy as somewhat presumptuous and, feeling a sense of resentment, reported the matter to Emperor Xiaowu, who immediately issued an edict ordering Huiyuan to return to the capital.

Although Sengyuan’s outward appearance was that of a layman, his mind dwelt upon dhyāna and the precepts, never failing in his observance of their integrity.
Shortly thereafter, the Emperor passed away, and Empress Dowager Zhao issued an edict permitting him to return to the monastic life.
In the sixth year of the Taishi era, Jiao Changsheng donated his residence to establish a monastery named "Zhengsheng" (Correct Victory) and invited Yuan to reside there.
As Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty personally served the young sovereign and constantly harbored apprehensions regarding unforeseen dangers, he frequently consulted Yuan on these matters.
Yuan said, "In seven months, things shall be settled."
It was exactly as he had said.
When Emperor Gao ascended the throne, he treated him with the rites due to a teacher.
When Emperor Wu succeeded him, he likewise showed him the utmost reverence as a teacher.
In the second year of the Yongming era, Huiyuan encountered the death of his elder brother and submitted a petition requesting to return to his hometown.
After he had been in his hometown for a short time, imperial edicts arrived one after another.
Huiyuan subsequently departed and stayed at Xianggong Monastery.

Thinking thus, he devoted himself with all his heart; consequently, while all three sides were ablaze, only the temple remained unburnt.
In the second year of the Yongyuan era of the Qi dynasty, he passed away at the age of eighty-seven.
10. Shi Fajing: Shi Fajing’s secular surname was Zhang; he was a native of Wucheng in Wuxing.
From his youth, he delighted in the Way, yet his aspirations had not yet been fulfilled.
Coinciding with the occasion when Huiyi performed self-immolation, he petitioned the Emperor to ordain twenty individuals, and Sengjing was one among them.
He took the Dharma as his teacher.
Having entered the Way, his conduct was as firm as ice and frost.
He cherished benevolence in his heart, making the salvation of others his primary concern.
Thereupon, he devoted himself to the study and practice of *chàngdǎo* (chanting and exhortation), surpassing all his predecessors.

Prince Wenxuan of Jingling of the Qi dynasty treated him with great courtesy and hospitality; Fajing vowed to propagate the Way with a sincere heart, never distinguishing between the noble and the humble. Whenever he was invited, he would certainly comply, showing no regard for cold or heat.
He did not accumulate private wealth, but constantly engaged in meritorious deeds.
At the beginning of the Jianwu era, a temple named Qilong was established for him using offerings from the faithful, where he resided.

Sengjing was by nature sincere and noble, making it his priority to welcome and appreciate others; thus, both monastics and laypeople became acquainted with him, all of whom held him in affection and esteem.
Although his scholarly studies were of shallow depth, his realization was spontaneous.
Even when confronted with sudden derision or difficult challenges, he invariably provided a fitting response.
He passed away in the second year of the Yongyuan era of the Qi dynasty at the age of sixty-four.

Your disciple, the orphaned Man Ying, bows his head in humble salutation.
One day, I was honored by the gift of your compiled *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), and you further commanded me to examine it closely.
Having searched through it from beginning to end with all my effort, I have seen nothing but magnificent talent.
Although the paper has grown worn and the ink faded, it has still not ceased to be transmitted.
As for the time when the Dharma was first spread and men of name and virtue had already arisen—
nearly five hundred years have passed, and six dynasties have come and gone.

From the time Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna set out from the Western Regions, down to An Shigao and Zhi Qian carrying their staffs to the Eastern Metropolis, although their traces appeared and vanished and the depth of their practice varied, [the Dharma was thus transmitted].
Acting as bridges and rafts for all, they bring about great benefit.

It is therefore fitting that both the monastic and lay communities transmit their excellence, that scholars fix their words with brush and inkstone, and that these deeds be illuminated for future generations to extol the virtues of those who have passed.

While there may be some deliberation regarding the principle of resonance and response (*yinggan*), the general outlines of the realms of the unseen and the seen (*youming*) remain incomplete; these peripheral texts are insufficient to illuminate and propagate the truth.
There are various biographies among them, yet they do not provide a comprehensive summary.

Jingxing happened to collect those who dwelt in the mountains, while Sengbao exclusively appended those who traveled afar; Faji only set forth the examples of lofty recluses, and Fa’an merely confined himself to the category of those with steadfast integrity.

Kang Hong’s work is exclusively devoted to individual accounts; Wang Xiu merely mentions the "High Seat" (the abbot); Sengyu stands out as uniquely recorded; and Xuanchang is preeminent as a solitary recorder.
Only that which was composed by Shi Fajin and written down by Wang Jin exists with the intention of providing a comprehensive synthesis, such that it may stand as a distinct school of its own.
However, while Jinming’s reputation was extensive, it was not yet broad; and although Jintie established his character, he did not achieve completion.
Among the authors since the Liang dynasty, there have likewise been those with flaws.
As for Sengyou’s compilation of the *Lanlü*, he already shares the responsibility for its shortcomings with Faji.
When Xiaoxiu dipped his brush, he again incurred the reproach of Jingxing.
His proposal for a public compilation is the most realistic and closest to the mark; yet, seeking my humble opinion, I find it even more cumbersome and redundant.

Your disciple, the orphaned Wang Manying, bows his head in prostration.
Your Excellency writes:

One day you presented me with a copy of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) that I had compiled, intending it as a means of admonition and correction; yet your reply, spanning several sheets of paper, has only served to further polish my work.
Reflecting upon this, I see that the Way relies on people for its propagation, and principle is made manifest through teaching.
In propagating the Way and expounding the Buddhist teachings, none are more esteemed than eminent monks.

Therefore, since the beginning of our cultural assimilation, those who have clarified the bequeathed Dharma—possessing extraordinary merit and exceptional conduct—have arisen throughout successive generations.
To earnestly exhort later generations, it is only right that this be compiled and arranged.

Since my youth, I have lacked the diligence of one who carries books and holds bamboo slips for self-instruction; yet throughout my life, I have admired the beauty of using lead and ink to record deeds of goodness.
Therefore, during the intervals between my studies and sightseeing, I have applied my mind to transcribing these records.
Whenever I encounter even a single section worthy of praise, I am immediately moved to reflect upon the three examinations.

However, as I have extensively searched through various chronicles, I find they differ in their degree of detail—some being overly prolix while others are too concise; some arrange the material inconsistently, while others omit or include certain actions. These matters have already been detailed in my separate preface, and I have also received your correspondence on the subject.
Therefore, without reckoning my own meager talent, I have hastily established these ten categories.
In deliberating upon their various streams and classifications, I have merely offered a brief exposition of my thoughts.
Yet, my literary path is vast and desolate, and my phrasing is both crude and unrefined.
I originally intended this merely as a personal record to prevent omissions; how could it be appropriate for it to intrude upon your lofty hearing?

Since you, the Dānapati, possess learning that encompasses both Confucianism and Buddhism, and your understanding penetrates both the profound and the secular, excelling in literary composition and being deeply versed in both internal and external studies, I hope that during your leisure from reading and perusing these works, you might deign to assist me in a detailed review.
Therefore, I have set aside my humble and rustic style to submit this to the Gate of the Dragon.
Yet, as the subject is lofty while the language is crude, I have long harbored much shame; that you now offer words of praise only serves to further increase my embarrassment.
I now present these ten sections of my authored commentaries and treatises for your further examination.
Should there be any errors or inaccuracies, I pray you will consider them with care.
Respects, [Your Name].
This biography was composed by the Dharma Master Huìjiǎo of Jiāxiáng Monastery in Kuàijī.

The Dharma Master’s learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular traditions, and he was skilled in lecturing on the sutras and vinaya. He authored ten fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* and commentaries on the meaning of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra Precepts*, both of which serve as guiding models for the world.
He also authored these thirteen fascicles of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.

In the second year of the Chengsheng era at the end of the Liang dynasty—the year of the Earth-Monkey (Guiyou)—he fled the turmoil caused by Hou Jing and arrived at Pencheng, where he lectured for a short time.
In the second month of the Jiashu year, he passed away at the age of fifty-eight.
The *Jiangzhou Sengzheng Huigong Jing* records that his remains were initially interred at the Mausoleum of Chanke Temple on Mount Lu.
